AMeffage from his Majesty, by the honourable Sir Henry Bellendeny Gentleman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty.

And being returned;

Several Members, returned upon new Writs, took the Oaths; and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectiial preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as follow eth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It would have given me the greatest Pleafur£ to have acquainted you, at the Opening of this Session, that our Success in carrying on the War has been equal to the Justice of our Cause, and the Extent and Vigour of the Measures formed for that Purpose.

I have tile firmed Confidence that the Spirit and Bravery of this Nation, so renowned in all Times, and which have formerly furmoiinted so many Difficulties, are not to be abated by some Disappointments; these, I trust, by the Blefiing of God, and your Zeal and Ardour for mv Honour and the Welfare of your Country, may be retrieved: It is nly fixed Resolution to apply my utmost Efforts for the Security of my Kingdoms, and for the Recovery and Protection of the Possessions and Rights of my Crown and Subjects in America and elsewhere, as well by the strongbit Exertion of our Naval Force, as by all other Methods: Another great. Object, which I have at Heart, is, the Preservation of the Protestant Religion, and the Liberties of Europe, and, in that View, to adhere to and encourage my Allies.

For this Cause I shall decline no Inconveniences; and in this Cause I earnestly desire yoUr hearty Concurrence and vigorous Assistance. The late signal Success in Germany has given a happy Turn to Affairs, which it is Vol. 28.

incumbent upon us to improve; and, in this critical Conjuncture, the eyes of all Europe are upon you: In particular, I must recommend it to you, that my good , Brother and Ally the King of Prussia may be supported in such a Manner as his Magnanimity and active Zeal for the common Cause deserve.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

It gives me the utmost Concern that the large Supplies, which you have already granted for carrying on the War, have not produced all the good Effects we had reason to hope for; but I have so great a Reliance on your Wisdom, as not to doubt of your Perseverance:

I only desire such Supplies as shall be necessary for the public Service, and, to that End, have oidered the proper Estimates to be laid before you; you may depend upon it that the best and most faithful (Economy shall be used.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have had such ample Experience of the Loyalty and good Affections of my faithful Subjects towards me, my Family, and Government, in all Circumstances, that I am confident they are not to be ftiaken; but I cannot avoid taking notice of that Spirit of Disorder which has shewn itself amongst the common People in some Parts of the Kingdom: Let me recommend to you to do your Part in discouraging and suppressing such Abuses, and for maintaining the Laws and lawful Authority. If any thing dial] be found wanting to explain or enforce what may have been misunderstood or misrepresented, I am persuaded it will not escape your Attention.

Nothing can be lb conducive to the Defence of all that is dear to us, as well as for reducing our Enemies to Reafoii, as Union and Harmony amongst ourselves.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty*, to return his Majesty the most humble Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to allure his Majesty, that this House fees with the deepest Concern the Success of his Majesty’s Arms so unequal to the Justice of his Cause, and to the Extent and Vigour of the Measures formed for that Purpose: That his faithful Commons firmly rely, that as his Majesty, in his royal Justice, has endeavoured to trace the Causes of palt Disappointments, lie will also, in his high Wisdom, open better Hopes of future Prosperities, by invigorating our En-terprizes, and animating the Attempts of the British Arms. That in this Confidence they will chearfully support his Majesty in the utmost Efforts for the Security of his Kingdoms, and for the Recovery and Protection of the Possessions and Rights of his Crown and Subjects in America and elsewhere, as well by the strongest Exertion of his Majesty’s Naval Force, as by all other adequate Methods: To assure his Majesty, that his faithful Commons,excited by Zeal for the Protestant Cause, and the Liberties of Europe, do with most unfeigned Joy

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Anns attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up;

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof* while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other Officers of Middlesexand Westminsterdo take Care, that from Eleven, of the Clock in the Morning to One in the Afternoon, and from Four to Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple-bar and Westminster-hallilmil be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars* Drays, Cart's, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminsterdiall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westmidfier-, and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order SatisfadLon to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be ele$ed or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness in,respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall fee, or be informed of to be, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Vol. 284

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into His Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post-Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the Rising of the House; and also on every Monday, Wednesclay, and Friday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the fame.

A Petition of the Commissioners of the Land Tax Lantl Tax acting in and for the Liberty of the Duchy of Lancaster, inhabitants in the Strand, in the County of Middlesex, on behalf of cf

themselves, and others, Proprietors and Owners of SomersetHouse Lands and Buildings within the said Liberty, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Liberty was charged, and did accordingly raise, by the Act of the 4th of William and Alary, towards the Land Tax for that Year, £.6,476 10s 6id. and so in proportion towards every Aid granted by a Land Tax since; and that the Lands and Hereditaments within the said Liberty have from time to time not only been affeftedat the utmoli improved Rents, but the empty Houses have been also rated at the Half thereof, of which many have been annually, and now.are, unoccupied; and that the Palace of Somerset House was rated and paid, in the said Fourth Year of William and Mary,

£.192, which was annually paid until the Year 1707, lince which time the Deficiency hath been raised by the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Liberty; and that Numbers of Families have for many Years resided in, and occupied most of, the Apartments and Buildings within, and belonging to, the said Palace, and that the said Palace hath been annually rated and assessed towards the Land Tax; but the said Inhabitants, and Occupiers of Apartments and Buildings within, and belonging to, the said Palace, have evaded orrefufed the Payment of the said Tax, to the Prejudice of the Proprietors and Owners of other the Lands and Buildings within the said Liberty: And therefore praying, That a Clausemav be added, in the Bill now depending, for granting an Aid to his Majesty, by a Land Tax to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year^S, to oblige the Inhabitants, and Occupiers of Apartments and Buildings within, and belonging to, the said Palace, to pay their Proportion of Land lax with the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Liberty, or to grant such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it he an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition.

A Message, by Mr. ghiarme, Deputy Gentleman Royal Assent Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty’sCommission for declaring his Royal Assent to an Act, agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty’s Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers:

Where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to a public Bill therein mentioned; and also impowering his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumber land,\he Lord Arch-bishop of Canterbury, the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, the LordPresidentoftheCouncil, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bill; and that the Archbishop of Canterbun/, the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, and Earl Gower, named in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bill; which Bill is as followeth; viz.

An Act for continuing certain Laws, made in the last Session of Parliament, for prohibiting the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch; and for prohibiting the making of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain, or from Meal or Flour; and to allow the Transportation of Wheat, Barley, Oats, Meal, and Flour, to the Isle of Man, for the Use of the Inhabitants there; and for reviving and continuing an A6, made in the same Session, for discontinuing the Duties upon Com and Flour imported, and upon Corn, Grain, Meal, Bread, Biscuit, and Flour, taken from the Enemy; and to permit the Importation of Corn and Flour into Great Britain and Ireland in neutral Ships; and to authorize his Majesty, with the Advice of his Privy Council, to order and permit the Exportation of such Quantities of the Commodities aforesaid as may be necessary for the Suftentation of any Forces in the Pay of Great Britain, or of those of his Majesty s Allies acting in Support of the common Cause; and to prohibit the Payment of any Bounty, upon the Exportation of any of the said Commodities, to be made during the Continuance of this Act.

That the Poor in the said Parish arc greatly increased:

That the Number of the Poor, in the Year 1750, when he was Overseer, was from 150 to 180; and that, in the Years 1749 and 1750, a Rate of is. in the Pound was sufficient for their Maintenance; but, in the prefen t Year, the Rate; is %s. 6d. and the last Year was 4-v. and their Number is increased to 250:

That it would he a great Advantage to the said Pa-riffi, if an equal Pound Rate could be laid on all the Occupiers of Houses, Buildings, and Lands; hut that such a Rate is not now established by Law: And,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Beriah Hills, being examined, said, That, for several Years past, many Disputes have arisen in the said Parish, in regard to the Legality of the Rates made for the Relief of the Poor; and that, in the Years 1756 and 1757, upwards of £. 100 was expended in Appeals to the Quarter Sessions, which were prosecuted on that account:

That the Poor in the said Parish arc greatly increased:

That the Number of the Poor, in the Year 1750, when he was Overseer, was from 150 to 180; and that, in the Years 1749 and 1750, a Rate of is. in the Pound was Sufficient for their Maintenance; but, in the prefen t Year, the Rate is ys. 6d. and the last Year was 4-v. and their Number is increased to 250:

That it would be a great Advantage to the said Pa-riffi, if an equal Pound Rate could be laid on all the Occupiers ot Houses, Buildings, and Lands; but that such a Rate is not now established by Law: And,

That he apprehends the Officers have not Sufficient Power at present to compel the indolent Poor to work, nor to punish them for Misbehvaiour.

Mr. William Diere, Vestry Clerk of the said Par iff], confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Hills; and said.

That many of the Poor would be capable of gaining a Livelihood, were they properly employed:

That, in the Year 1756, a Rate was quailiedby the Quarter Sessions, because personal Estates were not assessed: That they were assessed in the Year 1757, and the Assessment confirmed; but that the assessing them is attended with great Difficulties.

And the said Petition was read taking Notice, that an Act passed in the 29th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act to improve, widen, and enlarge, the Passage over and through London Bridge; and reciting several Powers given to the Petitioners, by the said Act* and alleging, that the Toll or Duty for loaded Vessels or other Craft, passing through the Arches of the said Bridge, being by the said Act dTrefted to be paid ever/Time they pass through the same; and the Tide being generally very strong at such Times, it is so extremely difficult, especially in the Night-time, to take an Account of such Vessels or Craft, that the Petitioners, though they have been at a very great Expence in endeavouring to find out a Method of ascertaining the fame, are unable to do it; by reason whereof, and of the Difficulties under the Act of recovering such Tolls, the Collection thereof is so very precarious, that they haveproduced from Midsummer 1756, the Time of the Commencement of the said Act, to Christmas last, no more than Eight hundred and Seventy Pounds, though estimated at the Gross yearly Sum of One thousand Six hundred and Forty-five Poundsyor thereabouts* and that the Charges of the Works judged necessary for the Improvement of the said Bridge, including the temporary Bridge already eFefted, and the Purchases to be made, will amount toa very considerableSum of Money, which the Petitioners will be obliged, from time to time, to borrow at Interest, in pursuance of the said Act: And, in regard the said Money cannot be borrowed upon the foie Credit of the Duty or Toll, for passing over the said Bridge* and as thesaidToll or Duty for passing through the Arches of the said Bridge is an ineffectual Toll, and

thfe Persons who may be inclined to lend the said Money* at a moderate Interest, cannot have the full Benefit of the Security intended thereby, without the further Assistanee of Parliament, therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering the said Act more effectual, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

That lie has navigated upon the River Thames from Henley and Marlow to London Sixteen YeanH That if a Bridge should be built, as direflect by the said Act, it would greatly obUruft the Navigation which is at'present carried on in the narrow Part of the River between the Aits and the Town of Brentford, there not being Justicient Depth of Water on the other Side: That iLa Pier was placed in such narrow Passage it would greatly obstruct the Navigation, and make it very dangerous; That they could not land their Men till they had got through the Bridge, for which they might frequently wait Half an Hour, and in such same might lose their Tide: That if a Bridge was built at the lower Ferry, called The Foot Ferry, and the Center Arch to be Fifty Feet wide, or even Forty-four, it would be sufficient; and at the Didance of about 150 Yards from the Ait, it would be no Obstruction to the Navigation, and be much more convenient.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, made in the 29th Year of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act to improve, widen, and enlarge, the Passage over and through London Bridge, was read; whereby it appears, that the Petitioners were empowered to appoint a Committee for putting the said Act in Execution.

James Hodges, Esquire, Town Clerk, produced to your Committee a Book, containing the Journal of the Common Council of the City of London; by which it appeared, that the Petitioners, soon after the passing of the said Act, and in pursuance thereof, appointed a Committee of Twelve Aldermen and 24 Commons of the said City to put the said Act in Execution.

Peter Roberts, junior, Esquire, being examined, said That the said Committee have proceeded to exercise the Powers given them, and have caused many of the Houses on the said Bridge to be taken down, and have contrafted with proper Workmen for improving the said Bridge; and; it being judged necessary to throw Two of the Arches of the said Bridge into One, a temporary Bridge has been erected, to preserve the general Passage in the mean time: That the Toll for Passage over the said Bridge has been duly collected, which from Midsummer 1756 (the Commencement of the Act) to Christmas last, has produced 'exclusive of about £. 400 for Charges ofcollefting)£. 1,600. or thereabouts: That it is so extremely difficult to collect the Toll for paffiftg under the Bridge, that, though it has been estimated at £.1,600. per Ann. yet it has produced in a Year and Half no more than the Sum of £. 6.15.

Mr. Glendonning, Inspector of the Tolls under the Bridge, being examined, informed your Committee, That, in order to know what the Toil ought to produce, he employed Three Men Night and Day, who took the Numbers of all the Vessels they could; and he is Lure so many went through in the Year, as, if they had all paid, would have produced £.1,650; but that it was impracticable to collect the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, made in the 29th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act to improve, widen, and enlarge, the Passage over and through London Bridge, was re ?d; whereby it appears, that the Petitioners were empowered to appoint a Committee for putting the said Act in Execution.

James Hodges, Esquire, Town Clerk, produced to your Committee a Book, containing the Journal of the Common Council of the City of London; by which it appeared, that the Petitioners, soon after the passing of the said Act, and in pursuance thereof, appointed a Committee of Twelve Aldermen and 24 Commons of the said City to put the said Act in Execution.

Peter Roberts, junior, Esquire, being examined, fai'd That the said Committee have proceeded to exercise the Powers given them, and have caused many of the Houses on the said Bridge to be taken down, and have contracted with proper Workmen for improving the said Bridge; and, it being judged necessary to throw Two of the Arches of the said Bridge into One, a temporary Bridge has been erected, to preserve the general Passage in the mean time: That the Toll for Passage over the said Bridge has been duly collected, which from Midsummer 1756 (the Commencement of the Act) to Christmas Jaft, has produced 'Vexclusive of about £. 400 lor Charges ofcollecting)£. 1,600. or thereabouts: That it is so extremely difficult to collect the Toll for paffitig under the Bridge, that, though it has been estimated at £. 1,600. per Ann. yet it has produced in a Year and Half no more than the Sum of £. 645.

Mr. Glendonning, Inspector of the Tolls under the Bridge, being examined, informed your Committee, That, in order to know what the Toll ought to produce, life employed Three Men Night and Day, who took the Numbers of all the Vessels they could; and he is lure so many went through in the Year, as, if they had all paid, would have produced £.1,650; but that it was impracticable to collect the fame.

James Hodges, Esquire, Town Clerk, produced to your Committee a Book, containing the Journal of the Common Council of the City of London; by which it appeared, that the Petitioners, soon after the passing of the said Act, and in pursuance thereof, appointed a Committee of Twelve Aldermen and 24 Commons of the said City to put the said Act in Execution.

Peter Roberts, junior, Esquire, being examined, fafd That the said Committee have proceeded to exercise the Powers given them, and have caused many of the Houses on the said Bridge to be taken down, and have contrafted with proper Workmen for improving the said Bridge; and; it being judged necessary to throw Two of the Arches of the said Bridge into One, a temporary Bridge hasEeen erected, to preserve the general Passage in the mean time: That the Toll for Passage over the said Bridge has been duly collected, which from Midsummer 1756 (the Commencement of the Act) to Christmas last, has produced ;exclusive of about £. 400 lor Chargesofeollefting)^. 1,600. or thereabouts: That it is so extremely difficult to collect the Toil for paffifig under the Bridge, that, though it has been estimated at £.1,600. per Ann. yet it has produced in a Year and Half no more than the Sum of £. 645.

Mr. Glendonning, Inspector of the Tolls under the Bridge, being examined, informed your Committee, That, in order to know what the Toll ought to produce, life employed Three Men Night and Day, who took the Numbers of all the Vessels they could; and he is sure so many went through in the Year, as, if they had all paid, would have produced £.1,650; but that it was impracticable to collect the fame.

High Price Sir John Philippe, according to Order, reported from otCnain, &c. the Committee of the whole House, to whorn it was referred to consider further of the orefent high Price of Grain, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Rifcuit, and Starch, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place;, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’sTable: Where the same were read; ami are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Corn and Grain be taught and sold by one and the same Weight throughout this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That whenever die several Sorts of Corn or Grain thall have continued to be sold at the London Market, for the fp'ace of Three W eeks, above certain Price*, to be fixed, the Ports shall be opened, for a limited Time, for the free Importation of foreign Grain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Bounty be allowed on the Exportation of Malt, Barley, live. Wheat, or Flour, unless, at the Time of such Exportation, the said several Sorts of Grain and Flour shall have been sold at the London Market, for flie spaee of Three Weeks, at lower Prices than are limited by an Act of the First Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Manj, intituled, An Act for encouraging the Exportation of Corn.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That whenever the several Sorts of Corn and Grain thall have continued to be sold at the London Market, for the Space of Three Weeks, above certain Prices, to be fixed, no low Wines or Spirits w hatsoever shall be made, extracted, or did died, within this Kingdom, from any Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Violences committed by Mobs in many Parts of this Kingdom have been one Cause of the present high Price of Corn, by preventing the proper and usual Circulation thereof.

Manchester APetition of several of the principal Inhabitants of the School ‘Town of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster,

Mills. Was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,'That, for 200 Years last past, certain Water Corn Mills within the said Town of Manchester have been settled upon Persons of-Honour and Quality, living near the said Town, as Feoffees in Trust, for maintaining, out of the Profits thereby arising, a free Grammar School within the said Town, and a Schoolmaster and Ulherfor the said School, and for other charitable Purposes; and that the said 17

Mills, at the Time of their being so first settled, and for a considerable Time afterwards; were, it is presumed, capable of grinding all the Cdrn and Grafin used arid con-filmed by the Inlwibitants of the said To wn-, and that the said Mills were originally only three in Number, and are in very bad Repair, and utterly incapable of supplying the Consumption of the said Town since the great Increase of the Inhabitants thereof, by the very extraordinary Extension of their Trade arid Manufactures; and that the Feoffees, soon after the making of the said Grant, claimed a Right, founded, as they pretended, on immemorial Custom,togrind, at the said Mills, all the Corn and Grain which should beconfumedby the Inhabitants of the said Town; and Decrees in the Dutchy Court of Lancaster were obtained in the Reigns of Queen Elizabeth, King James the First, and Queen Anne, whereby the said Right was either in the Whole, or in Part, confirmed; and a Bill has been lately filed in the said Court, against several Persons, for using Flour, in the said Town, which was not ground at the said Mills, and the Cause is now depending in the said Court; and that by means of the said Suits, and other Proceedings in the said Court, to enforce the Observance of the said Decrees, very considerable Sums of Money have been expended by the Parties, to the great Loss of the said Charity, and Prejudice to the Persons against whom such Suitsand Proceedings were instituted; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners intend not, by this Application, to interfere with, or anyways interrupt, the Proceedings in the said Cause, or to prevent or avoid any Decrees thereupon between the Parties concerned, the Petitioners only desiring that the Inhabitants of the said Town may not for the future be subject to any Right, or. Claim of Right, tending to a Monopoly, which will lay the Inhabitants under great Hardships and Difficulties in procuring Meal, Flour, and Bread, and consequently prejudice, if not destroy, the Trade and Manufactures there; and that the Petitioners, with many others. Inhabitants of the said Town, being sensible of the great Utility of the said School, are desirous to make ample Provision; by such Ways and Means as to the House shall seem meet, for supplying any Deficiency which may arise to the said Charity, by taking away all Claim to such exclusive Right aforesaid: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief as, upon Examination, shall appear just and necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon to the House:

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Fellowship, of the incorporated Society of Chandlers and Soap-makers, within the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That great Quantities of Candles and hard Soap were formerly made in that City, and exported to the West. Judies; but that, for some Years past, such Export Trade has been in great measure loft, occasioned, as the Petitioners apprehend, by the great Quantities of those Commodities that are constantly sent from Ireland, notwithstanding the Laws prohibiting the fame; and that, by the Loss of such Export Trade, his Majesty’s Revenue in the Duty on Salt is greatly diminished, and that the Price of British Tallow has, for some Years pad, been raised very high; and alleging, that the Petitioners apprehend the Importation of Irish Tallow Duty- free will be the only effectual Means of preventing these Evils, which are daily increasing: And therefore praying the House to take the Preniifes into Consideration, and to afford the Petitioners such Relief as, on mature Deliberation, shall appear to be reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to confvler of the Petition of several Tallow Chandlers, and Dealers in Candles, Inhabitants of the Cities of Londonmid Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and all the other Tallow Chandlers, and Dealers in Candles, within this Kingdom.

A Petition of the feverat Merchants, whole Names Exportatiati are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and 0 u all others, Merchants, in the County of Norfolk, City of Norwich^ and Burgh of Great Yarmouth, concerned in making or exporting Malt, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of a Proviso in an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, to prohibit, for a Time to be limited, the Exportation of Corn, Malt,

Meal, Flour, Bread, Bifciiit, and Starch, that nothing therein contained should extend to any Malt declared or made for Exportation on or* before the 4th Day of December 1756; and alleging, that at the Time the said Act passed, the Petitioner being at a great Difiance* and carrying on their Business in its usual Course, and being for feme time totally unacquainted with the Intention*of a Prohibition* had divers Parcels of Barley declared and making into Malt, after the said 4th Day of December, for Exportation, for the Holland Market, not exceeding in the whole 200 Lasts, all which was a&uallymade into Malt before the End of January 1757; and that, after they knew of the Prohibition, as the same was only to be in Force for a Year, and was not at that Time likely to be continued, they imagined that they should still have Time to export the above Quantity of Malt within the Fifteen Months allowed by the Malt<

Act; and that the said Malt hath ever since been, in pursuance of the said Act for grantingaDuty on Malt; under the Care of the Officers of Exdjfe, and by them locked upland if the said Malt be not exported in Fifteen Months after t he carry ing the same into Storehouses, the Proprietors thereof are by the last mentioned Act subjected to a Penalty of Fifty Pounds each; and that all the said Malt is in a perishing State, and is wholly unfit for Home Consumption, it being long Malt, of an inferior Quality, and proper only for the Market for which it was intended; and in case the Petitioners are not allowed to export the fame, they will not only become subject to the said Penalty, but all the said Malt will perish, and bea total Loft to such of the Petilionersas are interested therein, and also taking Notice, that by an Act, passed in this present Session, for further continuing the said Prohibition until the 2 jth Day of December 1758, it is provided, that, during the Continuance thereof, the Bou nty granted by any Law upon the Exportation of any of the Commoditiesbefore-mentioned(hall not be allowed or paid to any Person upon the Exportation thereof out of this Kingdom, to any Place whatfeever; and alleging, that attheTime of passing the said last mentioned A&t the Petitioners had severally made a Provision for employing their Malt-houses in the same Manner as they had done in the former Year, in making Malt for Ireland, and had bought several Quantities of Barley for that Purpose, ana had declared or made the same into Malt for Exportation, before the Expiration of the said Act of the last Sei-fion; and that the Petitioners bought the said Barley under the Bounty Price, and did not expeCl, nor had they an Opportunity of knowing in proper Time, that the Bounty upon the Exportation of Malt to Ireland, would be suspended; but imagined, that, if the Prohibition was further extended, such Prohibition would be in the same Manner as by the former Act; and that, if the Petitioners are not allowed the Bounty upon the Exportation of the said Malt to Ireland, they will be considerable Losers, having purchased such Barley at a much higher Price than they otherwise would have done, in Expectation of receiving the said Bounty; and that the said Malt was particularly prepared for that Market, and is of a different Quality, inferior to that made for Home Consumption: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and permit the Petitioners to export all such Malt as was a&nally declared or made for Exportation, on or before the 30th Day of January 1757, and to allow the Petitioners the Bounty thereon; and alfe to allow the Petitioners the Bounty on all such Malt, to be exported to Ireland, as was declared or made for Exportation, on or before the 25th Day o(Dc* cember last, lor continuing the former Act; or that the

ed to the House, and read; taking Notice, That a Petition hath been presented to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill for lepairing and widening the High Roads from the Town 0iGosport, throughFareham, BG shops Waltham, and the City of Winchester, to Stock-bridge, in the County of Southampton, and from the said City, through Otterborn, to the said Town and County of Southampton', which Petition, these Petitioners allege, was prepared without any previous Consultation with the Gentlemen and Inhabitants of that Town and County, and brought thither and signed by a few Persons there; and that these Petitioners have no Objection to the having the said Road,leading from the said City to Southampton, repaired and widened by the Aid of Parliament; but as the said Road has no Sort of Connexion with the other Roads in the said Petition mentioned, thpy apprehend it highly reasonable, that the Tolls ari-sing on the said Road between Winchester and Southampton should be applied to the Repairs of that Road only; and that the Meetings of the Trustees, for put- , ting in Execution so much of the said AS as relates to the said Road, lliould be held occasionally, as well at Southampton ns at Winchester; and that no Turnpike should be erected on that Road, whereby Persons, travelling only a few Furlongs thereon, may be compelled to any Tolls; that the chief Road leading into the said Town of Southampton, is through the Gate called Barg ate, being Part of the said Road from Winchester; and that, about Six Furlongs from the said Bargate, a considerable Highway, leading through Rockstone Lane to the said Town of Southampton, falls into the said Road leading from Winchester; and that the obliging Persons, coming through the said Lane, to contribute to the Repairs of the said Road from Winchester, for passing scarce Six Furlongs thereon, would be a very greatHard-ship: And therefore praying the House to take the Pre-miles into Consideration; and that, in case such Bill pass into a Law, Provision may therein be made, that the whole Road from Winchester to Southampton, may be repaired; that the Tolls arising thereon may be applied to the Repairs of that Road only, and in paying Alonies borrowed for, and applied in,those Repairs, under sufficient Penalties, to prevent any Misapplicatign; That the Trustees in the said Pill, if the same shall pass intoa Law, may be prevented from erecting or felting up any Gate, or taking any Toll, within Two Miles from the d own of Crediton.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to th£ Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

for which the advanced Price of Provifionhasbynomeans been an adequate Satisfaction; and that as the Distemper among the Homed Cattle is now intirely abated, and the Rot among the Sheep greatly decreased, the Petitioners are thoroughly convinced, that, from the present daily Increase of Tallow, the several Markets will be sufficiently flocked, without the Assistance of any imported from Ireland; and that the Petitioners conceive, should the said Bill pass into a Law, the Irish would be enabled greatly to undersell the Petitioners in their Tallow, as they pay no Land Tax, and have their Farms at a much cheaper Rate, and consequently the Petitioners, and others, must have their Rents proportionally abated, which will greatly affect the Landed Interest of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners apprehend,from the above and other Reasons, the passing such a Bill would be injurious to the Public, detrimental to the Revenue, and ruinous to the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

Encouraging Mr. Hanger reported from the Committee, who were me Growth appointed to consider of the Importation and Growth oi Madder. of Madder in this, Kingdom; that the Committee had considered the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

With respect to the Importation of Madder: By an Account from the Cullom House, and referred to the Committee, of Madder imported into England, from Holland, from Chrifmas 1749, to the 5th of January 1757, being Seven Years; it appears, that there has been imported in that Time, as followeth; viz.

And, with Respect to the Growth of Madder in this Kingdom,

Mr. 3/i//cr, Gardener and Botanist at Chelsea, informed your Committee, that lie has madeTrials with respect to the Cultivation of Madder in this Kingdom for 36 Years; that hehas planted Madder in dillerentSituations, and upon different Soils, and has had Roots of Two Years Handing, weighing 13/6. each; that he has seen the Method of cultivating it in Holland, and is sure that it may be cultivated easier here than in Holland; because there, the Ground being flat and watery, they areobliged to be at an extraordinary Expence of railing the Earth Three Feet, where the Madder is planted; and he observed, that when the Roots touch the Water, they stop growing; and that he is well allured Madder will grow as well in England, as in any Country whatsoever.

Mr. George Edwards, Merchant in London, informed your Committee, That he has imported Madder from l9

Holland; and that he lvas concerned in cultivating it here, from the Year 1738 to 1748; that the Ground made Use of for that Purpose was Thirty-four Acres and an Half, near Woolzvich, which produced in that Period, SixtyTons of Madder, which is 150 Calks, reckoning 800/6. Weight to a Cask; that he carried it to Market, and fold it to divers Persons, who gave it the Preference to what they had from Holland, because, they said, his was clean, and the Dutch adulteraied; that the Quantity raffed in the afore mentioned Period, employed 30 or 36 poor People all the Winter.

That he thinks Madder may be grown in this Kingdom, if the Tytlie was Fettled in a general Way, at or 5 s. per Acre per Annum; that One Piece of Ground will not answer for above Four Crops; that it will grow in any Soil, but thrives best in Fresh Ground, and a light sandy Loom; that he planted it in April, and took it up in the Months of November, December, and January, Twelvemonth following; that lie apprehends, if a general Cultivation of it was introduced into this Kingdom, it might be raised atOne Half the Expence it was when he cultivated it.

Mr. John Thorpe, Drtrggift, said, That he has been a' Grower of Madder for 16 or 20 Years, and is now concerned in about Ten Acres; that he has manufactured several Tons this Winter; and the Scarlet Dyers say, it exceeds the Dutch; that he has sent fometo East India, and is now preparing to fend more there; and a Captain of an East India Ship told him, it was the best Commodity he could carry; that he has had as good a Price as the Hollanders, and no Complaints made a gain ft it; that he has been obstructed in cultivating it, by having it intimated to him, that the Tythe thereof would be demanded in Kind; that he planted where there was a Modus, to prevent Disputes about Tythes; and that where Labour is cheap, it may be cultivated at half the Expence he does it.

Mr. Edwards being again called, said, That in 1741 and 1742, he fold couliderable Quantities of Madder for the East Indies.

Mr. Edmund Farmer, Callicoe Printer, being called before your Committee, said, That People of his Buline fs can’t carry on their Trade without Madder, it being the Ingredient that tynts the Callicoe; that there is used Two hundred and Fifty Tons, from 70 to £. 80 ptvTon, in a Year, within a few Miles of London, by the Callicoe Printers only; that the Price used to be about £.3 per hundred Weight, and is now from £.5, 5r.to £.5.105". thatitis frequently adulterated when lent from Holland; that lie has had f.zo allowed him for the Adulteration in Three Calks; that there are many Callicoe Printers in Ireland and Scotland.

Mr.....Broughton, Callicoe Printer, said. That

he uses 3 or 400 lb. of Madder in a Day, for Nine or Ten Months in a Y'ear; that it is absolutely necessary in their Business; that they can’t fix the Colour without it; that the Dutch Madder is frequently adulterated; that the Price has lately raised 14 or 15s. per hundred Weight.

Mr. William Tuck, Scarlet Dyer, said, That he dyes Cloth for Soldiers Cloaths, and can’t dye without Madder; that nothing will stand so well; that he ufesThree or Four hundred Weight a Day; that lie has used Mr. Thorpe's Madder; and being shewn some that Mr. Thorpe had produced to your Committee, said, he thinks itbetter than the Dutch ? that it excells it in Use; and that Madder is essential in dying Woollen Manufactures for Exportation; that there can be no better than Mr. Thorpe's; and that there are 2,000 Calks of Madder used in a Year in the Woollen Manufacture.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Madder is an Ingredient essentially necessary m Dying and Callicoe Printing, and of great Consequence to the Trade and Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Resolved

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Madder may he raised in this Kingdom, equal ih Good nets if not superior to any foreign Madder.

Resolved, That it is t he Opinion of this Committee, That encouraging the Growth of Madder in this Kingdom will be a Saving of a very large Sum of Money, which is now paid for that Commodity imported Duty free from Abroad.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, the Encouraging the Growth of Madder in this Kingdom will be a Means of employing great Numbers of poor Families in the Winter Months.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the ascertaining the Tythe of Madder will be the greatest Means of encouraging the Growth of that Commodity in this Kingdom.

Rejblvcd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to encourage the Growth and Cultivation of Madder in this Kingdom, by ascertaining the Tythe thereof.

County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners are informed by. the Votes, that the House has under Consideration,. a Petition of the Tallow-chandlers and Dealers in Candles of the Cities of London and Westminster; submitting to the House, Whether the Admiliion of Irish Tallow be not a likely Means of reducing the prefect Price of Candles , and these Petitioners pray the House, to take under their Consideration, Whether the free Importation of live Cattle into, this Kingdom from Ireland, ‘.would not be a Means of supplying the Pastures of this Kingdom with horned Cattle, so greatly diminished by the Distemper among them; and whether, by feeding them here, the Price of Tallow would not be greatly lessened, the Estates much better able to bear and pay their Taxes, and this Kingdom be enabled to supply our Fleets with Beef on reasonable Terms*, and the wicked Practice of supplying our Enemies with Provisions, and the Smuggling of Soap and Candles, from Ireland, greatly prevented; all which the Petitioners humbly pray the House to take into Consideration, and do therein as to them Ifiall seem meet.

Mr. Humpby Leigh, Clerk to the said Corporation, produced to your Committee, a Book of the Proceedings of the said Corporation, commencing 10th June, 10th William the 3d, wherein are entered the Proceedings of the said Corporation; whereby it appeared, that Elections have been made in Manner directed by the said AC; and it further appeared, that there was raised on the said City, in the Year 1695, £.2,709 123. 2 d. in 1696, £.2,907 193*. 3 d. and in 1697, £.2,908 is. o d.

Mr. Thomas Binford produced lo your Committee, several Bonds under the Corporation Sea!, for Money borrowed, amounting to £.644 8.?. od.; and said, That the whole Debt upon Bonds is now £.1,434 16X. od.; and that the Interest now due thereon is £. 936 11 s. 4 d. besides Three Years Interest more, which will be due at Lady Day 1761; at which Time the Principal and interest on the said Bonds is proposed to be paid off and . discharged: Then

John Brick dale Esquire, and Richard Leadbeter, Clerk to the said Corporation, being severally examined, said. And Mr. Leadbeter produced an Account, by which it appeared, that the Corporation have contracted a Debt of 917 £. 15s. 5d. within the last Two Years.

Yarmouth Sir Edward Walpole reported from the Committee, to Small Debts. w|lorn the Petition of the Traders and Inhabitants of the Borough of Gmz/ Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many other Traders and inhabitants within the said Borough, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the RefoJutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

William Mariyn Esquire, being examined, said. That many Persons take Advantage of the Difficulties that Creditors labour under in recovering small Debts, and frequently refuse to pay their just Debts:

That when Trade is bad, Labourers would not be able to subsist, unless their Employers were to advance them small Sums; and the Recovery thereof is attended with great Expence; and that he knows Instances of Persons being thrown into Prison for small Debts: and that it would be a great Advantage to the said Borough if a Court was established, there, for the Recovery of small Debts in a more expeditious and less expensive Manner. Upon the whole Matter your Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, ‘ That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the Borough of Great Yarmouth.

Ordered, Thai*Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts' within the Borough of Great Yarmouth: and that Sir Edward Walpole and Mr. Charles Townshend of Yarmouth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

In support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, made in the 5th and 6th Year of the Reign of King Edxvard the Sixth, against Regrators, Forestal-lers, and Engroffers, was read: Then

Thomas Nichols Esquire, a Farmer in Middlesex, informed your Committee, That there is no free Corn Market nearer to London than Brentford: And

Mr. Thomas Savage, a Corn Factor, being examined, said, That there is no public Market for Sale of Com and Grain nearer to London than Brentford: That he knows the general Practice of felling Corn at Mark Lane: That the old Place was Bear Key; but a Set of Gentlemen agreed together to build a private Place to fell Corn in: That they would not call it a Market; but gave it the Name of the Corn Exchange, on purpose to make a private Property of it: That whilst it was building he was told by Mr. Samuel Birch, One of the Proprietors, That he should not come to fell his Corn there: Accordingly, the First Day the Exchange was opened, Mr. Birch acquainted him, That, if he offered to fell his Goods there, he should be prosecuted: That several Persons agreed to try the Cause with the 1 Proprietors, whether they could make it a private " Property, or not: They refused coming to Tryal; but employed a Beadle, who, when the Witness and others were shewing their Goods, told them, They had no Right there; that it was a private Property; and that he had Ordersfrom the Proprietors to beat the Samples

Mr. confirmed the above Evidence in every Particular, being One of those who had been affronted in that Manner.

Mr. John Warren, Farmer at Shoreham, confirmed the above as to the Behaviour of the Beadle.

Mr. Scholey, Com Factor, being asked, if he was acquainted with the Manner of doing Business at Mark Lane, answered. That he has been there ever since it was begun; that it was never intended to be free Market; that his Reasons for thinking so were, that a Gentleman, who had served iz Years Clerkthip, applied to the Proprietors of the Exchange for a Stole or Stand, which they refused him: Another Instance he gave, viz. Mr. Gurney, who had served Five Years Clerkthip, applied as above, and was refused; and the Reasonassigned for such Refusal was, that he intended to take in a Partner: The Friends, of Mr. Burn, the Person Mr. Gurney intended to take in as Partner, doubting the Right of the Proprietors to make it a private Market, lent Word, that unless they admitted Mr. Bum to be in Parternship with Mr. Gurney, they would immediately enter an Action against them; upon which the Proprietors admitted him:

That there are 28 or 30 Leases given of the Exchange which do not descend to any Heir, but expire at the Death of the Possessor; nor can any Possessor, in case he becomes a Bankrupt, or in any Shape compounds with his Creditors, ever be admitted to fell there again: That he has seen Mr. Birch attempt; and hasfeen the Beadle turn People off the Exchange:

And the said Mr. Birch being called, declared to your Committee, That the said Exchange is the Property of private People, who think they have a Liberty to hinder People from coming the re.

Mr. Samuel Thoyts wras examined: Who said, He is employed in buying Beans for the West Indies: That the Method of felling Beans is on Board the Ken/ish Hoys at Wool Quay, near the Custom-house: That the principal Time for such Sale Day is on Monday, in the Morning: That there are a Set of People who make it their Business to go on Board the Hoys by Candle-light in the Morning, on their first hearing of a Convoy going for the West Indies, and buy the Beans, before other People can get on board the Hoys, and afterwards fell them at an advanced Price: And

Thomas NicholsYLtquke, beingagainfurtherexamined, said, That a Corn Market at Westminster would be of great Benefit to the Farmers; they would be encouraged to bring their Corn there, and could fell it cheaper; because they could carry Manure back, to improve their Lands; by which Means, he thinks, the Corn might be afforded One Shilling in ft Quarter cheaper.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine into that Part of the Petition which relates to Frauds and Abuses in the Sale of Hay and Straw. And,

The said Mr. Nichols informed }rour Committee, That the Methodof fell i n g Hay at t h e IIay market., Westminster,

is by assigning it to Saiefmeii, who are 7 or 8 in Number; who have is. $d. a Load for felling it, is. a Load for drawing it from the Market to the Buyer, and is. a Load allowed by the Farmer to be spent on the Buyer; so that the whole is a Tax of 3s. 3d. a Load for felling it; but never tell the Farmer who they fell it to: That he thinks, if a public Register was to be appointed, and a Prohibition laid upon buying Hay before it comes to Market, it would be a Check upon the Salesmen, and prevent Frauds being committed by Servants, who may now buy a Load of Hay for 52 s. and charge £.3, which Gentletpeli cannot prevent; but if a Register was established for the Sale of Hay, both the Farmer and Gentleman might have Reeourse to it, and fee the Price it fold for, and thereby prevent any Fraud by the Saiefmen or the Person buying: That it would be very useful vto have a weighing Place in the Market, to prevent Frauds in the Weight.

Vol. 28.

Mr. Daniel Hawkins, Farmer in Harrow Parish, con firmed Mr. Nichols's Evidence, withrefpe£t tot lie Manner of felling Hay in the Haymarkel\ and added, That he has heard the Salefrnen settle what the Price of the Market was to be: and that he thinks some Regulation necessary in the Sale of Hay.

Mr. Cordzvall being examined, said, That he has known the Salefrnen meet in a Morning, to settle the Price; and when he has called One of them, to buy a Load of Hay, that Salesman has allied the rest " How is " it to he to-day/’ mentioning the Price; that they then fixed the Price, and he paid it: That he suspetSls the Salesmen send to the Farmers, to prevent their fending their Hay too fall into the Market, that they may keep up the Price :That he has known the Saiefmen go to Smiihfield and Whitechapel in a Morning, in order to settle the Price of Hay at those Three Markets; and that if the Salefrnen were to fix the Price at £.3 or 4 a Load, they might do it, and the Buyer can’t help himself.

Mr. John Warrington, Stable-keeper, said, That he apprehends the Farmercan very seldom have a fairPrice for his Goods; for he has bought from 5 to 10 Loads of Hay in the same Market, in the same Day, at one cer-' tain Price per Load, which has often belonged to a.* many different Farmers, and the Quality of the 1 lay often from 5s. to js. per Load Difference; so that the Farmer mull have what Price the Salefrnen please to give him; and they are often Dealers in Hay themselves, and fell their own Hay with that of the Farmers:

That Salefrnen and Hay Jockies, who buy Hay in the Country for the London Markets, very often put Rubbish made wet into the Middle of the Truffes, which can’t be discovered ’till the Truss is unpacked: That he has seen 8 or lolb of such Rubbifti in One Truss; which, if not immediately found out, spoils the good Hay by heating:

That there is no Weight fixed for the Sale of Straw: That the general Rule is 361b. but has often found it deficient; and knows of no Method of Punishment for such Frauds: That the Jockey men buy the greatelt Part of the Straw to fell again, whereby that Commodity is monopolized; and that he thinks, the Price would be reduced, if a Prohibition was laid on buying to fell , again.

Mr. Wright confirmed Mr. Warrzng/on's Evidence with regard to Straw; and added, That he has often found it deficient in Weight; and has applied to Justices of the Peace, who declared they could not relieve him.

Mr. John Nezvport said, That he once saw a Man unbind Straw, water it, and bind it up again in less Quantities: And

Mr. Cordzvall, beingagain called, said, That he has seen Straw wet in the Middle of the Truss, and so hot that he could hardly hold his Hand in it: That when he has taken the wet Part out, the Remainder has been worth but is. 6d. per Truss.

Being asked. Whether lie had ever heard of any Stoppage on the Tadcaster River ? lie said, Sometimes there was? And being alked the same Question in regard to the Leeds River, he gave the same Answer.

He said. By a Monopoly, he did not mean that any one is prohibited from navigating on the said Rivers; but that the Lock Duties are so high, that the Proprietors make 30 or 40 per Cent, of their Money, so that the Duties might be lowered; and that if the Proprietors of the intended Navigation were ever allowed to make so much of their Money, he should apprehend it would then become a Monopoly; but it was proposed to prevent that, by lowering the Duties whenever they shall amount to more than a certain Sum per Cent.

Being asked, What the Rent of the old Navigation on thejir and Calder is at present ? he said, He has heard, jf. 6,000 a Year; and that at first, perhaps, it might not be 1,000 Pounds a Year: That he believes the Tolls have been lowered, but he does not know the Proportion.

Being asked. If he knew what the Proprietors divided for the first 20 Years ? he laid, He did not know, hut believes they loft about 20 or 30 per Cent.

Being asked. What Part of the County of Lancaster would be benefited by the proposed Navigation ? he said, Rochdale, and the Parts adjacent, would receive equal Advantage with Halifax; and that he believes the Navigation is capable of being continued to Rochdale, or even to Manchester; but he cannot speak to that with any Certainty, having never seen an v Plan.

Mr. John Smeaton, Engineer, being examined, said, That he lmd lurveved the River Calder, from Wakefield to Sailer Hebble Bridge; and he produced to your Committee his Survey, which he said was laid down with the utmost Care; and he said, that the Distance from Wakefield to Brooffmouth, by the Side of the River, is 23 Miles and an Half, and from thence to Salter Hebble Bridge Half a Mile:

That the Rife of the Surface of the River, from the Level Water below Wakefield Bridge, to the Level Water at the Mouth of Halifax Brook, is 154 Feet, and that from thence to the Level Water below Salter Hebble Dam is 24 Feet; in the Whole, 178 Feet; and consequently the Descent, at a Medium, is about One Inch in 20 Yards, or Onp Foot in 700:

That about One Half of the Descent above-mentioned is occupied by Fulling and other Mills, and that the other Half at present is unapplied to any Use:

That, when this Survey was taken, the River was remarkably low, yet that there was in general a Sufficiency of Water to keep Two Fulling Mill Wheels constantly going, and at the same time the Water afforded by the Brook, in 24 Hours, was as much a*> could be expended by Five Boats passing in that time:

That where the Fall of Water is not occupied by Mills, the Water is alternately divided into Pools and Streams: That the Pools are many of them deep enough for Navigation; and that the Streams are most of them upon Shingle or Gravel Beds, which are capable of being removed:

Tlwt there are every where flat Meadows on one Side of the River or the other, and generally on both Sides: Vol. 28.

That the Surface of the Water-side Meadow's have Cafdrr the same general Declivity as the River, and confe- ^av, Satioa’ qtiently that the Water cannot remain upon the Meadows, after the Current is retired within Bank, in the Decline of a Flood t

That the Bed of the River corresponds in general to the Soil of the Meadows: That it is a loomy Earth at the Top, and the same mixed with Gravel underneath:

That the most general Height of the Meadows above the Water, where it is not raised by Dams for the Use of the Mills, is about Nine Feet:

That he is of Opinion, from adtle Consideration of the Facts before recited, it is practicable to continue the Navigation of the River Cdldei', from Wakefield to Brooks-v\outh, for Boats and Barges (such as navigate from Raw-cliffe to Wakefield), that is, such as do not draw above Three Feet Six Inches Wat^r in dry Seasons, without fen-sibly affecting the Mills either by Back Water or Loss of Water, or the Meadows adjoining, by occasioning or continuing the Floods thereon sensibly longerthanusual; and that a Reservoir being formed below Suiter Hebble Bridge, for amassing the current Waters of the Brook in dry Seasons, the said Navigation may be carried up to Salter Hebble Bridge at all Seasons of the Year; and that the whole Expence will not exceed £. 30,000:

That the Survey was taken in October and November last; and that he inquired of the Millers, who said, there would be Water enough to supply Two Wheels:

That he made all the Observations on the River himself; thinks the Plan practicable, and would undertake to execute it.

' Being asked, What the Expence of perfecting the Navigation would amount to ? he said. He had estimated it at 29,000 some odd Hundred Pounds; but as it is difficult to ascertain the Expence of such an Undertaking within a few Hundred Pounds, he had delivered in the Estimate at £. 30,000.

Being cross-examined, he was asked, If he had ever been concerned in making a River navigable ? he said.

Not in the Execution of any Navigation; but that he had surveyed the River Clyde, about Two or Three Years ago, in order to the making it navigable, but the Scheme is not yet carried into Execution.

Being asked the Question, he said. He had been employed Seven Weeks in surveying the Calder, during which time he tfas three times up the River, and spent about a Month of the Time in taking the Measures.

Being asked. What was the general Rule of determining the Practicability of Navigations with regard to the Descent ? he said. That if there was a sufficient Quantity of Water, though the Descent be very great, a Navigation may be made; but the less the Fall the better, as it may be executed so much the cheaper.

Being asked. Whether a quick Fall was not more convenient for the Proprietors of the adjoiningGrounds? he said. It was, because the Floods would sooner pass away.

Being asked. What Water the Vessels to be employed in the proposed Navigation would draw ? he said, their Draughts would be various; but that, with Four Feet Water (whichDepthhe propofesto have by his Schema), they would carry from 20 to 25 Ton.

Being asked. Whether he had seen a Survey of this River, taken in the Year 1740 ? he said, He had; and that it differs somewhat from his Survey in regard to the Level, but not materially; and if he himself were to level the River again, he cannot say that, info great aDiftance, the Level would exactlycorrespond with his last Survey:

That he made some "Observations on the Quantity of Water necessary to turn the Fulling Mills; and thinks, that, in general, if a Clough be 29 Inches wide, and Eight Inches high, and a Four Foot Head of Water applied, it will not be more than sufficient for most of them; but they are not all alike. *

Your Committee then proceeded to examine the Matter of the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, and Manufacturers, residing in and near the Parish of Rochdale, in the County of Lancaster:

To prove the Allegations whereof, the Agent for the Petitioners examined,

Mr. George Stansfield: Who informed your Committee, That he was a White Kersey Maker, and lives near Sowerby Bridge, and is very well acquainted with the Country about Rochdale, which is very populous, and I he Inhabitantschiefly employed in different Branches of the Woollen Manufacture, particularly White Kerfeys and Bays, the Manufacture whereof is very considerable; and that these Manufactures are different from the Spccies of the Woollen Manufacture carried on at Wakefield and Leeds: That the Manufacturers are supplied with Wool and Materials chiefly from Lincolnshire, and the Eastern Parts of Yorkshire, Suffolk, Norfolk, and the Port of London, andfomefrom Nottingham/hire: ThatthefeMa-terials from Uncoln/hire, and the East Part of Yorkshire, are sent by Water to Wakefield or Leeds; and those from Norfolk, Suffolk, and the Port of London, are sent to Hull, and from thence also by Water to Leeds and Wakefield, from whence they are carried to Rochdale, and the Parts adjacent, by Land: That the Country about Rochdale does not produce Corn sufficient for a Tenth Part of the Inhabitants, who are supplied with a great Part of the Corn they consume from Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, which is conveyed to them in the same manner as the Wool: That their Manufactures are chiefly exported from Hull, in order to which, they are sent by Land to Leeds and Wakqfield, and from thence by Water to the Port of Hull: That the Distance from Rochdale to Wake-field, or Leeds, is 24 computed Miles; and that their Manufactures are sent thither by Land Carriage, and not bailed up till they come to Leeds or Wakefield:

That the Distance from Rochdale to Sowerby Bridge is 10 computed Miles; and that in the Road from Sowerby Bridge to Wakqfield there are Six deep Hills, which make it very inconvenient for Wheel Carriages, so that the Goods are generally carried on Horseback: That the Price of Carriage has increased, of late Years, from One Third to One Half, which be imagines to proceed from the Increase of the Trade; so that the Manufacturers are almost left to the Mercy of the Carriers, and cannot be served for want of convenient Carriage; and that he has known Wool lie Three or Four Months at Leeds and Wakefield, waiting for Carriage;

That the Di fiance from Sower by Bridge to Brook/mouth, by Land, is about Three Miies, over a steep Hill, and the Pack-horses from Rochdale to Sower by Bridge can go and return in one Day; whereas if they were obliged to go to Brooksmouth, they could not return till the next Day:

That their Goods are frequently damaged by Land Carriage, by Wet, and other Accidents on the Road, and foiled by packing and unpacking:

That Soivcrby Bridge lies on the great Turnpike Road from East to West, and, by extending the Navigation thither, an easy Communication would be opened between the Eastern and Western Parts of the Kingdom; and the greatest Part of the Parish of Halifax will receive an Advantageby this Extension of the Navigation to Sower by Bridge, equal to the Inhabit ants in and about Rochdale, and in some respects greater Benefit, as they will thereby be furnished with Coals, Lime, Stones, and Materials for building; and that by completing the intended Navigation, the Manufacturers in the Western Parts of Yorkshire? and in Lanca/hire, will be able to procure their Provisions and Materials at a cheaper Rate, and fend their Manufactures cheaper to Market: That the Witness himself is.a Proprietor of some of the Lands which join to the intended Navigation: That lie knows all the Proprietors of Lands and Mills, which will be chiefly affected byit, between Sowerby Bridge and Brook/mouth: That the Matter has been generally known in the Country; and that he never heard any Okjetlion made by any of the Proprietors of Lands or Mills, but, on the contrary, they generally approved it.

Being cross-examined, lie was asked, Whether, if the Navigation were completed to Sowerby Bridge, they should not be obliged to fend their Goods thither, without being baled ? he said. They should, in that Cafe, bale them at Iidme.

Being further asked, At what time he had known Goods lie so long at Leeds and Wakefield as he had mentioned in his Evidence? he said. It was last Spring, when they lay for want of Horses.

Being also asked. How many Mills were upon the River between Brook/mouth and Sowerby Bridge ? he said, Three or Four Fulling and Corn Mills.

Mr. John Eyes, Surveyor and Architect, being examined, said, That he furveved the River Colder,- from Brook/mouth to Sowerby Bridge (which isTwo Miles Four Furlongs and 34 Perches), in January last, and that the Fall of the Water, from the Mill Dam under Sowerby Bridge, is 29 Foot 2 Inches and an Half; and that, in his Opinion, it is capable of being made navigable for about £.3,400, and that there is no Dam intended in this Part of the Navigation: That he likewise measuredthe Road from Sowerby Bridge to Brook/mouth by Land, which is 5 Furlongs 26 Perches further than by Water; and that there is a Hill in the Road which rises 200 Yards perpendicular, in 1,890 Yards in Length.

Being asked, Why he fends Goods by Water, \Vheil Land Carriage is as cheap, and more convenient ? he said. He did it to prevent hig Warehouses being filled?

Being asked, Whether Two Ways of Conveyance would not be an Advantage to Trade ? he said. If one will supply the Trade, there is no Occasion for Two; and that he never knew Persons raise the Price of Land Carriage, when there have been great Quantities of Goods to carry;

That the Price of Carriage from London to Wakefield is reduced from 14s. to *js. 6d. a Pack; and from Wakefield to London they formerly paid is. and now pay 10 d. a Stone; and that the Price of Carriage from London to Wakefield fell about Six Months ago:

That a Waggon from Wakefield to Halifax can go with 25 Packs in a Day; and that he, the Witness, pays 20s. a Day for Two Carts, Eight Horses, arid Two Men; but they are not empk^ed in Carriage from Wakefield to Halifax:

That he would prefer Land to Water Carriage at the same Price, as it is more secure, and the Carriages will carry Goods baled; but that he can’t tell whether Goods can be carried from Rochdale to Wakefield baled.

Being asked. What the Proportion of Back Carriage from Halifax to Wakefield bore to the Carriage from Wakefield to Halifax ? he said. He could not exactly say, but thought it was not so much as One to Fifteen.

Being then asked. How he could know that it would be suficient to encourage the setting up of Stage Waggons? lie said, If they w ere loaded one Way, it would do:

That if Goods are packed at Rochdale, and again at Wakefield, the Expence of Package will make them a Trifle dearer at Market, and lie believes the People at Rochdale would chuse to bale their Goods at home if they could:

That he does not know what the Price of Water Carriage will be by the new Navigation; nor whether it will be cheaper than Land Carriage, having made no Calculation; nor does he know whether the Carriage will be cheaper, or not, when the new Navigation is made, blit that it is possible for Carriages to go from Halifax to Wakefield, and return the same Day, though lie had never known it done, but he has known them go as far in other Places:

That Goods come up the River Calder to Wakefield from many Parts, and are carried to Halifax by Land; but that he can’t tell whether carrying by Water would be cheaper, as he does notknow the PriceofWater Carriage.

Being asked. Whether, if the Navigation were extended to Halifax, Corn would not go up thither without being put in Sacks ? he said, That Expence would be the fame, as the Town of Halifax is a Mile from any Part of the intended Navigation, and the Corn mull be put in Sacks, to be carried from the Water Side; but that he did not know whether the Expence of Ware-house Room at Wakefield might not be saved:

That Wool is frequently brought from Knottingley to Wakefield^ which is Part of the old Navigation) by Land, and the Expence of Carriage from thence by Land or Water is exactly the same; but he does not know that any Corn has been sent from thence to Wakefield by Laud, nor does he know the Rate of Tonage on the old Navigation.

Then the Agents for the first-mentioned Petition, by way of Reply, examined,

Mr. Smealon, the Engineer: Who said, He proposed to have. Four Foot Water in the intended Navigation, in the shallowefl Parts, when the Dams are full, which is certainly suficient to carry Boats without flashing, fiuce there is'not Three Foot Water in many Places of t)ie old Navigation; and, if the Locks are made as they ought to be, there will be no need of flashing:

That the Quantity of Water to be taken from the Head, to let a Boat through a Lock, will be as much as VOL. 28.

will fill the Lock from the Level of the Water below to Calder that above; and that the Rife of the Locks on the in- Navigation* tended Navigation, on a Medium, is about Eight Foot:

That he hasobserved the Failing Mills, and apprehends that a Head of Water of Four Foot, with a Sluice Eight Inches high, and 29 Inches wide (which is about the Medium as to the Height of Water, and Dimentsions of the Sluice), will work the Mill with a proper Degree of Ve* locity; and that a Lock full of Water, Eight Foot high, will turn a Fulling Mill Wheel about Five Minutes:

That the Height of the intended Lock at Wakefield is proposed to be 10 Foot 5 Inches, and the Water contained in that Lock will work a Mill Wheel about Six Minutes and an Half:

That the Length of the Mill Pool at Wakefield is upwards of 17 Furlongs, and the Breadth unequal, in some Places 200 Foot, some 150, and in some scarce 100 Foot broad; and that the drawing off Water suficient to fill such a Lock, as is proposed to be built at Wakefield, will fink the Water in the Mill Pool, if no Supply comes in, the Eleventh Part of an Inch; and that he apprehends the Loss of a much greater Quantity of Water than that could not be perceived by the Working of the Mill:

That he was concerned in some Works at Wakefield Mills in the Year 1754: That the Soc Mill had then,

Four Wheels, and one new Wheel was then made for Flour on the North Side, and Two Fulling Wheels and one Prizing Wheel on the South Side: That he made an Experiment of the Quantity of Water suficient for the Soc Mill Wheels, and found it to be considerably more than what he mentioned above to be the Medium of the Quantity of Water used to turn the Mills upoix the Calder; for that the Head of Water was Four Foot Six Inches, the Clough 30 Inches wide, and drawn up 14 Inches and an Half, which ground Three Bushels of Corn (wanting One Sixteenth of a Bushei) in 40 Minutes; and that a Lock full of Water would turn that Wheel at that Rate about Four Minutes:

That, at the time he surveyed the River, there appeared to him to be Water suficient constantly to turn Two Wheels: and that, in going up the River Three times, he generally found Three, and sometimes Four,

Wheels going at the same time at the Mills in general; but that he apprehends they did not go in the Nights:

That tliedrawing off a Lock full of Water will have no immediate Effect on a Mill; but the Consequence will be (if the Mill Pool receives no Supply), the Mill will flop so much the sooner as that Lock full of Water4 would have kept the Wheels longer going, which, at a Medium, will be about Five Minutes if One Wheel were employed, and Two Minutes and a Half if Two Wheels were employed:

That some Mills will go when the Head of Water is funk a Foot, and some when it is funk Two Foot, according to their different Constructions j but it is the Interest of every Miller to keep the Head of Water as high as possible, because, when the Head of Water is low, a greater Quantity is necessarily expended, for what is loft in Velocity must be made up by Quantity:

That if a Lock full of Water is taken away from si Mill that is set down to collect a Head of Water, the Consequence will be, that such Mill must, at a Medium, stand Hill Five Minutes longer if the Pool is fed by One Mill Stream, and Two Minutes and an Half if the Pool is fed by Two:

That, supposing Ten Boats to pass in a Day, there will be a Loss of about a 57th Part of the whole Produce of that Day’s Water; for, if the River is capable of keeping Two Wheels going, the Loss of Water by One Boat is equal in Time to Two Minutes and an Half, and consequently 10 Locks full to 25 Minutes, which is a 57th Part of 24 Hours:

That if the Water flu>uld continue so low, as when he surveyed it, for 57 Days in a Year, the Loss of Work to the Mills, by the Palling of 10 Boats a Day, would be One Day’s Work in the Year; but it is not likely that O o so
