That he-had observed the present Locks on the Rivers Air and Colder* where in general there is very great Leakage, which arises from their not being properly made; for, if they were built on a proper Water Foundation, and the Gates properly made, though there would be some Leakage, it would be but very small in comparison to what he has observed on those Rivers; and that Leakage is in a great measure prevented at the King’s Docks, where there is a great Head of Water, and any considerable Leakage would Hop the Works: That the Witness has seen Several Locks in Flanders and Holland, where he could not observe any Leakage, and particularly One near Ypres, which pens tip a Head of Water of above 20 Foot, and that he could not fee any Leakage through the Gates; and that he fees too Reason why the Locks and Gates may not be made as good upon the Colder, and that they will be less expensive, as Stone, which isthemoftconsiderableMatcrial, is at Hand; and that the Leakage through a well-made Lock will not be more than a Lock full in 24. Hours: That he apprehends the Mills on the Colder, in general, are capable of Improvement; and that, by a proper Application of the Water to the Wheel, they might do the same Business with Two Thirds of the Water; for that he had been concerned in many Mills, and always found them capable of greater Improvement than he had mentioned; for that he built a Wheel for Sir Lionel Pilkington, in the Year 1754, and, upon an Experiment, the new Wheel ground Nine Bulliels while the old one ground Three, with the same Water from the same Pool; but that the new Wheel had a Descent of Eight Foot, and the old one of Five, but the Produce was as Fifteen to Five:

That Mills may be laid fall by Back-water; and that when a Frefli of Water comes down the River, it raises the Water both above and below the Mills, but more below than above: That this Addition of Water at the Tail of the Mill endeavours to press in where the Wheel works, and, in order to keep it out, a greater Quantity of Water is necessary to be drawn from the Head; and, so long as the Water can be kept from getting in at the Tail of the Mill, by drawing an additional Quantity from the Head, so long the Mill will work; but when the Pressure of Water at the Mill Tail prevails, the Mill flops; and that feme Mills will go with Three or Four Foot Back-water, scarcely any are affected by One Foot, and mofl of them will go with Two:

That where the Descent of a River is quick, it is not lbapt to subject Mills to Back-water as in flat Countries:

That, in his Plan for the intended Navigation, he had taken care not to raise any Dam so high as to make any stagnate Water, in the Race of the Mill Wheel, above each respective Dam, while the Mill is at Rest, except where the Water is pooled up into the Race of the Wheel above by a natural intermediate Shoal; and, in that Cafe, he has taken care not to raise the Dam below higher than such Shoal; and that by this Method, in the ordinary State of the River, the Mills will not be subjected to any new Inconvenience; and that the Dams he intends to make cannot affect the Mills by shoriening their Pools, since they are all placed upon Shoals, which naturally cut off the Communication between the Pool above and the Pool below:

That 12 Sets of Mills more may be built upon the 'River, if the intended Navigation shou Id be perfected, viz. One Sett at every Dam; and that no particular Difficulty will attend the Execution of the new Navigation: That the Number of Works will create a greater Expence, but no Difficulty.

Being cross-examined, he said, That he proposed to make the Locks better than most of the Locks he had seen on any River in England; and that he never saw worse Locks than those upon the Air and Colder: That *7

he had seen much better Locks at Exeter, but he thinks he can make better Locks than any he has seen in England.

Being asked, What lie took to be the belt Method of preventing Leakage where the Gates meet ? he said, To make the Gates flmt true to one another, and upon the Sill: That Cork or Flannel is fomerimes put where the dates meet, to prevent Leakage, but lie apprehends it may be sufficiently prevented without those Methods, but not quite so effectually; and that lie apprehends a well laid Foundation of a Lock will last a great Number of Years, and the Gates may last Seven Years without Repair; and that any considerable Loss of Water mu ft arise from Want of Repairs.

Being asked, Whether the Mills would not suffer in proportion to the Rapidity of the Stream ? he said. They would not; and Boats going through when the Mill Pools are near drawn off, will do the least Damage, as the Mills then employ the most Water, and a less Quantity in the Lock will bring the Water above and below to a Level:

That he apprehends Flashing is not made use of where there is no Necessity for it, as a Stream is no deflrable Thing; but a regular Stream is better than a Stream with Interruptions:

That several Brooks fall into the River Colder, between Halifax, and Wakefield', bnt the principal Stream is Huddersfield River, which works a Forge; and that there are Eight Mills between Huddersfield River and Wakefield, and Four between the said River and Hal fax Brook:

Being asked, Whether he was acquainted with the Nature of the Ground at all the intended Locks, so far as to say that it is proper for a Foundation ? he said, He apprehended Methods may be made use of to prevent Leakage, in a great measur, in any Ground: That Stone is a good Foundation, and he would deftre no better: That he had observed Dams undermined, but not where proper Care was taken; and that there are regular Methods of preventing it.

Being asked the Question, he said. He was acquainted with the Methods of setting Stones in Water, ami he itillanced what he had done at the Eddiftone Light-house, where, he said, the Foundation was very difficult; but that he had made one which he hopes will last as long as the Rock.

Mr. George Collett, Mailer House-carpcntor to his Majestyat Deptford, informed your Committee, That lie was acquainted with the Nature of Locks; and that about Two Years ago he made the Dock Gates at Dept-fiord, eaclvGate 31 Foot Three Inches w ide, and consequently the Channel 62 Foot 6 Inches, and the Head of Water from 14 to 17 Foot 6 Inches: That the Leakage is very trifling, if the Gates and Foundation are well made: That the Leakage through the Gates lie mentioned at Deptford, is not Two Butts of Water in 24 Hours; and, if the Gates were smaller, the Leakage would be leis: That the Leakage of a Lock 13 Foot wide, with a Head of Water from One Foot 'Fen to Twelve Foot Three Inches, would not be One Butt of Water in 24 Hours, if the Lock was well made; and that he has seen Locks at other of his Majesty's Yards; and that as good Locks as them may be made in Yorkshire.

Being cross-examined, lie said, He was not much acquainted with navigable Rivers, but that Locks may be made upon them as good its those at his Majesty’s Yards; and that, when he ipenks of Two Butts Leakage in 24 Hours, he speaks of the present Time, and for Seven Years to come; but When the Gates grow old, they admit something more: That they make new Gates once in 30 Years, and all that time can work down to the Keel of a Ship; and the Gates would last 50 Years with proper Repairs, so as to be Ranch; Land Locks may be made easier on smaller River-, where there are no Tides: That the Apron, or Sill, of the Gate, is secured with Dove-tailed Piles; that at Deptford having Four Tires of such Piles, and will lait 1 50 Years,

A Petition of the several Gentlemen, Clergy, and others, reftding in and near, and usually travelling, tbfc Roads from the Top of Whitejheet Hill, in the County of Wilts, to the Half-way House in the Parlfti of Nether Compton, in the County of Dorset, being the Turnpike Road from Salisbury to Shaftesbury, and Sherborne to Yeovil; and of the Tmftees and Creditors under an Act of Parliament, pasted in the 26th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for repairing and widening the Roads aforesaid; was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners have been at great Trouble and Expence in repairing and widening the said Roads; and that large Sums of Money remain due upon the Credit of the Tolls arising on the said Hoads; and observing, that as a Bill has pasted the House, for repairing the Road from Charmouth, through Lyme Regis, to join the Exeter Turnpike, the Petitioners are apprehensive that not only the Roads aforesaid, which they have with much Difficulty repaired, will again become ruinous and bad, but that the Money advanced thereon will thereby become much less secure, and be in great Dan* ger of beingloft; and that in order to put the Petitioners on as good a Footing as before the passing of the Lyme Act, they desire that the Bill for repairing and widening the Roads from Chard to Honiton may pass into a Law, which will not only strengthen the Petitioners Security, but be of the greatest public Benefit and Utility, being Three Miles nearer from Chard to Honiton, than the present Road through Axminster.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of Charles Dingleu, of London, Merchant; Exportation was prefen ted to the House, and read; setting forth. That; oi Cu*n)-since the late Earthquake at Lisbon, several Cargoes of Culm have been exported from Wales to the Kingdom of Portugal, to be there used in the burning or calcining 6f Lime, for the better and more speedy rebuilding of the said City of Lisbon; and that the same Duties have been taken for the Exportation of Culm, as by Law are charged on the Exportation of Coals, though those Commodities differ greatly in Value; and alleging, that the Petitioner cannot find any Statute whereby any Duty is charged on the Exportation of Culm to foreign Parts; and that the Exportation of Culm to Portugal, for the burning or calcining of Lime there, will be of great Benefit to the said Kingdom, as the same will greatly contribute towards the speedy and more effectual rebuilding of the said City; and the vend 1 ng of so 1 arge a Quantity of Culm, as muff necessarily be used for the Purposes aforesaid, will be of great Benefit to this Kingdom; and that if the same Duties, as are chargeable on the Exportation of Coals, ilia.ll continue to be taken on the Exportation of Culm, the Price thereof will be so far enhanced, that the future Exportation of Culm to Portugal will totally be prevented, and the whole Benefit arising therefrom mult be loft to the Inhabitants of Lisbon, as well as to this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take this Mat* ter into Consideration, and to make such Provision therein, as to the House shall appear to be just and necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the Whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Seven-night, the 3d Dav of April next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

A PETITION of the Merchants, Dealersin Leather, find Tanners, of the City of Edinburgh, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners have observed, that a Bill is ordered to be brought in, to take off the Duties now payable on the Importation of raw Hides and Skins into Great Britaiyi from Ireland; and representing many Advantages, which the Petitioners allege would arise, if the large Quantities of raw Hides and Skins, which are yearly exported from Ireland to foreign Parts, were to be tanned in Great Britain or Ireland: And therefore praying the House to take the Preraifes into Considera-Vol. 28.

tion, and that the Exportation of few Hides and Skins from Ireland to all Parts, except Great Britain, may be prohibited.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second time.

Copy of a Convention between his Majesty and the King of Prussia, concluded and signed at London, the 1 ith of April 1758; — and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation. were read.

The said Copy is preserved amongst the other Paper* of this Session, and the said Translation is as foL lo^veth; viz.

Translation of a Convention between his Majesty and the King of Prussia, concluded and signed at Lorb don, the i ith of April 1758.

Whereas

Treaty

with

Prussia.

; i Aprilis- A. 175 8*

Whereas a Treaty between their Bfltfl$\tfe fend P ruffian Majesties was concluded audfigned ontbe 16th Day of January 17 56, the Stipulat ions whereof tended to the Prefesvation of the general Peace of Europe, and of Germany in particular; and whereas, fiflce that Period, France has not only iuvaded the Empire with numerous Armies, and attacked their aforesaid Mqjeftjes and their Allies, but has also excited other Powers to act in like Manner; and whereas it is notorious, that the extraordinary Efforts made by his Prufian Majesty to defend imnfelf against the Number of Enemies, who lmve attacked him on so many Sides at once, have oc-cofioned a very great and burthensome Expence; whilst, on the other Hand, his Revenues have been greatly dSintnished, in those Parts of his Dominions which have been the Seat of the War; and their Majesties having mutually determined to continue their Efforts for their reciprocal Defence and Security, for the Recovery of their Possessions, for the Protection of their Allies, and the Preservation of the Liberties of the Germanic Body; His Britannic Majesty has rei’olved, in consequence of these Considerations, to give an immediate Succour, in Money, to his Prujian Majesty, as the speedieft and moll effectual; and their aforesaid Majesties have thought proper, that a Convention should be made thereupon, in order to declare and ascertain their reci-

Srocal Intentions in this respect; for which Purpose ley have appointed and authorized their respective Ministers; viz. In the Name and on the Part of his Britaniiic Majesty, his Privy Counsellors, Sir Robert Henley, Knight, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal of Great Britain, John Earl Granville, President of his Council, Thomas Holies Duke of Newcastle, First Lord Commissioner of his Treasury, Robert Earl of Holdernefe, one of his principal Secretaries of State, Philip Earl of Hard-wide, and William Pitt Esquire, another of his principal Secretaries of State; and in the Name and on the Part of his Prussian Majesty, the Sieprs Dodo Henry, Baron of Kni/phaufen, his Privy Counsellor of Embassy, and Mi niter Plenipotentiary at the Court of his Britannic Majesty, and Lewis Michell, his Chargi d'affaires at the said Court; who, after having communicated to each other their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles.

1.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to causeto be paid, in the Cityjof London, to the Person or Persons who shall be authorized for that Purpose by his Majesty the King of Prujia* the Sum of Four Mil-

lions of German Crowns, amounting to Six hundred and Seventy thou fond Pounds Sterling; which intirer Sum shall be paid, at once, immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications, upon the Requilitiou of his Prujian Majesty

2.

His Majesty the King of Prujia engages, on his Part, to employ the said Sum in keeping up and augmenting his Forces, which shall act in the most advantageous Manner for the Common Cause, and for the End proposed by their aforesaid Majesties of reciprocal Defence and mutual Security.

3-

The high contrafting Parties moreover engage; vbs. on the one Part, his Britannic Majesty, both as King, and as Elector, and on the other Part, his Prujian Majesty, not to conclude any Treaty of Peace, 1 ruce, or Neutrality, or any other Convention or Agreement whatsoever,with the Powers who have taken Part in the present War, but in Concert, and by mutual Conl’ent, and expressly comprehending each other therein.

4-

This Convention shall be ratified, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged on both Sides within the Term of Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Date of the Signing of this Convention, 01 looner, if possible,

In Witness whereof, We, the underwritten Ministers of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and of his Majesty the King of Prujia, by virtue of our full Powers, have signed this present Convention, and have set the Seals of our Arms thereto. Done at London, the Eleventh Day of April, in the Year of onr Lord 1758.-

(L. S.) Robert Henley* C, S.

(L. S.) Granville, P.

(L. S.) Holies Newcastle.

(L. S.) Holderneje.

(L. S.) Harduicke.

(L. S,) Wm. Pitt.

Richard Stradling said, He had been a Master Fiffier-man 35 Years; and that his Vessel is worth £.400, and is about 40 Ton Burthen; and that he navigates it with 7, 8, or 9 Men; and pays the Master One Guinea, and the other Men 13s. or 145, a Week; and that a Cargo of Cod is worth from £. 5 or £. 10 to £. 40; and that the Passage from the Nore to Gravesend sometimes takes Three or Four Days, and sometimes only Half an Hour; and that if a Vessel should arrive at Gravesend in the Middle of a Tide, the flopping to enter the same there may lose the Tide, which is a Prejudice to the Fish: That the Witness had been twice at the Office, to enter his Vessel; but found no Person there, and could not enter his Vessel; but left a Friend to enter her for him, and so run on to London; otherwise he must have loft his Market, or have run the Risque of losing his Vessel for not making his Entry: And added. That the Officers do not attend at Night:

Richard Pewrings, who has been Master of a Smack 24 Years, being examined, said. That he conduds his own Vessels, and that lometimes he is One Tide and other times Three Tides in coming from Gravesend to Billingsgate: That One of his Vessels is now on Sale, the Times being so bad that he cannot maintain or go on with his Trade:

That the common Method of setting up the Trade of a Fiihcrman is, by borrowing Money upon the Vessel; and that the Duty and Penalty affect the Fiflierman’s Credit; for if the Payment of the Duty ftould be omitted the Vessel is forfeited, and the Fisherman undone; and that the flopping to make the Entry sometimes loses the Market; and that if the Duty was took off it would be a great Ease to the Trade; and that this is the gene- ral Opinion of the Trade:

That the Duty is is. each Voyage, which amounts to about Four-and-twenty Shillings a Y'ear upon a Vessel;

but the Delay of entering is so great, that the Witness would rather pay a Duty of Three Shillings a Voyage at Billingsgate than the present Duty of Two Shillings at Gravesend.

Henry Thames, who has been Forty Years in the Fishing Trade, said* That out of Twelve Vessels, in which he has Shares, he hasonly received Interest this \ ear for his Money from Two of them/. That Ten Years ago the Fifliermen made their Payments regularly; and thak he will venture no more Money in the Trade unless the Penalty is taken off, as by the Neglect of a Servant a Vessel may be forfeited; and that this is the general Opinion of Persons concerned in this Business:

That for One thousand Pounds, he has now in this Trade, he should be glad to take Six hundred Pounds; but if the Duly and Penalty were taken off, he would continue the Business.

And being asked, Whether, if the Penalty was to be taken off and the Duty continued, he would go on in the Business? He said. Not in "lime of War: That the Duty is not much, and, if it was taken off, the Trade would not do in Time of War: That the great Number of Vessels employed in this Trade has hurt it, which is One Reason for his desiring to quit it; but that the Duty and Penalty hurt it worse; for though he never yet loft any thing by the Penalty, he is in danger of losing every Farthing he lends on a Veil'd, as long as the Penalty remains; and that, if the Duty and Penalty were taken off, more Vessels would be employed in Times of Peace than are at present.

Being alked, Yvhether the Duty doesnotfallupon the Consumers? He said, No, not a Farthing of it; it falls on the Mailers of the Vessels: And he added, That if the Penalty remains, he will not continue his Money in the Trade.

John Solletts, who has been Eleven Years in the Trade of a Fiflierman, and has a Smack worth about £. 500, said, That he is afraid of losing her, not being on board always himself; and that Six or Seven Vessels are no*w to be sold at Harwich for that Reason; and that if the Duty and Pena 1 t v conti nue, it w i 11 drive him, and several others, from the Trade; for that sometimes a Vessel is Five or , Vox,. 28,

Six Tides in getting from the Nore to Gravesend, though sometimes only Half aTide; but that they arrive oftener in the Night than in the Day, and no Person being at the Office to receive the Duty, they must lie by a Tide, or be liable to lose their Vessel; That this Delay is detrimental to the Fish, and is very burthensome to the Fifliermen; for, if they lose the Market on Friday, they are obliged to whit till Monday, very little Fish being fold on Saturday:

That before the Duty was laid on, they could fcareely get Bread by their Business, and the Duty enhances the Price of Fish to the Consumer, and has occasioned many Vessels to be laid by: That the Complement of Men is Nine to a Vessel; and though Eight could bring her from Gravesend, yet if a Man was sent on Shore, to pay the Duty, he would certainly be pressed:

That the Witness has known Seven or Fight and Twenty Vessels with Fish at Billingsgate at a time, as they were obliged to come up within a limited Time, otherwise they would not fend up so many together; and this makes Fish cheaper at sometimes, but dearer at others.

William Rutter, a Salesman at Billingsgate, said, He had been in that Business 23 Years; and that if a Vessel is detained a Night at Gravesend, flie can’t save the Market the next Day; which is a great Prejudice to the Fifliermen, and also to the Fish:

’ That the Witness was concerned in a Vessel which was seized aboutThree Weeks ago,worth above 300 Guineas: That the Master oflier went to the Office at Gravesend, to pay the Duty; but found nobody there but the Maid; and he came away, to save his Market, at Billings-gate, without paying the Duty; and the Vessel, seized as aforesaid, hath been since sold by Auction for £. 50: That the Master has the Vessel again at present; but the Witness could not say, whether he has any Concern in her or not; but said, he, the Witness, had got no Part of the £. 50 returned to him:

That the Vessel, so seized, went back to Gravesend as soon as her Cargo was fold, and the Master was going to the Office to pay the Duty, but met the Officer by the Wa v; who told him, he need not do it; That the Reason of the Witr.efs’s knowing this, is, the Master made Oath of the whole Tran faction before the Lord Mayor of London, in the Witness’s Presence:

That the Duty and Penalty are very great Hardships upon the Fishing Trade, as an Hour’s Delay may be often attended with a very great Loss; and that several Persons say, they will fell their Vessels if these Hard-ships continue.

1 hat if the Two Shillings was lobe paid at Billingsgate, it would be better for the Trade, than to have it paid at Gravesend; but could not always be paid at Billingsgate within Three Days from the Arrival atth eNore; for sometimes a Vessel cannot get up in Six Tides, as they can’t Tide it without coming to an Anchor; and iu Fogs they sometimes lay at an Anchor for Six Tides: That if the Duty and Penalty were taken off, it would encourage the Trade, as the Duty falls upon the Owners of the Vessels; and the Detention of the Vessels to pay it is a Grievance.

Arthur Chambers, of London, Fiflimonger and Salesman, said. That the Duty and Penalty a fifed the Trade, as the Delay in making the Entry sometimes is the Loss of aTide; and that it would be better if the Duty was to be collected at Billingsgate than at Gravesend: That the Loss of a Tide affects the Fish; and, if they lose the Market on Friday, little Fish being fold on Saturday, they must consequently wait till Monday:

That, he believes, if the Duty continues, many , People will fell their Vessels; and that Five or Six are now on Sale; but nobody will buy them:

That at present there are 100 Vessels employed in the Cod Trade; which, in general, make Niue or Ten Voyages in a Yrear each.

Then, in order to shew the Method of felling Fish at Billingsgate,

Mr. William Chancellor, an Officer under the Lord Mayorof Ltf/zctoz,said, That he had served the Office of Under Water Bailiff of the City of London, and had attended the Fish Market at Billingsgate several Years: That his Business there was, to fee that no Fish was fold before the Bell was run":

That the Market is free and open, and any Person may buy auy Quantity of Fish there he thinks fit: That in Summer the Market begins at Three o’Clock, and in Winter at Five, in the Morning, and continues till about Eleven:

That Turbots, and other Fish, are fold in Lots from the Forms or Stalls there, and that any Person may buy a single Fish there; but that single Fish are seldom fold there: That Cod Fish is there laid in Lots, from Four, to Four or Five Dozen, in each Lot, and sold to the belt Bidder:

That he believes a single Fish could not be bought early in the Morning; but at the latter End of the Market a single Fish might be bought; and that the Fishmongers buy the befl: of the Fish, and the Basket People buy the small Fish: And that he believed the Duty was prejudicial to the Trade.

MR. Hammond repprted from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many Hundred other industrious labouring Men employed in thp Unloading of Ships ami Vessels bringing Coals into the River Thames, commonly called Coal-heavers; ami also the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are subscribed, Undertakers for the Delivery of Ships loaded with Coals, in behalf of themselves and the rest of the Persons exercising the said Business; were fe-

One Shilling, and sometimes Two Shillings and She Pence, for uuloading One Score Chaldrons of Coals:

That the Coal-heavers work in Gangs of about Fifteen Men in each Gang; one of whom is called the Market-Man:

That there are Twenty Persons called Undertakers, Nineteen of whom keep Alehouses, in which the Labourers are obliged dailyto spend acertainSumofMoney:

That theie Undertakers agree with the Matters of Vefi’els for unloading their Coals, and apply to the Market-Men, who furnish labourers to unload the Coal Ships; and that, during the Time the Vessels are unloading, the Undertakers supply the Labourers, front Day to Day, with some Part of their Wages then due to them; which Money, so paid, they deduct from the Labourers Wages when the whole Ship is cleared:

That the Undertakers also make other considerable Deductions from their Wages upon several other Accounts, amounting to upwards of£. 7,000per Annum:

That the Price of Labour varies according to the Number of CoalShipsin the River; and that sometimes, when the Price of Labour is low, a great Number of Ships arrive, and then the Labourers insist on higher Wages than they had contracted to work for; afitVif their Terms are not complied with, will leave the'Ships they had engaged to unload, and the advanced Trice of Labour falls upon the Owners of the Vessels; but that, if there was one settled Price for the Labour, the Business would be done cheaper, which would be of great Benefit to the Coal Trade.

Then several Coal-heavers appeared before youf Committee; who said, That it w as the Desire of them* as w ell as of all the Persons employed in that Bofmefs, that the same should be regulated, their Wages ascertained, and that they might be enabled to make such PiQvision for such of them as maybe sick, lame, and past their Labour, and for Relief of their Widows and Orphans, as should be thought proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Relief of the Coal-heavers w orking upon the River Thames, and for ascertaining the Price of their Labour; and for enabling them to make Provisioii for such of themselves as shall be sick, lame, or past their Labour, and for their Widows and Orphans: And that Mr. Hammond, Sir John Philipps, Mr. Cooke, Mr. John Pitt, the Lord Regitter of Scotland, Mr. John Hartei/, Mr.* Morton, Mr. Ridley, and Mr. Buiccs, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A PETITION of the Governor, Deputy Governor, Aflitiants, and Guardians of the Poor, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners are, by several Acts of Parliament, constituted and continued Corporation for the Care and Maintenance of the Poor in the said City, and apprehend they are a fair representative Body of the Inhabitants 0 f Bristol, being composed of the Mayor and Aldermen, Forty-eight Persons elected by the Payers to the Poor’s Rates, and of thefenior Churchwardens of the several Parishes in the said City; and that the said Corporation hath had, from its first Institution, the foie Care and Management of the Poor in the said City; and that a Committee of the said Corporation is, in Obedience to the Act of the 18th of his present Majesty, annually elected, and meets regularly to hear the Complaints of the Poor, and to order them proper Relief; and that the Petitioners are apprehensive, the Bill now depending in the House, for the more effectual compelling Overseers of the Poor to obey Orders, made by Justices of the Peace, for the speedy Relief of impotent and necessitous Poor; and to explain the Law with regard to the Power of Justices of the Peace to order Relief on sudden andemer? gent Occnfions; will, as it now bands, give each of the Justices of the Peace in that City a distinct and particular Power to order Relief for poor Persons, and to summon the Governor, Deputy Governor, Committee, and Churchwardens, at his Pleasure, to shew Cause why such Relief should not be given; which the Petitioners allege is not only mincerllary, but also will occasion great Confusion in the Relief and Ordering of the Poor, will tend to inhance the Poor’s Rates in the said City, and may be attended with many other Inconveniences; And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confuleration; and to make Provision that the said Act may not extend to that Corporation, or grant such other Relief as to the l louse shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the adjourned Debate be resumed, which arose upon the Motion made upon Wednesday lab, that the Bill for the more effectual compelling Overseers of the Poor to obey Orders, made by Justices of the Peace* for the speedy Relief of impotent and necessitous Poor; and to explain the Laws with regard to the Power of Jnllices of the Peace to order Reliefon sudden and emergent Occasions; with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Sir John Crosse reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, Vestry-men, and other Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Margaret, Westminster, in Behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Parish ioners, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. Fcarey,\eHry Clerk to the said Parish, produced to your Committee, several Workmens Bills for repairing the Parish Church of Saint Margaret's, Westminster, amounting to £. 516 and upwards: which have all been paid within these 8 Months, as appears by the several Entries of the Proceedings of the Vestry, in a Book which was produced before your Committee:

And he informed your Committee, That the necessary Repairs of the said Church cannot be completed by the Parishioners without the greatest Difficulty, by reason of the great Expence they are at on Account of their Poor; they having maintained last Year near 450poor People in their Workhouse; and gave Quarterly/Relief to about 150 out of the Workhouse; and that the Whole Parochial Rates of the said Parish were then, and are still, assessed at 2 s. 3d. in the Pound on Rack-rent; and that for several Years preceding that Time, the said Rates amounted to is. 7d. in the Pound:

That the Debt contracted by the said Parish, on Account of their Poor, between the Years 1740 and 1748, amounted to £.1945. 8$. 3 d. notwithstanding an additional Rate of id. in the Pound was levied annually during that Time, and till 1756, upon the Inhabitants, for the Relief of the Poor, which additional Rate amounted to above £. 2,400; but that the said Debt is now reduced to £. goo:

And the Reason alleged by Mr. Feareij, for having contrafted the said Debt, and making the said additional Rate, was, that 325 Houses {landing in the said Parish had been pulled down, to open Streets and Avenues towards Westminster Bridge, for the Use of the Public; and that above 200 other Houses have been, or are liable to be, taken down, in pursuance of the Act for opening a Square near Dean's Yard.

And your Committee having been informed, That the said Church is now in a decayed and ruinous Condition, notwithstanding the large Sums of Money so lately laid out thereon; called before them,

Mr. Kenton Couse, a Surveyor, who said, That he had surveyed the said Church within these Two Months; and that the Floors, Pews, and Seats, of the Gallery on the North Side of the Church, belonging to the House of Commons, and the Gallery ou the opposite Side, together with the Stairs leading to the said Gallery, are in a very decayed Condition, and are so bad, that they cannot be repaired, but mull be entirely new; and as the Seats in the Members Gallery are at present very narrow and incommodious, it is proposed to alter them in such Manner, that they will be more fitting for tile Reception of the House of Commons:

That the Floors, Pews, and Seats, in the Body of the Church below, are intirely worn out, and mull be made new:

That the Pavement of the Church being partly Brick, is become extremely bad; and as Graves are now frequently made under the fame, the Piers which support the Roof of the Church, may in time be endangered thereby; and the Witness laid, it was therefore proposed to make a Vault under the Middle lfle, by which Means, when the Church is new pewed and paved, the Pews will not be damaged by' the removing them at any Time for Burials:

And the Witness further said, That the East End of the Church is very ruinous, and the great Window and Altar decayed; and as the said Ealt End of the Church is

That the Windows of the Church are most of them at present glazed with ordinary small Glass, and are itl a very bad Condition, and ought to be glazed in another4 Manner; and the Stone Work of the Window Frames likewise wants repairing:

That the Church, from the great Number of Doors, is at present very cold; and from its great Length, very difficult to be heard in, especially in the Pews at the East End of the North and South iiles, for which Reason they are at present empty:

Thru the (hutting up Two Arches on each Side, as it will add to the Symmetry of the Church, will also con-tribue to make the same much warmer, and will make the Hearing in those Pews extremely easy:

And the Witness further said, That it was proposed to make a Portal at the West End of the Church, and to erect Waffs round the dark Vestry, at the South West Corner of the Church, to secure the Church from Accidents by Fire from the adjacent Buildings:

And he informed your Committee, That he apprehends the Expence of the Whole of the Repairs and Improvements proposed to be done to the said Church, may amount to about £.6,000.

Mr. Samuel Peirfon, one of the Churchwardens of the said Parish,-informed your Committee, That several Corpse lie so near the Surface of the Ground in the Church, that the Pariffiioners have frequently complained to him of the Stench occasioned thereby.

That the Petitioners have been informed, that the Surveyors and Workmen now employed in widening and amending Vol. 28.

the said Bfidgfe, h£t\fe found odt the true Principles on which it is bnilt; and that the Foundation of the Piers are built of a hard durable Stone, well cemented together, and ate adjudged by the Surveyors as found and fuftantial a Building as ever was or can be erected; and that the Piers are not built on wooden Piles as formerly believed and asserted, but on a Stone Foundation, now as strong and firm as when first built; and that when the said Bridge is finished, great Savings will be made in keeping it in Repair from what hath been formerly expended, being then judged necefikry from the mistaken Opinion of a wooden Foundation; and that the Petitioners are informed, there are very confidefable Estates, amounting to a very large Sum, appointed solely for the Repairs of the said Bridge, which the Petitioners apprehend will be very sufficient to maintain the fame, without the said Tolls uponWaggons, Carts, and Drays* and that if the said Estates shall not be thought sufficient for the Repairs of the said Bridge, Ihe Petitioners hope ' the said Tolls may not remain a Burthen on Trade and Commerce; but that such necessary Toll, if any, may be laid on Coaches, Chariots, Chaises; and Horsefi: And therefore praying the House. to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief therein, as to the House diall seem meet.

Mr. Auditor Watson reported from the Committee, to Bndgeford whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Free- Lane, holders, and others; and also of the Trustees appointed &c. by an Act of Parliament, passed in the 27th Year of his ®k0a<*# present Majesty, for repairing the Road from the North End of Briageford Lane, in the County of Nottingham, to and through several Towns and Places in the Counties of Nottingham, Leicester, and Rutland, and through Rockingham to the Bowling Green at Kettering, in the County of Northampton,vthok Names^are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of several of the Trustees named in an Act of Parliament, passed in the 27th Year of his present Majesty, for repairing the Road from the North End of Bridgtford Lane, in the County of Nottingham, through several Places therein mentioned, to the BowlingGreenaXKettering, in the Coun tyof Northampton, and of the several other Persons, whose Narties are there* unto subscribed; were severally referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions *, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’sTable:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, the said Act was read: And,

Mr. John Smith, and Mr. Henry Shortney, being severally examined, said, That the Trustees have already borrowed £.3,300 on the Credit of the Tolls, granted by the said Act; which, together with the Tolls, has been applied in repairing the said Road; but that it will be impossible to repair and support the said Road, unless the Term and Powers, granted by the said Act, are enlarged.

Mr. Smith being examined, said, That several of the Trustees appointed by the said Act, and other Gentlemen, are desirous that the Road should be carried through the Town of Plumtree, through Stanton Lane, leading into Widmoor Pool Field, to the Town of Upper Broughton, instead of going through Normanton; that this will be as near as the old Road, within a few Furlongs, and more easily repaired, the Materials lying nearer thereto, and the Soil being better.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That the Duty of Six Pence per Ounce Troy, on all Silver Plate, made or wrought, or which ought to be touched, allayed, or marked, in this Kingdom, granted by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of his late Majesty’s

Reign, shall, from and after the First Day of June 1758, cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it if the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in Lieu thereof, the Sum of Forty Shillings yearly shall, from and after the First Day of June 1758, be paid to his Majesty, for a License to be taken out by every Person grading in, felling, or vending, Gold or Silver Plate.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Sums to be paid for the said Licenses shall be applied to the same Uses and Purposes, as the present Duty on Silver Plate made or wrought in this Kingdom, is no\v liable, and appropriated unto, and in the same Manner.

Drawback Mr. Hammond reported from the Committee,to whom °Q the Petition of Thomas Watson, of Morris's Causeway, in Callbu<^t&C* the County of Surrey, Callicoc Printer, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fa6t contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the

Report in his Place; atii afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. George Tuppenni), Book-keeper to Mr. Watson, informed your Committee, That a sudden Fire broke out . at Mr. Watson s Workshop, in the Evening of the 8th Day of September 1755, which destroyed a considerable Quantity of East India Callicoes and German Linens, amounting to between 7 andj£.8,000 Value, which were in the Workshop, and were intended for Exportation.

Then,

Mr. William Steed, Merchant, produced an Account of Callicoes and German Linens destroyed by the Fire in Mr. Watson's Workshop, which he informed your Committee he had taken from his own and the other Proprietors Books, and had also chequed it with the Books at the Custom-house; and found, that the several Pieces in the said Account were not wrote off there for Exportation, and the Word " Burnt" was wrote against the several Lots, to prevent their being wrote off.

And by Mr. Watson's Book of Account of Goods received, in order to be printed, and of the Time when re-delivered, it appears, that the several Lots specified in the above Account delivered in by Mr. Steed, had been received byMr. Watson% and not delivered back; but that he had paid the several Proprietors the Value of their respective Goods, with the Custom Duties paid upon their Importation, in Money.

And by the Account delivered in to your Committee, by Mr. Steed, it appeared, that the whole Value of the Callicoes burnt was £.2,249, 15s. 11 d.\ and that the Drawback upon Exportation would have been £.736.

4.?.; and th&t the Drawback upon the Exportation of the broad and narrow Germany Linens con fumed in the said Fire would have been £.46. 16y. 7d.

And your Committee were informed. That Mr. Watson had applied both to the Commissioners of his Majesty’s Customs, and to the Lords of the Treasury, and their Lordships were satisfied of the Reasonableness of Mr. Watson's Application, to be allowed the Drawback upon such of t he said Goods as he could prove to have been destroyed; but that their Lordships apprehended themselves not sufficiently impowered to give him that Relief, without the Authority of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders in and about the City of Chichester, in the County of Suffer, who are Exporters of Corn, Flour, Xc. on behalf of themselves, and others within the said County, who are in the like Circumstances, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by an Act passed in the Fourth Session of this present Parliament, all Sorts of Corn, Meal, Malt, and Flour, were prohibited to be exported from Great Britain before the 25th of December 1757; in which said Act was a Proviso, that the same should not extend to any of the said Commodities which should be exported from Great Britainto Ireland; and alleging, that the Petitioners, relying 011 the said Proviso, did, at different times during the Continuance of the said Act, buy, and export to Ireland, large Quantities of Wheat and Flour, under the Limitations, Restrictions, and Requisites, therein di-rested; for which the Collectors of the several Ports, from whence the same were exported, for want of Money in their Handsfrom the proper Branches to pay the Bounty, have granted them the necessary Debentures and Certificates, in order to obtain the Bounty from the Custom-houl'e in London, according to the usual Method in such Cases; and taking Notice, that, by an Act passed in this present Session of Parliament, the aforesaid Act was continued to the 24th of December 1758, with this further Direction, that no Bounty should be allowed on the Exportation of any of the said Commodities to any Place whatsoever; and further alleging, that the Petitioners, not being immediately advertised of the said last mentioned Act in its first Commencement, did continue their Trade to Ireland, where they were in great Want of Supplies, till the 25th of December 1757* and shipped off many large Cargoes of Wheat and Flour, between the First Day of this present Session of Parliament and the said 25th of December, in full Expectation that the Bounty would be allowed agreeable to, and under the Proviso in, the said former Act; and the Petitioners, having obtained Debentures for the greatest Part of their Cargoes that were so shipped during the said Month of December 1757, duly transmitted the same to London, for the Acceptance of the Commissioners of the Customs, in order for Payment thereof; but the said Commissioners have refused Accept- -ance thereof, signifying it to be their Opinion, as well as of the Solicitor of the Customs, that the Act of the present Session, for discontinuing the Bounty, did commence and take place from the First Day of the Session, to wit, the First of December 1757, and, m consequence thereof, the Collectors of the several Ports where the said Cargoes were shipped havelikewife refused to grant the Debentures remaining in their Hands for the Refulue of the said Commodities so exported before the 25th of December 1757, although all the Requisites of Law have been duly complied with; and that if the said Debentures are not paid, the Petitioners will become very heavy Sufferers: And therefore praying. That the House will take the Preraifes into Consideration, and make fuchProvision for the said Bounties being paid, for so much of the said Commodities as were exported to Ireland between the First Day of this present Session and the said 25th of December 1757, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition bereferred to the Con-fideiation of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Merchants, whose Names are thereunto sub-

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for taking into C^nfidemtion the Report from the Committee, who were appointed to inquire into the original Standards of Weights and Measures in this Kingdom, and to consider the Laws relating thereto; and to report their Observations the-eupon, together with their Opinion of the most effectual Means for ascertainingand enforcing uniform and certain Standards of Weights and Measures to* be used for the future; be now read;

And the fair! Order being read accordingly;

The House proceeded to take the said Report into Chhfiderattotr.

And the Boxes, containing the Standards referred to iii the said Report, were brought to the Table.

And the said Report was read; and the Refolunions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

~ Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is necessary, in order effectually to ascertain and enforce Uniform and certain Standards of Weights and Measures to be used for the future, that all the Statutes relating thereto should be reduced into One Act of Parliament, and all those now in being, subsequent to the great Charter, repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Distance between the Two Points in the Gold Studs in the Brass Rod described in this Report, and delivered herewith, ought to be the Length called a Yard, and the Instrument also herewith delivered adjusted to the same Length, ought to be preserved and used for fizing Measures of Length at the Exchequer; and that One Third Part of the said Length, called the Yard, should be a Foot, and the 12th Part of that Third or Foot deeded One Inch.

‘ Resolved; That it is tile Opinion of this Committee, That all Measures of Length whatsoever should be taken in Parts, Multiples, or certain Proportions of the said Standard Yard.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Measures, called Measures of Capacity, should be dfeertaihed according to the Number of cubical Inches therein contained.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Measures of the same Determination, whether of Liquids or of dry Goods, ought to contain the same Number of cubical Inches; and that the Gallon ought to contain 282 such Inches, and the Quart One Fourth Of the Gallon, and the Pint One Half of the Quart.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bulliel ought to contain Eight of the said Gallons, and the Quarter Eight such Bushels; and all other Measures, called Measures of Capacity, ought to be take 1 iu Parts, Multiples, or proportional Parts of the said Gallon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Goods, measured by any of the said Measures of Capacity, should not be heaped, but stricken with a round Strike of the same Diameter from one End to the other.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standard of Weight ought to be the Pound herewith delivered, described in this Report, and made hpbn the Examination and Review of the several present Standard Troy Weights therein mentioned *, and that the 12th Part of the said Pound should be an Ounce, the 20th Part of such Ounce a Pennyweight, and the 24th Part of such Pennyweight a Grain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all other Weights should he taken from Parts, Multiples, orcertain Proportions, of the said Standard Pound,

Refilled, That it is the Opinion of this*Committee, , - 18; -

That all Contrafts, Bargains, Sales, and Dealings, ought ' to betaken and adjudged to be according to the Stand-. ards aforesaid; and that no Person should recover the Price of Goods fold, Or the Goods themselves, or any Damages, on account of any Contrafts, Bargains, Sales* or Dealings, but according to the said Standards.

Resolved, That it is tile Opinion of this Committee, That it ought to be made penal for any Person to have in his Possession any Measure or Weighs that is not agreeable to the aforesaid Standards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Comrhittce; That it ought to be made highly penal for anV Perfoil to make or fell any Measure or Weight that is not agreeable to the aforesaid Standards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That no Person onglit to be permitted to make Weights, or Measures, without having first obtained a proper Li* cence for that Purpose, upon the Payment of a certain Sum, for the enfQrcing an Uniformity in the Weights and Measures to be used.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee1,’' That all Measures, called Measures of Capacity, to be* hereafter made, ought to be marked with the Name of the Maker; and, after a proper Examination of the* Measure, the same to be stamped with the initial Letters of the Name of the Person who examined it.

A Petition of the subscribing Planters and Merchants, African

interested in, and trading to, the British Sugar Colonies forts and in America, was presented to the I louse, and read; tak- Sett emcft S< ing Notice, That the Petitioners are informed, that the State and Condition of the Forts and Settlements in Africa is under the Consideration of the House; and alleging, that the Price of the moll valuable Negroes, so much lyanted in the Sugar Plantations (and even of the inferior Sort), is greatly advanced since the Forts and Settlements have been under the Direction of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, which greatly distresses and alarms the Petitioners, prevents the Cultivation of the Britfi Colonies, and is of great Detriment to the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom; which the Petitioners are fearful, and believe, is in some Measure owing to the ruinous State and Condition the Brit if 1 Forts and Settlements were in, as appears from a Survey taken in the Years 1755 and 1756, by Jufly Whtfon Esquire; and, from a Sur- -.5,1 vey taken by Captain Weller, of his Majesty s Ship Afjifiance, in 1757, it does not appear they were then in a better Situation; and that the Petitioners fear the British Settlements are not kept in that respectable State it is absolutely necessary they should be, nor will any further Sums granted for that Service answer the Purposes intended, unless other Measures are pursued, and the Money more properly accounted for; and that the Petitioners presume the most proper Method to execute that great End, next to that of an incorporated Company, with a large capital trading Stock, tinder certain Restridious and Regulations, will be that the Care and Management of the British Forts and Settlements in Africa, be put under the foie Di red ion of the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations; and further alleging, that the Petitioners Interest in preferring and extending this Trade is closely connected with that of Great Britain, and is of such a Nature as makes it impossible for them to have any other Views, but such only as are for the Honour and Interest of this Nation, and such as will be most conducive to the improving this Branch of Commerce, as their Preservation or Ruin go Hand in Hand with that of the African Trade; and that by an Act, passed in the Year 1 750, for extending and improving the Trade to Africa, the British Subjects are debarred from lodging their Merchandize and Slaves in the Forts and Settlements in Africa: And therefore praying, That such Part of the said Act maybe repealed; and that all Commanders of Britfi and American Vessels; free Merchants, and all other his Majesty *s Subjects, who are settled, or may at any time hereafter settle, in Africa, shall have free Liberty, from Sunrise to Sunset, to enter the Forts and Settlements, and todepufit their Goods and Merchandize in the Warehouses thereunto belonging; also to secure their Slaves or other Purchases, without paving any Consideration for the fame; but the Slaves tobevidualled at the proper Cost and Charges of each of the Proprietors thereof; and further alleging, that if the aforesaid Method be approved, and the Commanders of the Ships of War stationed on the Coast of Africa have proper Powers and full Inilrudions to assist the Governors of the several Forts and Settlements, and to preserve the Rights of the Crown of Great Britain, and of the trading Britfi Subjects, to prevent the Er«

Your Committee find, That from the Year 1730 to the Year 1743, both inciufive, the Royal African Company of England had£. 10,000 per Annum granted them byParliament,tovvardstheMaintenanceoftheir Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, and in the Year 1744 they had £.20,000 for the same Purpose; in 1745 nothing; and in 1746 £. 10,000, which was the last Sum granted by Parliament to the said Company; the wholei amounting to £. 170,000: And it appears, by the Establishment of the said Company for their Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, for the Year 1735, that the Total Charges of the said Company’s Eftahliftiment, for the Maintenance of their Forts and Settlements for that Year, amounted in Sterling Money to£. 12,310 17 4.

Your Committee observing, that the before-mentioned were all the Forts on the Coafi o f Africa that had been inspected at that Period of Time, had Recourse to the Return made by Captain Pye, of his Majesty’s Ship the llumber, to the Admiralt y, in 1749-50; and find, that, besides the afore-mentioned Forts, he had 111-speded the Fort of IVkydah; and reported the State and Condition of it to be as followeth; viz.

Whida/i, surveyed 27 February 1749:

2 Officers, 3 Soldiers, Blacks; Castle Slaves, 32 Aten, 46 Women, 27 Children; 12 Canoe Men; 35 Guns, from 2 to 9 Pounders; 380 Shot, from 2 to 9 Pounders; 2401b. of Gunpowder; 56 Muskets, 5 Biuuderbulies; Military Stores, 6 Copper Ladles, 2 Worms; Vessels,

1 Eleven Hand Canoe, bad; Goods in Trade to the Value of £.27 supplied from Cape Coast Four Years ago, and none since; in consequence whereof the Trade is almost loft.

And Captain Pye observes, that the Forts in general are very irregular; and what Repairs are made, for want of skilful Workmen, are badly executed, particularly Bricklayers and Masons Work; and that whatever Sums are granted can be of no Signification, till proper Persons are sent from Europe, to inllrud the Natives; and the Bricks they make are quite familly, for want of being properly made, as there are different Sorts of Earth, and seemingly very proper for the Purpose: Carpenters and Sawyers are very much wanting, there being Wood proper for Building, though most of it is to Windward of the Forts: They have likewise Stone in some Places plenty, but nobody that understands working it; and, for want of an experienced Surveyor, every Chief makes Alterations for his ownCon ven iency,without considering whether such Alterations are detrimental to the Fortificat ions or not: The Negroes in general are very tradable to learn Trades; and, were there a suficient Number of Artists sent out to instrud them, and a competent Sum of Money allotted for this Service, they would undoubtedly, in Two or Three Years, render the Forts complete:

And Captain Pye, having been instrucled to communicate his Observationson the Coastin general, observes, in his Letter to Mr. Clevland, dated 18 March 1749-50, in the First place. That a Company is moll certainly necessary; nor, in his Opinion, can the Trade be properly carried on without it.

He then observes particularly upon every Fort and Settlement: And as to Gambia, he found it in a most mile-rable Condition; the People in a most melancholy Situation,

3iGe6.IL 8° Juniu275

tion, for want of Goods to carry on a Trade to support th^ir Garrison, not having any Supplies for upwards of Five Years, nor allowed to trade for schefnselves; the Consequence of which was, they were obliged to call in all their Out Factors on the Continent, which were many, and, if properly supplied. One of the bed Branches of Trade, on the Coast, for Wax, Slaves, Teeth; and Gold; but, by being so long ne^le&ed, the chief Trade is gone down the River Senegal to the French Factory.

At Sierra Leone is a prodigious Trade for Slaves, and some Teeth, carried on by Ships of different Nations; of which, he believes, the Trading Ships of England, have their Share.

O11 his Arrival on the Gold Coast, he found from Dix-cove (which is the Fil'd Fort on the Coast) to Whidah, all the Forts belonging to the Royal African Company in a much better Situation than he expelled, from the miserable Condition he found Gambia in, though far shortof the Dutch and Danes) which he soon found was owing to the Leave the African Company had granted in the Beginning of the Year 1749 to Mr. Stockwelly their Governor, and Company to carry out Goods 0:1 their own Account, and trade for themselves, on Condition to maintain the Forts and Settlements belonging to the Roy<\\African Company* which were represented to be in lb miserable a Condition for want of Goods to trade with, that the Council at Cape Coast, which Mr. Stock well superceded, had applied for Goods to be sent out, or they lliould be obliged to abandon the Forts, as they declared to Captain Pye they mud inevitably have done, had not Mr. Stockwell and Company brought out Goods justr as they did.

But Captain Pye observes, that the Method took by Mr. Slockzvclly was, making the Remedy almost as bad as the Disease, as the chief of the Trade was with the French Ships, for which he had numerous Complaints from the English Ships trading on the Coad, thatitruined their Trade; and by the above Means the GuldCoaft had got into the Hands of the French; and when Captain Pt/eremonftrated to them the Consequence ofcarryingon that illicit Trade with the French Ships, so prejudicial for the Nation in general, they made for Answer, they were fenlibleof the Injury it did the Nation in general, promising to do so no longer till Supplies came out; but it Was their lad Effort; and that it was impodible by any other Method to maintain the heavy Expence that attended the keeping open the Forts and Settlements.

And your Committee observe, That Mr Justly Watson, who, by Direction of the Board of Ordnance, took a Survey of all the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa in 1755 and 1756, gives in his Reports the following Accounts with respect to the Situation and Condition of the several Forts, together with their Platforms, the Pra&icabihty of getting Materials upon the Coast necessary for the Repair thereof, and to the Quantity and Condition of Cannon in the several Forts; viz.

James Fort, Gambia, 1755:

The West and North circular Batteries, with the Battery between them, seem to be well situated for the Defence of the River, but are in a fad Condition; and the Want of proper Judgment in the first erecting of them, and the little Care that appears to have been taken of them since, has occasioned the Sea to undermine the Foundations, and several Parts of the said Batteries have already fallen down, and the rest likely to ftiare the same Fate in a little Time: That the Magazine, as far as he could observe, is the worst he ever met with, having neither Light nor Air: That there are no frefti Water Springs on the lstand, and but very little Provision for catching Rain Water, which might be saved in great Abundance: That the Fort might be made confulerably stronger than it is; and, when properly finished, might be kept up in good Repair at no very considerable Expence; and that, as the Situation is such as to command the whole Trade up the River Gambia, if it was properly kept up, he gives it as his Opinion, that it should be forthwith taken under proper Consideration.

And Mr. Watfony in his Letter to the Council at Gambia, 20 October, 1755, desires to know, if Building Materials can be procured on or near the lstand, and on what Terms, and whether any Handicraft Men can be procured thereabouts.

In answer to which, the Council at Gambia say, that all Building Materials may be had there, most of them upon very reasonable Terms; but that a few Vessels of 7 or 8 Tons each, will be absolutely necessary for the Purpose of gathering Oyster Shells, to make Lime: That there is Stone in Plenty; Timber is to be had, but with some Difficulty, it being situated in-land, for which Reason it would be necessary to have some Sort of Wheel Machine, which will not only save Time but Imposition; Clay is to be had at the neighbouring Shore, very proper for making Bricks, Straw always at hand, and Plenty of Wood; but proper People must be sent to make them, there being none in those Parts; what few there are who have any Judgment that Way belong to the Fort: That there are no Handicrafts Men to be had in those Parts.

N° 9. Commenda Fort, April 1756:

In very indifferent Repair; there are'fwa considerable Breaches in the main Wall, and several Cracks and Bulges in the other Parts; the Mortar goes in but a very little way, and loomy Earth is used instead of Mortar, which never binds or makes a Cement; the East Curtain was begun tube carried up, which he presumes had fallen down, but they left off when Annamaboe Fort was first begun; the Magazine is very small, and without Light or Air; the Fort might be greatly enlarged if thought proper; the word Particular there is the Landing, which hi general is but very indifferent; it is much nearer the jDutch Fort than ours, so that they have it in their Power to annoy us with small Anns in Landing; and Mr. Wat-fan was informed, that they have had sundry Disputes and Conferences on that Subject with our Chief, and want greatly to exclude usof the Privilege of landing the re, which if they effect, our Fort will differ greatly, hs the Shore thereabouts is rocky and very bad.

And it was Mr. Watson's Opinion, That the English Fort ffrould be kept up, as it is not only near the Dutch principal Settlement of Elviina, but also about 587 Yards Distance from their Fort at Commenda:

Sufficient Quantities of Stone may be got near the Fort; neither Lime Stones, nor Shells, to be found there; blit there is at present a large Quantity of Oyf-ter and Cockle Shells, which were brought in the iate Company’s Vessels from Whmebah, in 1747 and 1748; no other Sand to be got near the Fort, but what is gathered off the Sea Beach, and which has been usually made use of to mix with Lime for Mortar; no Bricks made there; but such as have hitherto been made use of at that Place, have been brought either from Cape Coast Castle, or Dixcove; Plenty of Frefli Water; no Timber to be had nearer than Dixcove, or else 8 or 9 Miles in-land, which would be attended with very considerable Expence; small Joists for light Flooring might be got thereof proper Hands could be procured to hew and saw them; that as the Fort is in several Places in a ruinous Condition, the Repair of it muff be referred to future Resolutions from England.

N° 10. Succondcc Fort, April 1756:

Is in such a dismal ruinous Condition, as to be quite irreparable, and nothing but rebuilding can answer any End, the Foundation being of a loose,landy Nature, intermixed with Stones of the same Quality; the violent Rains waft away the loose Ground, and the Stones follow, so that in a few Years more, most of the Fort will be carried away, or* more properly speaking, fallen down; but if the Trade was considerable enough, a new Fort ftould be erected, and there is a very proper Spot for that Purpose on a Hill, about 3 or 400 Yards to the North Eastward, which commands our present Fort, and in such a same might be reduced to a good ftroug Battery, and would be serviceable on several Accounts: ift. And he believed many more Reasons might be offered to prove the Advantage we ftould have in building a new Fort; the Landing Place at this Fort is fovery safe, that in his Opinion, we fhottld not quit our Possession on any Account; but he afterwards gave it as his Opinion, that for the present, and until some Resolution is taken on that Plead, the only thing to be done was, to secure the Barracks from faffing in, to the Danger of the Soldiers Lives; the Magazine is excessive small, and very bad, without Air or Light; the Fort might to be rebuilt, as i t is within MulketShot of a Dutch Fort, which is both stronger, and in a great deal better Order than ours; neither Lime nor Timber to be had nearer than Dixcove; Bricks might be made there, but it is believed they would prove bad; plenty of fresh: Water:

Nfc 11. Dixcove Fort, May 175b,

Appears outwardly in good Order; is situated on a rifrng Ground, in a Cove or Bay, between 2 and 300 Yards wide, where small Vessels may careen, and a very good Landing Place; the Magazine like all the others* without Air or Light; this Fort ought to be kept up and supported in the best Manner possible, it being from hence that most of our other Forts get Lime and Timber for their sundry Repairs, and if this Fort is neglected, the others mull suffer greatly; as Lime isfcarce in this Part of the World, some Steps ftould be taken towards settling the Right of the English to Atchumah, a Village about a League to the We ft ward of Dixcove, that in case the last mentioned Place should be exhausted of Lime Stone, we might not be deprived of the only Place we can get it at besides, which is Atchumah; this is a Circuinftance highly deserving Consideration, as it will have great Weight with the Natives, for if we have really a Right to the Village of Atchumah, as by our keeping the Caboceers there in the Committee’s Pay, it seems we have, notwithstanding which, the Chief of Acqueda fends and takes the Inhabitants Fift, Fowls, &c. and in every Respect acts there the same as at any Dutch Village; the Negroes are continually making Complaint to the Chief, but all he can do is to make them as easy as possible, by telling them, they may be affurecl the Dutch will be obliged to quit all Claim to that Village very stortly; Stone and Sand to be had at Dixcove; our not supporting, but neglecting them, will not only induce them, but those at other Places, to leave us and fly to the Dutch, who are continually on every Occasion bringing on Disputes with the English at Dixcove; and Mr. Senior the Chief, in his Letter to Mr. lVatfony fays, he imagines that 60 Men Slave* might be able to get near 2000 Iiogftieads of Lime in a Twelve-month:

Timber fit for building at about Four Miles from Dixcove, which it is imagined the English have a Right to; but the Dutch keep the Natives in Awe, so that we are deprived of any Benefit therefrom.

Upon the Whole, Mr. Walfon adds, that in the present Condition of our Forts upon the Coast of Africa, Three or Four Men of War of 40 Guns each, might take every one of the Forts with ease, and dispossess us of all our Settlements in that Part of the World:

And Mr. Rednap having informed your Committee, That he had been employed in passing Mr. Roberts's Account, by the Auditor of the Imprelt for the £.6,000 granted him by Parliament; your Committee enquired . whether Mr Roberts did produce the same Sort of Vouchers as the old African Company used to do; to which he dec lared in the Affirmative, saying, that Mr. Roberts left his Vouchers in the Auditor’s Hands, and the^Company only presented Copies of the Charges paid in Africa, sworn to by their Accomptant.

And Mr. Cujl being again called, and asked, Whether the African Committee’s Servants have any Arrears due to them ? declared, That by the Books, ending 30 June 1756, there appears to be due £.1,918 to the Servants, which, at 60 perCent. is £.1,200 5 and that there is now due in Arrears about £.6,000.

Your Committee having proceeded thus far in their Enquiry into the Matters referred to their Consideration, had an Account referred to them, from the House, of the State and Condition of the Forts and Settlements, as inspected by Captain Barton, of his Majesty’s Ship the Lichfield, dated the 13th of Januai'y 1758; and your Committee find no material Difference between Captain Bartons Account, and Captain Weller's, except that Captain Barton reports the Forts and Guns to be in rather a worse Condition than Captain Weller found them; that this Difference is owing to the xAlteration in the State of Bance Island ,* and that the Guns in the Forts under the Direction of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa are in better Order, and more in Number, than they were when in-speCled by Captain Weller.

And Captain Barton, in a Letter to Mr. Clevland, 13 Januai'y 1758, fays, That in January 1756, Cape Co aft Castle was attacked by Four Sail of French Men of War $ that the Castle hulled the Intrepide, one of the said Men of War, half a Dozen Times, and then they sheered off: Fie further fays, That he was informed by the Governor and Council of the said Caftlr, that the French -had no Trade upon the Coast; and that they were certain there had not been a French Merchantman tipou the Coast for near Two Years before.

Your Committee, upon the Whole, observe, That the Forts and Settlements on the C oast of Africa were so ill supplied with Goods and Stores by the late Royal African Company, that the Servants of t|le said Company , were, before March 1749-50, permitted to trade on their own Accounts, in order to support the Forts and Settlements on the Gold Coast, which Trade is chiefly carried on with the French, manifestly to the Detriment of the Trade of Great Britain. 1

That the Forts in general on the Coast of Africa were originally ill constructed, and are very irregular; and

that they were delivered to the Committee of the Com- African

pany of Merchants trading to Africa, oil the 20th June 1751, in bad Condition.

That the Attempts of tht French to build a Fort at Annamaboe, the principal Place of Tra e on the Gold Coast; and the Insults and Intrigues of the Natives to obstruCb the Proceedings of the Engljh in build -n one, made it necessary for the African Committee to apply their chief Attention to the expediting, by all poiiibie Means, the Erecting the said Fort, and to employ great Part of the Artificers in the African Committee’s Service at that Fort, whereby so much Money was expended, as to make a Balance of £.7,140 14. 3. dne from that Fort, to the other Forts and Settlements on the Coali of Africa.

In respect to this particular Fort of Annamaboe, your Committee must observe. That Stone might be had, but it depends upon the Pleasure of the fupe ftitious Natives* who deem many of the hocks sacred; and Mr. Waffon thinks it would be the utmost folly to undeceive them; that no Lime is to be had nearer than Winnebah ovDtx-cove, to procure which, the Committee must have had a Number of Slaves and Canoemcn, and Vessels to transport it from’thence to Annamaboe, and on that Coast there are do Materials fit for making Bricks, cither for inside, or any other Kind of Work, the Dampness of the Weather being such, that Brick made there crumbled ^way, though covered: Your Commttee oifferve further that no Spot could be found at Annamaboe; so < onve nient for the Building a Fort upon, as that where the present Fort is built; that the Fort commands all the Landing Places, and the Roads; and though there is an Irregularity in one of the Bastions, th&t was unavoidable, by the Nature of the Place, and the Dispofuiou of the Inhabitants, the Work of the Fort itself is executed in a solid, good, and substantial Manner, and what no Person need be ashamed of.

Your Committee observe. That Repairs have been made at several of the other Forts, by Order of the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa.

That upon an Account of Four Years Expenditure of the Money granted by Parliament to the African Cdmpany7 there. has been on an Average, annually expended for Charges of Management in England, and JFees to the Exchequer - - - £.1^140

That the French no longer trade within the Distrirts of the British Forts and Settlements upon the Gold Coalt; and that the Trade to Africa is now carried on Free and unmoiefted, and perfectly to the Satisfaction of the British Merchants trading to that Coast.

That the late! African Company received from Parliament between the Year 1730, and the Year 1746, £.170,000, for the Support of their Forts and Settlements; but after the Year 1746, no further Sum was granted by Parliament to the said Company.

Mr. William Knight, being examined, said. That he is near 63 Years of Age, knows the School Mills, and was born near the highmost Mill: That there are Thiee Buildings, and the Mill called the Middle Mill (lands on the River Irke, and adjoins to Walkers Croft, and (lands on the Right Hand in going up the Stream: That he remembers it a Logwood and Walk Mill, and to have ft*en Tenters for Cloth in Walkers Croft, and had then only One W ater Wheel: That betw een 40 and 50 Years ago, and thinks it uras when Mr. Bailey was Steward to the Feoffees, they took it into their own Hands, it was then made a Corn Mill to grind Malt: That he knows the highmost Mill; and, to the bed of his Know lege, one Mr. Moseley made an Alteration in it,byaddingT\vo Stones and One Water Wheel, and an additional Building to the old one:

That the Number of Inhabitants in the Town of Manchester are greatly increased, and the Trade and Manufactures of the said Town are since his Memory, increased near one Half.

Being cross examined, he said, He did not know who was the Letfee of the said Mills when Mr. Bailey was Steward to the Feoffees.

Being a(ked how he knew that the Feoffees took the Middle Mill into their own Hands, or whether they ever did? he said, Aged People had told him so.

Being asked, When he (irft knew the Mills, if there were not Three ? he said, There were Three Buildings: That there were in the higher Building Two Pair of Stones, and in the lower only One Wheel and One Pair of Stones; and that, in the Middle Mill, there were no Stones, it being applied for Logwood and Cloth.

Mr. Thomas Wood, being examined, said, That he is a Miller, and lives at Chedle Mills: That about Four Years since, he lived with Mr. Dazvfon, the present Tenant of the School Mills, as his Miller, and continued with him about Three Years and a Half, and worked at the highmost Mill, which was employed in grinding Wheat and' Barley: That there were Three Pair of Stones and Three Water Wheels, but that they could not be all worked at one time in a fearce Time of Water: That in Freihes Two or Three could work; but that 'only One can work in June and July, and can grind then, on an Average, about Three Buthels an Hour: That he never worked at the Two lowermost Mills, and don’t know what Work they can do: In the highmost Mill there is only One Miller; and that they work about 55 Bushels before the Mill is (lopped to cool and to grease, which is for about Two Hours, but can work 16 Hours out of 24, exclusive of cooling and greasing: That they make no Oatmeal at
