this Mill, neither can they grind all the Corn brought there within 1 he Time, Which is 24 Hours, and that Corn had been Fetched away from him twice, but that Tome-times it had remained longer than 24 Hours: That the Mill ground Wheat well, and never heard any Complaint to the contrary: That the said Mills could not supply all the Bakers in Manchcfier with Flour for Bread, for, while he was there, they often had Flour from other Places: That private Persons did not fend Corn to grind, the Mills being chiefly employed by the Bakers: That he has often stood (till for want of Water in the Months of June and July, sometimes Four, Five, or Six Hours; and if the highmost Mill (lands, the others mud, that having the Water lirft: That he has often known the Joweft Mill (lopped by Back-water, and sometimes the other Mills: That they chiefly grind Malt at the middle Mill, but sometimes Wheat on a Sunday, and at the lower Mill Wheat and Barley: That in June and July they can’t work the Three Mills unless in Frefhes, and then not long together; That lie has known, when the Mills have been fully employed, the Bakers have been obliged to Airniili them selves with Flour elsewhere, and that great Quantities of Flour are brought Weekly from other Places to Manchcfier That he works at present at Checile Mill, which is Five computed Miles from Manchcfier, and has known Flour carried from thence to Manchester to be sold, and also great Quantities of Grain brought from Manchcfier Quay to the said Mill, and which was ground there, and carried back to Manchester; and that several other Mills thereabouts fend Flour to Manchcfier: That he has lived at Manchester; and said, that the School Mills are not sufficient to grind Corn enough for the Inhabitants, nor even for the Bakers there.

Being cross-examined, he laid, That it is Four Years, and better, since he was discharged; and the Reason was, that his Master and he could not agree: That he never knew that all the Wheels could work at the highmost Mill in June and July,

Being alked, If there were Five Pair of Stones at the higlimoii Mill, whether Three Wheels, properly con-itrutled, could not set them to work in wet Weather ? he said. Perhaps they might: That he never knew any Corn fetched away but twice as aforesaid, and it was in June or July, and Water was then very fearce, and the lowermost Mill repairing, and has known other Mills upon t!iis Stream have flood still at the same time, but could work the highmost Mill when the lower was repairing: That lie supposes People who live near Man-chciter, go and luy Flour there: That they have sent Flour from Chedle Mill to Manchester at all times of the Year: That there was very little Corn (not above a Measure in a Month) ground at the School Mills,but for the Bakers, while he was there: That he has been at Manchester upon a Market Day, and has seen Bread brought there which was not ground at the School Mills, and never heard that the Country Bakers was threatened to be prosecuted for it: That the common Reputation of the Country is, that the School Mills are not sufficient to grind lor the Conlumptiun of the Town of Manchester, and that more Flour is brought there than is fold out from the School Mills: That he never knew Oatmeal ground at the School Mills, there being neither Kilns or Scives for the making of it, of which much is eat in and about the said Town.

John Bagjhaiv, being examined, said, That he served h is A pprent icefh i p with Daniel Fanjhazv, a Baker at Man-chester, and left him Six Years ago, and at present lives in London: That they made line Bread, and used great Quantities of the lined Flour, which was ground some at Derby, Nottingham, Liverpool?, and Preston, and had all they tiled from those downs for the fined Bread, and that, no Part of it was ground at the School Mills, as they could not grind it without fpoilingthc Colour of it; and never knew them attempt to grind fine Flour, becanle, from the bell Wheat ground there, they could not make the bell Bread: That the Flour ground there was to make llouffield Bread: That he has known School Mills fully employed, and never knew them Hand still for want of Corn to grind: That he has sent Wheat

to be ground, which has continued there a Week, and sometimes Ten Days, before he could get it back; and has tried to have it sooner, and has been answered sometimes that they wanted, and sometimes that they were so full of Corn, they could not grind it sooner: That his Master kept a great Stock of Flour by him, having some from Sheffield and other Mills, and that other Bakers had it from these Places as well as the Plates above-mentioned: That he apprehends the School Mills are not able to grind for all the Inhabitants of Manchester, not even for the Bakers only: That One Half of what his Master used was ground at other Places: That he had been at the Mills frequently during his Apprenticeship, and never remembers to have seen private People bring Corn to grind there, nor never knew any Oatmeal ground there, or saw any Conveniency for it: That a great deal of Oatmeal is used iii Manchester, and is used in the Manufactures as well as for Bread: That they have had Oats ground at Chedle Mill, which is Five Miles from Manchester, which they should not have done, if they could have had it ground at the School Mills, and had also bought it ground as it came into the Town.

Being cross examined, he said, That the School Mills consist of Three, and no more, but don’t know how many Stones there are: Thai he formed his Opinion of their not being capable to grind for the Inhabitants of Manchester, from his ow n Knowlege that the Bakers were never supplied from them:

That some Bread was brought into Manchester by Country Bakers, but not a great deal; That the lower Sort of People eat Wheat Bread and some Oat Cakes, and Bread called Jannick, which is made of Oats; but that Oats are not the Growth of the Country about Manchester: That, he has known Corn detained at the School Mills in Winter, and all times of the Year, but that there are sometimes Floods in the Winter:

That great Quantities of Flour, which are brought into Manchester on Market Days, is brought by People who live out of Manchester: That if he had applied for fine Flour at the School Mills, he could not have had it, but that he never tried to make fine Bread of the Corn ground there: That he never saw all the Stones at the Mills, but that there are blue Stones, which he said are not proper to grind fine Flour, and never heard that Corn might be taken away from thence if not ground in 24 Flours: That they have fold Bread to the Country People who came to the Town, but never carried any out of Town to fell; and that he never followed the Business of a Baker in Manchester for himself; but that the general Reputation of the Country is, that the School Mills cannot supply the Town of Manchester.

That Mills built upon this Principle cannot do Work well, neither can they do much:

Being cross-examined, he said, That he formed his Opinion of the Badness of the School Mills from the Goodness of Travis Mill; but that Travis Mill was built upon a different Principle, and there being more Head and Fall, and that being an Overlhot Mill, and the School Mills Underfhot: That he saw them in 1754 a great many times, Half an Hour at a time, but never saw the Flour measured: That when he saw them on the 1 ft of April instant, it was not a very dry time, there being Snow on the Hills, and that the Water was neither low nor high.

Being asked, If any Improvement could be made in the Head and Fall between the upper and lower Mills ? he said, Not to Advantage: That the Bed of the River might be lowered, but it would not increase the Fall: That it might be lowered below the lower Mill, perhaps Two Yards, but it would then bring the Broad Water back:

Being asked, Whether, if the River was lowered, and the middle Mill destroyed, it would pen up the upper Mill ? he said, it would not; but as it is between Two Rocks, it would be liable to bring Back-water, it being now liable in Flood time; and that if the Bed of the River below the lower Mill was dug ever so deep, the Level of the Water would be the fame, because -the Water behind would come up flowing to the Wheel: That there is a little Fall at present, which is wanted in Floods:

That he believes, when he saw the River Irk on the First of April, it was all Spring Water; but that Springs are not always the same Height, and did not take particular Notice, whether the Springs were as low then as he had everfeenthem; but that his own Mill was then scarce of Water: That he had never attended much to the Rife and Fall of Springs, nor does not know when they are at the highest* but said, they are at the lowed in August.

Being asked. How he could say what the School Mills would do in the short Water Months, if he had taken no Notice of the Height of Springs ? he said, Because the Water was clear, and there having been no Rain for Seven or Eight Days; but that the Water would have been as clear, if the Springs had afforded only Half the Quantity; and that he does not know how low the M ater would be, but from what he has heard; and that his Calculation was made, from supposing the Body of Water, on the said ift of April, the same it would be in the short Water Months.

Speech of And afterwards a Speech of the Lords Commissioners

oJa&Mn, was delivered to both Houses by the Lord Keeper of I the Great Seal; which is as folio wet h:

I Vol. 28.

— 3° Jugujli.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We have received the King’s Commands upon this Occasion to affureyou, That his Majesty has the deepest Sense of the Loyalty and good Affections demonstrated by his Parliament, throughout the whole Course of this Session. The Zeal which you have fhewnjor his Majesty’s Honour and real Interest in all Parts, your Earn-eftness to surmount every Difficulty, and your Ardour to carry on the War with the utmost Vigour, in order to a safe and honourable Peace, must convince all tlm World, that the ancient Spirit of the British Nation is still subsisting in its full Force.

His Majesty has also commanded us to acquaint you. That he has taken all such Measures, as have appeared to be raoft conducive to answer your public spirited Views and Wiffies.

Through your Assistance, and by the BJeffing of God upon the Conduct and Bravery of the combined Army, his Majesty has been enabled not only to deliver his Dominions in Germany from the Oppressions and De-vaftations of the French, but to push our Advantages on this Side of the Rhine.

His Majesty has cemented the Union between him and his good Brother the King of Prujia, by new Engagements, with which you have been already fully acquainted.

Qur Fleets and Armies are now actually employed in such Expeditions, as appeared likely to annoy the Enemy in the most sensible Manner, to promote the Welfare and Prosperity of these Kingdoms, and particularly to preserve our Rights and Possessions in America, and to make France feel our just Weight and real Strength in those Parts. His Majesty trusts in the Divine Providence, that they may be blessed with such Success, as will most effectually tend to these great and desirable Ends. Gentlemen of the House of Commons;

We are particularly commanded by the King to return you his Thanks for those ample Supplies, which you have so freely and unanimotifly given: His Majesty grieves for the Burthens of his People; but your Readiness in supporting the War is the most probable Means, the sooner to deliver you from it. You may be assured, that nothing will be wanting on his Majesty’s Part to secure the most frugal Management.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

His Majesty has directed us to repeat his Recommendation to you, to promote Harmony and good Agreement amongst his faithful Subjects, and to make the Upright-ness and Purity of his Intentions and Measures rightly understood. Exert yourselves in maintaining the Peape and good Order of the Country, by enforcing Obedience to the Laws, and lawful Authority; and by making the People sensible, how much they hurt their own true Interest by the contrary Practice.

For their Sakes the King has commanded us to press this upon you; for their true Interest and Happiness are his Majesty’s great and constant Object.

After which the Commission was read, for proroguing the Parliament until Thursday the 3d Day of August next: And the Parliament was accordingly prorogued until Thursday the 3d Day of August next.

Proceedings Mr. Speaker reported. That the House, at the Desire in the Peers of the Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty’s reported. Commission, that the House might hear the Commission read, had been at the House of Peers: Where the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, fitting with several other Lords, on a Form between the Throne and the Woolsacks, said to the Effect following:

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We are commanded by his Majesty to let you know, That as it is not convenient for his Majesty to be present here this Day in his Royal Person, he has been pleased, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, to authorize his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, and several Lords therein mentioned, to do every thing in the Name of his Majesty, which ought to be done on the Part of his Majesty, in this Parliament, as may more fully . appear by the Letters Patent.

That then the said Letters Patent being read, which were to the Purport of what the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal had said, the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, 3s One of the Commissioners, made a Speech to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In pursuance of the Authority given to us, by his Majesty’s Commission under the Great Seal, amongst other Things, to declare the Causes of his holding this Parliament; his Majesty has been graciously pleased to direct us to assure you, that he always receives the highest Satisfaction in being able to lay before you any Vol. 28.

Events that may promote the Honour and Interest of his Kingdoms:

That, in consequence of your Advice, and enabled by that Assistance which you unanimously gave him, his Majesty has exerted his Endeavours to carry on the Waf in the most vigorous Manner, in order to that defirablo End always to be wished, a safe and honourable Peace. It has pleased the Divine Providence to bless his Majesty’s Measures and Arms with Success in several Parts; and to make our Enemies feel, that the Strength of Great Britain is not to be provoked with Impunity.

We have it also in Command from his Majesty to acquaint you, That the Conquest of the strong Fortress of Louifbourg, with the Islands of Cape Breton and Saint John, the Taking of Frontenac, of the highest Importance to our Operations in North America, and the Reduction of Senegal, cannot fail to bring great Distress upon the French Commerce and Colonies, and, in proportion, to procure great Advantages to our own: That Nation has also been made sensible, that, whilst their Forces arefent forth to invade and ravage the Dominions of their Neighbours, their ownCoafts are not inaccessible to his Majesty’s Fleets and Armies: This they have experienced in the Demolition of their Works at Cherbourg, erected at a great Expence, with a particular View to annoy this Country; and in the Loss of a great. Number of Ships and Vessels; but no Treatment however injurious to his Majesty, could tempt him to make Retaliation on the innocent Subjects of that Crown.

In Germany his Majesty’s good Brother the King of Prussia, and Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick, have found full Employment for the Armies of France and her Confederates, from which our Operations both by Sea and in America have derived the most evident Advantage: Their Successes, owing, under God, to their able Conduct, and the Bravery of his Majesty’s Troops, and those of his Allies, have been signal and glorious.

His Majesty has further commanded us to observe to you, That the common Cause of Liberty and Independency isftiil making noble and vigorous Efforts against the unnatural Union formed to oppress it: That the Commerce of his Subjects, the Source of our Riches, has, by the vigilant Protection received from his Majesty’s Fleet* flourished in a manner not to be paralleled during such Troubles. In this State of Thin gs, his Majesty, in his Wisdom, thinks it unnecessary to use many Words to persuade you to bear up against all Difficulties, effectually to stand by and defend his Majesty, vigorously to support the King of Fruffia, and the rest of his Majesty’s Allies, and to exert yourselves to reduce our Enemies to equitable Terms of Accommodation.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The uncommon Extent of this War in different Parts occasions it to be uncommonly expensive. This, his Majesty

My Lords and Gentlemen-,

His Majesty has, in the last place, graciously commanded us to assure you, that he takes so much Satisfaction in that good Harmony which fubfills amongst his faithful Subjects, that it is more proper for him now to thank you for it, than to repeat his Exhortations to it. This Union, necessary at all times, Is more especially so in such critical Conjunctures; and his Majesty doubts not but the good Effects we have found From it will be the strongest Motives to you to pursue it.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of Four Shillings in the Pound, and no more, upon Lands, Tenements, Herditaments, and personal Estates, and also the Sum of Four Shillings in the Pound upon Offices and Pensions,beraised in that Part of Great Britain called England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, within the Space of One Year from the 25th Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-nine; and that a proportionable Cess, according to the Ninth Article of the Treaty of Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Sup ply granted to his Majesty, the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, which, by an Act of Parliament of the Thirty-first Year of his Majesty’s Reign, have Continuance to the 24th Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-nine, be farther continued and charged upon all Malt which shall be made, and all Mum which ilia.ll be made or imported, and all Cyder and Perry which shall be made for Safe, within the Kingdom of Great Britain, from the 23d Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-nine, to the 2 4th Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petitions,

An Act, made in the Tenth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for making navigable the River or Brook called Worjley Brook, from Worjley Mill, in the Township of Worjley, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, to the River lrwell, in the said County, was read; whereby certain Persons therein named, their Heirs and Assigns, were appointed Undertakers of the said Navigation, and impowered to take Duties for Tonage for Coals, Goods, Wares, Merchandizes, and other Commodities conveyed thereon.

Mr. William Tomkinfon, being examined, said, That he knows Worjley Brook, and i’aw the same about a Fortnight since; and that no Part of it is made navigable, nor has any thing been done towards making such Navigation:

That the Duke of Bridgewater is Lord of the Manor of Worjley, and is Proprietor of several considerable Coal Mines within the said Manor, and is also Proprietor of Worjley Mill, and of a great Part of Worjley Brook, which is supplied with a considerable Quantity of Water from the Tunnel which drains his Grace’s Coal Mines:

That the said Mines are Seven Miles, or more, from Manchester and Salford, to which Places Coals are conveyed by Land Carriage at a considerable Expence:

That the Price of Coals at those Places is generally 5Jtf. per C. Weight, or more:

That the Inhabitants in Lymm, Thelwelly and other Places in the County of Chester, are supplied with Coals from Worjley, or other Mines in that Neighbourhood, at a very considerable Expence, the Distance being full Ten Miles, and the Roads in very bad Condition:

Then Mr. John Gilbert produced a Plan of a Canal or Vol. 28.

And the said Mr. Gilbert, being examined, said, That he attended at the levelling and measuring the Ground; and that he is of Opinion it is very practicable to make a Canal sufficient for the Navigation of Boats and Velfcis of considerable Burthens, whereby the Carriage of Goods will be greatly facilitated, and become less expensive; and that the same may be supplied with Water from the said Worjley Brook, and other Brooks communicating with, or adjacent to, such Canal, and also by the Water which will drain from Chatt Moss: That it is not proposed to take any Water from the River Incell:

That the Duke of Bridgezvater will be able to deliver Coals at Salford, and other Places, at 4 d. per Hundred Weight: That the said Canal will be a more advantageous Navigation than the Navigation which was intended to be made on Worjley Broo/c, because the Canal will be made without any Locks; and that thore irmft be several Locks on Worjley Brook to convey Vesselsdown to the River lrwell, the Fall of Water from the Tail of Worjley Mill to the Irxoell being Forty Feet at lead in the Distance of about Two Miles, and that Vessels may be navigated on the Canal with greater Ease and lei's Delay:

A Petition of the Malt Distillers of the City and Suburbs of London, \vh >fe Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the retl of the Paid Trade* throughout Great Britain, was pro fenced to the House, and read; alleging, That it having been deemed expedient to prohibit (he (Milling of Spirits from Wheat, Malt, and other Grain, to the a^th Day of December inliant, some of the Petitioners have intirely era fed the Distilling Business; whilst others, merely for t he fake of preferring their Ctiftomers (the Compound Distish rs), and of employing feme of their Servants, Horses, and Utensils, have submitted to carry on the Distillation of Spirits from Moloffes and Sugars under great Di fad vantages, in full Hope that the said Restraint would cease at the Expiration of the limited Time, or at lead when the Necessity, by which they conceived it to be occasioned, should be removed; and that it is with great Concern the Petitioners observe, that a Bill is brought iu for further continuing the said Prohibition, at a time when the Price of all manner of Grain, and particularly of Wheat and Barley, is considerably reduced, and, as the Petitioners humbly conceive; at a reasonable Medium; and reprefen ting the great Loss which, the Petitioners allege, themselves, and many Traders and Artificers dependent upon them, mull sustain, in case the said Bill be puffed into a Law: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Cousideration, and either to permit the Petitioners to carry on the Distillation from Wheat, Malt, and other Grain, in such Degree, and under such Restrictions, as shall be judged necessary and proper; or to grant them inch other Relief, in respect of their several Lodes and Incumbrances, as to the House shall seem meet.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

St. Mary Lambeth, and St. Mary at Rotherith, in the County of Surrey, and the several Precincts and Liberties of the fame, was read; whereby it appeared, that certain Persons, therein named, were appointed Commissioners to hear and determine all such Matters of Debt as are therein mentioned, and were constituted a Court of Justice, by the Nameof the Court of Requestsfor the Town and Borough of SoutInvark, in the County of Surrey; and,

Mr.«Middlemarsh, being examined, said, That the said Court has been of great Service to the Traders and Manufacturers living within the Limits of the said Jurisdiction; and that, if the same was extended to the several Parishes of Streatham, Clapham, Camberwell, and the Manor of Hatcham, in the Parish of St. Paul Deptford, within the County of Surrey, it would be of great Utility and Benefit to Trade, and prevent great Expences attending Suits at Law.

I with I could do it in a Manner suitable to the Occasion; and as they ought, to be given to vou now Handing in your Place, as a Member of this tioufe.

A Petition of the several Sheriffs, whose Names are Collefling of thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and the Poll Fines, rest of the Sheriffs^ and of the Grantees of Post Fines under the Crown, of that Part of Great Britain called England, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having beeu informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives his Consent, as far as his Majesty’slnterest is concerned, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; reciting the Manner of suing out Writs of Covenant for levying Fines in the Court of Common Pleas; and allege ing, that the Sheriffs of the several Counties of this Kingdom, and the Grantees under the Crown of Post Fines levied in the said Court, are put to great Trouble and Expence in collecting and getting in the fame, as the Fines levied in their respective Counties and Liberties are frequently of small Parcels of Land in very distant Parts’ of the Counties; so that it is difficult to find out thewery.

Lands whereof such Fines are levied; and that it frequently happens that Fines are levied of Reverfionarylnterefts only, in the Lands comprised in the said Fine, whereby such Sheriffs and Grantees gre utterly deprived of getting in and receiving the Post Fines due thereon, until such time as such Reverfionarylnterefts are come into Pofeffipn, which may be, and often is,a great Number of Years after the levying of such Fines; so that many of them are totally loft, as the only Manner to compel the Payment of such Post Fines is by distrainingon the Lands whereof such Fines are levied, which always is attended with great Trouble and Expence; and that, on a moderate Computation, the Chargeattending thecolleftingandgetting them in by Distress amounts to about Five Shillings in the Pound: and that in many Cafes it is a Burthen on the Owners and Proprietors of the Lands so distrained, as the Post Fine is, at all Times, a Charge 011 the Lands whereof such Fines are levied; and which Lands often go through many Hands before the Sheriffs or Grantees under the Crown can certa'inly know the Lands liable to, and charged with, such Post Fine; and that when the Post Fine is paid the Officer who receives the same is entitled to Four-pence for a Receipt in Discharge thereof; and that notwithstanding the great Trouble and Expence attending the collecting

and

45$ 18° — -i 90 D

ami getting in the fltid Post Firies, the respective Sheriffs are obliged every Year to account for, and pay into his Majesty’s Exchequer, all Sums of Money whatsoever set on them for the Pod Fine due to the Crown, for the Fines levied in their respective Counties during the Year of their Sheriffalty, whether they have received them or not, before they can obtain their Quietus: And that forstfmnch as the said Post Fines are well ascertained, the Petitioners conceive, that if an Officer was appointed to receive the same in or near one of the In ns of Court, before the Fine be palfed to the King'sSilverOffice, and the said Officer on receiving thereof to acknowledge the Money he so receives on the Back of the said Writ, and to have the said Fee of Four Pence, payable to the Sheriffs or their Bailiffs on their giving Acquittances for such Post Fines allowed him, and al so the furt her Fee of Six Pence in the Potnid, payable by the Sheriffs or Grantees of the Crown, for his Care and Trouble in receiving, accounting, and paying thereof to them, when the Extracts of such Fi nes are fen t in Process to them from the Exchequer as aforesaid, (which the Petitioners on their own Parts are very ready and delirousto pay, and humbly apprehend ever}7 Sheriff will be glad to comply with) and as by appointing such an Officer with such Allowance as aforesaid, no one of his Majesty's Subjects will be any way burthened, nor any Officer prejudiced by erecting such an Office, and the same will be no Chargeor Incumbrance on the Crown, nor any way alter the present Method of passing Fines (except the going to such Office therewith to pay the said Poll Fine) and the same wiil tend to the manifest Ease of the Petitioners, and all other Sheriffs and Grantees of Pod Fines under the Crown; therefore praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the moreeafy coIleCling, accounting for, and paying of, Post Fines* that shall be due on levying of any Fines in his Majesty *s Court of Common Pleas at Westminster, of any Manors, Messuages, Lands, Tenements, Rents, Commons, and other Hereditaments, to his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, or the Grantees thereof under the Crown; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Ptemifes as to the House shall seem meet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two thousand Nine hundred Fifty-eight Pounds, Nineteen Shillings and Seven Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying jthe Charge for Allowances to thefeveralOfficers and private Gentlemen of the Two Troops of Horse Guards, and Regiment of I Jorfe, reduced, and to the superannuated Gentlemen of the Four Troops of Horse Guards, for the Year 1759.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Thirty-four thousand Three hundred Sixty-seven Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Ten Pence be granted to his Majesty, upon Account of the reduced Officers of his Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year 1759.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two thousand One hundred and Twenty-eight Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, for the paying of Pensions to the Widows of such reduced Officers of his Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, as died upon the Establishment of Half-pay in Great Britain, and who were married to them before the 25th of December 1716, for the Year 1759.

Chappel Mr. Hetvett reported from the Committee, to whom Bar the Petition of the Justices of Peace, Clergy, Gentle-oads' men, Freeholders, Tradesmen, and Inhabitants, of the Towns of Nottingham, A If re toil, Matlock, and Winder, and several other Towns and Places, in the several Counties of Nottingham and Derby, whose Names are thereto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-rested him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Anthony TiJJington, being examined, said, That he is well acquainted with the Roads mentioned in the Petition, which are ruinous and bad: That in the Winter Season they are almost impassable for Carriages, and dangerous for Passengers on Horseback; and that they cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law.

Mr. Joseph James said, He is well acquainted with the Roads, and confirmed the above Evidence.

Mr. Tifflington, being further examined, said, That from Nottingham to Newhaven is about 38 Miles: That the usual Way is through Nut hall, Watnall, Moorgreen, Selfton, and Somercoates, to Afire Ion: That Lead comes this Way from Derbyshire to Nottingham, when the Roads are passable: That he was at the Meeting about the Petition, and that it was then understood the Road was to be carried the Way he mentioned, and so expressed in the Advertisement for that Meeting: That the Petition was prepared, and the Money subscribed accordingly: And, he apprehends, if this Plan should be altered, the Subscriptions would be withdrawn, especially by the Inhabitants of Alfreton, who have subscribed £. 1,600: That £.3,900 is subscribed, and£.600 more ready: That he estimates the Expence at £.6,000: That there is no Doubt but the Toll proposed will repair the Road, as the Materials are good, and, for the most part, near the Road: And that this Road (with another, which is intended to be applied for) will open a Communication with Chester and Liverpool:

That there is no public Road between Nuthall and Alfreton, but through Selston; and if the Road should not be carried through Selston, the Branch to Annejley cannot be made, which is a great Object, as a Communication will be thereby opened with the Forest, where the Roads are naturally good.

Mr. James being further examined, said, That the Intention of the Subscribersand the Country in general was to have the Road repaired the Way Mr. Tifflngtoy. had mentioned.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and widening the Roads from Chappel Bar, near the West End of the Town of Nottingham, to Newhaven; and from the Four Lane Ends, near Oakerthorpe, to Ash-bourne; and from the CroJ's Post on Wirksworth Moor to join the Road leading from Chesterfield to Chappel en le Frith, at or near Langston, in the County of Derby; and from Selston to Annejley Woodhouse, in the County of Nottingham: And that Mr. Hewett, the Lord George Vol. 28.

fort. ttou an Act of Parliament, made and passed in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Preservation and improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behatfpf themselves and the several other Commissioners named.and appointed by and in pursuance of the said Act; hnd also of the Coal Owners and y Coal Fitters, interested in the Navigation of the'feid

Hiver, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House* and read; reciting, That by the said Act the Commissioners thereby appointed are required, before the 24th Day oijune 1759, to remove all Sands, Shoals, and other Obffrilftions and Impediments between a Place xstlledSouth Biddkk, or Biddkk Ford, andaPlace called New Bridge, and effectually to make the said River navigable to carry Beats,. Keels, and Vessels, of the "Burthen then used upon the said River, and from time to time to keep and maintain it so navigable between the said Two Placescalled Biddkk Ford ami New Bridge, for and during the Residue of the Term of Twenty-one Years; and alleging, that the said Commissioners have, at a very great Expence, deepened the Channel of the said Port or Haven, - and have made considerable Additions andnecessary Alterations to and in the Pier at the Mouth of the said River, and have expended divers considerable Sums of Money in and about the fame, and other necessary Works, for the Improvement of the said Port, Haven, and River; and that, in order to render the said Port and Haven safe and commodious for Ships of any considerable Burthen now used in the Coal Trade, and the Mouth of the said River effectually navigable, it is necessary that the Channel should be further deepened,

the present Pier further lengthened, and new Pier or Piers built, and that divers other Works Should be made at or near the Mouth of the said River; and that the Charge of such Works will, upon a moderate Computation, amount to the Sum of Thirty thousand Pounds and upwards; and that the Petitioners are advised, chat the Commissioners are not authorized or impowered by the said Act to erect any Locks, Dams, or Piers, in, upon, or near, the said River, and the Gronmb contiguous thereto; and that the making of the said River navigable from Riddick Ford to New Bridge aforesaid ^if practicable without Locks or Dams) cannot, according to the Judgment of fkilftil Engineers, be effected but at the Expence of Nineteen thousand Pounds and upwards; but that the fame, according to the Calculation of such Engineers, might be effected by a Lock and D&m at the Expence of Six thousand Pounds, or thereabouts; and that the Money to arise by the Duties imposed by the fitjd Act, during the Continuance of the Term therein, wfli pot be fttffieient to defray the said several Expence*; and that great Damage hath been done to the Works carried on, and great Obllrtiftrons have beeiioccafioned to the Navigation in the said Port, Haven, and River, by Reason that no Power is vetted in the said Commissioners to appoint One or more Harbour and River Matter or Matters, for the regular Government of the said Port, Haven, and River, and to direct Ships, Keels, and other Vessels, to moor, lay, and anchor, in a proper Manner, and at proper Places; and that the said Commissioners are not enabled to complete the Improvement of the said Port and Haven, and the Navigation of the said River Wear, up to the said Place called New Bridge, for want of Powers necessary for that Purpose:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by the said Act, and for making the said Act more effectn&l; anil for the granting to the now Commissioners, and such others as this l louse shall nominate or appoint, and their Successors, to be elected according to the Directions of the said former Act, fitch Powers and.Authorities for the Purposes aforesaid; and for making Orders, By-laws, Rules, and Regulations, for carrying oft and completing the Navigation of the said River, and the better Preservation and Improvement of the said River, Port, and Haven, as to the House foal! seem meet:.

Mr. AldermanDickinson reported from f he Committee, to whom the Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Manor and Liberty oiNorton Falgate, otherivifc Norton Fotlcy, in the County of Middhfex, on behalf of ihem-selves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Manor and Liberty, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in attheClerk’sTable; Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

In support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Lawrence Holker, and Mr. Thomas Abraham Ogier said, That the Liberty and Manor of Norton Falgate is out of the City of London, and great Part thereof is extra-parochial: That at present it is very ill lighted and watched, as there is no Method of compelling the Inhabitants to contribute to those Purposes; and is also' very dangerous to Passengers in the Night time.

Mr. Zachaiy Agace and Mr. James Payton confirmed the foregoing Evidence; and added, That it would be of great Utility to have the said Liberty and Manor well lighted and watched, and also the Streets well cleaned and paved; and that this is the Desire of the Inhabitants in general within the said Manor and Liberty; but that the same cannot be effected without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

Ordered That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better enlightening and cleansing the open Places, Streets, Squares, Lanes, Courts, and other Places, within the Manor and Liberty of Norton Falgate, otherwise Norton Folley, in the County of Middlesex; and for regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said Manor and Liberty: And that Mr. Alderman Dickiri-son, Sir Robert Ladbroke, and Mr. Cooke, do prepare* and bring in, the larne.

Borough of Nezv Shoreham, in the County of Suffer, and of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, and Farmers, residing near the Port and Harbour of New Shoreham aforesaid, and of the Matters and Pilots of Ships usually navigating to and from the same, was presented to the House, and read: setting forth. That the said Port and Harbour, by a late Alteration in the Entrance, is become so difficult and dangerous, as to be scarce navigable, whereby the Petitioners are not only deprived of the Ship-building Trade, but of a Market for their Com and Timber, with which the Country greatly abounds; and also labour undergreat Difficulties in receiving Coals, and other Commodities, which that and the neighbouring Towns arefupplied with by means of the said Harbour; and alleging, that the said Harbour being situated in the deepest Part of the Bay, between Spilhead and Beachy, were Ships are frequently cast on ShoVe, might, if made good and secure, by forming ah Entrance with proper Pier Heads, be a Means of saving many Ships and Cargoes, of preserving the Lives of many of his Majesty’s Subjects, and be of Advantage to Trade and Navigation in general: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioners to erect Piers, and other Works, for the Security awd Improvement of the said Harbour, by laying afmall Tonnage on all Ships and Vessels, and also a small Duty on allGoods and Merchandizes brought in or carried out of the said Harbour, and by appropriating the said Tonnage and Duties, to serve as a Security for such Sums as shall be necessary to be borrowed for completing the said Work, and keeping the same in continual Repair, or to make such other Provisions for the same as to the House shall seem meet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of Six million Six hundred thousand Pounds be raised by trausferrable Annuities, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum; and that an additional Capital of Fifteen Pounds be added to every One hundred Pounds advanced; which additional Capital shall eonfiftof Ten Pounds given in a Lottery Ticket to each Subscriber, and of Five Pounds in like transferable Annuities at Three Pounds per Centum: The Blanks and Prizes of the Lottery to be attended with like Annuities, after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, to commence from the 5th Day of January 1760; and that the Sum of Six million Six hundred thousand Pounds, together with the said additional Capital of Five Pounds per Centum, amounting to Three hundred and Thirty thousand Pounds, making, in the Whole, Six million Nine hundred and Thirty thousand Pounds, do bear an Interest after the Rate of Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, which Interest shall commence from the 5th Day of July 1759: The said several Annuities shall be transferable at the Bank of England, and charged upon a Fund to he established in this Session of Parliament for Payment thereof, and for which the Sinking Fund shall he a collateral Security, and shall he redeemable by Parliament in the Whole, or in Part, by Suras uot less than Five hundred thousand Pounds at one time, Six Months Notice having been first given of such Payment or Payments respectively: That the Lottery shall coniift of Tickets of the Value of Ten Pounds each, in a Proportion not exceeding Eight Blanks to a Prize, the Blanks to be of the Value of Six Pounds each:

That every Subscriber shall, on or before the r3th Day of February instant, make a Deposit of Fifteen Pounds per Centum on such Sum as he shall clmfe to subscribe, towards raising the said Sum of Six million Six hundred thousand Pounds, with the Cashiers of the Bank of England, as a Security for his making the future Payments on or before the Times herein after limited; that is to say,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act of Parliament, passed in the 2 2d and 23d Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act foi* settling and preserving the Navigation of the River Wey, in the County of Surrey, was read: Then the Agent for the Petitioners called,

Mr. RichardStedman: Who, being examined, said. That the River Wey is now navigable from the Thames to within 100 Yards of the great Bridge at Guildford, and that it is intended to continue the said Navigation up to Godalming, which is Four Miles and about 200 Yards.

And he produced a Plan of that Part of the River intended to be made navigable, surveyed and drawn by himself, which he explained to your Committee; and said, that the Undertaking was very practicable, there being no Rocks or other Obstructions in the Way, and the Ground very level, the Fall not being more thaii about Four Feet and an Inch in a Mile; and, when the Fall is the greatest, the Whole of it between Godalming and Guildford is between 16 and 17 Feet:

That there will be Three Locks wanting; and that the Navigation may be completed for £. 4,500, and the Wharfs will cost about £. 1,500.

Mr. Thomas Wilkinson, Dealer in Timber, said. That if the River was made navigable from Guildford to Godalming, it would be of great Advantage to the Public, and particularly to the adjacent Parts of Surrey, SuJfexy and Hampshire:

That the Difference between Land and Water Carriage would be is. 6d. in each Load of Timber in the Space of Five Miles; and if the Timber be brought 8, 10, or 12 Miles, beyond Godalming, the Saving will be 4 s. a Load, for that the Timber can be carried 10 or 12 Miles in One Day to Godalming; but if ’tis carried to Guildford, it will take Two Days:

That the Method at present is, to drop their Timber upon the Roads, great Quantities being dropped about Gofden Common, about Three Miles from Guildford, and not Half a Mile from the intended Navigation, and likewise at Hambledon Common, at and near which latter Place there are at present 900 Loads of Timber, and sometimes it remains there Six Months, for the Farmers will only carry it off just when theypleafe.

And that Mr. West, a Ship-builder, having begun to build a 74 Gun Ship for his Majesty’s Service, was obliged to flop the Building for Three Months, though he had bought the Timber, not being able to get it carried:

That the intended Navigation would also be a great Advantage to the Landholders in those Parts, as it would enable them to procure Chalk to burn to Lime for manuring their Ground at acheaper Rate, by which means the Expence of manuring an Acre of Land would be reduced 6s. 8 d. as near as can be computed.

Mr. Thomas Chandler, being examined, said, He was employed by Mr. West to get Timber; and that if the intended Navigation were completed, it would cause a Saving in the Carriage of Timber of Five or Six Shillings a Load at an Average; and that in the Instance mentioned by the last Witness, in regard to Mr. West's Timber, it would have been a Saving of more than 6 s. a Load in the Carting:

That there are great Quantities of Timber dropped on and near Hambledon Common; and that Mr. West has had 1,000 Load at a time lying the re, the Stages being too long to go in One Day; but that if the River had been navigable to Godalming, the greatest Part of this Timber would have been carried thither:

That

30 — 50 Februarii.



4°4

Tlrat the intended Navigation will be a great Advantage to the adjacent Landholders of Surrey and Suffix, as, liy means thereof, they may be furnished with Chalk to burn to Lime for Manure, is. a Load cheaper than they are at present:

That it would likewise be a great Advantage to the Bark and Tanning Trade, great Quantities of Bark being at present left in Suffix, because it will not answer the Expence of Carriage:

Being asked, What the Difference in the Price of the Carriage of a Load of Timber by Land and Water would be, in case the same could be carried to Guildford in One Day ? he said, That he could not answer precisely to that Question, unless he knew the Terms of the intended Navigation; but, supposing the Expence of the Water Carriage to be is. the Saving will be 45.

William Ockcnden Esquire, being examined, informed your Committee, That he had viewed the River from Godalming to Guildford, which may very easily be made navigable; and that it is evident, that the completing the said Navigation will be of great Utility to the Public.

That he did not level it with an Instrument; bu,t believes, from his View, that the Measures given in Evidence by Mr. Stedman are exact, and thinks the Work may be completed for the Sum mentioned by Mr. Stedman.

Stort Mr. Nicholson Catvert reported from the Committee, Navigation. wjlorn Petition of several Gentlemen, Traders, and others. Inhabitants of the Comities of Hertford ' and Fffc.r, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Yeomans, being examined, said. That he is a Surveyor, and has been employed in making several Navigations, particularly in the Rivers Nene and Ivel: That he surveyed the River Stort in December last, from Bishops Stort ford, to a Place called the Rye, at Hoddef-don, where it falls into the River Lea: That it is capable of being made navigable; and that he estimated the Expence of completing the Navigation at £. 10,000; viz.

That there are at present 10 Mills on the proposed Navigation, and was formerly another: That it will not be necessary to raisethe Water higher than it is at present at any of the Mill Dams: That the Puffing of Boats will not beany Prejudice to the Mills in full Water Time: That there is Plenty of Water from November to May, except in very dfy Springs, and in hard Frofts.

Beingafked, What would be a sufficient Satisfaction to the Millers for the Loss of Water sustained by the

Passage of a Boat through a Lock ? he said. He apprehended Six Pence for the Passage of every Barge up or down at every Mill: That the shortest Mill Pool in the River would not fink -j-th of an Inch by filling a Lock; and that this would be supplied by the Stream in Four Minutes, in case the Mill was flopped: That, when he mentioned 6 d. as a proper Satisfaction for the Passage of a Boat, his Meaning was, that 3 d. would be sufficient for the Loss of Water, and the other 3 d. for the Miller’s Attendance as Lock-keeper, it being pro.-posed to let the Millers have the Charge of the Locks, as it was apprehended they would be more careful of the Water than other Persons.

Being asked, What Number of Boats, he imagined, would be employed on the Navigation ? he said. He apprehended Six Boats every Week would be sufficient to carry all the Goods down the River.

Mr. Thomas Adder ley, being examined, said. That he had lived at Hockerell 11 Years, and 20 at Bishop Stort-ford; and that he is well acquainted with that Part of the Country:

That, if the proposed Navigation should take Effect, it would be a great Advantage to the neighbouring Country, as it would enable them to fend their Malt, Wheat, and other Grain, much cheaper to Marker: That great Quantities of Malt are made in the Bishop Stort ford and Saffron Walden Di drifts: That he had made a Calculation, from which it appeared, that about 66,000 Quarters of Malt are sent from thence to the London Market annually.

And being asked, How he made this Calculation ? he said, That he had examined the Excise Books of those Districts; by which it appeared, that, upon an Average of the Years 1754 and 1757, 41*528 Quarters of Malt were made in the District of Bishop Slortford, and 35,681 Quarters in Saffron Walden District; and, in Confirmation of this Part of his Evidence, he produced the following Account, taken from the Excise Books, and signed by the Supervisor of Excise.

either to Stanflead Deal, or to Ware, by Land; and that it is difficult to get Carriers; for the Maltsters cannot afford to pay more than One Shilling a Quarter, and the People who carry it, being all Farmers, will not work for that Price, when they have any other Employment: That, when the Malt is got to Ware or Stanjiead, there is frequently some DifficuItyin gettingitto London; for the Proprietors of Barges, being many of them Maltsters, or Factors for the London Markets, will not carry for other People till they have served themselves: That the Expence of Warehouses falls upon the Malt-fter; and that, when the Witness has had a Commission from London for Malt, he has not been able to get it carried thither till the People at Stanjleadhad sent their own: That there are the same Difficulties in lending Wheat to London, of which great Quantities go from thisCoun-try, the Proprietors of Barges being commonly Factors or Maltsters: That the chief Commodity on this Navigation will be Malt, and the great Demand for it is in the brewing Season, from October to March, when the River is full of Water:

That this Country is very ill supplied with Coals: That the Witness has bought them at London, Maldon, and Lyn; but that they all come very dear, as they are mostly brought by Land Carriage, which colt i6r. &d. a Chaldron; viz. 10s. to Starrfield, and 6s. 8 d. to Stort-ford, and that upon back Carriage only, 4 s. of which, lie apprehends, will be saved by the intended Navigation; and that this Navigation would reduce the Price of Carriage from Stortford to London about Six Shillings a Ton:

That the Navigation would be of Advantage to the Public in general, and to the Poor in particular, in regard to Firing r That, within the Iaft 17 or 18 Years, Wood for Fuel israised in general about Six Shillings a Load: That the Malt Trade is likely to increase, and they dry it all with Wood; and, if no other Fuel is introduced, they will be in great Distress:

That the Proprietors of Lands and Mills wereap-prised of the Application to Parliament; fora Meeting was held to consider of the Application, which was sfd-vertifed a Month before in the Chronicle, the General Evening Pofi, and the Ipswich Journal.

A Petition of the High Sheriff and Grand Jury of the County of Flint, assembled at the Allizes at Flint, on Monday the 21st Day of August lait, was presented to the House, and read; reciting, That by an Act, passed in the 30th Year of his present Majesty, to render more effectual the several Laws now in being for the Amendment and Preservation of the public Highways and Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, One HalfVnore than the respective Tolls payable by any Act or Acts for repairing . Turnpike Roads, are to be paid for every Waggon, Wain, Cart or Carriage, having the Fellies of the Wheels thereof of less Breadth or Gage than Nine Inches from Side to Side, at lead, at the Bottom or Sole thereof, or for the Horses or Beasts of Draught drawing the fame. Tolls or Duties which were or should be payable for the same respectively, by any Act or A6is of Parliament made or to be made, for repairing Turnpike Roads, are to be paid before the same shall pass any Turnpike Bar or Gate; and representing to the House, That the Trade and Manufacture of that 1 Country chiefly consists in its Mines and Minerals, and in the Carriage thereof; and alleging, That by reason of the Ascents and Unlevelness of the Roads, together with the Straitness of the Passages through Rocks ^nd Hollow-ways leading from the Turnpike Roads to Places where Carriages to the Mines are required, the Use of Nine Inch Wheels is rendered impracticable j and that Voi. 28.

the being subje61; to such large additional Tolls is a very great Burthen to the Commerce and Trade of the said County; and that the Weights on Carriages used in that Country are npt so excessive, and consequently not so prejudicial to the Turnpike Roads as in England y and that if Wheels with Fellies of Six Inches was admitted upon the same Terms as those of Nine Inches by Law are now admitted, it would in that Country effectually answer all the Purposes intended by the said A6i, and would he in all other Reflects of greater Utility: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give the Petitioners such Relief, as to them shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Farmers, and other Inhabitants dwelling and residing near certain Turnpike Roads, in that Part of Great Britain called North Wales, was also presented to the House, and read; representing to the l louse, That the Petitioners are willing and desirous to conform to the Law as far as they are able; but alleging, that in the present Situation and Circumstances of the Bye Roads in that Country, the using Nine Inch Wheels is in many Cafes utterly impracticable; and that the Weights commonly drawn on Carriages in that Part of the Kingdom, as the Petitioners conceive, are oftener under than exceed Twenty hundred Weight; and that Wheels of Six Inch Fellies would as efle&uali v preserve the Roads, as those of Nine Inches with additional Weight proportionable, and would in every other RespeCl be of much greater Utility and Conve-nienev: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioners such Relief as shall seem meet.

Bejblved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider the Act passed in the 30th Year of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act to render more effectiuil the several Laws now in being for the Amendment and Preservation of the public Highways and Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom; and also to consider of the Execution of the said Act

Ordered, That the said Petitions he referred to the said Committee of the whole House.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Ralph William Grey Esquire, and John Cuthbert Esquire, being severally examined, said, That the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne is very large and populous; and that many Strangers resort to it:

That if a regular Watch were kept in the said Town, and the Streets sufficiently enlightened, it would be a Means to prevent Robberies, Burglaries, and other Misdemeanours, and greatly tend to the Preservation of the Persons and Properties of the Inhabitants:

And that it would be a great Convenience to the Inhabitants, if the Hackney Coachmen, Chairmen, Carmen, common Porters, and W atermen, within the said Town,were under proper Regulations:

But that the said several Purposes cannot be effected without the Aid of Parliament.

And several Members present confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for establishing, regulating, and maintaining, a Nightly Watch J and for enlightening the Streets and open Places within the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne; and for regulating the Hackney Coachmen, Chairmen, Carmen, common Porters, and Watermen, within the said Town and Liberties thereof: And that Sir Walter Blackett and Mr. fiidley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Bojlock Toller being examined, said. That he has been Clerk to the Trufrees of the said Navigation ever since the Commencement of the Act; that 201 Meetings have been appointed, 76 of which have only done Business, the remaining 125 being obliged to adjourn, for want of a sufficient Number of Trufrees:

That the Navigators have come to make Complaints of Defects in the Navigation, which could not be heard for want of a sufficient Number of Trustee3; and that there were not above Three or Four Meetings between 1754 and 17.57:

That the Fund establifried for the Navigation is only £. 300 a Year, payable by the new River Company, and agrofs Sum of £.2,500, £. 1,000 of which was appropriated by the Act for Services performed previous to the passing of it; so that there remained to be employed in the Works only £. 1,500:

That since the Commencement of the said Act One Wear has been re-built, which coll £. 1,259; another at Broxbourne, which colt £. 699; and another at Stanjlead, which cost £.472; and that the Trufrees have now in hand £. 726, besides their £. 300 a Year:

And by an Account of their Expences, at an Average, for 19 Years, viz. from the Commencement of the Act, it appears, that their ordinary Expence amounts to £.265 a Year; so that there remains only £.35 a Year, together with the said £. 726, to answer all extraordinary Expences:

That the Expence of the Navigation for 19 Years past, amounted annually to about £. 265, exclusive of building and purchasing Staunches or Turnpikes.

Mr. John Clark, Surveyor to the Trufrees, being examined, said, That the Repairs necessary to be performed at Broxbourne and Stanstead Gates, will require 140.

Mr. Hankin being again examined, said. That Vessels are very often flopped for want of Water between Ware and London; that a Vessel, with a proper Quantity of Water, may perform a Voyage in Five Days; but that sometimes they areThree Weeks, and sometimes a Fortnight, owing to the Shallovvness of the River; that Goods have frequently laid at JVare in Warehouses, from the Uncertainty of Water Carriage, and have at last been sent by Land.

Being asked, If the River was deepened, how much it would reduce the Price of Carriage between Ware and JLondon f

He said. One-fifth.

Being asked, What would be the Consequence if a Gate was to be blown up, and the Trufrees had not a sufficient Sum of Money in their Hands to repair it.

He said, The Vessels in that same would not carry half a Load.

Being further examined, he said, That the River is very crooked, and daily grows worse; that the Floods move the Ground from one Point to another, which makes it very difficult for Boats and Barges in turning up the River; and that several Barges have been damaged by the Sharpness of the Points of Land.

Mr. James Hewson, a Bargemaster, being examined, said. That he remembers the River 50 Years, and that Horses have been used to tow Vessels all that Time; that Horses do less Damage to the Lands, than Men, as the Horses make but Offe Tract, and tow from the Body of the Barge, whereas the Men pull from the Mall Head, and go 8 or 10 Pole further on the Lands, and do more Damage };han the Horses; and that the Navigation cannot be carried on by the Men so well as by Horses, for One Horse will draw as much as Ten Men.

And Mr. Hankin added, That exorbitant Demands have lately been made for the Liberty bf towing with Horses; for which nothing was paid formerly:

That Mr. Jijfop an Attorney at JValtham, rents Lands, over which the towing Paths lead the Length of 40 Pole, or upwards, and demands One Shilling for passing over it with a Horse; that he remembers about Eight Years ago nothing was paid; that a former Tenant demanded 3 d. a Horle, then 6 d. and now Mr. JeJfop demands 1 s. Vol. 28.

and has brought several Actions against the Bargemen; that the Witness went to the Person who rented the Laud before Jeffbp, who told him, That Mr. Jejfop took the Land over his Head, in order to extort Money from the Bargemen.

William Pturner, junior, Esquire, said, That his Father has an Estate, over which there is a towing Path, and that he had no Objection to towing with Horses over his Ground in the usual Paths.

Thomas PlumerByde, Esquire, said, he had no Objection to towing with Horses over his Laud, and has heard no Gentlemen object to it.

A Member present informed your Committee, That he has several confulerable Tracts of Land on the River Side; that every Vessel pays him for the Use of his Wear and going through the Grounds together, by Agreement, and he has no Objection to the towing with Horses through his Ground, provided the same Satisfaction be made him which he receives at present; that the Wear and Ground go together, with respect to the Toll; that they pay i.v. for every Voyage going and coming; and that the Tenant of the Wear receives the Money, and the Tenant of the Lands has nothing to do with it; but that his Tenant cannot give a Passage without. hisConfent.

Sir William JVake being examined, said, That the Horses do more Mischief by towing than Men; and that he has had frequent Complaints thereof.

To prove that the Navigation of the said Rivers Colder and Ayre is an Eft ate of Inheritance, an Act, pafi’ed in the 10th and 11 th Y"ear of the Reign of King William the Third, intituled, An Act for the making and keeping navigable the Rivers Aire and Calder, in the County of York, was read; by which Act several Persons therein named, One Half of which were Inhabitants of I.eeds, and the other Half Inhabitants of Wakefield, or the Neighbourhood thereof, and their Heirs and Aliigns, were apointed Undertakers for making the said Rivers navigable from Weeland up to the Towns of Leeds and Wakefield, and impowered to take the several Tolls and Duties therein mentioned: Then,

The said Mr. Warburton, being further examined, said.

That he lives at Leeds: That the Profits of the Navigation are alTefted there at £. 600 a Year: That he paid the Assessments from 1741 to 1751, as Agent to the Lessees of the Navigation; That the Navigation was af* sessed in the Parochial Assessments, and for the Highways

That the Rent of the Navigation was paid by the Lessees, to the Proprietors of the Navigation, in equal Moieties, at Wakefield and Leeds:

That he has several times seen the Books of the Col-le6iions of the Lock Dues, and that it is always diltin-guished in such Books where the Boats come from; and that he has frequently seen the Boats passing and repairing upon the Rivers; and that more Tolls are taken in respect of the Boats passing to and from the Wakefield Branch than of those to and from the Leeds Branch: That One Moiety of those Tolls is taken at the Lock at Knot ling ley, and the other at Beale Lock, and that both these Locks are upon the united Stream; but that he did not include the Farmers Boats, for the Passage whereof noToll is paid; and that he could not tell which would produce most, if Toll was paid for those Boats.

He then produced several of the Town Books and Assessments for Wakefield, from the Year 1731 to the Year 1757, both inclusive; by which it appeared, that the Profits of the Navigation were assessed at, and paid for at £. 50 a Year, until the Year 1739, inclusive; and that the Navigation was assessed from the Year 1739 to 1757, both inclusive, at £. 600 per Annum; and all these Assessments are confirmed by Two Justices of the Peace.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

An Act, passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, was read, for repairing several Roads near the City of hath; and also another Act, of the Thirtieth Year of his present Majesty*£ Reign, for the Preservation of public Highways and Turnpike Roads; were read: And,

Richard Hclfon, being examined, laid, That the Village of Bathwicke lies about Haifa Mile from the City of Bath, and the only Road is through Bathwicke Lane, which is near Haifa Mile long, and from thence on the Turnpike Road near Two Furlongs:

That the Inhabitants of the said Village carry the Produce of their Gardens, and other Grounds, to the said City, and bring from thence moll of the Dung and Soil used for manuring their Gardens and Grounds:

That the said Lane is so very ruinous and narrow, that it is impossible to, pass the same with broad Wheels, and sometimes very difficult for narrow Wheels: ThataTurnpike being placed between the End of the said Lane and the City of Bath, the Inhabitants of the said Village (being under a Necessity of using narrow Wheels) are not only obliged to pay One Half more than the usual Tolls, but are also deprived of all the Exemptions in the said first-mentioned Act:

That it would be a great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Village, if the said Lane were repaired and widened, but that it cannot be done by the ordinary Course of Law.

In Support of the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition,

Isaac Dodjley, being examined, said, That the Road leading from the Turnpike Road from Bath to Bradford, on the Top of Munition Hill, and also the Road from the London Road at the North End of Walcot Church-yard to the Landfdown Road are at present very ruinous, and cannot be repaired by the Laws in being:

- That if the said Roads were repaired, it would be a great Advantage to the Public, as by that means all the Turnpike Roads round the City of Bath would be united.

Mr. Bowes reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Execution an Act of Parliament, made and passed in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of 6underland, in the County of Durham, whole Names are thereunto iiibfc.ribed,ou Behalf of themselves, and the several other Commissioners named and appointed by and in pursuance.of the said Act; and also of the Coal Owners and Coal Fitters, interested in the Navigation of the said River, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Mailers of Ships, Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants, in and near the Town of Sunderland,in the County of Durham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Mat*-ter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards' delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the first mentioned Petition,

Part of an Act, passed in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Preservation and Improvement of the Riyer Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, was read.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners called, Mr. Isaac Thompson, Land Surveyor at Newcastle, who being examined, said, That he has been acquainted with the Port and Haven of Sunderland, and the River Wear, upwards of Twenty Years: That the Port and Haven in the Year 1746 were in a very bad Condition: That the Commissioners have been at great Expence in deepening the Channel, and in making necessary Alterations to the Pier:

That Part of the End of the old Pier, which was in a ruinous Condition, has been taken down and erected in a different Direction:

That Two Currents have been laid into One, by removing Rocks., and taking up Sands:

That the Witness apprehends these Improvements Lave been Very advantageous to Trade, and by opening the Channel, Snips can go in and out with much greater Ease:

That he surveyed the River from the Bar to New Bridge§ in the Year 1736, and found it in a very bad Condition, and choaking up with Sand:

He produced a Survey to your Committee, which is hereunto annexed: Appendix, N° 1.

And said. That he had the Perusal of the Books of the Commissioners under the former Act, and took Extracts from them: That in the Year 1746, the Amount of the Expence of the Pier was £.19,787. 2.?. 5 id; and the whole Expence, including the Pier, between 1717 and 1733, winch was during the Term of the former Act, was£. 27,847.14^. 1 \d.-, and from 1733 to 1738, £. .5,086 was laid out in the River and Port:

That he believes these were thewholeof the Expences; and that the Money was raised by a Duty on Coals, and was paid by the Coal Owners and Coal Fitters:

And being asked, How far the Tide flows from the Mouth of the Harbour, up the River ? he laid, Very differently; that he has fecn the Tide rife Six Inches at Newbridge, when it has been 16 Feet and an Half at the Bar; that it commonly flows at Neap Tides up to Mr. Lamblon's High Staith, about Half a Mile above Biddickford:

That he surveyed the River at the Time the late Act passed, when no Commission had been subsistingfor Eight or Nine Years; and that the Harbour was in so bad a Condition, that Ships could not go out with Safety, as they could not take in the necessary Quantity of Ballaft, and get over the Sands:

Vol. 28.

That there is about One Foot Nine Inches "Water at Low-water at Biddickford in a dry Season: That he founded it in February last, and found it of the same Depth, as when he surveyed it:

That a loaded Keel cannot navigate from Biddickford to Newbridge, when a Spring Tide flows Six Inches at Newbridge:

Being asked; Whether there are any Parts below the Staiths, at Forfeits Sands, so low as at Biddickford t he said. Much lower, being in some Parts not above Ninelnchesdeep: ThatSir Ralph Millbank's, Mr. Do-ni/on' s, Mr. Allens, Mr. Peareth's, Mr. Henry Lamb ton's High Staith, and Mr. Nicholas Lamblori's Staiths, are all above Forfier's, Sands; and that Mr. Smith's, Mr. Ncfham's, Mr. Temper's, and Mr. Henry Lambtons Low Staith, are below the Sands:

That the Tide flows at Neap Tides at. Forfier's Sands, One Foot Eight Inches, and at Spring Tides it rises Five Feet Eight Inches:

That loaded Keels draw about Three Foot Water j and that they sometimes lie at Forfier's Sands, Five or Six Days for want of Passage; and that Forfier's Sands are now as bad as ever.

Mr. Joseph Robson being examined, said, That he lives at Sunderland\ and is the Engineer there for the Commissioners of the River Wear 5 and that he has known the Port and Haven of Sunderland Yearsand upwards: That £. 6 ,522 and upwards have been laid out in his Time; and that a Rock, which lay in the Way of Shipping, has been cut through in the deepest Part, about Three Foot Nine Inches; That the Direction of the Pier has been altered, and an Addition made to it; and that great Quantities of Gravel have been taken up, and the Channel made deeper: Thatfmce the Rock has been, cut through, the Channel is almost Three Foot deeper, and is in a better Direction: That Ships can come in now with Winds that they could not come in with before, and can take in larger Quantities of Coals:

That the Trade on the River is considerably increased: That the Witness has feeti 200 Sail of Ships come in with Winds which they could not have come in at all, if the Channel had not been deepened:

That the Channel has been Ailed up with sL Ftefli, but the Stream keeps it open, in Consequence of its being made deeper.

Mr. Jacob Spencely being examined, said, That he has known the Portand Haven of Sunderland 25Years: That in the Year 1746 they were in a very bad Condition; and that the Commissioners have been at a very considerable Expence in deepening the Channel:

That he was employed by the Commissioners in the Year 1750, in deepening Part of the North Channel 2 That it was made deeper by taking up the Gravel, but was of ffiort Duration:

That he received between 3 and ^.400 for deepening Part of the North Channel, and other Works carried on by him: That he was permitted to look at the Treasurer’s Books, where he saw that upwards of jT. 4,000 had been laid out from the Year 1750, to the Time Mr; Robson was concerned:

That by making the Channel in a direct Line* Ships can go out better and with greater Burthens.

Captain Henry Moore being examined, said, That he saw the Port and Haven of Sunderland, mNovember last; and that if a Pier was built upon the North and South Rocks, it would inclose a much greater Quantity of Water, and a very fine Harbour might be made, as the Expence would be greatly moderated by having Materials upon the Spot: That it is capable of Improvement, and might be rendered Safe for Ships of greater Burthen, and might load with greater Safety than in the open Sea, as Nature has contributed greatly towards it:

And being asked, In what Direction it would be proper to lengthen the present Pier ? he said, He would leave it as it is, provided new ones were made; and when a Pier was made to secure the South arid North Winds, Ships might lie in the Harbour with greater Safety.

That the Works have received as much Damage in One Tide, as would take up Five, Six, or Ten Tides, with an Hundred Men to repair: That he has remembered great Stoppages to Trade by the Irregularity of the Mooring and moving of Ships; and that there are sometimes Three or Four hundred Ships in the Harbour, and when the Wind has been fair, they have beOn all ready to go out at one Time; and that every Ship endeavours to get out as fast as possible, by which Means they have been entangled together, and the whole Padage been Hopped for Four Days: And that if a Harbour-master had been appointed to direct a proper Number of Ships to go out together, these Stoppages might have been prevented: That there is a Person appointed to prevent Nuisances: That the Commissioners have no Power to oblige Persons to make good Damages; but that he has paid Five Pounds for his Ship laying Two Tides by the Pier.

Sunderland, 24 June 1758.

Gentlemen,

According to your Order, I have taken the necessary Surveys up ttie River; and, for a better Underhand ing; it may be necessary to mention the Four Methods of making the Water in a River deeper: And,

First. By adding more Water.

2d. By contracting the Breadth.

3d. By lowering the Bed.

4th. By making Dams or Locks.

The Frrli of these is seldom practicable.

The Second, in some Cafes, is adviseable.

The Third is the belt Method,provided it can be don© at a reasonable Expence.

The Fourth is most^practised.
