And it appeared to your Committee, That in the 13th Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, inConsequence of a Petition of the Commissioners, appointed by the aforesaid Act, an Act of Parliament passed, giving them a Power to contract for Lands, and other Powers, for the more effectual Prefer vat ion and Improvement of the said River I Tear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland.

That, by another Act, passed in the 20th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, which wasalfo read; certain Comtnifliuners therein mentioned, and their Successors, were authorized and impowered to causeaSurvey to be made of the said River, as far as a Place called New Bridge, and no farther; and to cause the said River to be made and kept navigable for the Term l 21 Years, from the 24th Day of June 1747; and by aClause in the said Act, the said Commissioners are particularly directed, before the 24th Day of stine 17,59? to remove all Sands, Skoals, and other Obstructions and Impediments; and to make and maintain the said River effectually navigable for Boats, Keels, and Vessels. of the Burthen then used upon (he said River, between a Place called South Biddick or Biddickford, and New Bridge aforesaid, for and during the Residue of the said Term of 21 Years, with such Powers and Authorities for carrying the said Act into Execution, as is therein mentioned.

Then in order to {hew to your Committee, That the Commissioners have not yet complied with the Directions of the laii mentioned Act, so far as the same relates to extending the Navigation from Biddickford to New Bridge aforesaid, the Agent for the Petitioners called, Mr. John Smurfit, who said, That he had lived within Three Miles and an Half of Biddickford, for 40 Years, and knows the River from t lie nee to Newbridge very well; and that nothing has been done by the Commissioners appointed by the said Acts, towards making any Part

of the River Wear navigable between Biddickford and Newbridge aforesaid; and the Witness said, that the River is not at present navigable to Newbridge, nor ever was in his Memory:

And being asked I he Question, he said, In Spring TidesfomeKeelsmay have gone as high asM v.Lampion's Staith, which is a little above Biddickford; but that, the River has never been navigable higher than M r.Lampton's Staith in the Witness’s Time; and that the Tides don’t so much as swell the River up to Newbridge.

Then to Ihevv the great public Utility ofextending the Navigation from Biddickford to the City of Durham,

The said Mr. Smurfit informed your Committee, That there are several Mines of Coals on each Side the River Wear, between the City of Durham and Biddickford; that the bringing Coals to the present Navigation is attended with a very f^reat Expence, as several Collieries lie at a very great Distance from the present Navigation, and the making of Way-leaves is attended with a very great Expence: That several of the Collieries now in use are above Miles from the present Navigation; and that the moll distant Part of (hole Collieries would not be above T#o Miles from the Navigation, if it was extended as far as the City of Durham; and the Witness mentioned several Collieries which lie close to the pro-pofecl Navigation; and said, it was his Opinion, that if the proposed Navigation was effected, it would reduce the Price of Coals at London.

Mr. John Shirley, an Architect, said, That the making the proposed Navigation from Biddickford to the City of Durham will be of great Utility, both as to the Carriage of Coals and other Merchandize, particularly in the Carriage o Coals to Sunderland, as there are Collieries all the Way 01 each Side the River between Biddickford and Durham; and that if these Collieries were opened, the Witness said, he believed the Coals would be fold cheaper at the Port of Sunderland,than they are at present. Then, Mr. John Smeaton, Engineer, fair). He had viewed the River proposed to be made navigable between Biddickford and the City of Durham, in which V iew he had aflilled himself by a Plan made by Mr. Shirley. in the Year 1731; and where (lie River had varied its Course, or appeared to differ from that Plan, he had shewed the Variations in a Plan, both which Plans he laid before your Committee; and Mr. Smeaton gave it as his Opinion, That it was practicable to make the said River navigable for Keels of about 20 Tons and a Quarter Burthen, being such as are at present used upon the River between Sun-derland and Biddickford aforesaid: That these Keels draw less Water than any Vessels he ever saw; and that there is Water enough to carry any Number of them that can be wanted; that he apprehends 48 of them may pass a Lock in 12 Hours Time:

That some Parts of the River will easier be made navigable than others; but that he is satisfied the Whole is practicable:

That from Biddickford to Cocking ford is about 7 Miles; and he said, lie apprehended the Expence of making that Part of the Navigation would not exceed £. 8,000; but as to the Expence of continuing it from Cockingford to Durham, lie said, that was very uncertain, as it will be difficult to cut through the Rocks, and to make the Locks; but that he believes the Expence will be about £. 20,000; it may be more or less; but he thinks it thereabouts.

And Mr. Shirley being again examined, said, That the Plan, by which Mr. Smeaton aflilied himself, agrees with the Survey taken by the Witness in the Year 1731, by the Direction of the Gentlemen of the City and County of Durham; and he produced to your Committee the Original, containing an Account of the Levels; and he gave it as his Opinion, that the whole Navigation might be completed for £. 20.000; for that the Rocks may be of Advantage, by furnishing large Blocks of Stone, for various Purposes.

Sir Charles Mordaunt reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Merchants and Manufacturers in the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the several Merchants and Manufacturers of the Town of Sheffield, in the County of York, whoseNames are thereunto subscribed; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petitions, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Upon the First of the said Petitions,

Mr. John Taylor, and Mr. Samuel Garbett,being examined, informed your Committee, That there are at lead 20,000 People employed in the Toy Trade at Birmingham, and the neighbouring Towns about, 6,000 whereof are employed in making Toys, confiding in general of Articles in which Gold or Silver is manufactured; that the Witness, Taylor, employs 600 himself in that way; and the Witnesses produced to your Committee several Kinds of such Toys, and gave Evidence that the Gold manufactured into 20s. worth of Seals is not w.orth id. that in a Snuff Box of 18.9., Value from the Maker the Silver is not worth ild. that they make many Articles wherein the Silver is not worth more than . 1 per Cent, of the Value of the Goods, but that in some Instahceis it is worth 5 per Cent, and though the Quantity of Gold or Silver used in ornamenting such Goods is lo small, in proportion to the Value of the Goods, yet the Sale of them depends upon the Neatness and Elegancy of the Ornaments:

That there are Two or Three Drawing Schools efta- blished at Birmingham, for the Instruction of Youth in* tj\e Arts of Designing and Drawing, and 30 or 40' Frenchmen, and Germans are constantly employed in Drawing and Designing; that the Whole of the Toy Trade at Birmingham and the neighbouring Towns, amounts to about £.600,ooooperAnnum, about £.500,000 per Annum of which is exported to foreign Markets; that the Matgrials worked up amount to about £.150,000 . per Annum,ythe Whole of which, except the Gold and Silver, are the Produce of our own Country; viz. Copper, Brafe, Spelter, Steel,8Cc,

That the.Custom of the Trade is to work from Orders taken.from Patterns; that the Patterns font to Correspondents abroad are from 6 to 12 Months before they are returned; but the Patterns for Home Trrfde are generally returned in: a Month or less, whereby, constant Employ is found.for the Workmen, and the Home Trade.supports the Foreign t - That Girlsfrom 7 fco ra Year§ old are employed in the Manufacture, and earn from is. te 4s. per Week, and from that Age upwards, they earn from 4s. to 8s. per Week, that Boys from. 7 to 12 Years of Age earrv from 1.9. to 7s. per Week, and from that Age upwards from 7to 42$. per Week :*

That many of the Goods are made by the Help of Machines or Engines, invented by the people of Birmingham, which lessens the manual Labour, and enables Boys to do Mens Work, and sometimes more:

That the same kind of Manufactures which are made at Birmingham are likewise made in several Places in Germany, though not in so great a Variety as here, and used to be imported into England, but since the Invention of the above Engines very few have been imported:

That many Attempts have been made by Foreigners to decoy our Manufacturers from hence; and that some have been prevented going, but some are gone, particularly one Matter Workman from Birmingham, who used to employ 3 or 400 Men, is gone, and took some of his Men with him; and the Witnesses were of Opinion that if Ten of our Workmen were to go to any one Place abroad they might raise a Manufactory, from whence they might lbpply Britain with some of the same Sort of Toys made by the Petitioners:

Then the Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, which directs, That every Person who shall fell or vend any Goods or Wares, in which Gold or Silver is manufactured, shall take out an annual Licence, was read;

And the before-mentioned Witnesses said. That the Excisemen declare who must, or who need not, take out a Licence; that all Persons following the Plating Business, peculiar to Birmingham, are obliged to take out a Licence:

That many of the Master Workmen have not taken out Licences, because the Excisemen have, by Orders from the Commissioners of Excise, declared, that Gilders, Silverers, and Refiners, of Gold and Silver, who deal for many Thousand Pounds per Annum, are not liable to s the Penalty of the Act, but that any who plate, though ever so thin, are liable, notwithstanding that it is impoffiblefor the most knowing Workmen, in many instances to distinguish between silvering and plating, and some lilvered Work hath a larger Quantity of Silver upon it than plated:

That there was a Dispute on this Matter, and Two Justices were inclined to think all liable, and proposed to find it Special, to make a same for the King’s Bench -y

' that was thought too expensive for the Parties, and therefore dropped.

To prove that their Goods past through Five or Six Hands who pay the l ax, the Witnesses further gave Evidence, That the Mailer Workmen of their Manufactures fells to the Factor, the Factor to the Merchant, the Merchant to the Country Dealers or Shop-keepers in large Towns, who fell to Shop-keepers of inferior Rank in small Towns and Villages, every one of whom are obliged to take out a Licence; and the Quantity sold by each Individual being in general too inconsiderable to bear the Expence of a Licence, many have laid down their Business, and many Orders have been Countermanded; and unless the Act is altered in that respect, few People will care to engage in that Business.

To shew that every Branch of the Toy Trade at Birmingham has been increasing till the said Act passed, the Witnesses said. That the Town had increased more than One-half since the Toy Trade began amongst ’em, and that the Petitioners know at least 100 People who began Trade without any Fortune, and have raised themselves by their Ingenuity and Indftftry.

Upon the Second of the said Petitions,

Mr. Ebenexer Roebuck, Factor in London for tlfe Sheffield Manufactures, being examined, said. That the Inhabitants of Sheffield amount to about 20,000, and that in the Town and Neighbourhood about 15,000 People are employed in the Cutlery and Toy Trade; and amongst the great Variety of Wares made there, some of them are decorated with small Ornaments of Gold or Silver, and he inflanced some particularly, that in a Do-zea of Knives, which the Maker fells for 6s. the Silver, of which the Ornaments thereon are made, is not worth 3d. and he said, that in most of their other Goods, the intrinsic Value of the Ornaments is near the same Proportion:

That they give good Wages to the Workmen, fora tolerable Hand can earn from 15 c/. to 18 d. between 6 in the Morning and 3 in the Afternoon; hut the great Advantages of being well supplied with Coals and Water, com pen fates to the Maher Workmen for the Dearness of Labour, and enables them not only to afford good Wages to the poor Labourer but to vie with Foreigners at other Markets; and he gave it as his Opinion, that the Situation of Sheffield for the Purpose of carrying on their Manufacture, is preferable to that of any oth* r Town in the W’orld:

He added, That the English can fell the low-priced Wares cheaper than the French, or any other Country, but in many Countries the high-priced Wares are to be had on cheaper Terms than we can make them.

As to the Difficulties the Toy and Cutlery Trade lies under, from being obliged to take an annual 405*. Licence, Mr. Roebuck's Evidence was much the same as the Two former Witnesses, wherefore your Committee decline repeating it.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That thislloufe will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Wye A Petition of several Persons Owners of Lands upon Navigation. or adjoining to such Part of the River Wye as lies between Guildford and Godalming, in the County of Surrey, was prefen ted to the House, and read; taking Notice, That a Bill has been presented to the House, for extendingand continuing the Navigation of the said River to the Town of Godalming; and representing to the House, that no public Notice, either by Advertisement or otherwise,was given of the Intention to petition Parliament for the said Bill, nor Application made, or Plan of the said intended Navigation produced, or any Information with respect to the Purport or Provisions of the said Bill, given to the Petitioners, whereby theycould form anyJudgment how, or in what manner, the said Navigation may affect their respective Interests and Properties; and that as no public Meeting was called, whereby the Sense of the Country could be taken with respect to this Matter, and as the Petitioners and other Land-owners are yet Straugers to the Plan and Scheme of the said Navigation, and as the Bill contains very extensive and general Powers, the Petitioners humbly hope, that the said Bill will not pass, until the Country in general and the Land-owners in particular have, as is usual in Matters of this kind, been acquainted with the Nature of the said Scheme, in order that a Judgment may be formed whether the most proper and effectual Provision is made for the Advantage of the Public and the Property of Individuals: And therefore praying the House to take these Matters into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief as to the House shall seem necessary.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Con-fideration of the Committee to whom the Bill for extending and continuing the Navigation of the River Wey, otherwise Wye, in the County of Surrey, to the Town of Godalming, in the said County, is committed.

SI R William Peere Williams reported from the Co n-mittee, to whom the Petition of the Constable and Inhabitants of the Borough of New Shoreham, in the County of Sussex, and of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, and Farmers, redding near the Port and Harbour of New Shoreham a fore fa id, and of the Masters and Pilots o Ships, usually navigating to and from the same, was eferred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr Jeremiah Siya?i, Matter of a Ship, being examined, said, That he has known the Port and Harbour of New Shoreham Forty Years; within which Time the Entrance of the Harbour has been carried above a Mile further to the Eastward, occasioned by the Sands being thrown up by the Sea:

That Ships of 300 and 400 Tons Burthen have been built there fmee the Witness knew the Harbour; but that it cannot be done now, there not being Water enough to carry them out of the Harbour.

And he further said, That the Town of New Shoreham is deprived of its Market for Corn and Timber, with which that Country greatly abounds; and the Inhabitants lie under great Difficulties in receiving Coals and other Commodities for the Supply of New Shoreham, and the neighbouring Towns, by Reason of the Harbour being so (hallow: That the said Harbour is situated in the deepest Part of the Bay between Spithead and Beachy; and that if agood Entrance and proper Pier Heads were made to the fame, it would be a Means of preventing many Ships from being drove on Shore, and the Saving of the Lives of many of his Majesty’s Subjects, and be of public Utility: And,

Mr. Richard Stafford, a Pilot, being examined, confirmed the aforesaid Evidence; and added, That he founded the Harbour the 18th Instaut, and would not take Charge of a Ship which drew more than Eight Feet Water.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for erecting Piers and other Works, for the Security and Improvement of the Harbour of New Shoreha7n, in the County of Sussex, and for keeping the same in Repair: And that Sir William. Peere Williams, the Lord Carys-fort, and Mr, Robert Bristow, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Commoh Council, of the City of Exeter, in Chamber assembled, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners observe, that a Petition is now depending, for a Bill for making and completing the Navigation of the River Wear, from, and including, Biddickford, to the City of Durham; and that the Petitioners conceive that such an Improvement will be of great public Utility: And therefore praying, That a Bill may be brought in, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition now before the House; and that such Bill, under such Regulations as to the House shall seem meet and just, may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Nathanael Rowe Esquire, Clerk of the Warrants, Inrollments, and Estreats, of his Majesty’s Court of Common Pleas at Westminster, was presented to the House,andread; representing to the House, That the Office of Clerk of the Warrants, tic. is a very ancient and public Office, kept in Clifford's Inn, and held for Life by the Petitioner, by virtue of a Grant from the Lord Chief Justice of the Court of Common Pleas for the Time being, and through which all Fines do and must pass, in order to file Warrants of Attorney for the Conuzee in such Fines, which are and have always been entered iu Books which remain in the said Office; and, in the next Term, the Rolls upon which the said Fines are ingrossed, and the Poll Fines marked thereon, are delivered to the Petitioner, to make Estreats thereof, with the Sums thereto affixed for the said Poll Fines; and whichEftreatsare, the laltDay of the said Term, carried by the Petitioner up to the Court of Exchequer; and that the Praefine upon every Writ of Covenant being affixed at the Alienation Office long before the Warrant of Attorney can be filed, and is always the Standard for fixing the Post Fine thereon, and can thereby be certainly known; the Petitioner therefore apprehends, that such Post Fines would be most properly paid at his said Office by the Attorney concerned therein, without any additional Trouble to him, or Expence to his Client, at the same time that such Warrants of Attorney are filed; but if such Post Fines are set and paid before the Fine has been brought to the Petitioner s said Office, and such Fine shall be deemed good and valid in Law, from the Time of Payment of such Post Fine, it will be attended with great Injury to the Petitioner, by depriving him of great Part of the Profits of his said Office, as, when the Fine is known to be valid in Point of Law, the Conuzees, or their Attornies, might be wholly negligent of bringing the same to the Petitioner’s said OfficeAnd therefore praying, That he may be appointed to receive such Post Fines i or that, if the Office were the Praefine fe set or indorsed shall be appointed to receive the same 30

(as by the present Bill is prop’ofed), such Provision may be made in the said Bill, for saving the Estate of the Petitioner, in his said Office, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report, which was made from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the more regular and easy collecting, accounting for, and paying of, Post Fines which shall be due to the Crown, or to Grantees thereof under the Crown, and for the Ease of Sheriffs in respect to the fame, was committed, be taken into Consideration.

And Mr. Coale said, That of late Years the Poor of Plymouth are much more numerous, and the Expence of maintaining them much greater, than heretofore.

And he produced to your Committee an Account of the whole Receipts of Monies for the Maintenance of the Poor aforesaid, from the Year 1753 to the Year 1758, both inclusive, and also of the Diiburlements during the same time; and it appeared, that the Disbursements had exceeded the Receipts, during that Period, upon an Average, £.323. 18s. g^d. per Annum.

And Mr. Coale further laid, That ’tis necessary to amend the said Act in several respects, particularly as to the Methods of holding Courts, and the Election of Officers, which at present are very inconvenient; and also to compel the Payment of the Rates assessed upon Persons who are Lodgers, and who carry on considerable Trades within the Town, and also to oblige the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor to account, within a limited Time, to the Treasurer of the said Corporation, for the Monies by them received for the Use of the Poor.

And Mr. Benjamin Way, a Clerk belonging to the said Office, attending your Committee, produced an Account of all Sums detained in the said Office, pursuant to the Act passed last Session, granting Rates upon Offices and Pensions for Half a Year, ending the 10th of October 1758, and amounting to the Sum of £. ,528. 9. 6; which Account, he said, contained all the Pensions on the Establishment above 100 a Year, and from which they had retained the Shilling in the Pound; except in Two or Three Instances, where the Pensions had not yet been called for:

That foreign Protestant Churches receive £.500 a Year, which is distributed to several Persons in small Sums, of £. 20 or £.30, and none of them amount to £.100 a. Year: That it is not yet determined whether this Money shall be taxed or not, upon which Account it has not yet been paid; but he said, that this Money has been assessed to the Land Tax:

That there is another Sum of 8,000 and odd Pounds a Year paid to the French Protestant Refugees in England, which has never been charged to the Land Tax;.and therefore the Witness said, he apprehended, they were not chargeable by this Act; That this Sum has been paid without any Deduction; but he is informed, no OnePerson receives100 a Year out of this Money: That £. 800 a year is paid to the Lord Almoner to be distributed to the Poor, and no Peduftion has been made from that Money.

Your Committee proceeded to inquire how the said Act had been executed by the Commissioners of the Land Tax, acting for Offices executed in Westminster Hall, who are directed to assess "311 Perquisites of Offices:

And Mr. John Feary, attending your Committee, said, That he was Clerk to the Commissioners of the Land Tax for the City and Liberty of Westminster, acting for Offices executed in Westminster Hall: — That the Commissioners met early in July last; but that they made no Assessment then, because they could not tell what Stoppages had been made for Salaries upon the several Offices; for, the Commissioners being only impowered to assess for Perquisites of Offices, they could not know what the Perquisites were till a Deduction was made of Salaries; and they could not learn what the Salaries were, and what Stoppages had been made from them, till February, and as soon as they knew it they made an Assessment upon Perquisites.

And he produced the said Assessment upon Perquisites for the Offices of the Exchequer and King’s Bench, for the Year 1748; by which it appeared, that the whole Money, assessed for Perquisites, amounted only to £. 566. 4 s. and he also produced the Assessment to the Land Tax for the Year 1757.

And he said, That the Chancellor of the Exchequer is charged nothing for Perquisites, his Salary paid at the Exchequer, as certified from the Auditor’s Office, exceeding the Charge upon his Office to the Land Tax for the Year 1757:

That the Auditor of the Exchequer is charged in the Year 1757 to the Land Tax for £. 1,600; and by the Certificate the Witness received from the Exchequerthey had retained the Shilling in the Pound from 3,765, so that the Commissioners charged nothing for Perquisites:

That Peter JLeheup Esquire, Comptroller of the Exchequer Bill Office, is charged to the Land Tax in 1757 at £.120; and that the Witness was certified by an Officer acting under Mr. Leheup, that they had retained One Shilling in the Pound from £. 350; so that no Assessment was made for Perquisites — For wherever it appeared, by the Certificates, thatthe One Shilling in the Pound had been retained from particular Officers for as large or larger Sums than such Officers stood charged with to the Land Tax for the Year 1757, the Commissioners had made no Assessment for Perquisites in any of those Cafes; of which he mentioned the following Instances: -

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Seven hundred and Eight Pounds Three Shillings be granted to his Majesty, to enable the Commissioners, appointed by virtue of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, for the better securing his Majesty’s Docks, Ships, and Stores, at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Plymouth, and for the better fortifying the Town of Porff mouth and Citadel of Plymouth, in Trustees, for certain Uses; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; to make Compensation to the Proprietors of such Lands and Hereditaments, at and near Chatham, as have been purchased for the Purposesmentioned in the said Act, and for Damage done to the Lands adjacent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Six thousand Nine hundred Thirty-seven Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Seven-pence Halfpenny be granted to his Majesty, to enable the Commissioners, appointed by virtue of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, for the better securing his Majesty’s Docks, Ships, and Stores, at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Plymouth, and for the better fortifying the Town of Portsmouth, and Citadel of Plymouth, in Trustees, for certain Uses; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; to make Corapenfa-tioti to the Proprietors of such Lands and Hereditaments at and near Portsmouth, as have been purchased for the Purposes mentioned in the said Act.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the ^Sum of Twenty-five thousand One hundred Fifty-nine Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence, be granted to his Majesty, to enable the Commissioners, appointed by virtue of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, for the better securing his Majesty’s Docks, Ships, and Stores, at Portsmouth, Chatham, and Plymouth, and for the better fortifying the Town of Portsmouth, and Citadel of Plymouth, in Trustees, for certain Uses; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; to make Compensation to the Proprietors of such Lands and Hereditaments, at and near Plymouth, as have been purchased for the Purposes mentioned in the said Act.

General A Petition of the Gentlemen, Tradesmen, and Far-Tumpike mers, in the West Riding of the County of York, on Be-Acts. half0f themselves, and other Persons resident in the said

Riding, was presented to the House, and read; reciting, That by an Act, passed in the 30th Year of his present Majesty, to render more effectual the several Laws now in being for the Amendment and Preservation of the public Highways and Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, One Half more Tolls are to be paid for Carriages having the Fellies of the Wheels thereof of less Breadth or Gauge than Nine Inches, than are appointed to be taken \>y any Act or Acts of Parliament upon such Roads respectively; and representing to the House, that a great Part of the West Riding of the said County of York is mountainous, and very uneven, by Reason whereof, and of the Bye Roads being very narrow, the using Nine Inch Wheels is in many Cafes utterly impracticable; and that the Weights commonly drawn on Carriages in that Part of the Kingdom, as the Petitioners conceive, veiy rarely exceed One Ton, except such Carriages as travel for Hire on Turnpike Roads only; and that a Cart drawn by Three Horses, and a Waggon by Four, with narrow Wheels, not used or travelling for Hire, might be permitted to pass for the usual Tolls in that Country, without much Prejudice to the Roads; and that Wheels of Six Inch Fellies would as effectually preserve the Roads asthofe of Nine Inches, with proportionable and additional Weight, and would, in every other respect, be of much greater Utility and Conveniency to the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to take the said Premises into Consideration, and grant to the Petitioners such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from and after the 5th Day of July 1759, all Persons may trade in, fell, or vend, any Goods or Wares, in which t he Quantity of Gold in any One separate and di-ftinct Piece of Goods or Ware shall not exceed Two Penny Weights, or the Quantity of Silver in any One separate and distinct Piece of Goods or Ware shall not exceed Five Penny Weights, without being liable to take out a Licence for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from and after the 5th Day of July 1759, every Person who shall trade in, fell, or vend, Gold or Silver Plate, or any Goods or Wares, in which any Gold or Silver shall be manufactured, and the Quantity of Gold in any One inch Piece of Plate, or Goods, or Ware,shall be of the Weight of Two Ounces or upwards, or the Quantity of Silver in any One such Piece of Plate, or Goods, or Ware, shall be of the Weight of Thirty Ounces or upwards, shall pay Five Pounds for each annual Licence, instead of the Forty Shillings now payable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from and after the 5th Day of July 1759, all Pawnbrokers trading in, vending, or felling. Gold or Silver Plate, and all Refiners of Gold and Silver, shall be obliged to takeout annual Licences, for each of which they shall pay a Duty of Five Pounds, instead of the Forty Shillings now payable.

Kingdom, and to consider the Laws relating thereto j and to report their Obfenations thereupon, together with their Opinion of the moll effectual Means for ascertaining and enforcing uniform and certain Standards of Weights and Measures to be used for the future*

And the said Report was read; amj the Resolutions OF the Committee are as follpweth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That the EU ought to contain One Yard and One Quarter, according to the Yard mentioned in the Third Resolution of the former Committee, upon the Subject of Weights and Measures, agreed to by the House the 2d Jane 1758, and the Pole* or Perch, in Length Five such Yards and an Half, the Fiirlong 220* such Yards, and the Mile 1760 fiidh Yards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;

That the superficial Perch should contain 30 Square Yards and a quarter, and the Rood should Contain 1210 Square Yards, and the Acre 4840 Square YardsUforesaid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;

That according to the 4th, 5th, and 6th, Resolutions of the former Committee upon the Subject of Weights and Measures, agreed to by the House the id June 1758, the Quart ought to contain 70^ Cubical Inches, the Pint 35 and a Quarter, the Peck 564, and the BusheJ 2,256.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Parts of the Pound, which is mentioned in the Eighth Resolution of the former Committee upon the Subject of Weights and Measures, agreed to by the House the 2d June 1758, examined and adjusted in the Prefence of this Committee, and herewith produced; viz. the Half Pound or Six Ounces, Quarter of a Pound or Three Ounces, Two Ounces, One Ounce, Two half Ounces, the Five Peny Weights, Three Peny Weights*

Two Peny Weight, and One Peny Weight, the Twelve Grains, Six Grains, Three Grains, Two Grains, and Two of One Grain each, ought to be the Models of the several Parts of the said Pound, and to he used for filing or adjusting Weights for the future.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;

That all Weights exceeding a Pound should be of Brafs;

Copper, Bell Meta], or Call Iron, and all those which shall be of Call Iron, should be made in the Form, and with a Handle of hammered Iron, such as the Pattera herewith produced, with the Mark of the Weight cast in the Iron; and all Weights of a Pound, or under, should be of Gold, Silver, Brass, Copper, or Bell Metal.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;

That all Weights of Cast Iron should have the initial JLetters of the Name of the Maker upon the tipper Bar of the Handle, and all other Weights should have the fame, together with the Mark of the Weight, according to the Standard, upon some convenient Part thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Yard, mentioned in the Second Resolution of the former Committee, upon the Subject of Weights and Measures, agreed to by the House the 2d June 1758, being the Standard of Length, and the Pound mentioned in the 8 th Resolution of the former Committee, upon the Subject of Weights and Measures, agreed to by the House the 2d June 1758, being the Standard of Weight, ought to be deposited in the Court of the Receipt of the Exchequer, and there safely kept under the Seals of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and of the Chief Baron, and the Seal of Office of the Chamberlains of the Exchequer, and not to be opened, but by the Order, and in the Presence, of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the Chief Baron, for the Time being.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the moil effectual Means toascertain Uniformity in Measures of Length and Weight to be used throughout the Realm, would be to appoint certain Persons at one particular Office, with Clerks and Workmen under them, forthePurpose only offizing and adjusting, for the 7 A Ufo

5 jo I2° — 23d A. 1739.

TJfe of the Subjects, all \teaCures of Length, and all Weights being Parts, Multiples, or certain Proportions, of the Standards, to be used for the future.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of thifc Committee, That a Model or Pattern of the said Standard Yard, mentioned in the Second Ilefolution of the former Committee, agreed to by the House 2d June 1758, And now in Cul-tody of the Clerk of the House; and a Model or Pattern of the Standard Pound, mentioned in the Eighth Resolution of the former Committee, agreed to by the House 2d June 1758, together with Models or Patterns of the Parts of the said Pound, now presented to the House, and also of the Multiples of the said Pound, mentioned in this Report, when the same are adjusted, should be kept in the said Office, in Custody of the said Persons to be appointed for fizing Weights and Measures, under the Seal of the Chief Baron of the Court of Exchequer, for the Time being, to be opened only by Order of the said Chief Baron in his Presence, or the Presence of Oue of the Barons of the Exchequer, on the Application of the said Persons, for the Purpose of correcting and adjusting, as Occasion shall require, the Patterns or Models used at the saidOffice for fizing Measures of Length or Weight, delivered out to the Subjects.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Models or Patterns of the said Standard Yard and Standard Pound aforesaid, and also Models or Patterns Of the Parts and Multiples aforesaid, of the said Pound, should be lodged in the said Office, for the fizing of such Measures of Length or Weights, as being Parts, Multiples, or Proportions* of the said Standards, shall hereafter be required by any of his Majesty’s Subjects.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Measures of Lengths and Weights sized at the said Office, should be marked in some convenient Part thereof, with such Marks as shall be thought expedient, to shew the Identity of the Measures and Weights sized at the said Office, and to discover any Frauds that may be committed therein.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Office should be kept within a convenient Distance of the Court of Exchequer at Westminster,nu(i that all Measures of Length and Weights, within a certain Distance of London, shall he collected and re-affized, as Occasion shall require, at the said Office.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in order to enforce Uniformity in Weights and Measures to be used for the future, all Persons appointed by the Crown to Act as Justices of the Peace in any County, or City, or Town Corporate, being respectivelyCounties within themselves, throughout the Realm, should be impowered to hear, and determine, and put the Law in Execution, in respect to Weights and Measures only, without any of them being obliged to sue out aDedimus, or to act in any other Matter; and the said Commissioners should be empowered to fine and imprison, and to inflict or mitigate such Penalties as shall be thought proper, and have such other Authorities as shall be necessary for compelling the Use of Weights and Measures, agreeable to the aforesaid Standards.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Models or Patterns of the said Standard Yard and Pound, and of the Parts and Multiples thereof before mentioned, should be distributed in each County, in such Manner as to be readily used for Evidence, in all Cases where Measures and Weights shall be questioned, before the said Commissioners, and fqr adjailing the same in a proper Manner.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Thomas Hopkins junior, Thomas Lucas, John Lucas senior, and John junior, were, according to Order, brought to the Bar; where they, upon their Knees, received a Reprimand from Mr. Speaker, and were ordered to be discharged out of Custody, paying their Fees.

Plymouth A Petition of the Land-owners and Inhabitants who Poor, pay to the Poors Rates in the Town and Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, does, if his Majesty's Interest is concerned therein, recommend the Consideration of the said Petition to the House, and likewise gives his Consent, that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; alleging* That, for many Years past, there hath been assessed and raised on the Land-owners and Inhabitants of the said Town, from time to time, before the Year 1757, several Sums of Money on account of the Land Tax, over and above what the said Town hath annually paid as their Quota; and taking Notice, that a Bill is now before the House, concerning the Poor of thesaidTown: And therefore praying, That such surplus Money as aforesaid, which now remains in the Hands of divers Persons, may be applied for the Use of the Poor of the said Town, in such Manner, and by such Ways and Means, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the undersigned Persons, belonging to his Majesty’s Islands of Guernsey and Jersey, for and on behalf of many of his Majesty’s Subjects of those Islands, Owners of, and interested in, Privateers fitted out from the same, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That those Islands lie in the midst of the British Channel, and within Sight of the French Coast, and that those Islanders have now and in former French Wars embarked their Fortunes in fitting out small Privateers, which run in close to the French Shores, and, by making their Vessels resemble the French fishing Boats, and not to appear like Privateers, or likeShips of Force, or giving any Alarm to the Coast, they hav.e taken many Prizes from the French to their own private Advantage, to the Annoyance of the French Coasting Trade, and to the great Benefit of this Nation, not only in the Value of the

Vol. 28.

Prizes so taken, and in distressing the Enemy, but also far more considerably in gaining materia! Intelligence of the Enemy’s Designs on several Important Occasions; and that these Services cannot be performed by large Vessels, who dare not approach so near to the Coast; and the very Appearance of which alone would be a sufficient Notice and Alarm to the French, who would instantly, by Signals, communicate such Alarm all along ' their Coast; and that the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is now depending in the House to prohibit Privateers of small Burthen and Force, which the Petitioners humbly conceive, if extended to Privateers belonging to those Islands, would ruin the Persons who have invested their Fortuues in small Privateers; and would not only deprive this Kingdom of the before-mentioned Advantages, but would also produce many and great Disad -vantages to Great Britain, by the Numbers of like small Privateers, which in such same the Enemy would then spread over the Channel, to the great Annoyance of the Navigation and Commerce of this Kingdom, and which they have of late been pretty generally prevented from fending out: And therefore praying, That such Privateers as do, or shall really and truly, and without any Deceit, belong to the Inhabitants of the Islands of Guernsey or Jersey, may be wholly excepted out of the said Bill, or that the Petitioners may be heard by their Counsel against such Bill, and may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to explain and amend the Act of the 29th Year of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of Seamen, and the more speedy and effectual Manning his Majesty’s Navy, is re-committed.

Admeaftire- A Petition of the several Inhabitants of the City and "coal* Liberty of Westminster, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster adjoining thereto, and of the several Parishes of Saint Giles in the Fields, Saint. Mary le Bon, and such Part of the Parish of Saint Andrew Holboum as lies in the County of Middlesex, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, waspre-fented to the House, and read; reciting, That, in the 19th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, an Act was made for more effectually preventing Frauds and Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals within the Limits aforesaid; which said Act has, by several subsequent Acts, bedn continued until the 24th Day of June 1759, and is now near expiring; and taking notice, that a Bill is now depending for further continuing and amending the said Act of the 19th Year of his present Majesty; and representing to the House, that, by the said Act, Four Pence is laid upon every Chaldron of Coals bought, as Wharf Measure, within the Limits aforesaid; which amounts annually to a large Sum of Money, and is a Charge upon the Petitioners, for which they apprehend they receive no Benefit; and that in case the said Bill should pass into a Law, it would be in no respect beneficial to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners are the only Persons within the Bills of Mortality who are compelled to pay for the Admeasurement of their Coals by Land Coal-meters, unless where the Buyer of Coals requires the personal Attendance of such Coal-meters: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third time.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third time upon Thursday Morning next.

Sir, Next) York, April 16th 1759.

I had the Favour of receiving your very obliging Letter of the 6th of December, inclosing a Resolution the House of Commons came to that Day, in a Packet from Mr. Wood on the 3d of April.

It is with the deepest Sense of Gratitude I receive that highest Mark of Honour, the Thanks of the House; and I hope my future Conduct, in the Service of my Country, will best acknowledge it, and render me more deserving of so very great an Honour.

I must beg Leave to return you, Sir, my most sincere Thanks for the gracious Manner in which you have been pleased tofignify to me the Resolution of the House.

I am, with the utmost Respect,

Sir,

Your most humble,

and most obedient Servant,

Jeff. Amherst.

Table: Where the same were read; and areas followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Methods of relieving the Poor, in the respective Parishes where no W01 khouses or other proper PI aces have been provided for their Reception and Employment, are in general very burthensome to the Inhabitants of fuel) Parishes, and tend to render the Poor miserable in themselves, and useless to the Community.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Method of giving Money out of the parochial Rates to Persons capable of Labour, in ordeT to prevent such Persons claiming an intire Subsistence for themselves and their Families from the Parishes, is contrary to the Spirit and Intention of the Laws for Relief of the Poor, is a dangerous Power in the Hands of parochial Officers, a Misapplication of the Public Money, and a great Encouragement to Idleness and Intemperance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Employment of the Poor, under proper Direction and Management, in such Works and Manufactures as are suited to their fespective Strengths and Capacities, will be of great Utility and Advantage to the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Placing of the Poor in Workhouses, to be provided within fud) Districts as shall be deemed most convenient in the several Counties and Ridings in England and Wales, under the Direction and Management of Governors or Trustees, to be particularly appointed or chosen for that Purpose, will be the most effectual Method of assisting and relieving such poor Persons as by Age, Infirmities, or Diseases, are rendered incapable of supporting themselves by their Labour, of employing the Able and Industrious, reforming the Idle and Profligate, and of educating poor Children in Religionand Industry.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Poor in such Workhouses will be better regulated and maintained, and managed with more Advantage to the Public, by Guardians, Governors, or Trustees, to be specially appointed or chosen for that Purpose, and incorporated with such Powers, and under such Restrictions, as the Legislature shall deem proper, than by the annual parochial Officers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Erecting of the Workhouses upon waste Lands, and appropriating a certain Quantity of such Lands to be cultivated, in order to produce Provision for the Poor in the said Houses, would not only be a Means of inilructing and employing many of the said Poor in Agriculture, but Ieflen the public Expence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Controversies and Law Suits, concerning the Sett lements of poor Persons, occasion a very great, and in general an useless, Expence to the Public, to the Amount of many Thousand Pounds per Annum; and that often more Money is expended in aleertaining such Settlements by each of the contending Parishes, than would maintain the Paupers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, if Workhouses should be established for the general Reception of the Poor within Diflri6ts in the respective Counties and Ridings, the Laws relating to the Settlement of the Poor, and the Pafling of Vagrants, may be repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That whilst the present Poor Laws subsist, the compelling Parish Officers to grant Certificates to the Poor,

Then the Residue of the Report from the Committee, appointed to consider of the Laws relating to Bankrupts, and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; and to whom the Petition of the several Bankrupts, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others in their unhappy Situation; was referred; was read.

The said Report is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee called before them Francis Capper, Esquire, a Commissioner of Bankrupts,

’ Junii. A. 1759.

Who informed your Committee, That the Act of the '5th of his present Majesty is the prevailing Act relating to Bankrupts — By that Act it is made Felony, where a Bankrupt, after 42 Days Notice, published in the Gazette, does not surrender himself to the Commissioners, and make a full Discovery of his Estate and Effects for the Benefit of his Creditors, and in case of any Omissiorij to the Amount of Twenty Pounds and upwards, he is to be adjudgeda Felon-that upon Application to the Great Seal by the Bankrupt, within Six Days before the Expiration of the 42 Days, the Keeper of the Great Seal has Power to enlarge the Time, not exceeding ^oDays after the 42 Days — the latter Clutife is for the Benefit of the Bankrupt, to prevent his being surprized, if in the Country, and not havingNotice to come up; if Time enlarged, the Penalty does not extend to the enlarged Time — that he has heard of a Trial of that Kind, and an Acquittal upon it, at the Old Bailey; that he was concerned as Cotmfel in that Bankruptcy before the Lord Keeper, and was told by the Solicitor, that, upon the like Exception, the Party was acquitted — another Thing he apprehends would save the Parties great Expence in the Commission, Commissions frequently issue against Partners, which are called joint Commissions, and likevvile fe-parnte Commissions against the same Partners, in their private Right; that there‘is no positive Statute, as he remembers, that directs t he Marshalling the joint and separate FHefts, so that the joint Creditors may be paid out of the joint Estate, and the separate Creditors paid out of the separate Estate; this Difficulty occurred early to the Great Seal, who have taken this Method, to prevent the double Expence of taking out Two Connnission.s against the same Persons, where a joint Commission has been taken out, or vice versa a separate one, upon Application of a different Clals of Creditors, to order the Creditors of both Sorts to come in and prove their Debts, under one Commission; but under these Directions, that the Commissioners do take an Account of the joint and separate Estate, distinguishing the one from the other; so that the joint Creditors be paid out of the joint Estate, and the separate Creditors out of the separate Estate; and if there is any Surplus of either Estate, such Surplus is brought to Account, and in Aid of the deficient Estate; as for Instance, if there shall be any Surplus of the separate Estate, that Surplus is brought into the joint Estate, to satisfy all thejoint Creditors; the Reafuti is, because a Commission of Bankruptcy, in the first Instance, is in the Nature of an Execution, and the joint Creditor may take his Remedy against the joint or separate Estate, or both; if there is a Surplus of the joint Estate, and any Creditor of the separate Estate remain unpaid, the Share of the Bankrupt in such joint Estate, is to be applied in Dischargeofhis separate Creditors only: If Provision was made by Statute, it would favc the Parties the Expence of an Application to the Great Seal; that the particular Creditor would be save.I all that Expence, which is not allowed him out of the Bankrupt’s Estate, the Order of Court extends only to the Relief of the Party applying: It is very frequent to have several distinct Applications in respeel to One Commission; that Creditors of both Kinds would have this further Benefit, they might vote in the Choice of Affigileesi, and likewise oppose the tigning of a Certificate; whereas under the Order of Court, it frequently happens they are deprived of that Benefit, as such Order of Court may not be obtained in lime:

That he has known several I nstances where Persons have taken the Benefit of the Bankrupt Laws, under colourable Trades: But it is for the Benefit of Creditors that a Commission should issue, because they have immediate Execution; and hefubmitted whether such Bankrupts ought to have their Certificat.es, unless they have been in Trade Twelve Months at least, or unief* their Effects limit amount to a Dividend of Twelve Shillings in the Pound.

Christopher Loft, Esquire, informed your Committee, that some Tliings haveitruck him ns Defeats in the Bankrupt Laws, those relate to the Creditor, the Bankrupt, and, in some Degree, to the Commissioners — with

rospect

2 Geo. II. 1° Junii. 6>5i

respect to Creditors, as the Law now stands, the Bankrupt has the Privilege of0 giving a Preference to any One or more of his Creditors; and, as frequent Experience (hews the Commissioners that their Adjudication is founded upon a very stale Act of Bankruptcy, and if between the Time of that Act and the Ad judication; the Bankrupt has assigned his |>erlbnal,or conveyed his real, Estate, for valuable Consideration, the Creditors who have thus advanced Money, without a Possibility of guarding against the Act, are over-reached by it, which, in his Opinion, might be remedied, by confining the Act of Bankruptcy to some final! Period of Time, anterior t.o the suing out of the Commission; and that no Bankrupt should be at Liberty to exercise the Privilege of prefering his Creditors on the Eve of a Bankruptcy; and for the Eafe of Creditors he should propose, that, upon the Removal of old Commissioners by the Great Seal, Death or Refusal to act, the new Commissioners might act without the Expence of a renewed Commission.

With relation to the Bankrupt, its principal Object seems to be the Certificate, and appears to be but One Curb which the Legislature has put into his Mouth, under all the Statutes, which have made these Three Requisites; viz.

TheConfent of Four-fifths in Number and Value of his Creditors, and their Request to the Commissioners to sign such Certificate — the Discretion of the Commissioners to be guided by the Behaviour of the Bankrupt before them, and the Allowance of the Great Seal — and that if either of these Powers were refeinded, it would induce great Misbehaviour in the Bankrupt, and Prejudice to his Creditors; and it is submitted that a further Check might be put upon the Bankrupt; viz.

That a Certificate should in no same be allowed, till the Assignees of the Bankrupt had declared at leali One Dividend of his Estate and Effects for the Benefit of his Creditors; for though the Statute dire6!s the Assignees to declare a Dividend after Four Months, and within Twelve Months, as they can get the Estate and Effects in, and which within that Time may generally be done, yet it rarely happens that a Dividend is declared under Two Years, and in many Cafes much longer, and in many none at all.

Under this Head a further Amendment might be made; viz.

As the Law stands, the original Time allowed the Bankrupt for diiclosing his Estate, is within 42 Days after being advertised a Bankrupt in the Gazelle; and a Power is given in the Statute for the Great Seal to enlarge the Time 49 Days from the Time of Application, which mult be Six Days before the Expiration of the 42 Days; and though a capital Felony is incurred hv Concealment of Estate or Effects, to the Amount of £. 20, and the Bankrupt should be so peculiarly circum-ttanced as not to be able to fin it h his Examination, and conform to the Statute as the Law now stands, neither the ' Commissioners nor the Great Seal can enlarge the Time.

That this might he remedied by veiling a Power in the Great Seal, or the Commissioners (which latter would lave great Expence) to enlarge the Time.

For the Ease of the Commissioners,

As the Law stands, if the Bankrupt does not surrender to finish his Examination till 12 o’Clock at Night of the last Day, the Commissioners are bound to set till that Time, and perhaps all Night, to take it; should therefore propose, that if the Bankrupt will not surrender till the last Day, he should surrender at 10 of the Clock in the Morning of that Day:

And at present, if the Bankrupt be in Execution, the 'Commissioners must attend him in Gaol, where ’tis very difficult to take an Examination with any Degree of Accuracy; he therefore would propose, that the Sheriff should be obliged to bring the Bankrupt up, upon the Commissioners Warrant, and not be liable to an Escape, which may be done by striking out the Words " Pro-u vided he is not in Execution."

Edward Green, Esquire, formerly a Commissioner of Bankrupts, informed your Committee, That he thinks Vol. 28.

there are many Hardships attending Bankrupts, as well those who have not obtained their Certificate, as those that have, blit chiefly those who have not: First Objection; that it is confined to the Content of Four-fifths in Number and Value, whereby it may be in the Power of One Creditor, without giving any Reason, to obstruct the Certificate, and at the same Time to take the Benefit of the Commission: The Remedy he would propose, is, to oblige such Creditor lo make his Objection, within a certain Time, before the Commissioners; and if they don’t think the Objection reasonable, it should be in their PovVer to overrule it, and consequently grant the Certificate: Second Objection; leaving the Creditor the Liberty of appealing to the Great Seal: By the Act of the 4th and 5th of Queen Anne, the Bankrupt is not entitled to his Certificate, unless the major Part of the Commissioners certified to the Great Sea), that the Bankrupt had conformed; 5th of Geo. 2d confined it to the Consent of Four-fifths of the Creditors in Number and Value, which is the First Act of that Nature; that he thinks it would be right to leave it on the footing of the 4th and 5th of Queen Anne\ for as the Law how stands, too great a Power is lodged in One or Two Creditors: Another Hardship attending Bankrupts is, being obliged to get the Certificates at their own Expence, after having delivered up their All; that he thinks it reasonable it should come out of the Effects, or out of the Allowance which Bankrupts are intitled to: The next Hardship is, that the Assignees have it in their Power to refrain making a Dividend till they are compelled by Application to the Great Seal by the Bankrupt, or any Creditor; and before any Certificate is granted, the Effects are often divided, to prevent the Bankrupt having the Benefit of his Allowance.

With regard to such Bankrupts as have obtained thei Certificates, the following Hardship attends them, in respect to their Bail:

If Judgment is obtained against the Bankrupt by Suit at Law, pending the Commission, the Bail remains liable, and must either surrender the Prisoner, or apply to the Court in which Judgment is obtained for an Exoneratur, that the Bail-piece may be discharged, which often costs more than the Bankrupt is able to pay.

That where a Creditor has a Demand on Bond or Note, and proves that Debt under the Commission, and yet proceeds at Law for Recovery of the same Bond or Note, the Bankrupt may be detained in Custody thereupon, and has no other Relief than by applying to the Great Seal; that the Creditor may make his Election to proceed at Law, or under the Commission; and the Order usually is, that the Creditor shall have Time to make his Election in about a Week, but with Liberty to assent or dissent to the Certificate, let him make his Election the one Way or the other.

That he thinks, upon producing of the Commission and Proof of such Creditor’s having proved his Debt, to any Judge of that Court where the Suit is instituted, that Court or Judge at his Chambers should be obliged to discharge him.

Upon the Matter of the said Petition,

Robert Clibborn being examined, said, That he obtained his Certificate the 1 ith of July 1758, after having been confined in Prison Six Years and an Half, occasioned by an Agreement between Two of his Creditors, that One would not sign till the other was satisfied: That the Debts under the Commission amounted to about £. 3,700, and his Effects produced about £, 2000, and that a Dividend of only Five Shillings in the Pound has been made.

Richard Clough beingexamined, said. That he was a Bankrupt about 20 Years ago; that he was sent for by the Corporation of York, to set up his Trade there in the Manchester Business; that his Stock was £.1,000, the Corporation allowed him £.100 for moving, and £.250 per Annum for carrying on the Trade, for which the Corporation bound themselves for Twelve Years; that this gaveDifgnft to the Lancashire Traders, they thinking it would interfere with them, and therefore occasioned a Commission to be taken out against him, although he had Effects sufficient to pay 20s. in the Pound, and a Surplus of Fifteen hundred Pounds:

That in Aprilfoft the Commission against him was renewed, which occasioned a second Commission to be taken out by his later Creditors against himself and his Sons, who were then Partners with him; and he is now under Two Statutes of Bankruptcy.

Mr. Thomas Jordan, Keeper of the Fleet Prison, produced to your Committee a List of Bankrupts, Prisoners in the King's Bench and Fleet Prisons, whereby it appeared that 15 are confined in the King's Bench Prison, and 17 in the Fleet Prison.

JohnFish and RichardCtough being further examined, said, That many Bankrupts have been obliged to go abroad, on Account of Hardships they labour under by the Bankrupt Laws, and mentioned One who abfconderi, after having paid io^. in the Pound; and the Witnesses both said, they would have gone abroad if they had had no Families; and that they have heard of Bankrupts going abroad to set up Manufactures.

Samuel Higgins, a Bankrupt, being examined, said, That he failed for£. 1,300, that his chief Creditor was his Assignee, and has upwards of £.400 of the Bankrupt’s Effects in his Hands, and that the Witness has Two Freehold Houses, let at £.8. 10$. per Annum. besides outstanding Debts; that his Assignee has refused signing his Certificate, without giving any Reason; his other Creditors, who have not iigned his Certificate, have promised him they would, if his Assignee would; and that there is no Dividend made of his Efiects.

Thomas Bell and James Oliver being examined, said, That they had been declared Bankrupts, and the Reason why they have not obtained their Cerficates is, because they would not each of them give their principal Creditor (One of the Assignees) £. 50 for signing.

Then one of the Agents for the Petitioners produced to your Committee, an Order made by the Lord Chancellor upon the 14th Day of September, 1748, in the Matter of Da?iiel Lindsay, a Bankrupt, wherein it is recited, That the Bankrupt was, about the Year 1744, taken in Execution for a Judgment Debt, unfairly set up by one Tilman Henckell; that in the same Year a Commission of Bankruptcy issued against him, when the said Henckell, who had him in Execution, proved the said Judgment Dv^bt under the said Commission, although, upon a just and fair Account, he would be found indebted to the Estate of the Bankrupt; whereupon all Parties concerned attending the Lord Chancellor, and being heard, and the said Henckell making his Election to proceed against the Bankrupt atLaw, the Lord Chancellor ordered, that the said Henckell lliould be excluded from receiving any Dividend under the Commission, but should, nevertheless, be considered as a Creditor under the said Commission, so far as to be at Liberty to assent or dissent from the Bankrupt’s haying his Certificate:

*7

And your Committee was.informed. That the Bankrupt has remained inCustody, upon the said Execution, from the Year 1744 to this Time:

Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That some Amendments may be made to the Laws relating to Bankrupts, to the Advantage of the Creditors, and in Ease of the Bankrupts.

The same of George Walker, a Bankrupt, mofl humbly submitted to the Consideration of Parliament, Sheweth,

1. That the Bankrupt, in the last War with Fraiice and Spain, had the Honour to be Commodore and Commander in Chief of a Squadron of Four private Ships ot War, called the Royal Family Privateers, and, in the Year 1746 and 1747, had the good Fortune to take several very rich Prizes, and thereby became intitled, as Commodore and Quarter Matter of the said Squadron, to a very large Sum of Money out of the Produce of the Sale of said Prizes; and also to £. 7,247. 4*. out of the Prize money due to the Officers and Crews of said Privateers, on Account of Goods furnished and Money advanced to them, and which was to be repaid.

2. That William Belchier, Israel Jalabert, and James Talbot, together with other Owners and Managers of said Privateers (fmce dead), caused the aforesaid Prizes to be condemned and fold, and received the whole Produce of the fame, amounting to £. 200,000 Sterling, or thereabouts, whereby they became Debtors to the Bankrupt in a large Sum of Money, on Account of his own Shares, and other Allowances as Commodore and Quarter Matter; and also on Account of the said £. 7,247. 4*3 due to him; of which the said Managers had early Notice, long before any Dividend was pretended to be made, or any of the said Officers and Crews were paid their Shares.

3. That the Bankrupt, knowing the Managers to be possessed of a large Sum, his Property, on Account of said Prizes, and having a pressing Occasion for some Money, prevailed on them to advance him £. 2,550 on the Credit of his Interest in said Prizes; for which they not only obliged him to execute a Bond, bearing Date the 16th of March 1748-9, in the penal Sum of£. 5,100, but also to execute to them an Indenture, of the same Date, by way of collateral Security, whereby he assigned over to them his Interest of £.2,878. ijs. 5dM in said Prizes; and also the said £. 7,247. 4s.; with this Proviso, that the said Indenture should be void so soon as the £. 2,550 was paid.

4. That the said Managers soon after had several other large Sums of Money paid in to them, on Account of the said £.7,247. 4^. and also £.2,610. 6s. gd. was paid into their Hands, the 15th of March 1750, by Henry Cafamajor, in Discharge of the said Bond, by which Means the same and also the said Indenture became void, and ought to have been delivered up; but the said Cafamajor, being wholly under the Influence of the Managers, and acting in concert with them, collusively suffered the said Bond and Indenture to remain in their Hands everfince.

5. That the said Managers, though often applied to by the Bankrupt to account with him touching his Interest in said Prizes in their Hands, they have con-

6. That in the Year 1754 the Bankrupt, having been informed, that Mr James Goddard, Agent to the said Royal Family Privateers, was, by several malicious Perfections, driven into Obscurity, he came to London in 1755, to settle Accounts with the Managers, and to take out of their Hands his said Bond and other Securities, which were satisfied and paid; and accordingly he applied to them for that Purpose; but they, dreading the

Consequence of his Appearance, and of his joining with other Officers and Seamen in a Suit of Chancery, insti-tuted by Mr. James Goddard in their Behalf, to compel the said Managers to account for the Produce of the said Prizes; threatened to put his said Bond of £.2,550 in Suit against him, and to imprison him thereupon, on the least Sign of Molestation against them; and that the aforesaid William Belchier, pretending to be much his Friend, did, under that specious Colour, and the alluring Offers of Friendship and Assistance in the Prosecution of a Plan which the Bankrupt had then in view, endeavoured to persuade him, that it would be for his Interest to make a ftiort End of all Matters in dispute between him and said Managers; and, for that Purpose, to consent to sign their general Account of the Prizes, and to execute mutual Releases to one another; for that it would be impossible ever to adjust or settle the Accounts of said Prizes.

7. That the Bankrupt, findinghimself thus threatened, and disabled, by the unjust Detention of his Property im the Hands of the Managers, to contest the Matter in Account with such powerful AdverCaries and at the same time relying on the proffered Friendship and Affiftance of the said William Belchier, agreed to his Proposal; and, in the Month, of November 1755, did enter into the following Agreement with the said William Belchier, in behalf of himself and the other Managers of the said Royal Family Privateers, by which it was agreed " That the Managers of the Royal Family Pri-<c vateers and the said George Walker should make an " end of all Matters in dispute between them in Manner following; that is to say, That the said Managers " and the Bankrupt George Walker should mutually

" execute each unto the other general Releases, for and in respect of all Claims and Demands whatsoever u between them touching the said Privateers and their €t Prizes, or otherwise howsoever; and that the said " George Walker should in the Interim sign their Books " till the said Releases could be prepared, for which,

of said William Belchier told the Bankrupt, he had *c given Orders to Mr. Rayner."

8. That the Bankrupt, not suspe6ling any Fraud, and being desirous to be left at Liberty to prosecute his other Affairs, did, at the Request of said William Belchier, and in pursuance of such Agreement, lign such Books as were presented to him for that Purpose; but without any previous Examination or Inspectioti thereof, or of the Vouchers of the fame, in hopes that the said Managers would have executed to him such general Release as aforesaid; but the said Managers, after the Bankrupt had been thus prompted and induced to lign their Books, refused to execute the fame; and, instead thereof, the said William Belchier, Israel Jala- . bert, and James Talbot, being at that time the only surviving Managers, soon after caused him to be arrested, in a fictitious Action, for £. 833. 12 s. 11 d. pretended by them to be a Balance of an Account current; which pretended Account the Bankrupt never saw or heard of, till after he had been Fifteen Months in Prison on said Action: He therefore does not think himself in any ways bound by his having signed the said Books, in the Manner and upon the Motives above-mentioned; but more especially as the said Managers have not on their Part performed the Agreement or Conditions upon which they were so ligned.

9. That the Bankrupt, for want of Bail, found himself under the Necessity of being removed by Habeas 16

Corpus to the King's Bench, where lie has been detained a Prisoner, at the Suit of the said Managers, ever fmee the 21 ft May 1756.

10. That the said George Walker, the Bankrupt, was no sooner become a Prisoner, than the said William Belchier, Israel Jalabert, and James Talbot, charged him in Custody not only upon the said pretended Debt of £.833. 1 is. 11 but,most unjustly and oppressively, set up the aforesaid Bond of £. 2,550 (which had been paid several Years before) against him, and also charged liim in Custody in £. 5,100, being the Penalty thereof, in order to preclude him of any Chance of obtaining Bail; and have since signed Judgment, and charged him in Execution upon both the said Actions.

11. That the Bankrupt, being greatly distressed, and unable to make any Defence against the said Actions, and being advised, that his only Relief was in a Court of Equity, he therefore made no Defence at Law, and was preparing a Bill to be filed in Chancery against the said Managers; but being unable, by Reason of his distressed Circumstances, to commence and prosecute such Suit in Equity, lie was, as aforesaid, charged in Execution on the Penalty of the said Bond for ,£.5,100, and also on said other Action for £. 850 Damages and Costs; which said Executions so greatly distressed the Bankrupt that (after remaining upwards of Twelve Months in close Confinement, whereby his Health was greatly impaired, and his Life endangered), he was at last forced to find Security for about £. 8,000 before he could obtain the Liberty of the Rules.

12. That aCommission of Bankruptcy issued against the said George Walker, on the 27th Day of May 1757, upon the Application of James Contts, Banker, whereupon he was declared a Bankrupt; and, pursuant to Notice in the Gazette, all the Creditors who had proved Debts under the Commission did, at the SecondSitting of the Commissioners, chuse the said James Coutts and John Cruikjhank, of London, Merchant, Assignees of the Bankrupt’s Estate and Effects; who have accepted of the said Trust^and executed a Counter-part of an Assignmenfc to the major Part of the Commissioners.

43. That the said William Belchier, Israel Jalabei't, and James Talbot, appeared before the Commissioners, and offered to prove a Debt of £. 850 by virtue of the said Judgment obtained against the said George Walker; but the Commissioners refused to admit them to prove such Debt, unless they would agree to discharge the Bankrupt out of Custody, from the Execution upon that Judgment;. which they refused to do; but did not offer to prove any Debt under the other Judgment upon the Penalty of the Bond of £. 5,100, well knoiving that the same had been discharged several Years ago, though the Bankrupt still continues to be charged in Execution upon the fame.

14. That the said William Belchier, Israel Jalabert, and James Talbot, on the 17th June 1757, petitioned the Great Seal; by which Petition, after many false Allegations contained therein, they pray to be at Liberty to prove their Debt under the said Commission, in order to oppose the Bankrupt’s Certificate, and to dissent from the same, they waving all Benefit of any Dividend of his Effects; a Condition which they might very safely propose, as they were largely indebted to the Bankrupt.

15. That the Bankrupt, together with the said Assignees of his Estate, preferred, at the same time, a cross Petition to his Lordship, praying, a general Account of the said Prize Monies as between the said Managers and the Bankrupt; and, notwithstanding the said last mentioned Petition was supported by several Affidavits, whereby it appeared, that, upon a just and fair Account, there would be found a very large Balance owing from the said Managers to the Bankrupt’s Estate, yet his Lordship declared, that he would not direct any Account to be taken in a summary Way upon that Petition; for that the proper Remedy was by Bill ift Equity to compel such Account, and reduce the said Debt of £. 850 set up by the Managers; and therefore his Lordship was pleaftd to refuse the Desire

of

of the said cross Petition, and (o admit the Managers to prove their said Demand, as prayed by their Petition.

16. That the Commission against this Bankrupt has issued fairly, and without any Fraud or Collusion, with a View to procure his just and lawful Creditors Satisfaction for their respective Demands: That the Bankrupt has in every Respect complied with the Law, by surrendering up his All for their Benefit; who werefo well satisfied of his just and honest Dealings with them in that Respect, that all of them who have proved their Debts under the said Commission, have very readily signed, or given Authorities to sign, his Certificate; and that the only Creditors that oppose the Bankrupt’s Certificate are the Managers of the Royal Family Privateers; who were the original and only Cause of his Bankruptcy, by the unwarrantable Detention of all his Property in their own Hands; those very Managers who threw him into Prison, and (till detain him there upon the aforesaid Two fictitious Causes of Action.

That the unfortunate Bankrupt humbly conceives his Cafe, as well as that of his fair and just Creditors, /will appear to be attended with such Circumstances of great Cruelty, Oppression, and Injustice, as call aloud for Red refs; and from which, as the Law concerning Bankrupts now (lands, there is no Relief to be expected, otherwise than from the benign Interposition of the Legislature. He therefore most humbly begs Leave to submit the same to the Wisdom and Consideration of the Parliament.

George Walker.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time; was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The King has commanded us to put an End to this Session of Parliament; and at the same time to affine you, That as yourConduft during the Course of it has highly deserved his Royal Approbation, so his Majesty now returns you his hearty Thanks for it.
