all Europe, to come to equitable and honourable Terms of Accommodation.

By your Assistance the combined Army in Germany has been completed, powerful Squadrons as well as great Numbers of Land Forces are employed in America, iu order to maintain the just Rights and Possessionsofhis Majesty and his People, and to annoy the Enemy in the moll sensible Manner in those Parts *, and, as France is now making confklerable Preparations in her Ports, his Majesty has taken Care to put his Fleet at Home in the best Condition, both of Strength and Situation, to guard against and repel any Attempts that may be meditated against his Kingdoms.

The King's Measures have all been directed to aifert the Honour of his Crown, to preserv the eflTeirtial Interests of his faithful Subjects, and to support the Cause of the Protestant Religion and public Liberty:

His Majesty therefore trusts, that the Uprightnefsofhis Intentions will draw down the Blessing of Heaven upon his Endeavours.

We have it also in Command from his Majesty to set you know. That he hopes the Provisions you have made? to prevent and correct the Exceflfes of the Privateers will be efifeftual to that desireable End. The King has had it much at Heart: For though his Majesty is sensible of the Utility of that Service, when under proper Regulations, he is determined to do his utmost to prevent any Injuries or Hardships being done to the Subjects of neutral Powers, as far as may be practicable, and confident with his Majesty s just Right to hinder the Trade of his Enemies from being collulively and fraudulently covered.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

We are commanded to affiire you, That when his Majesty considers the large Supplies which you have founanimously given, he feels himself under theftrongeft Obligations, not only to thank you for them, but also to applaud the Firmness and Vigour with which you have acted, as well as your Prudence in judging, that, notwithstanding the present Burthens, the making ample Provision for carrying on the War is the most probable Means to bring it to an honourable and happy Con-elusion. No Attention will be wanting on his Majesty s Part for the faithful Application of what you have granted.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

His Majesty has been graciously pleased to order us to add, That he has nothing more to desire of you, but that you would carry down the same good Dispositions, and propagate them in your several Counties, which you have shewn in your Proceedings during your fitting here.

After which the Lord Keeper said:

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Desire of the Lords, authorized by virtue of his Majesty’s Commission, that the House might hear the Commission read had been at the House of Peers: Where the Lor I Keeper of the Great Seal, fitting, with several othe Lords, on a Form between the Throne and the Wool-sacks, said to the Effect following:

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We are commanded by his Majesty to let you know. That as it is not convenient for his Majesty to be present here this Day in his Royal Person, he has been pleased, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, to authorize his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, and his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, and several Lords therein mentioned, to do every thing in the Name of his Majesty, which ought to be done on the Part of his Majesty, in this Parliament, as may more fully appear by the Letters Patent.

That then the said Letters Patent being read, which were to the Purport of what the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal had said, the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, as One of the Commissioners, made a Speech to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In pursuance of the Authority given to us, by his Majesty’s Commission under the Great Seal, amongst other Things, to declare the Cause of his holding this 15

Parliament; his Majesty has been graciously pleased to direct us to allure you, that he esteems himself particularly happy in being able to cal! you together in a Situation of Affairs so glorious and advantageous to his Crown and Kingdoms.

His Majesty fees and devoutly adores the Hand of Providence in the many signal Successes, both by Sea and Land, with which his Arms have been blessed in the Course of the last Summer; and at the same time his Majesty reflects, with much Satisfaction, on the Confidence which you placed in him, by making such ample Provisions, andentrufting him with inch exteniivePowers for carry ing on a War, which, the Defence of our valuable Rights and Possessions, and the Preservation of the Navigation and Commerce of his Majesty’s People, had made both just and necessary.

We have it also in Command from his Majesty to acquaint you. That the happy Progress of our Successes, from the taking of Goree, on the Coastof Africa, to the Conquest of so many important Places in America, with the Defeat of the French Army in Canada, and the Reduction of their Capital City of Quebec, effected with so much Honour to the Courage and Conduct of his Majesty’s Officers, both at Sea and Land, and with fa great Lustre to his intrepid Forces, together with the important Success obtained by his Majesty’s Fleet off Cape Lagos, and the effectual blocking up, for so many Months, the principal Part of the Navy of France in their own Ports, are Events which must have filled the Hearts of all his Majesty’s faithful Subjects, as well as his own, with the sincerest Joy; and, his Majesty trutts, will convince you, that there has been no Want of Vigilance or Vigour on his Part in exerting those Means which you, with so much Prudence and public spirited Zeal, put into his Majesty’s Hands:

That our Advantages have extended farther, and the Divine Blessing has favoured us in the East Indies; where the dangerous Designs of his Majesty’s Enemies have mifearried, and that valuable Branch of our Trade has received great Benefit and Protection:

That the memorable Victory gained over the French, near Minden, has long made a deep impression on the Minds of his Majesty’s People; and that, if the Crifis in which that Battle was fought, the fu peri or Numbers of the Enemy, and the great and able Conduct of his Majesty’s General Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick, are com-fidered, that Action must be the Subject of lasting Admiration and Thankfulncfs: N

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, to be heard at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient time, to be appointed either by the House, or the Committee of Privileges and Elections, as the Matter to be heard Hia.ll be before the House, or the said Committee, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lifts of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objetted to, who voted for the Sitting Members, giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distin-guifiiing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners, or their Agents.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Vol. 28.

Resolved, Thai it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall fee, or be informed of to he, in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back Door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other Officers of Middlesex and Westminster do take care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning to One in the Afternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon* during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall be kept free and open; and that no Obstru6tian be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in Waiting do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Fbotmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Htgh Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Stibjefts, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our most humble Thanks for the Speech delivered by your Majesty’s Command to both Houses of Parliament

17

Permit us, Sir, with the sincerest Zeal and Duty, to congratulate your Majesty on the glorious and uninterrupted Series of Succels and Victory which hath attended your Majesty’s Arms during the whole Course of this distinguished and memorable Year.

With the deepest Reverence, and most devout Gratitude to Divine Providence, we acknowledge that manifest Blessing and Protection which God hath vouchsafed to bellow upon your Majesty’s Councils and Arms, and offer up our most ardent Vows and Prayers for its Continuance.

Your Majesty’s faithful Commons will not attempt to enumerate all the AdvantagesandGloriesderived toyotir Majesty and these Kingdoms from the various Successes which have been extended into every Quarter of he World; but we humbly beg Leave to allure your Majesty, that our Hearts are 'filled with the moil grateful and lively Sense of the happy Consequonces, which, under God, are owing to the Wifiiom, Vigilance, and Vigour, of your Majesty’s Measures in the Prosecutiuii of this just and necessary War; particularly,

The taking of thelfland of Goree, and the Extension of our Commerce on the Coast of Africa, the Defeat of Ttie French Fleet in the East Indies, and the Repulse of their Laiwi Forces before Madrass, whereby the dangerous De/ignsofour Enemies there have mrfearried, and Protection hath been given to our Trade and Settlements in those Countries; the valuableConquest of Gaadelnpe and Marie Galante in the West Indies: the Reduction of so many Forts and Places in North America, completer! and crowned by that glorious and decisive Victory over the French Army in Canada, and the Surrender of their capital City of Quebec, affected with so much Honour to the Courage and Conduct of your Majesty’s Officers by Sea and Land, and with so much Lustre to your intrepid Forces; the important Success of your Majesty's Fleet, in pursuing, taking, and destroy ing, a considerable Part of the French Squadron off Cape Lagos, and the blocking up, for so many Mouths, the rest of the Navy of France in their own Ports, which hath greatly augmented the Distress of our Enemies, whilst it has protected and secured our Commerce and Navigation.

Nor can we ever forget that critical, figual, and memorable, Defeat of the Frc?wh Army near Mindtn, so j u ftly the Subject of lading Ad m irat ion and Thankful ness, if we consider the superior Numbers of the Enemy, the great and able Condu6t of his Serene Highness Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick, or the unconquerable Valour of your Majesty’s Troops.

When we reflect upon this continued Train of Suc-ceffes, Part of which would have been sufficient to have signalized this long and a&iveCampaign, it is impossible for us not to express the highest Satisfactionat the great Ability Resolution, and perfect Harmony, so coufpicuous in your Majesty’s Admirals aodGenerals throughout the Execution of your Commands, and at the ardent Courage which hath man ifelled it self in the Behaviour of the Officers and Forces both by Sea and Land, with such personal and national Glory: Nothing but this Spirit could have enabled them to surmount every Difficulty arising from the superiorNumber and advantageous Situation of the Enemy; ami we are fully persuaded, that the like Resolution, Ardour, and Zeal, excited and animated by thofebeft Incentives, your Majesty’s gracious Acceptance and Royal Approbation of their eminent Services, followed by the warmest and most universel Applause of their Country, will continue to give Terror to the Enemies, and Confidence to the Allies, of Great Brit am.

We view with the higheftAdmiration the Magnanimity and unexampled Efforts of that great Prince, your Majesty’s Ally, the King of Prussia, whose consummate Genius, unwearied Activity, and unlhaken Constancy of Mind, seconded by the Bravery of his Troops, have been able, in every Situation, to supply Resources sufficient to refill the united Forces of so many and such formidable Powers.

Your Majesty’s faithful Commons feel with due Gratitude your paternal Care and Concern for the Peace and Happiness of your People; and cannot too much admire that true Greatness of Mind, which disposes your Heart, in the Midst of Prosperities, to wish that a Stop may be put to the Effusion of Christian Blood, and that public Tranquillity may be restored.

We intirely rely on your Majesty's knownWifdom and Firmness, that this desirable Object, whenever it shall fee attained, will be on such Terms as shall be just and honourable for your Majesty and your Allies, and shall bring along with them full Security for the future on solid and durable Foundations, by procuring such Advantages as may in Reason and Equity be expected from the Successes of our Arms, and which will fix in the Minds^of a grateful People the lading Remembrance of this happy Era, and of the Benefits derived to them tinder your Majesty’s glorious and auspicious Government.

In order to effect this great End, we are thoroughly sensible that ample Provision tnuft be made for carrying on the War in all Parts with the utmost Vigour; and we assure your Majesty, that we will chearfully grant your Majesty such Supplies as shall be found necessary to sustain and press with Fifed all our extensive Operations against the Enemy, and at the same time, by the Blessing of God, to repel and frustrate their daring Defisrns against these Kingdoms; convinced from the long Experience we have had of the Wisdom and Good-Xiefs of your Majesty, that they will be applied in such manner as will best answer these great Purposes.

We can not sufficiently testify our grateful Seufe of the fcigh Satisfaction which your Majesty has been pleased to express in that perfect Union and good Harmony which so happily subsists amongst your faithful Subjects, the salutary vffeds of which have been most conspicuous; and the pleasing Kxperience we have had of them, joined to your Majesty’s paternal Recommendation, must be the rood powerful Motives to enforce the Continuance of fhofe Dispositions, so essential to the full Exert ion of our utmost Strength, as well as to the Tranquillity,.good Order, and Happiness'of your Majesty’s People.

A Petition of several Noblemen, Gentlemen, and Removing others, Inhabitants of East Greenwich, and Places adja- Gunpow.ier cent, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the w;ch l0 pUr-Inliabitants, was presented to the House, and read: set- fleer, ting forth, That in the Parish of East Greenwich, and within a Quarter of a Mile, or thereabouts, of the Town, in which there is a Royal Palace, and Royal Hospital for Seamen, there is a Storehouse or Magazine, wherein is frequently kept very great Quantities of Gunpowder, to the Amount, as the Petitioners are informer!, of Six thou fund Barrels or more; and that, betides the great Danger which muff attend all Places of that Kind, the said Magazine Hands in an open Field, not inclosed by any Fortification or Defence whatsoever, whereby it is exposed to Treachery, and every other Accident; and alleging, that the Petitioners apprehend, if, through Treachery, or by Lightning, or any other Accident, the said Magazine should take Fire, among many great Mischiefs which would follow, not only the Lives.and Properties of the Petitioners, but the said Palace and Hospital, the King’s Yards and Stores at Deptford and Woolwich, and the Banks and Navigation of the River Thames, and the Ships failing and at Anchor therein, would be inevitably destroyed, and inconceivable Damage accrue to the Cities of London and Westminster; and further alleging, that the said Magazine is now in a dangerous Condition, being propped on all Sides: That the Props are, as the Petitioners are credibly informed, decaying at the Foundation; and that, in case it should fall, the Powder must most certainly take Fire, and all the before-mentioned Calamities inevitably happen: And therefore praying the House to take the Premiles into Consideration; and that the said Magazine may be taken down, and removed to some more convenient Place, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall feetn meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

A Petition of the Mayor, Magistrates, Merchants, Distillation Manufacturers, and other Gentlemen, of the City of from WI,eats Norwich, was prefeuted to the House, and read; fitting &c‘ forth, That the Petitioners apprehend that the Scarcity and Dearness of Corn (the principal Motive which occasioned the Act for the Prohibition of the making of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain) has ceased; and alleging, that particularly the Price of Wheat is reduced below the necessary Expence of producing it, and tends rather to renew the Complaint of Scarcity, as it d ifeou rages the Hulb an d-man from tilling so much Land as he would, by a reason-ablePrice, be induced to do; and that, in case the House should think fit to permit the diddling from Malt or Corn (which the Petitioners allege would be highly beneficial to this Kingdom, and more advantageous than the drilling from a foreign Produce, and evidently preferable to the present necessary Practice of importing large Quantities of foreign Brandies) the Petitioners confide in the Wisdom of the House to make such Provisions and Rfc-strictions as may prevent the pernicious Abuse of such Liquors by the common People; all which the Petitioners submit to the Judgment and Discernment of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petitition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to take into Consideration so much of^n Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled.

An Act to continue, for a farther Time, the Prohibition of the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread,

Biscuit, and Starch; and also to continue, for a farther Time, the Prohibition of the making of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain, or from Meal or Flour; and to prohibit, for a limited Time, the making of low Wines and Spirits from Bran; as relates to the Prohibition of the making of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain, or from Meal or Flour, or from Bran.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of King's Lynn, in Norfolk, in Council assembled; end also,

A Petition of the Mayor and Bailiffs of the Borough of Berwick upon Tweed, in behalf of all the Inhabitants of the said Borough;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; representing to the House the good Effects which the Petitioners allege have arisen from the Prohibition of the making of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain, or from Meal, Flour, or Bran: And praying, That the said Prohibition may be further continued.

A Petition of the several Land Owners and Holders of the South-weft Parts of the jCounty of Essex, whose Names arethereuutosubscribed,on behalf of them selves, and the rest of the Landed Interest, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the continuing the Prohibition of the Distillation of Corn beyond the Necessity which appeared to require it, will be a vast Loss and Discouragement to the Petitioners and the rest of the Landed Interest: And therefore praying. That the Malt Distillery of this Kingdom may be again opened, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Freeholders of the Counties of Ross and Cromartie, in North Britain, was also presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners are convinced, from Fa6ts and Experience, that the temporary Causes which produced the Prohibition of the making of Spirits from Wheat, Barley, or any other Sort of Grain, have long ceased in North Britain, and that a further Prohibition thereof rauft in its Consequences be very grievous to the Inhabitants of that Part of the Kingdom; and further alleging, that no spirituous Liquors are made in that Part of the Kingdom but those called Aqua vita, which are never exported, and are always distilled from Malt made of pig or Bear (a Grain of inferior Quality to Barley), which is the chief Growth of that Country; and that the Climate or Circumstances of a great Part of that Country render the Use of Spirits more necessary, as well aslefs pernicious, than in more Southern Climates: And therefore praying, in Const-

14

deration of the particular Circumstances before stated, That the Distillation of the Spirits called Aqua vita, may be permitted in the North Parts of Great Britain, in the same Manner as before the late Prohibitions were laid on, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to take into Consideration so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act tocontinue, for a farther Time, the Prohibition of the Exportation of Corn, Malt, Meal, Flour, Bread, Biscuit, and Starch; and also to continue, for a farther Time, the Prohibition of the making of low Wines and Spirits from 'Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain, or from Meal or Flour; and to prohibit, for a limited Time, the making of low Wines and Spirits from Bran; as relates to the Prohibition of the making of low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or any other Sort of Grain, or from Meal or Flour, or from Bran.

Tranllation of a Convention between his Majesty and the King of Prussia, concluded and signed at London, the 9th November 1759.

YPftfln ]t knovvn to whom it concerns, or may con- u ia' cern: That the burthensome War wherein his Prussian Majesty is engaged, putting him under the Necessity of making new Efforts, for his Defence against the great Number of Enemies by which his Dominions are attacked; and being the refore obliged to enter into a new Concert with his Britannic Majesty, in order to provide reciprocally and jointly with him, for their common Defence and Safety; and his Majesty the King of Great Britain, having made/ known at the same Time the Desire he had to strengthen the Bonds of Friendship which subsist between the Two Courts, and to come to a new Agreement on this Occasion; and for this End, by an express Convention, relating to the Succours, by which he may give to his Prussian Majesty most expeditious and most efficacious Assist-ance, their said Majesties have therefore, for this Purpose, named and authorized their respectiveMinisters; to wit. In the Name and on the Part of his Britannic Majesty, his Privy Counsellors, Sir Robert Henley -Knight, his Keeper of the Great Seal of Great Britain; John Earl Granville, President of his Counsel; Thomas Holies Duke of Newcastle, First Lord Commissioner of his Treasury; Robert Earl of Holdernesse, oue of his

A, 1759.

principal Secretaries of State; Philip Earl of Hard wid/cc; and William Pitt, another of his principal Se- cretaries of State: And in the Name and on the Part of his Prussian Majesty, the Sieurs Dodo Henry, Baron of Knyphaufeit, his Privy Counsellor of Embalfy, and Mi-11 ifter Plenipotentiary at the Court of his Britannic Majesty, and Lewis Michell', his Charge9 d'Affairs at the said Court; who, after the Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles.

1.

It is agreed. That all the preceding Treaties whicfr subsist between the Two Courts, of whatever Date or Nature they may be, and particularly that of Westminster, of the 16th of January, in the Year 1756, as well as the Convention of the nth of April of the last Year, and that of the 7th of December of the same Year, shall be deemed to be renewed and confirmed by the present Convention, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses; and shall be of the same Force, as if they were inserted herein Word for Word.

2.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to cause to be paid in the City of London, into the Hands of the Person or Persons who shall be authorized for that Purpose by his Majesty the King of Prussia, the Sum of Four Millions of German Crowns, amounting to Six hundred and Seventy thousand Pounds Sterling; which intire Sum shall be paid at once immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications, upon the Requisition of his Prussian Majesty.

3-

His Majesty the King of Prussia engages, on his Part, to employ the said Sum in keeping up and augmenting his Forces, which shall act in the most advantageous Manner for the Common Cause, and for the End proposed by their aforesaid Majesties, of reciprocal Defence and mutual Security.

4-

The High contracting Parties tporeover engage; viz. on the one Part his Britannic Majesty, both as King and as Elector; and, on the other Part, his Prussian Majesty; not to conclude any Treaty of Peace, Truce, or Neutrality, or any other Convention or Agreement whatsoever, with the Powers who have taken Part in the present War, but in Concert and by mutual Consent and expressly comprehending each other therein.

5-

ThisConvention shall be ratified, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged on both Sides, within the Term of Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Date of the signing of the present Convention, or sooner, if possible.

In Witness whereof, We, the underwritten Ministers of his Majesty the King of Great Britain,\and of his Majesty the King of Prussia, by virtue of our full Powers, have signed the present Convention, and have set the Seals of our Arms thereto. Done at London, the Ninth of November, in the Year of our Lord 1759.

(L. S.) Robert Henley, C.

(L. S.) Granville, P.

(L. S.) Holies Newcastle.

(L. S.) Holdernesse,

(L. S.) W. Pitt.

Separate Article.

The Experience of what has passed, having shewn the Necessity of having for the Good of the Common Cause, a Body of Troops, for covering the Dominions of thje most Serene Landgrave of Hejfe-y and his most Serene Highness having represented his Inability to maintain a, Body of his own Troops, for aufwering in part so indispensable an Object, his Dominions having been totally exhausted, in consequence of the enormous

Contributions and Deliveries the French have drawn fro.n\ thenceAxi* Britannic Majesty promises and engages to cause to be paid to the most Serene Landgrave of Heffey without any: Deduction,th e Sum of Ninety-feveu thousand Five hundred ^Eighty-two. And in Consideration of the said Sum of £.97,582 17 iof to be advanced as usual, from Two Months to Two , Mopths, and of the Payment of the extraordinary Expenses in the Manner settled by the Treaty of 1755, the most Serene Landgrave of Hejfe promises and engages on his Part to keep the said Body of 6,992 Men in Readiness, to act every where for the Good of the Common Cause, according to the C^ronmftanoes of the War.

With regard to Forgge, and other Things neoeff*ry to be furnished for the said Body of Troops his Majesty will provide for the fame; gnd the most proper Mea-. fares shall be taken, as shall be agreed upon between the two Courts for that Purpose.

Moreover, the King of Great Britain having northing more at Heart than to facilitate the Means by which the most Serene Landgrave of Hejfe may rggain the hislResidence in his own Dominions, ana give frefliCourage to his faithful Subjects by his Presence, which is so tnuch wished for; his said Majesty, in order to contribute4o-wards so interesting an Object, grants to the said most Serene Landgrave the Sum of Sixty thousand Found* Sterling, to be paid as his mpft Serene ILghnefe {shall think it most convenient.

The present separate Article shall be of the same Force, as if it was inserted Word for Word in the Treaty concluded and signed this Day. Importation An ingrossed Bill to continue, for aTime to be limited, of Beef, Uc. an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An A6fc to continue, for a limited Time, an Act, made in the Jaft Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act to permit the Importation of salted Beef, Pork, and Butter, from Ireland, for a limited Time; and to amend the said Act; was read the Third time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Rider, providing, That the Continuance of the Act might be ihortened by the King, or by the Parliament, during the present Session.

And the Question being put. That the said Clause be brought up;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to continue, for a limitedTime, the Importation of salted Beef, Pork, and Butter, from Ireland.

Ordered, That Mr. Bacon do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

The said Report is as followeth: viz:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. JoJ'eph Martyr, and Mr. John Shipman, being severally examined, laid, That there is a Magazinefor Gunpowder within a Quarter of a Mile of the Town of Greenwich, where tiiere is a Royal Palace, and a Royal Hospital for Seamen, a new Church, and other considerable Buildings.

Mr. Thomas Furnis, Store-keeper at the said Magazine, being examined, informed your Committee, That the usual Quantity of Gunpowder, kept in the said Magazine, has, upon a Medium, for some Years past, been from Four to Sixthousand Barrels; that the only Security to the said Magazine, is an open Fence, Eight Feet high, which is at the Distance of about Eight or Ten Feet from the Building; but that there are Cen-tries constantly placed there.

Then a Copy of a Report made to the principal Officers of his Majesty’s Ordnance, by William Skinner, JuJily Watson, Archibald Patowi, J. P. Defmaretz, Engineers, which was presented to the House, upon the 13th Day of December 1754, and now referred to' your Committee, was in Part read; whereby it appears’ to have been the Opinion of the said Engineers, that as to the Damage which might arise, in case the said Magazine was to blowup* with Six or Eight thousand Barrels of Powder in it, it would not be easy to deter- mine the dreadful Eft’eft, but were unanimously of Opinion, that the Town of Eafi Greenwich and Royal Hospital adjoining, would greatly suffer by such Ex-plofion and Re-action of the Air, which would not only cause many Houses to fall, but destroy the upper Struftures of the neighbouring Buildings* and endanger the Lives of the Inhabitants; and that it would destroy the Banks of the River Thames, and lay under Water the whole Level of Marsh Land, situated between Greenwich and Woolwich, which would greatly obstruct the Navigation of the River, by making a Breach as difficult to flop as that at Dagenham was.

A Member present, one of the principal Officers of his Majesty’s Ordnance, informed your Committee, That he agreed in Opinion with the said Engineers, and added, That he thought the Explofion would extend as far as the lower Part of Deptford; and would also affest the opposite Shore.

And the said Member further added. That the said Magazine is in a very bad Condition; that it has been examined into by Direction of the Board of Ordnance* and the Foundation found to be very bad; that the Building stands merely upon Shoars, which have lieen lately replaced, the former ones being decayed; that if the said Magazine was to fall, in his Opinion it would fire the Powder; that where there is a Proof House for Gunpowder, there must be a Magazine sufficient to hold 2000 Barrels.

Mr. William Robinson, a Surveyor, being called, informed your Committee, That he, together with Mr* Joseph Pratt, Bricklayer, and Mr. James Morrifs, Carpenter, had, pursuant to Direction from the Board of Ordnance, lately surveyed the said Magazine; and he delivered in to your Committee, a Paper, which he said contained their Remarks, Observations, and Opinion relating thereto, which are as follow; viz.

' Then the Residue of the before-mentioned Report was read, whereby it'appeared. That the said Engineers had viewed the River from Greenwich to Grave]end, and found at Purjleet, a most proper Place for erecting a Magazine, it being situated on a riling Ground, near the Border.of the River, on the Essex Shore, at the North End of Long Peachy where the Men of War generally take in their Powder; and that Pur fleet was preferable to any other Place they could find, on Account of its folicl and dry Foundation, which would not only greatly preserve the Powder, but that likewise a considerable Expence would be favcd bjr erecting a Magazine tilers, mon* than wool i be any where between Greenwich And GravefrnJ, as the Foundation of the other Places they examined were Clay or Mailli;

besides which, in case of any Accident, the Damage Would not affefil the Navigation of the River, as there are no Banks to destroy; and that Purfleet is likewise free from any of the Objections made against Greenwich, as it lies Four Miles from Grays, Three from Erith, and Two from Avely, the nearest Towns or Villages.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the present Magazine for Gunpowder, near the Town of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, is very improperly and dangerously situated.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That notwithstanding great Care has been taken to support the said Magazine, the same is utterly incapable of being effectually repaired.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Purfleet, in the County of Essex, is a proper Place for the erecting of a Powder Magazine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for taking down and removing the said Magazine at Greenwich.

The Three First of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question.

Admiral Vice Admiral Saunders, Rear Admiral Holmes, and

8aunder», Brigadier General Toiovjhend, being come to the House, Ac. thanked. Mr. Speaker acquainted them. That the House had unaniinouily resolved, that ihe Thanks of this House be given to the Admirals and Generals employed in the glorious and successful Expedition against Quebec-, and Mr. Speaker gave the said Members the Thanks of the House accordingly, as followeth; viz.

Vice Admiral Saunders, Rear Admiral Holmes, Brigadier General Townshend!

The House has unanimously resolved, that their Thanks be given to the Admirals and Generals employed VoL. 28,

in the glorious and successfulExpedition against 2we5ec, with a Direction to me to communicate those Thanks accordingly; and I am to db it to you, Sirs, in this Place, as you are Members of this House, and now present; but with a Reference also to those other great Officers who are likewise included within this Refo-lntion; in the doing of which Service, I never had more Pleasure, as it regards the Subject of it, or more Difficulty, as it respects my Performance of this Command;

What Sentiments or Words shall I life equal to the Occasion f I scarce dare trull to my own*especially after what has been said here, by several honourable Per* fons, on this great and animating Event to us — The Conquell of Quebec: And I do moll earnestly wilh, for my own fake, for yours. Sirs, and for the House, that t might avail myself of their Eloquence, and refer you to that; let it, however, supply my Defers in complying with thisUfage, and Duty of my Office*

The able and valiant Leader, whom the House has so justly celebrated by an Act of public Piety, is, unfortunately for his Country, beyond the Reach of all our Praise: — He is gone fromus; but you providentially remain; and the public Pi aise,so much your Due also, you Sirs, happily for us all, receive in Person — O ur Joy in you is uninixed with any Impressions of Sorrow, except for him your Companion, and those other brave Men who fell with him, but fell with him in Battle, and in Victory — Glorious Deaths, although bemoaned; he and they died for their Country; you hazarded your Lives also for it, but survive for our Security: Continue, then, Sirs, the Honour you have already acquired — Pursue your own Spiritand Ardour whenever the publicDanger shall again call you forth: The Reduction of Quebec, so im* portant to the British Empire and Interestsin that Part of the World, and where the Cause of the War began, and which is our primary and ultimate Consideration of it, mull ever be remembered to your Fame — Ybur grateful Countrymen here, and of America, will, through all Times, recount the Names, the bold and perilous Ad~ ventures, and the amazing Succelfes, of those who conducted this hardy Enterprize — Emulation mufl follow it.

These are Merits worthy the high Acknowlegements of them I am to deliver'to you, which are the Unanimous Thanks of the Commons of Great Britain; and I do give you their Thanks for the Part you had in the glorious and successful Expedition against Quebec

The other Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for granting to his Majesty several Duties upon Malt; and for raising a certain Sum of Money, by way of Annuities and a Lottery, to be charged on the said Duties 5

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause for making forth Duplicates of Exchequer Bills, Lottery Tickets, Certificates, Receipts, Annuity Orders, or other Orders, loft, burnt, or otherwise destroyed.

Mr. Charlton took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Charlton reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

IR Edward Hawke being come to the House, Mr. Adirfal Speaker acquainted him, That the House had un-animously refotved. That the Thanks of this House be an given to him for the fate signal Victory obtained by him over the French Fleet; and Mr. Speaker gave him the Thanks of the House accordingly, as followeth; viz.

Si r Edward Hawke t 1 The House has unanimously resolved, That’ their Thanks be given to you, for the late signal Victory, obtained by you, over the French Fleet.

You are now, Sir, happily returned to your Country, after a long, but moll important Service; and are returned, victorious and triumphant, and full of Honour.;

You meet the Applause of your Countrymen, in their Minds and Hearts, and which they had manifested, before, in all the outward Demonstrations of public Joy and Congratulation. ‘

Your Expedition was for the neared and most affecting Concern to us — The immediate Defence of his Majesty's Kingdoms, against a disappoiuted and enraged Enemy, meditating, in their Revenge, our Definition at once: Your Tnift, therefore, Sir, was of the highed Nature; but to which, your Characters of Courage, Fidelity, Vigilance, and of Abilities, were known to be equal. You soon freed us from Fears; and have answered all our Hopes, that Bravery and Conduct could give, or turbulent Seas and Seasons would admit of — even the lad did not disturb or diminish your Spirit and Vigour. You had over-awed the Enemy in their Ports — in their chief naval Force, till Shame, perhaps, or Defpcration, brought them forth at lad. You fought them, subdued them, and, in their Confusion and Dismay, made those, who could escape, to seek their Security in Flight and Di(grace.

Thus their long-preparing Invasion was, then, broken and dispelled; and which cannot but bring to our Remembrance the Design and the Fate of another Armada, (in a former Age of Glory) whose Defeat was, at that time, the Safety of England, and the lading Renown of the English Navy.

These, Sir, are your late eminent Services to your King and Country, and have been, now, enumerated, not from any Imagination that they are unknown anywhere, or can be ever forgotten, but that your Presence with its makes them to rife, with their first Strength, in our Thoughts, as the Recounting of them mult give us afrelh

33 Geo. II. 28° Januafti.

733

Spirit of Joy, in our Acknowledgements of them. Our Acknowlegements, then, Sir, you have, for these your pad Services: Permit us to add our Expiations, too, of what may be your future Merits, in Defence of the Rights and Honour of your Country, where-ever you shall, again, command.

It is a very pleufing Office to me, to convey these Thanks of the House to you; and I do give you, in the Name of the Commons of Great Britain, their Thanks, for the late signal Victory, obtained by you, over the French Fleet.

Upon which Sir Edward Hawke ftiid.

Mr. Speaker!

I own myself greatly at a Loss, as to the proper Manner of acknowleging the great Honour conferred on me, by this august House, in their distinguished Approbation of my Conduct, on the 20th of November Iaft. In doing my utmost, I only did the Duty I owed my King and Country, which ever has been, and shall be, my greatest Ambition to perform faithfully and ho-neftly, to the bed of my Ability — I can only a dure this honourable House, that I receive this Mark of Honour, with the greated Respect; and shall ever retain the most grateful Sense of it.

Before I fit down, permit me, Sir, in particular, to return you my most respe&ful Thanks for the obliging Manner in which you have communicated to me the great Honour done me by this House, which I shall always edeem as the highed Obligation.

Ordered, Nemine contradicente, That what has been now said by Mr. Speaker, in giving the Thanks of this House to Sir Edward Hawke, together with Sir Edward Hawke's Answer thereto, be printed in the Votes of this Day.

A Petition of the Justices of Peace, Freeholders, and other Heritors, of the County of Forfar, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners are convinced, from Fa6ts and Experience, that the temporary Causes, which produced the Prohibition of making Spirits from Wheat, Barley, or any Sort of Grain, have long ceased in North Britain; and that the further Prohibition of Distillation of Spirits from Grain mull, in its Consequences, be very grievous to the Inhabitants of that Part of the Kingdom; and further alleging, that no Spirituous Liquors are made in that Part of the Kingdom, but those called Aqua Vita9 which are never exported, and are always distilled from Malt made of Big or Bear (a Grain of inferior Quality to Barley) which is the chief Grow th of that Country, and cannot be applied to any other Use, or be sent to any foreign Market: And therefore praying, That the Distillation of the Spirits, called Aqua Vita, may be permitted in the North Parts of Great Britain, in the same Manner as before the late Prohibitions were laid on, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet:

A Petition of the several Land-ow ners and Holders in the Ne ghbourhood of the East Riding of Yorkshire, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the landed Interest, was also presented to the House, and read; representing to the House several ill Consequeiices, which, the Petitioners allege, will arise from the Suppression of the Malt Distillery: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Malt Distillery maybe again restored, to such Degree, and under such Recti i&ions, as may prevent all Abuse thereof; or that the House will grant the Petitioners, and the rest of the landed Interest, such other Relief, as shall teem meet.

A Petition of the several Land-owners and Holders of the Isle of Sheppy and Milton, in the County of Kent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the landed Interest, was also presented to the House, and read; expressing the Hope of the Petitioners, That the Land-owners and Farmers of Great Britain should*not be treated with less Indulgence than the Sugar Colonies, but be allowed the same Opportunities of d ifpofing of the Produce of their Lands: And therefore praying. That the Malt Distillery of this Kingdom maybe again opened, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to take into Const-deration the State of the Distillery.

Mr. Barrow reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and the rest of the Trustees for putting in Execution an Act, made in the 20th Year of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for continuing the Term and enlarging the Powers granted by an Act, passed in the 12th Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Roads from the City of Gloucester to the City of Hereford, and for repairing other Roads, in the County of Gloucester; and also of several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Freeholders or Inhabitants of the said County of Gloucester; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The said Acts were read: And,

Mr. Edward Driver, being examined, said. That he has been Clerk to the Trustees for repairing the said Roads 14 or 15 Years — That about £. 500 a Year has been expended upon the said Roads for many Years — That there is at present a Debt of above£. 700 on the Tolls; and that some Parts of the Roads are now almost impastable.

That the said Act, of the 20th of his present Majesty, does not impower the Trustees to borrow Money'; nor to punish Persons passing through private Grounds, to evade the Payment of the Tolls:

That the said Act is in many other Respects defective; and it will be impossible to repair the said Roads, unless the Term and Powers thereby granted are further enlarged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Term of, and enlarging and altering the Powers granted by, an Act, made in the 20th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for repairing and widening certain Roads leading from the City of Gloucester towards the City of Hereford, and for repairing other Roads in the County of Gloucester, in the said Act mentioned; and for making the said Act more effectual: And that Mr. Barrow, Mr. Prolan, and Mr. Foley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present high Price of spirituous Liquors is a principal Cause of the Diminution in the Home Consumption thereof, and hath greatly contributed to the Health, Sobriety, and Industry of the common People.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in order to continue for the future the present high Pride of all Spirit& used for Home Confomption, a large additional Duty belaid upon all spirituous Liquors whatsoever, distilled within, or imported into, Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be a Drawback of the said additional Duties upon all spirituous Liquors, distilled in Great Britain, which shall be exported.

Resolved, That it is the Opinkm of this Committee, That an additional Bounty be granted, under proper Regulations, upon the Exportation of all spirituous Liquors drawn from Corn in Great Britain.

The said Reflations, being severally read a Second 4ime, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition,

 An Act of Parliament, passed in the n& and 23d Years of the Reign of Kin gCharles the Second, intituled, An Act for settling and preserving the Navigation of the River Wei), in the County of Surrey, was read.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners called,

Mr. Richard Stedman: Who, being examined, said. That the River Wey is navigable from Guildford to the Thames, at Wey Bridge; and that it is very practicable to continue the Navigation up to Godalming, which is about Fout* Miles from Guildford: That he has surveyed the River, and thinks there are no more Obstructidns than are common in all Navigations.

Mr. John Smeaton said, That he has been frequently employed in making Rivers navigable; and that he has surveyed the River Wey, from Guildford to Godalming, which he takes to be about Four Miles: That the River is very capable of being made navigable for £. 5,000; in which he includes £.800, for contingent Expences; but that there is an Alteration necessary to be made at Guildford Bridge, which will make an additional Expence of £.600: That there are no particular Inconveniences attending this Navigation, which he thinks as practicable as any other.

Mr. Thomas Wilkinson said, That he lives at Godal-viing; and that the CountryTen or Twelve Miles to the Shuth and South-eastof that Totvn abounds with Timber: That if the River was made navigable from Guildford to Godalming, there would be a Saving of 2$. 6d. in the Carriage of each Load of Timber in the Space of Five Miles, viz. from Godalming to Guildford; and if the Timber was brought from Eight Miles South of Godalming to Guildford, 4 s. would be saved in the Carriage of every Load, allowing is. per Load for Water Carriage: That there will be the same Kind of Saving in the Carriage of Chalk, which will come to is. 6 d. cheaper from Guildford Pit to Godalming than at present, allowing 15*. 6d. per Load for Water Carriage, of Chalk, which would make a Saving of gos. in every Kiln of Lime: That more than Half of the Timber brought to Guildford comes through Godalming; and that there are great Quantities of Timber left on Commons, which cannot be brought to Guildford in One Day; and at present there are near 3,000 Loads on Hambledon Common, and Places adjacent, which might ba brought to Godalming inOne Day, if the Navigation was made, which would save the Expence of loading and unloading, which occasions great Delay, and colls is. per Load.

Upon the 2d mentioned Petition,

Mr. John Holies said. That he lives at Lodfworih, in Sussex: That if the River Wey was made navigable from Godalming to Guildford, it would ihorten the Land Carriage from the several Parishes mentioned in the Peti-. tion, so that the Farmers, who are now obliged to lay out a Night with their Carriages, might return home in Ope Day, by which 6 5*. or 7s. would be saved in each Journey: That about 4 s. a Load would be saved in the Carriage of Timber, Charcoal, Meal, and oth^r Things: That Chalk may be had at Godalming for 3 s. 6 d. per Load by Water Carriage, which would be a Saving of 6 s. or 7 s. a Load on all the Chalk which the Witness is obliged to carry to an Estate he now occupies at Lurgu-falc\ and that there would be a Saving of bet ter than 50$. in each Kiln of Lime: That the completing the said Navigation will be a general Benefit to the whole Country, from the South, South-east,and South-weft of Godalming: That the Advantages would extend i6*or 17 Miles from

And the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as lolloweth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the general Admission of all Children indiscriminately, under a certain Age, into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Children, to be maintained there at the public Expence, has been attended with many evil Consequences, and ought to be prevented.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Children should be received into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of exposed and deserted young Children, after the Twenty-fifth Day of March next, to be there maintained at the public Expence.

THE Lord Strange reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners appointed by and in pursuance of an Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for rtiaking the River Weaver navigable, from Frodsham Bridge to Winsfard Bridge, in the County of Chester, and of several Gentlemen, Manufacturers, and other Inhabitants, of the said County, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for making the River Weaver navigable, from Frodsham Bridge to Wins-ford Bridge, was read: And,

Mr. John Barrow, being examined, said, That the River Weaver was made navigable in pursuance of the said Act, and that the Navigation was once very good; but that One Lock is quite destroyed, by the falling in of the Koof of a Salt Rock Pit, which was funk by the Proprietor of the Land near the Lock, and worked under the Bed of the River.

Mr. Thomas Kent, Clerk to the Commissioners for executing the said Act, being examined, said. That One Half of the said Lock is fallen into the Rock Pit, and there buried: That the Lock is destroyed, and cannot be repaired or rebuilt in the same Place; and that it will cost above a thousand Pounds to erect a new Lopk, as he apprehends:

That Persons using the Navigation frequently damage the Works, by running their Vessels again (I them:

That the Ad is defective in many Respects, particularly, that there is not any Method appointed for the Recovery of Satisfaction for the Damage done by the Destruction of the said Lock, or for any other Damages of the like Nature; and that the present Undertakers cannot support Actions with respect to Damages done to the Works of the Navigation, such Undertakers not having any legal Property therein: That there is not any Penalty on Persons sinking Boats, and leaving them so as to obstrud the Navigation: That the Commissioners have noControui over the Undertakers, with respect to the making or maintaining the said Navigation: That there is not any Penalty on Persons unnecessarily opening, or leaving open, the Locks: That the Owners of Vessels are not obliged to set their Names, or mark the Tonnage, on their Vessels; and that the Commissioners have not Power to make By-laws or Orders for regulating the said Navigation.

Mr. Barroxo, being again examined, confirmed Mr. Kent's Evidence in respect to the several Defects in the Ad.

Then several Clauses in the said Act were read; setting forth. That after the said River was made navigable, the Highways leading to the said River, between Frod-sham Bridge and Winsford Bridge, would be more used by Carriages bringing Salt and Salt Rock, to be conveyed on the said River, and consequently the Expences of repairing inch Highways would become a greater Burthen to the Persons who are to repair the same than theretofore; and enading, that after the said Navigation

14

should be completed, and all the Expenses attending the fame, and all Money borrowed on the Credit of 1 lie said Act, fully paid and satisfied, that so much of the clear Produce of the Rates and Duties granted by the said Act, as the Justices, at their Quarter Sessions, should think fit, should be employed in amending the said Roads: And,

Mr. Barrow, being again examined, said, That there is not any Road to the North Side of Witton Bridge (were that Part of the Navigation terminates) but by Witton Brow, which is at present very dangerous:

That, by the sinking of the Roof of a Salt Rock Pit,

Part of the said Road fell in, and the Remainder is now so narrow, that a Cart can hardly pass along it; and that if the said Road was repaired, or a new Road made, great Quantities of Salt would be brought that Way to the Navigation.

And both the Witnesses said, That it will be impossible to improve and preserve the said Navigation, unless the said Act be amended and rendered more effectual.

And Mr. Barrow, added, That he thinks the most proper Method to improve the Navigation would be, to put it under the Direction of the Commissioners and Trustees: And that he apprehends, it could not be carried on so well if it were made private Property.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for making the River Weaver navigable, from Frodsham Bridge to Winsford Bridge, in the County of Chester; and for the more effectual preserving and improving the Navigation of the said River: And that the Lord Strange, Mr. Thoroton, and Mr. Grosvenor, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

S*?«ing mittee, to tyhom the Petition of the several Fishermen > grading to Billingsgate Market, whole Names are thereunder written, qp Behalf of tfiepiselves, and all others the Fishermen trading to that Market, was referred, /jT^iat the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as feUoweffi; viz.

To prove tfye Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act passed in the 2zd Year of his present Majesty’s Reign^for jqaking a Free Market for the SaleofEilh in the City of Y^efiminster, and for preventing the Fore-stalling and Monopolizing of Fish, and for allowing the §ale offifli, under tkeDipaenfionsmentioned inaClause, qontainedmap Act of the First Year of his late Majefry’s Ij^eign, in case the same are faken with a Hook \ and also an Act, passed in the 29th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for explaining, amending, and rendering more effieaual, the said Act-, were read: And,

Mr. Isaac Cook, aFilherman, trading to fy'llingfgate Market, being exaraiued, said, That being obliged to make their Entry at Gravesend, subjects them to great Hardships, as they are liable, for the Omission thereof, to forfeit both Ship and Cargo; and it frequently happens, they are obliged, by Wind or Tide, to come tq . Woolwich, before (.hey can ftpp their Veffejs: And, that

if they were to Hop at Gravesend, when the Wind and Tide are fair for the London Market, they would lose the Market, as it would take an Hour or Two to stop; and the Searchers at Gravesend are not constantly at their Office there, to receive the Entries! And that the Witness has gone there Three or Four Times in a Day, and found no Officer there: That if a Vessel arrives at Gravesend in the Night, and no One is at the Office to receive the Entry, the Ship is liable to be seized, as forfeited, for not making the Entry: And that the heavy Penalties inflicted by the said Acts, are a great Discouragement to the Fifliing Trade, as moll Vessels built for such Trade, used to be built on Credit, and on Loans made thereof; and now, if a Man has not Money to build a Fishing Craft himself, nobody chooses to lend him any thereon, as the Vessels are liable to be forfeited for the Omission of Entering thereof; and the Penalty being so great, most Mailers of Vessels go themselves to make the Entries, as they are not willing to trull to their Servants going to do the fame; and the said Inconveniences occasion the Fish to come much dearer to Market: That the Witness has Two Vessels, both which he is obliged to trull to the Care and Management of very indifferent People, often taken from the Parish, not One in Ten of whom can write: And that he has known several Fifliing Vessels seized by the Omission of Servants in not making their Entries at Gravesend; and that lately the Mailer of a Vessel having differed with his Owners, omitted, with a fraudulent Design, to make the Entry, in order to subject the Owners to the Penalty.

M v.Joseph Clark confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Cook.

Wolverley A Petition of tVie Inhabitants of Wolverley, in the Road. County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners find, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill, for the amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, several Roads leading from the Market House, in the Town of Kidderminster, in the County of Worcester; and setting forth, That the Roads branching out of and leading from the High Road leading by Broad Waters, intended to be repaired by the said Bill, through the Breach Lane to Wolverley, and from thence to Wrib-benhall, in the Way to Bewdley Bridge, in the said County, also intended by the said Bill to be repaired, are in divers Places so ruinous, that in the Winter Season, Carriages, and PersonS on Horsebcck, cannot pass without great Danger; and that the said Roads are in many Parts very narrow and incommodious, and cannot be effectually amended and kept in Repair, by the Laws now in being: And therefore praying, That in the said Bill Provision may be made for the better amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the said Roads leading from Broad Waters through the Breach Lane to Wolverley, and from thence to Wribbeniiail aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Sir Robert I.tidbroke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition;' and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where , the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr, George Dance, Surveyor, and Mr. Benjamin Blag-den, Builder, being severally examined, said, That there are several Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the City of London, and Liberties thereof, which are very narrow and incommodius for Foot Passengers, and also for Coaches and other Carriages.

Then two Papers, containing an Account of the proposed Openings and Enlargements, together with a Plan thereof,(which1 are hereunto annexed, and marked N° 1, N* 2, and N° 3,) were produced; and the Witnesses informed your Committee, that if Openings and Enlargements were made in the Places and Manner described in the said Papers, it would be very advantageous to the Trade of the City of London, and to the Public in

Jeneral.

Mr. Alderman Gojling and Mr. Richard Peers, eing examined, said. That there are many Houses within the said City and Liberties, wherein the several Floors or Rooms are the Property and Freehold of different Persons, whereby Disputes are frequently occasioned between them, touching the pulling down and rebuilding the Fremifes, or the Party Wallsthereof; and such Rebuilding is thereby often prevented, to the great Injury of such of the said Owners as are desirous to rebuild; and the Witnesses gave several Instances of Houses so circumstanced, and particularly mentioned Four Houses in the Parish of 2ueenhith, which belong to the City, except One Chamber up One Pair of Stairs, which is private Property, and which the City were desirous of purchasing, in order to rebuild the said Monies; but the Person who treated with them not being able to make a legal Title thereto, the said Houses remain in a ruinous condition, and cannot be rebuilt.

Mr. John Philips confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Alderman Gojllug and Mr. Peers; and added, that, in some Houses, the upper Stories project further than the lower, so that no Defence can be made by Party Walls to secure such Monies from Fire.

Then an Act 110 Georgii 1 ‘ relating to the building of Party Walls, was read: Aud,

Leeds Bridge. Mr. Wilkinson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, and Inhabitants, of the Borough and Parish of Leeds, in the County of York, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was re-ferred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Hr. Henry} Stables, being examined, said, That the Bridge over the Riverwithin the TownlhipofLa?flfr, called Leeds Bridge, is a Riding Bridge, and stands in the public Road from London to Edinburgh, by way of Derby, Sheffield, Wakefield, Leeds, Knaresborough, and Boroughbridge, or Ripon.

Mr. Robert Parker, being examined, said. That, by Length of Time, and the great Number of Waggons and Carts frequently passing over the fame, the said Bridge is greatly decayed, and requires a speedy Repair, and that the Passage over the said Bridge is greatly confined, by reason of the Narrowness of the Road over, and the Buildings, and other Encroachments made and erected at both Ends, and upon the Abutments of, the said Bridge, and that it is very dangerous to Passengers on Foot and on Horseback.

Then a Copy of an Order, made at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the West Riding of the County of York, held at Pontefract the 23d of April 1759, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Sum of £.1450 was granted for repairing and widening the said Bridge: And,

John Lee Esquire, being examined, said, That the said Sum of £.1450 will not be sufficient to repair and widen the said Bridge, as it will be absolutely necessary to purchase and take down some Buildings (landing upon, or adjoining near to, the said Bridge, to open the Avenues thereto; and that it is pfoposed to raise a Sum of Money Vol. 28.

on the Township of Leeds, sufficient for that Purpose, which cannot be done without 'the Aid of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a.Rill for raising Money, for the fin idling and completing the Repair of Leeds Bridge, in the County of York, and for the purchasing and taking down the^doufes and Buildings which straiten and obstruct the Passage to and over the said Bridge: And that Mr* Wilkinson, Mr. Re- . corder of London, the Lord Carysfort, and Sir George r Savile, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And an Amendment was made by the House to the Bill.

Sir William Peere Williams reported from the Com mi t-' tee, to whom the Petition of the Constable and Inhabitants of the Borough of New Shoreham, in the County of Safer, and of several Persons, Inhabitants of the Boroughs of Horsham, Bramber, and Steyning, and other Places in the said County, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petition,

Captain Henry A rthur. Commander of a Custom -hou fe Sloop at Shoreham, informed your Committee, That the Harbour of New Shoreham hath been (till within these Seven or Eight Years pad) a commodious and safe Harbour for Shipping; but that the Navigation into the same is now become very dangerous and difficult, occasioned by Shoals being thrown up at the Entrance of the said Harbour — That the said Harbour is situated in the most dangerous Part of the Channel, and the deeped Part of the Bay between Spilhead and Beachy, where the Witness has seen Twelve Vessels alhore at a time; and that, by constructing a proper Pier or Piers, the said Harbour might be rendered safe and commodious for Ships of considerable Burthen, and as good as any in England, and be of great Utility and Advantage to that Part of the Country, and Parts adjacent — That where the intended Harbour is proposed (which is opposite to Kingstone, and a Mile and an Half below Shoreham) there is Nine Feet Water at low Water, and is Two Miles to the Eadward of where the Harbour now is — That the Duties that might have been raised, upon an Average, for Twenty Years pad, according to the Duties of Hampton and Newhaven, would have been sufficient to pay the Interest of £.10,000.

And, being alked the Quedion, he said. He apprehended the lay ing a Duty only upon Ships coming into the Harbour, would not be sufficient to maintain the fame; but that it is proposed to lay a Duty upon all Vessels that land or ship Goods within the Limits of the Harbour, which Limits extend Eight or Nine Miles to the Eadward, and Five or Six Miles to the Wedward, of the present Harbour.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for erecting Piers, and other Works, for the Security and Improvement of the Harbour of Nezo Shoreham, in the County of Suftx, and for keeping the same in Repair: And that Sir William Peere Williams, Mr. Brifiozve, Mr. Frederick Montagu, the Lord North, and the Lord Jlowe, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Justices and Grand Juries, present at Poor Law. the General Quarter Sefiio ns of the Peace, and the several Adjournments thereof, holden for the County of Norfolk, next after Epiphany One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty, was prefen ted to‘the House, and read; alleging, That the Charge of maintaining the Parochial Poor of this Kingdom is become so extremely burthensome, that the Occupiers of Lands and Houses are scarce able to bear it: That an Evil of this Nature should be so long and so fenflbly felt in a trading Nation, which wants Hands in Husbandry, and in every Branch of Business, the Petitioners apprehend must be owing to some Defect in the Poor Laws, and to the Want of a more eflfectual Method of providing for the Poor, by which the Aged and Impotent may be better sustained, and the Idle and Profligate in some measure made serviceable to the Community; and that it was with the utmost Satisfaction the Petitioners observed the serious Attention paid in the last Session, to this important Matter: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into further Consideration, and grant such Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, T[\2X the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Charterers, Land-owners, London Leaseholders, and Inhabitants, of the Township of Long- Indofwt ton, in the County of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunder severally subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners take Notice, that a Petition has been presented to the House, to inclose or dint certain Parels of wade Ground in Long-ton aforesaid, containing about 750 Statute Acres; and representing to the House, that although the said common or waste Grounds be open and uncultivated, yet the same (especially the Higher Marsh) are very good Pasture Lands, and cannot.in any respect he more improved; and that the same have been immemorially used and enjoyed as Common of Pasture, as well by the Charterers and Land-owners, as also by the Cottagers and Inhabitants living within the said Township, for all their Cattle and Geele, without Number, as they were able to keep (but confiding chiefly of Sheep and Scotch Cattle), without any Molestation from the Lords of the Manor, or any of the Landholders within the said Township, to the very great Relief and Maintenance of several Families redding within the said Township; and that that Part of the said common or waste Grounds, called the Lower Marsh, is so near to the Sea, that One Half of the fame, or more, is overflowed at Spring Tides, on which account it will be impossible to inclose or Hint the same with any Certainty; and that although by the inclosing or dinting the fame, in Exclusion of the Inhabitants and Cottagers, the Charterers, Land-owners, and Leaseholders, would reap greater Benefit from the Common than they do at present, yet, as the inclosing and dinting the same w'ould be attended with many great Inconveniences and Lofies to the Inhabitants and Cottagers, by depriving them of their Right of Common (to which they apprehend they have an indisputable Right, as having a prescriptive Right of Common of Pasture in the said waste Grounds) and, in its Consequences, would tend to the great Impoverishment, and utter Ruin of many Families, and cauling the greatest Part of them to become chargeable to the said Township: In Consideration whereof, and forasmuch as the greatest and heaviest Part of the Taxes would, in that Cafe, fall upon the smallest Land-owners; as the Lord*

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford, was also presented to the House, and read; representingto the House the great Detriment which, the Petitioners allege, the Exportation of Iron Chapes for Buckles is to the Buckle Manufacture in this Kingdom; since, if Chapes were not exported as an imperfect Manufacture, an equal Quantity at lead would be exported when finished with the Buckles: And therefore praying, That such effectual Measures may be taken for Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matters thereof; and report the fame, as they shall appear to them, to the House:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That there shall be granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of LowWines or Spirits, of the First Extraction, made or drawn from any Sort of Drink or Walh, brewed or made from any Sort of Malt or Corn, or from
