Brewer Wadi or Tiits, or any Mixtures with such Brewers Wash or Tilts, Five Pence, over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Oilfillers or Makers thereof.

Refdved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there shall be granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Strong Waters or Aqua Vine, made for Sale*, of the Materials aforesaid, One Shilling and Three Pence, over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there shall be granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Low Wines or Spirits, of the First, Extraction, made or drawn from any foreign or imported Materials, or any Mixture therewith, One Shilling and Three Pence, over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there shall be granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Spirits, made or drawn in Great Britain from any foreign or imported Materials, or any Mixture therewith, Eight Pence, over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there dial I lie granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Low Wines or Spirits, of the First Extraction, made or drawn from Cycler, or any Sort or Kjud of British Materials, except those before mentioned, or any Mixture therewith. Six Pence Three Farthings, ever and above all other Duties charged or chargeable j thereon, to he paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be-granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Spirits, made for Sale, from Cyder, or any Sort or Kind of Briti/k Materials, except those before mentioned. One Shilling One Penny Three Farthings, over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to he paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof. ‘

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Encouragement of the Exportation of Spirits, drawn or made in Great Britain, the like Drawbacks and Allowances be made, under proper Regulations, upon the Exportation of rectified Spirits drawn or made in Great Britain, as are now payable upon the Exportation of Home-made raw Spirits.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the further Encouragement of the Exportation of Spirits, drawn or made in Great Britain, an additional Drawback or Allowance of Twenty-four Pounds Ten Shillings per Ton, be paid and allowed, under proper Regulations, upo^n the Exportation of all such Spirits.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there shall be granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Single Brandy, Spirits, or Aqua Vitae, imported from beyond the Seas, over and above allother Duties payable for the fame, One Shilling.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there shall be granted and paid to his Majesty, for every Gallon of Brandy, Spirits, or Aqua Vitas, above Proof, commonly called Double Brandy, imported from beyond the Seas,over and above all other Duties payable for the fame, Two Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said several additional Duties shall Hand appropriated, and be applied, to the same Uses and Purposes respectively, as the present Duties on Spirituous Liquors are now applicable and appropriated unto.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

Wheel* on Farmers, and Occupiers of Land, in the County of Wor-Hig ways. C€jier^ ;n behalf of themselves and Numbers of others, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That by several Acts of Parliament lately passed for the Amend-c ment and Preservation of the public Highways and

Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom, the Petitioners find themselves greatly aggrieved by b^ing obliged to make Use of Waggons with Wheels the Breadth of Ninelnches on Turnpike Roads, although they come through Ways to reach the fame,almost impracticable for fuchWaggons to pass, being very narrow, and in many Places deep hollow Ways, the Widening of which would not only be an immense Expence to the several Parities, but would otherwise lay an insupportable Burthen on the little Farmers of 2o, 30, or 40 Pounds a Year, by occasioning them to procure broad wheeled Carriages, which is absolutely out of the Power of too many of them, who would consequently be rendered incapable of carrying the small Produce of their Farms to Market, and Manure to their Lands; that the Use of broad Wheel Carriages, in the Manner they are now drawn, instead of improving, have greatly damaged, even the Turnpike Roads in ihat Part of the Kingdom, which before were generally in good Repair, occasioned, as the Petitioners apprehend, by the said Carriages being drawn double, and as they are restrained to no Weight, carrying such prodigious Burthens,asno lload, however well constructeu, canbear; and that, by quartering the y totally destroy the Horse Road, making Two Ruts too narrow for a Horse to go in, instead of the old Path, so that travelling on Horse-back, on the best Roads in that Part of the Kingdom, is

become notohly disagreeable,biit extremely dangerous; and that, notwithstanding all the Advantages granted by Parliament to broad Wheels, few or none in that County use them (common Stage Waggons excepted), on account of the Inconveniences above set forth, which the Petitioners apprehend would, in a great Measure, if not wholly, be removed, were ail Waggons obliged by Law to be drawn by Horsesat Length, and confined, at lead in those Parts, to certain Weights, and were the Drivers of Carriages obliged to keep such Part of the Road, without crofting or quartering, as shall be directed on Stones or Polls to be set up for that Purpose: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into p

Consideration, and fix the W eight to be carried by all 0

Carriages; and that such Carriages may, as formerly, be ll

drawn at Length, and prevented quartering or crolfing, under the Direction of the Commissioners, or to grant such other Relief as shall seem meet:

Bridge, in the said Township of Stretford; and representing to the House, that the extending the said Navigation to the said Township of Stretford as aforesaid, will be a Means of supplying the Petitioners, and others, residing in and near Altringham, Nether Knutsford, and Stretford aforesaid, and a considerable Part of the said County of Chester, with Coals, upon much better Terms than at present they are capable of procuring the fame, and will be attended with many other beneficial Consequences to the Petitioners and the Public: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may pass into a Law.

; the said former Act; and alleging, that the Tolls, already granted by the said Acts, are as large as the Trade carried on by the Petitioners, and others iifing the said Road, will admit, without being greatly prejudiced thereby; and that fmee the passing the said Acts, the Price of Coals, which is the Fuel chiefly used in those Pacts, and for the Carriage *; 1: whereof, the said Road is the nearest and most commodious for the Inhabitants upon or near the Road, as well as the Rates of Carriage of other Commodities on the said Road, have been considerably increased, and that any further Increase of the said Tolls, especially if the same should be great, or should be applied in the same Manner and Proportion as the said Tolls already granted by the said Acts are made applicable, would not only very greatly distress the Petitioners, if not be totally rn-consistent with the Trade and Welfare of the said Road, but would also be particularly unequal and injurious with regard to the Petitioners, and all other Persons, living in the several Towns and Parishes through, or near which, that Part of the said Road which lieth between Market llarborough aforesaid, and the Market Cross in Thrapston aforesaid, doth pass, in regard that Three-seventhsof the net Produce of all the Tolls granted by the said Acts ;. are appropriated to the Repairs of such Part of the said Road as lieth between the said Market Cross in Thrapston aforesaid, and the said Pound in Brampton aforesaid; and that it hath beenfouud by constant Experience, ever ft bee the palTing the said Acts, and the same will, as the Petitioners apprehend, clearly appear from the Books and Accounts of the said Trustees, and their Receivers and Clerks, that the said Proportion of Three-sevenths of the whole Tolls, hath every Year greatly exceeded the Money that has been annually collected upon that Part of the said Road, to the Repairs whereof the said

Upon examining, on the Part of the Earl of Dyfart,

Mr. Martyr, that he was very willing to accommodate the Public with such Part of his Estate, as should be necessary to carry the said Act into Execution, but did not choose to part with more.

In Cotifequence of which Answer, the Commissioners, upon the 11 tli Day of April 17 58, offered his Lordship £. 2,100 for such Part of his Estate as they adjudged necessary to be possessed of; but his Lordship being informed by his Agent, that the Ground the Coramifliouers thought necessary to be possessed of, was considerably more than the Public had Occasion for, refused the said Offer; whereupon the Commissioners summoned a Jury, wrho viewed the Premisses, for which the said Sum of £.2,100 wfas offered as aforesaid, and the said Jury awarded to his Lordship £.1,517. 11s. o d. for the fame, together with £. 135 to John Lambert, as Lessee of the said Premisses, for his Interest therein.

Mr. Wilkinson reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Freeholders, Inhabitants, and Re* fiants, within the Hundred of High Peak and Manor of Cafileton, in the County of Derby, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mi*. Michael Hall, Deputy Steward of the several Courts Baron belonging to the Hundred of High Peak and Manor of Cafiletom, said, That Plea hath been held in the said Courts every Three Weeks, or as often as requisite, in all perfortal Actions arising within the Jurisdictions of the said Courts, where the Debt hath been under Forty Shillings; and that Justice hath been administered in the most impartial Manner; but that the Method of compelling Persons to appear before the said Court, and the Expences of prosecuting Causes to Judgment, and the removing such Causes afterwards to iu peri or Courts, hath greatly discouraged Creditors from attempting to recover their just Debts: And the Witness added, that the regulating the Proceedings of the said Courts would be very advantageous?to the Persons residing within the Jurisdiction of the tame. Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Method of Proceedings in the several Courts Baron, hi the Petition mentioned, are tedious, expensive, and ineffectual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, for Leave to bring in a Bill for regulating the Proceedings in personal Actions in the said Courts Baron.

The Second Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second time, was upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House,

and for the making and repairing thereof were impowered to take the Toll mentioned in the Petition; and also reciting, that by another Act, made in the 13th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, the Undertakers were impowered to take another Toll, also mentioned in the Petition, to be from time to time applied for and towards the repairing the said Road; and alleging, that the said Navigation being completed up to Tinjley, the Petitioners, in obedience to the said Acts, have made a good Road from Sheffield to Tinjley aforesaid, and havehitherto kept the same in Repair at an Expence amounting to the Sum of £. 3,500 and upwards, over and above all the Income.arisen from the said Tolls; but that, notwithstanding the utmost Care is taken by the Petitioners to maintain the said Road in good Condition, the same is so cut and torn by the great Number of narrow wheeled Carriages passing thereon with Loadings, not only to and from the said Wharf, and subject to the Tolls aforesaid, but also to and from other Places, and not subject to any Toll for the Repair of the said Road; that it is almost impossible for the Petitioners to prefers the said Road as it ought to be, without same legal Restraint, to prevent or discourage such frequent and excessive Use of narrow wheeled Carriages there-oa-; To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Samuel Skye, beingexamined, said, That he knows the Road from Bewdlexj Bridge to Tit (on Brooke: That it is in a ruinous Condition: That it is narrow in divers Places for 30 or 40 Yards, and in one Place for 100 Yards together: That there are hollow Ways, which cannot he avoided, without going some Hundred Yards about: That the Road is frequently overflowed, and that People have been drowned in it; and that when he came out of the Country the Water was Five Feet deep; and that there is not any Bridge for Carriages:

That he apprehends a Toll of an Halfpenny aHorfe and Six Pence a Carriage will be fuftkient to repair the said Road, without interfering with the other Roads:

That he does not know this Road was ever indicted:

That he does not believe the Statute-work sufficient to repair the said Road; but does not know certainly.

Mr. Joseph Oldham, being examined, said, That the Soil of the said Road is loose: That the River is sometimes out for a Month together: That there is only a Horse Bridge; and that the Road is so narrow in some Places, that a Horse cannot pass by a Carriage.

Sir Edward Winnington Baronet, being examined, said. That the Road is very narrow, and bad; and that there is only a Horse Bridge; but he never saw the Water out:

That this is the common Road from Bewdley to Worcester:

That he does not know, that this Road was ever indicted; but believes it cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law.

And Sir Edward Winnington and Mr. Skye both said. That they think it will be proper to make Provision in the Bill, for repairing the several Roads from the Market House in Kidderminster, for applying the Tolls separately to the respective Roads on which they shall be collected.

And he moved the House, That the said Petition be now read.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, with great Pleasure, observed the happy Consequences produced upon the Morals, Behaviour, Industry, and Health, of the lower Class of People, fi nee the Prohibition of the Malt Distillery; and alleging. That the Petitioners observe, that a Bill is brought in to allow the distilling of Spirits from Corn; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Encouragement given

Vol. 28.

Petitioners conceive the Advantages proposed to be allowed upon the Exportation of such Spirits, being lb much above the Value of the Commodity, will lav such a Temptation for Smuggling and Perjury, as no Law can prevent; and expressing the Fears of the Petitioners, that should such a Bill pass into a Law, the excessive Use of Spirituous Liquors will not only debilitate and enervate the Labourers, Manufacturers, Sailors, Soldiers, and all the lower Class of People, and thereby extinguish Industry, and that remarkable Intrepidity and Courage which has lately so eminently appeared in our Fleets and Armies, but also inflame those intoxicated with its malignant Efficacy, to perpetrate the moll heinous Crimes, Whereby the Opulence and Power of the Nation, which mud always depend on the Vigotir and Industry of its People, and its Liberty and Happiness, which cannot be supported without Temperance and Morality, will be, as the Petitioners apprehend, in the utmost Danger of being destroyed; and that the Petitioners are also further apprehensive, that the extraordinary Consumption of Bread Corn, by the Still, will not only so raise the Price, as to oppress the lowerClafs of People, but will be fuel) a Bar to the Exportation thereof, as to deprive this Nation of a great Influx of Money, at this Time so essential for carrying on the present just and necessary War, and thereby highly injure the landed and commercial Interest: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and that the present Prohibition of distilling Spirits from Corn may be continued, or that Wheat may not be permitted to be used inDistillation,or that the Petitioners ttiay have such other Relief, as to the House shall feeni meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That all Committees have Leave to fit, not* Committees, withstanding any Adjournment of the House.

praying for Leave to bring in a Bill for prohibiting the Exportation of such Iron Chapes; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, if such a Bill should pass into a Law, the whole Body of Iron Chape Manufacturers, would be rendered entirely dependent on the Buckle-nmkers, and be reduced to the melancholy Alternative of seeking t heir Support in some other Way of Business at Home, or transporting themselves and Families into foreign Countries; and that the Profits arising to the Petitioners from the manufacturing and vending of Chapes are so very small, that it is with great Difficulty the Petitioners, with the utmost Exertion of their. A Petition of the Merchants, Factors, and Traders, of the Cities of London and Westminster, was also presented to the House, and read; representing to the House, several Disadvantages, which, the Petitioners allege, have arisen to the Trade of Buckle-making, from the Exportation of Iron Chapes; and alleging. That the Chape Makers, taking Advantage of the great foreign Demand for Chapes, and well knowing that they are not able to get up asufficient Quantity toanswer the home as well as the foreign Demand, have advanced their Prices to such a Degree, that the Buckle Makers cannot afford tocome up to, by which Means a great Number of Hands employed in the making of Buckle Rings, stand dill for want of Chapes, to complete the Buckles, and will, if some Relief be not found out,be obliged to desert the Business, whereby the foreign Buckle Trade muff, as the Petitioners apprehend, be greatly lessened in this Country, if not totally loft: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Jarrit Smith reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Citizens of Bristol, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; and also the Petition of the Mayor, Rurgeffes, and Commonalty, of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal; were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and Ire read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

L To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions,

Abraham Elton Esquire, being examined, said. That the Bridge at Bristol, over the River Avon, leads from the County of Gltficester, and from Wales, to the Western Parts of England:

That the Passages over the said Bridge, and through the several Streets and Avenues leading thereto, are extremely narrow and inconvenient; and that Accidents frequently happen to Persons and Carriages passing to and over the said Bridge, to the great Hindrance ot Trade and Commerce:

That the Foundation of the said Bridge has been examined by several experienced Workmen, and appears to be good; and capable of such Improvement, by rebuilding thereupon, ns will be of great Advantage to the Navigation; That taking down the Houses on the said Bridge, and widening the Streets, Lanes, Ways, and Passages, leading thereto, and removing other Annoyances and ObstruCHons, will be very advantageous: That it will be necessary to build a temporary Bridge while the old one is repairing:

And that, after the rebuilding of the said Bridge, and opening the said Passages (if the several Inconveniences . should not be fully remedied), it may be very necessary to build another Stone Bridge over the said River, and ' open proper Avenues thereto.

Several Members present confirmed Mr. EUon's Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for rebuilding, widening, and enlarging, the Bridge over the River Avon, in the City of Bristol, and erecting a temporary Bridge adjoining, and for widening the Streets, Lanes, Ways, and Passages, leading thereto; and for building another Bridge over some other Part of the said River, within the said City, if necessary, and for opening proper Ways and Passages thereto: And that Mr. jarrit Smith, the Lord Carysfort, and Mr.

Nugent, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

and also that Transfer Books should be kept, in which, and not otherwise, the Proprietors should, by Writing under their Hands, assign and transfer their Shares to any Person who should accept the same in the said Transfer Books, likewise in Writing under their Hands; and, lastly, that no Benefit of Survivorship should be claimed by any of the Proprietors, except the Trustees, in respect of the Trust Estateoniy; but that the Persons to whom the Proprietors should by Will, or Writing under their Hands, give the fame, or in Default there- of, their Heirs at Law, should be intitled to the fame, and to all Privileges thereunto belonging, it being the express Intent of the Parties that theundisposed of Shares of the Proprietors should go to their Heirs at Law, but not to their Executors or Administrators.

That he had carefully looked over the said Minute Book, but had not found therein any Order, either of a general Meeting or grand Committee, to warrant or authorize fuqh Division or Multiplication, save as aforesaid -y but that it appeared by the first of said Leidgers, that in fast the said 220 old Shares were so divided or multiplied, and by the subsequent Leidger, that the said 8^00 new Shares were therein polled to the several Accounts of the Persons in whose Names the said 220 old Shares then flood.

And the said Mr. Paterson produced and laid before vour Committee an Account in Writing,which he said he had drawn from the said Transfer Books and Leidgers; and believed to be a true Account, containing the Names of the original Proprietors of the said 220 old Shares in the Year 1699, and the respective Proportions of Shares they were severally intitled to, and also the Namesof the Proprietors of the said Shares, who in the said Year 1720 fold the said 220 old Shares to a new Set of Proprietors; and also the Names of the Proprietors whose 220 old Shares were divided or multiplied into 8,800 new Shares; and also shewing that of the said 8,800Shares?, 233 Shares still remain in the said Books, in the Names of the original Proprietors thereof; and that 1158 Shares have been expunged or annihilated; and that 3,681 Shares have been transferred to, and now Hand in, the Books of the said Partnership, in the Name of Jcihn Belt, in Trust for the said Partnership; and that 3,728 Shares, Hefidue of the said 8,800 Shares, have been transferred to, and now Hand in, the said Books, in the Names of sundry Persons, as Proprietors thereof.

And the said Mr. Paterson produced and laid before your Committee a List of the several Persons Names, who, as appears by the said Leidgers, were, in the Year 1726, intitled to Shares in the said Partnership, by virtue of Transfers thereof made to them.

And the said Mr. Paterson said, that there being several Persons who, by virtue of such Receipts as aforesaid, figued and given by the said Thomas Storey in the said Year 1720, claimed to be intitled to Shares in the said Partnership, which had never been transferred to them, Notice was given in the following public Papers, which he produced and laid before your Committee; to wit, the London Gazettes of the 19th of August and 20th of September 1 735, and the Daily Advertisers of the 2 ill and 28th of August, and of the 3d and 12th of September, 1755, for the Proprietors of Shares, or the Receipts for Shares, in the Penjylvania Land Company of London, to apply unto the said Thomas Hyam and Son, in order for the preparing of an Account of the whole Number of Shares and to whom they belonged.

A Petition of the Noblemen, Gentlemen, Justices of Scotch Peace, and Commissioners of Supply, of the Shire of Ayr, met at Ayr the 19th of March One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty Years, was presented to the House, and read; testifying the Approbation of the Petitioners of that wife and salutary Measure which has lately taken place in South Britain, the Establishment of a regular Militia; and alleging, that the Petitioners lliould think themselves wanting in their Duty to their Country, lliould they on this Occasion omit representing to the House the Petitioners ardent Willies to fee the Benefit of that wife and salutary Measure extended to North Britain; and which they have the greatest Reason to hope for, as by the Articles of Union they are undoubtedly intitled to be on the same Footing; and that the just Dread which that defenceless Part of the Country was thrown into from the late threatened Invasion, by a contemptible Number of French, under Thurot, will, the Petitioners hope, open the Eyes of those who perhaps never thought of it before, and convince them, that, both from Necelftty and Justice, the Power of Self-defence ought to be equally granted ro the whole People of the United Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Connderation, and to do therein as to them shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better ordering of the Militia Forces, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, be read a Second time.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Bonner and Mr. Browning:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for preventing the excessive Use of spirituous Liquors, by laying additional Duties thereon; for Shortening the Prohibition of making low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or other Grain, and from Meal, Flour and Bran; for encouraging the Exportation of British-made Spirits; and for more effectually securing the Duties payable upon Spirits, and for preventing the fraudulent Re-landing or Importation thereof; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for extending and continuing the Navigation of the River Wey, otherwise Wye, in the County of Surrey, to the Town of Godalming, in the said County, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Roads from Hale-worthy, in the Parish of Davidstow, in the County of Cornwall, to the East End of Wade Bridge, in the said County, and from the West End of Wade Bridge aforesaid, into and through the Borough of Mitchell, in the said County, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing several open Fields, Meadows, and Commons, within the Lordship and Liberty of Sea-grave, in the County of Leicester, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the dividing and inclosing the open Fields, Meadow, and common Pasture Grounds, and waste Grounds, in the Manor and Parish of Hawksworth, in the County of Nottingham, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Amendments, made by this House, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing a certain Common, or open Piece of w’afte Ground, in the Parish or Township of Hartjhill, with Woodhall, in the County of York.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinburgh, was presented to the House, and read; reciting, That, by an Act, passed in the 29th Year of his Majesty’s Reign, " for the better " supplying the City of Edinburgh with fresh and wholesome Water," the Petitioners were impowered to collect any Springs of Water, within a certain Distance of the Reservoir therein described, and to convey such Water to the said City, by Pipes, for the Use of the Inhabitants; and that a Method is therein laid down for ascertaining the Value or Consideration to be paid to the Proprietors of any Lands, from or through which such Springsand Water may be collected and conveyed; and alleging, that the Necessity of providing this further Supply of Water never appeared so remarkable as within these few Months past; for, during that Period, the inferior and most numerous Class of the Inhabitants have been reduced to Extremity, and those of the highest Rank have suffered the greatest Inconveniency by want of Water; and that, while this Distrefe continues, the whole City mull be exposed to the greatest Danger by every accidental Fire, which, from the Height and Closeness of the Buildings, may be more fatal there than in any other City; and that the Petitioners, in prosecuting the Purposes of the above Statute, were opposed by a Gentleman, from whose Grounds they proposed to derive a Supply of Water to their Reservoir, which they could find no where else so good and so convenient; that this became the Subject of a Law Suit before the Sheriff of the County, and afterwards before the Lords of Session, which rendered the Petitioners uncertain, whether the above Statute would be effectual for the Purposes thereby intended, or not; which Uncertainty has been only removed by a Judgment of the Lords of Session, pronounced upon the Twelfth Day of February loft, whereby the Petitioners are now at Liberty to prosecute the further Execution of the above Statute; and that the Petitioners find, from a late Survey and Estimate, that the Expence of providing the City with Sufficiency of Water will be . attended with much greater Expence than was apprehended, at the time the above Act was passed; and that such Expence cannot be provided for without Authority of Parliament; and that, as these Reasons for an immediate Application to Parliament have but lately occurred, the Petitioners thought it their Duty, without . further Delay, to do every thing in their Power for the immed iate Relief of the Inhabitants, and the Preservat ion of the City itself, and flatter them selves, that the Necessity of the same will move the House to allow a Bill to be brought in for rendering more effectual the Purposes of the former Act, notwithstanding their Resolution, of the 14th of November last, to receive no Petitions for private Bills after the 26th Day of January now past: And therefore praying, that in respect of the special Circumstances, and great Necessity of this Cafe, to receive their Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the more effectual carrying into Execution the Act of the 29th of his Majesty above-mentioned, and for providing a Fund for carrying the Purposes of that Act into Execution.

And the House being informed by several Members of the House, That the several Circumstances set forth in the said Petition had happened as is therein described; and that, if some further Provision be not speedily made, the said City will, from want of a sufficient Supply of Water, be exposed to great Danger by Fire;

Ordered, That, upon Consideration only of the very particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinburgh, and of the Information now given to the . House, Leave be given to exhibit aPetition for bringing in a Bill, as desired by the said Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinburgh, in their laid Petition just now read.

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council, of Edinburgh, was presented to the House, and read; containing the same Recital, as i mentioned in the said last preceding Petition; and alleging, that the Petitioners find, that a considerable Sum will be necessary for carrying the said Act into Execution, and particularly a great Expence must be laid out in digging for and collecting the Springs, and laying the Pipes through the fame, building Reservoirs and erecting Stopcocks, and for defraying the Expence of the Carriages which will be wanted, and for purchasing and laying the Pipes, besides what must be paid to the Proprietors, in whose Grounds the Springs are found, or through which it may be necessary to conduct the Water; and a further annual Expence will be necessary for keeping these Works in Repair; and that the Petitioners find, that the ordinary Revenue of the Town is altogether insufficient for answering those Purposes; and that, as the providing the Town with fresh and wholesome Water, is of the utmost Importance to every Individual, so it is just and reasonable, that the Expence should be levied from the Heretors, and other Inhabitants, in such Manner as the House shall judge proper: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting to the Petitioners a Power to levy from the Heretors, or other Inhabitant?, of Edinburgh, such Sum as shall be necessary for executing the Purposes of the said Act of the 29th of his present Majesty, and such further annual Sum as shall be required for keeping in Repair the Pipes, Reservoirs, and other Works, employed for providing the City with Water.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Ofxvald, Mr. Pole, Lord Advocate of Scotland, Mr. Fuller, Mr. Veilch, Mr. For-refier, Lord Middleton, Mr. Hope, General Cornwallis, Mr. Nor they. A Petition of the Freeholders and Heretors of the Shire of Edinburgh, legally convened by the High Sheriff at Edinburgh, the 19th Day of March 1760, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners being fully convinced, that, in Times of Danger, no Expedient for the Defence of the Kingdom is more constitutional and effectual, than a-well disciplined Militia; and that the Petitioners have observed, with Pleasure, how far an Establishment of this Kind has contributed towards the Safety of One Part of the Island, while they behold, with Regret, the Danger to which the other Part of it has been exposed from their want of the same Means of Safety; and representing to the House. the defenceless State of Scotland, whose extensive Coasts

lie open to the Invasion of the Enemy, while the regular Troops areneceflarily employed in protecting the distant Possessions of Great Britain, or are prudently drawn towards the Center of the Kingdom; and that the Inhabitants of that populous County discover the most ardent Zeal to exert themselves-in maintaining our happy Confutation, and insupporting our most gracious Sovereign: And therefore praying, That a Law may be enacted for establishing a Militia in Scotland, under such Rules and Regulations as to the House shall seem proper, that thereby such an Addition may be made to the internal <and constitutional Strength of the Nation, as will render it more secure in itself, and more formidable to its Enemies.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better ordering of the Militia Forces, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland. be read a Second time.

nburgh A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Water- Council, of the City of Edinburgh, was presented to wor 8‘ the House, and read; reciting, That, by an Act, passed in the 29th Year of his Majesty's Reign," for the better " supplying the City of Edinburgh with fresh and wholesome Water,*' the Petitioners were impowered to collect any Springs of Water, within a certain Distance of the JRefervoir therein described, and to convey such Water to the said City, by Pipes, for the Use of the Inhabitants; and that a Method is therein laid down for ascertaining the Value or Consideration to be paid to the Proprietors of any Lands, from or through which such Springs and Water may be collected and conveyed; and alleging, that the Necessity of providing this further Supply of Water never appeared so remarkable as within these few Months past; for, during that Period, the inferior and most numerous Class of the Inhabitants have been reduced to Extremity, and thofeof the highest Rank have suffered the greatest Inconveniency by want of Water; and that, while this Distress continues, the whole City must be exposed to the greatest Danger by every accidental Fire, which, from the Height and Closeness of the Buildings, may be more fatal there than in any other City; and that the Petitioners, in prosecuting the Purposes of the above Statute, were opposed by a Gentleman, from whose Grounds they proposed to derive a Supply of Water to their Refer-voir, which they could find no where else so good and so convenient; that this became the Subject of a Law Suit before the Sheriff of the County, and afterwards before the Lords of Session, which rendered the Petitioners uncertain, whether the above Statute would be effectual for the Purposes thereby intended, or not; which Uncertainty has been only removed by a Judgment of the Lords of Session, pronounced upori the Twelfth Day of February last, whereby the Petitioners are now at Liberty to prosecute the further Execution of the above Statute; and that the Petitioners find, from a late Survey and Estimate, that the Expence of providing the City with Sufficiency of Water will be attended with much greater Expence than was apprehended, at the time the above A6fc was passed; and that such Expence cannot be provided for without Authority of Parliament; and that, as these Reasons for an immediate Application to Parliament have but lately occurred, the Petitioners thought it their Duty, without further Delay, to do every thing in their Power for the immediate Relief of the Inhabitants, and the Prefervation of the City itself, and flatter themselves, that the Necessity of the same will move the House to allow a Bill to be brought in for rendering more effectual the Purposes of the former Act, notwithstanding their Resolution, of the 14th of November last, to receive no Petitions for private Bills after the 26th Day of January now past: And therefore praying, that in respect of the special Circumstances, and great Necessity of this Cafe, to receive their Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill for the more effectual carrying into Execution the Act of the 29th of his Majesty above-mentioned, and for providing a Fund for carrying the Purposes of that Act into Execution.

And the House being informed by several Members of the House, That the several Circumstances set forth in the said Petition had happened as is therein described; and that, if some further Provision be not speedily made, the said City will, from want of a sufficient Supply of Water, be exposed to great Danger by Fire;

Ordered, That, upon Consideration only of the very particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinburgh, and of the Information now given to the House, Leave be given to exhibit aPetition for bringing in a Bill, as desired by the said Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Council, of the City of Edinburgh, in their said Petition just now read.

A Petition of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council, of Edinburgh, was presented to the House, and read; containing the same Recital, as i mentioned in the said last preceding Petition; and alleging, that the Petitioners find, that a considerable Sum will be necessary for carrying the said Act into Execution, and particularly a great Expence must be laid out in digging for and cohering the Springs, and laying the Pipes through the fame, building Reservoirs and erecting Stopcocks, and for defraying the Expence of the Carriages which will be wanted, and for purchasing and laying the Pipes, besides what must be paid to the Proprietors, in whose Grounds the Springs are found, or through which it may be necessary to conduct the Water; and a further annual Expence will be necessary for keeping these Works in Repair; and that the Petitioners find, that the ordinary Revenue of the Town is altogether insufficient for answering those Purposes; and that, as the providing the Town with fresh and wholesome Water, is of the utmost Importance to every Individual, so it is just and reasonable, that the Expence should be levied from the Heretors, and other Inhabitants, in such Manner as the House shall judge proper: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for granting to the Petitioners a Power to levy from the Heretors, or other Inhabitants, of Edinburgh, such Sum as shall be necessary for executing the Purposes of the said Act of the 29th of his present Majesty, and such further annual Sum as shall be required for keeping in Repair the Pipes, Reservoirs, and other Works, employed for providing the City with Water.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Ofxvald, Mr. Poky Lord Advocate of Scotland, Mr. Fuller, Mr. Veitch, Mr. For-refier, Lord Middleton, Mr. Hope, General Cornwallis,

A Petition of the Freeholders and Heretors of the Shire of Edinburgh, legally convened by the High Sheriff at Edinburgh, the 19th Day of March 1760, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners being fully convinced, that, in Times of Danger, no Expedient for the Defence of the Kingdom is more constitutional and effectual, than a-well disciplined Militia; and that the Petitioners have observed, with Pleasure, how far an Establishment of this Kind has contributed towards the Safety of One Part of the Istand, while they behold, with Regret, the Danger to which the other Part of it has been exposed from their want of the same Means of Safety; and representing to the House. the defenceless State of Scotland, whose extensive Coasts

lie

Ire open to the Invasion of the Enemy, while the regular Troops are necessarily employed in protecting the distant Possessions of Great Britain, or are prudently drawn towards the Center of the Kingdom; and that the Inhabitants of that populous County discover the most ardent Zeal to exert t hemfelve&in maintaining our happy Constitution, and insupporting our most gracious Sovereign: And therefore praying, That a Law may be enacted for establishing a Militia in Scotland, under such Rules and Regulations as to the House shall seem proper, that thereby such an Addition may be made to the internal and constitutional Strength of the Nation, as will render it more secure in itself, and more formidable to its Enemies.

Ordered, That the fetid Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better ordering of the Militia Forces, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Freeholders and Commissioners of Supply, of the County of Stirling, met at Stirling this 12th March 1760, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners, being fully convinced, that, in Times of Danger, no Expedient for the~Defence of the Kingdom isfo constitutionai and effectual as a well disciplined Militia; and that the Petitioners have observed, with PJeafure, how far an Establishment of this Kind has contributed towards the Safety of One Part of

the

aviation.

High Peak, &c. Courts Baron.

33 Geo. II. 3 Aprilis 857

the Kingdom, while they behold, with Pain* the Danger to which the other Part of it has been exposed from their want of the same Means of Safety; and representing to the House the defencelels State of Scotland, whhfe extend ve Coasts lie open to the Invasions of the Enemy, while the great Body of regular Troops are necessarily employed in protecting the distant Possessions of Great Britain, or are prudently drawn towards the Center of the Kingdom; and that the Inhabitants of that populous County discover the moll ardent Zeal to exert themselves in maintaining our happy Constitution, and in l’upporting our gracious Sovereign: And therefore praying. That the Laws xnow in Force, fot* the raising and training the Militia in England, may be extended to Scotland, that thereby Fuch an Addition may be made to the internal andconllitutiona! Strength of the Nation, as will render it more secure in itself, and more formidable to its Enemies.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better Ordering of the Militia Forces, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, he read a Second time.

Mr. Hewclt reported from the Committee, to whom Costock the Bill for dividing and inclosing the open Fields of Incl0Iufc‘ Cojlock, otherwise Cortlingstock, in the County of Not* tingham, and all the Lands and Grounds within the said open Fields, was committed, That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; except Four Persons, whose Properties in the said Fields consist of about Eleven Acres, who having been applied to, refused to sign the Bill; and that the whole of the Lands intended to be inclosed consists of about 726 Acres, or thereabouts; and that no Person appeared before the Committee to oppose the Bill; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, to impower the Proprietors to charge their Lands with Money for defraying the Expences of passing and executing the Act.

And the said Clause was twice read, with Blanks; which being filled up, the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

A Petition of the Freeholders and Commissioners of Sc?^ Supply, of the County of Stirling, met at Stirling this 12th March 1760, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners, being fully convinced, that, in Times of Danger, no Expedient for the'Defence of the Kingdom isfo constitutional and effectual asawell disciplined Militia; and that the Petitioners have observed, with Pleasure, how far an Establishment of this Kind has contributed towards the Safety of One Part of

Googte-

33 Geo. II. 3° Apr Ms. 857

the Kingdom, while they behold, with Pain., the Danger to which the other Part of it ha.s been expo fed from their want of the same Means of Safety; and representing to the Mouse the defenceless State of Scotland, whole extensive Coafis lie open to the Invasions of the Enemy, while the great Body of regular Troops are nOceflarily employed in protecting the distant Possessions of Great Britain, or are prudently drawn towards the Center of the Kingdom; and that the Inhabitants of that populous . County discover the moil ardent Zeal to exert them-felvos in maintaining our happy Constitution, and in supporting our gracious Sovereign: And therefore praying. That the Laws xnow in Force, for the raising and training the Militia in England, may be extended to Scotland, that thereby such an Addition may be made to the internal and constitutional Strength of the Nation, as will render it more secure in itself, and more formidable to its Enemies.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better Ordering of the Militia Forces, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Commissioners of Supply, Justices liUtiaLawa ^Fthe Peace* an^ Freeholders, of the County of Perth, Was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the prefen t naked and defenceless State of Nor ill Britain in general,'and of that populous County among others; and that the Petitioners observe the happy Effect already arising from a Militia in South Britain, and, considering that Measure as the most wife, effectual, and constitutional, humbly propose, that a Law may be passed for establishing a Militia, upon proper Regulations, for that Part of the united Kingdom called Scotland; and alleging, that though by the Petitioners local Situation the disarming Act reached that County, there is none in in Great Britain wherein the Seeds of Disaffection are more totally eradicated; and that, united now in Sentiments both of Loyalty and Zeal, the Petitioners make their Requests to the Commons of Great Britain, not doubting that their wife Deliberation, to which the Safety of our Lives, Liberties, and Laws, are intruded, will give due Attention to the ardent Wishes of well-affected Subjects, who anxiously delire to share in the Rights which our happy Constitution intitles them to claim.

An ESTIMATE of the Expence of maintaining, from the 8 th Day of February 1760, exclusive, to the 3 ift of December 1760, inclusive, such Children as were received into the Hospital for the Maintenance and Education of ixposed and deserted young Children, between the said 8th Day of February and the 26th Day of March 1760.

The Number of Children received into the said Hospital, between the 8th Day of February 1760, and the 26th Day of March 1760, is - - - - - - - 834

The Charge of maintaining which 834 Children, from the Time of their FiriT taking in, to the

31st Day of December 1760, inclusive, is imagined may be estimated at - - - - £. 3,127 10 —

being after the Rate of £3. 15. for each Child: The Reason of so Iowan Estimation being ' founded on the very tender Age of the Children so brought in, and the great Mortality which will probably be consequent on the fame.

N. B. The Governors and Guardians beg Leave to observe to this honourable House, that in this, as also in the lateEstimate delivered into Parliament, nothing is computed for Buildings or Repairs of the Houses belonging to them; yet they are sensible an additional Expence will attend the Providing of Lodging for the Children under their Care, whether it be under the Article of building, finishing, or enlarging Houses already erected, or hiring of Houses for their Maintenance and Education, inasmuch as the Hospital at London will not contain above 600 Children.

Signed, by Order of the General Committee,

Thomas Collingwood, Secretary.

Aprilis. A. 17

Translation of the Convention between his Majesty and the Landgrave of HeJJ'e Cajfel, concluded and signed at London the lft of April 1760.

Whereas his Majesty the King of Great Britain has judged it to be conducive to the Interests of his Crown, and of the common Cause, to reinforce his Army in Germany, under the Command of his Serene Highness Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick Lunebourg, by a new Corps of Hessian Troops; and his Serene Highness the Landgrave of Hejfe Cajfel, having agreed to the Propofol made him on the Part of the King of Great Britain, and being earnestly desirous of entering into the Views of his Majesty in this respect, his Serene Highness has engaged to furnish an additional Corps of Troops, confiding of 3,392 Men, to be employed in the same Service, and to the same Purposes, as the other Hessian Troops. In Consequence thereof the respective Ministers, duly authorized to that Efl’eft, have agreed upon the following Articles.

1.

Agreeable to prior Treaties, and namely to that of the 17th January 1759, there shall be, between his Majesty and the Serene Landgrave, their Successors, Heirs, and Subjects, a sincere Friendship and strict Union, in-so much that the one shall consider the Interests of the other as his own; and shall faithfully use his Endeavours to advance them as much as pofiibie, and to prevent and remove all Trouble and Damage.

2.

HisSerene Highness the Landgrave of Hejfe Cajfelfl lall raise, and add to the HeffianTroops,already in the Payof Great Baitain, a new Body of Troops, according to the State hereto joined, conflfiing of 2,520 Foot, of 416 Horse, of 16 Cannoneers for the Chasseurs, of 240 Huffars, and of 200 Chasseurs mounted; which said Body of Troops, excepting the Hussars and Chasseurs, that are already complete, f7ia.ll be in a Condition to serve, at farthest, by the End of the present Month of April.

3-

His Britannic Majesty engages on his Part to pay, for the railing and equipping this new Corps of Troops, the Sums specified in the State hereto annexed.

4-

His Majesty likewise charges himself with the Support of the said new Corps, as well with regard to their Pay, as to the ordinary and extraordinary Treatment every Year (during the Continuance of the War) beginning from the ill of January 1760, intirely upon the same Footing as the other llejjian Troops are at present.

5*

His Majesty, in order to give the Serene Landgrave a convincing Proof of his Friendship, and in Acknowledgement for the Zeal he has shewn, promises farther to continue to pay, during a Year after the Peace shall be made (according to the States already delivered, and likewise adjoined hereto) the actual Pay, as well of the present Augmentation, as of the additional Body of 6,692 Men, now with the Army; which were not comprehended in the Number of the 12,000 Men, in regard to which t here is already a Treaty subsisting with Great Britain.

6.

The Ratifications of this Convent ion shall be exchanged here at London, in the Space of Four Weeks from the signing hereof, or sooner, if possible. In Testimony whereof. We the underwritten, authorized by the full Powers of his Britannic Majesty and the Serene Landgrave of Hejfe Cqffel, have signed the present Convention, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be hereunto affixed. Done at London the 1 ft of April 1760.

(L. S.) Holies Newcastle.

(L. S.) Holdernefje.

(L. S.) Hardwicke.

(L. S.) W. Pitt. (t. S.) H. Alt.

Trauflation of a Treaty between his Majesty and the reigning Duke of Brinificick, concluded and signed at Marpurg the 14th of January 1760.

HIS Majesty the King of,<Great Britain, having judged it necessary, for the Support and Safety of the Common Cause, to augment his Forces in Germany, and having caused Intimations thereof to be made to hisMoft Serene Highness the Duke of Bnmfvoick and Lunenburg, and his said Moll Serene Highness, having entered with Zeal into his Majesty’s Salutary Views, they have thought proper to direct their respective Ministers; that is to say, His said Majesty, John Manners Marquis of Granby, Lieutenant General of his Forces, Commander in Chief of his British Forces in Germany, Colonel of his Royal Regiment of Horse Guards, and Member of the Parliament of Great Britain, and James Durand Esquire, Major General of his Forces, and his Commissary for the Muster of his German Troops; and the Most Serene Duke of Brunswick and Lunenburg, Gottlieb Lebrecht de Stammer, Lord of IVahren, Lieutenant General of his Highness’s Troops, and Governor of the Town and Fort refs of Wolfenbuttel; to enter into Conference thereupon; who, after the Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles.

Art. 1.

His Most Serene Highness promises and engages, by virtue of this Article, to yield to his Britannic Majesty a Body of Troops amounting to 2,413 Men; to wit.

Men.

The Second Battalion of Zaftrow’s, of - - 754

A Battalion of Grenadiers, of - 4 87

A Body of Chasseurs, Infantry, of - - - 213

A Regiment of Carbineers, Cavalry, of - - 515

A Regiment of Hussars mounted, of 334

Which Body of Troops/hall be held in a Condition to march on the ift of May next, or sooner, if possible, upon his Majesty s Requisition; which is to be understood to be made, with regard to the Infantry, Two Months bdore they march, and, to the Cavalry, Six Months VoL. 28.

before they march; the Two aforesaid Battalions shall not be separated from those of Brunswick, which are actually with his Majesty’s Army, commanded by his Most Serene Highness Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick, unless Reasons of War require it; and the whole shall always remain under the Orders of the Brunswick General, who shall command the Troops of his Most Serene Highness; and the said Troops shall take the Oath of Fidelity to his Britannic Majesty immediatelyupon their being first muttered by an English Commissary, without Prejudice, nevertheless, to the Oath which they have taken to his Most Serene Highness the Duke: His said Highness reserving besides to himselfthe Disposal of all the Employments which shall become vacant; the Administration of Justice shall be also reserved to him.

Art. 2.

Each Battalion of Infantry of this Corps shall be provided with Two Pieces of Field Artillery, with the Officers, Gunners, and other Persons, and the Train thereunto belonging.

Art. 3:

Towards defraying the Expences to which the Most . SereneDuke will be engaged for mounting, railing, and equipping, the said Corps of 2,413 Men, his Majesty promises to pay to his Most Serene Highness, for every Carabineer, Huffar, and Chasseur, on Horseback, duly armed and mounted, 80 Crowns Banco; and for every Foot Soldier, or Chasseur on Foot, 30 Crowns Banco, in the Manner following; that is to say, upon Account, for Levy-money for the Infantry, Artillery, and Cavalry, 60,000 Crowns Banco, shall be paid as loon as possible, in Consideration that the Most Serene Duke, thro* a Zeal necessary in the present Circumstances, has already advanced the greatest Part of the necessary Expences, and the Remainder w hen the said Troops shall march.

Art. 4.

Besides what is stipulated in the preceding Article, his Britannic Majesty engages to pay to the Most Serene Duke, during the Time that this Treaty shall Jaft, an annual Subsidy,‘in the Manner and Proportion following; that is to say, this Suhfidy shall commence from the 1st oi' November of the present Year, and shall be paid at the Rate of 61,287 Crowns Banco, per Annum, the Crown reckoned at 53 Sols of Holland, from the Time of the

When-the said Troops shall be sent back by his Britannic Majesty, from the Day of their Return into the Territories of his Most Serence Highness, until the Expiration of the Treaty, the Subsidy shall be again raised and continued on the Foot of 122,574 Crowns aforesaid per Annum, and the respective Payments shall be made regularly, without Diminution, and Quarterly, in the City of Brunswick, to the Person authorized by the Most Serene Duke fof the Receipt thereof.

Art. 5.

% With regard to the Pay and Treatment, as well ordinary as extraordinary, of the said Troops, whilst they shall be actually in the Pay of his Britannic Majesty, it is agreed, that, as long as they serve in the Empire; they filial! enjoy the same Advantages and Emoluments as his Majesty allows to his Gema/rTroops, according to the efte&ive State in which the Body of the said Troops shall be delivered; which shall be ascertained by a Tabelle, signed by the respectiveMinisters of the high contracting Parties, which shall have the same Force as if it was inserted, Word for Word, in the present Treaty: Whilst; they shall be employed in the Lozv Countries, X\^ey shall be treated in the said respect on the foot of the Dutch Troops. His Majesty also shall cause to be paid to the Officers of this Body the same Advances and Emoluments granted to his German Troops, to put themselves in a Condition to march; the whole as has already been practised on the March of the former Body of 6,000 Men of the Most Serene Duke.

DECLARATION.

The Words L’Annee Courante, having been made use of in the 4th Art. of the Treaty between his Majesty the King of Great Britain and his Most Serene Highness the Duke of Brunswick, signed at Marpurg the 14th of January last; which Words were inserted at a Time* w hen it was probable, that the said Treaty would have been signed in the Ceurfe of the Month of December last, which did not happen on account of the Messenger,' who-was charged with carrying the Treaty to his Majesty’s Plenipotentiaries, having been detained by contrary Winds; I have the King's Orders to declare, in the Name and on the Part of his Majesty, That the Words L'Annee pajfee ought to be substituted and inserted in the room of those V Annie courante. Done at London this Eighth Day of February in the Year 1760^ Signed, by the King’s Command,

HoldemeJfe\

If it should happen unfortunately, that any Regiment, Battalion, or Companies, of the above-mentioned Corps, should be ruined or destroyed, in Whole, or in Part, or that the Pieces of Cannon, with which they shall be furnished, should betaken by the Enemy, his Majesty the King shall cause to be paid the Expences of the necessary recruiting and remounting them, as also the Value of the said Field Pieces, in order forthwith to reinstate the Artillery and the Troops.

Art. 7.

As well in this respect, as in every other Point, the said Body of Troops shall be treated as favourably as the other Troops of his Majesty, and particularly as the Hejfian Troops, on the Foot of which they are engaged.

Art. 8.

His Britannic Majesty shall keep this Body of Troops in his Service, the whole time that the present War shall continue; and when his Majesty shall think fit to fend back the said Troops, he shall give Notice thereof Three Months before hand to his Most Serene Highness, and shall cause to be paid to them One Month's Pay for their Return.

Art. 9.

In case the Most Serene Duke shall be attacked, or disturbed in the Possession of his Dominions, his Britannic Majesty promises and engages to give his Most Serene Highness all the Succour which the same shall require, and that the Circumstances of the present War shall permit.

Art. 10.

This Treaty shall subsist as long as the present War shall lad, and his Majesty promises and engages to continue, for Two Years longer (to commence from the End of the last Winter Quarters that shall be due to this Body of Troops), the Payment of the aforesaid Subsidies of 122,574 Crowns Banco to the Most Serene Duke, in the Manner before expressed in the 4th Art. it being to be understood, that his said Most Serene Highness engages, that thesaidTroopslhall bekept in aCondition to march, and shall enter into the Service of the King immediately on the Requisition which shall be made for that Purpose,

Translation of the Ulterior Convention between his Majesty and the reigning Duke of Brinswick, concluded and ttgned at Fader born, March 5th, 1760, and of the Declaration thereto annexed.

ULTERIOR CONVENTION. SINCE the Conclusion of the Treaty between his Majesty the King of Great Britain and his most Sereue Highness the reigning Duke of Brunjivick Luneburghf signed by their respective Plenipotentiaries, at Marpurg, on the 14th of January last, his most Serene Highness paving made it known, that he was able to make a farther Augmentation to the Body of Brunswick Troops which his Majesty has taken into his Service, in the following manner j to wit.

Men.

To the Eight Battalions of Infantry, Eleven Men per Company, which would make, for 48 Companies - , 528

To the Battalion of Grenadiers granted by the

above-mentioned Treaty - - - 86

To the Body of Chasseurs, Infantry - - 100

To the Body of Chaffeure, mounted -; - 100

To the Regiment of Hussars mounted, Two more inferior Officers per Troop being included - - - - 146

Which would make, in the Whole, an Augmentation of - - - 96O

And his Majesty, having readily agreed thereto, promises and engages, by this ulterior Convention, to cause to be paid to his most Serene Highness the Levy-money for every Foot Soldier and Trooper of the present Aug*-mentation, agreeably to the Stipulations in the 3d Article of the above-mentioned Treaty; apalfo to augment the Subsidy in proportion to the said Augmentation; and to extend the whole Tenor of the said Treaty, and of the Declaration in Explanation of the Term immediatement, made use of in the 10th Article of that Treaty, with regard to this Augmentation, as far as both of them are applicable to it: And his most Serene Highness, on his Part, promises and engages, by these Prelenla, to hold this farther Augmentation of 960 Men in Readiness to march on the 1 ft Day of May next, at least the Infantry,

Part, That his Majesty agrees to his said most SerenQ Highness’s Proposal; and also that the Stipulations in the ulterior Convention above-mentioned shall extenq. as well to this Augmentation of 40 Men, as to the Augmentation of the Subsidies proportionally. " as aforesaid, for the Continuation of the Payment of " the Subsidiesafter the present War shall be terminated." And as it may be presumed, that Peace being once efta-bliilied upon a solid Footing, his Majesty’s Service will not require that the Troops in quedion should immediately begin to march, his Majesty will grant the Term of Two Months for the Infantry, and of Six Months for the Cavalry, of the said Body of Troops, to put therm-selves in a Condition to march, being fully persuaded,

Aprilis. A. 1760;

that, if the same should require it, his most Serene Highness will do every thing in his Power to shorten the Term which is mentioned in this Declaration. Done at London, this Eighth Day of February, in the Year 1760.

Signed, by his Majesty’s Command,

An ingossed Bill to amend an Act, made in the 29th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, made in the 22d Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for making a Free Market for the Sale of Fish in the City of Westminster, and for preventing the Forestalling and Monopolizing of Fish, and for allowing the Sale of Fish under the Dimensions mentioned in a Clause contained in an Act of the First Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, in case the same are taken with a Hook; and also for better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with FiOi; and to prevent Abuses of the Saleiiuen of Fish for Fiiliermen; was read the Third time.

Vol. 28. v

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act to repeal so much of an Act, passed in the 29th Year of his present Majesty’s Reign* concerning a free Market for Fish at Westminster, as requires Fishermen to enter their Fifliing Vessels at the Office of the Searcher of the Customs at Gravesend\ and to regulate the Sale of Fish at the First Hand in the Fish Markets in London and Westminster; and to prevent Salesmen of Fish buying Fish to fell again on their own Account; and to allow Bret and Turbot* Brill and Pearl, although under the respective Dimensions mentioned in a former Act, to be imported and fold; and to punilli Persons who shall take or fell any Spawn, Brood, or Fry, of Fish, unlizeable Fish, or Fish out of Season, or Smelts under the Size of Five Inches; and for other Purposes.

Ordered, That Mr. Alderman Dickinson do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

The House proceeded to take into Conficleration the Report which was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, Manufacturers, and other Inhabitants, of the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick; and also the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of Wolverhampton, in the County of Stafford; and also the Petition of the Factors, Traders, Manufacturers, and other Inhabitants, of the Borough of Waif all, in the County of Stafford; and also the Petition of the Manufacturers of Iron Chapes for Buckles, residing in the several Towns of Wolverhampton, Waif all, and Bil/lon, in the County of Stafford, and of Birmingham, in the County of Wanoick; and also the Petition of the Merchants, Fa6tors, and Traders, of the Cities of London and Westminster \ were referred.

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In Support of the Allegations of the Three first-mentioned Petitions,

Mr. Matthew Bolton, a Toymaker of Birmingham, being examined, said, That upwards of Eight thousand People are employed in Buckle-making in the Counties of Warwick and Stafford, the Returns of which are £. 300,000 per Annum, exclusive of the Hands employed in making Tools, and preparing Materials: That Buckles, are composed of Copper, Brass, Iron, Tin, Spelter; and that great Quantities of Buckles are set with Glass, in Imitation of Jewelry: That, on an Average, Chapes are One Third of the Value of the ordinary Sort of Buckles; but there are Buckles made, that the Chapes are not One Tenth of the Value:

That the Home Consumption of Buckles bears no Proportion to the Exportation, as the greateit Part of the £.300,000 is exported out of the Kingdom:

That the Witness believes there are about 2,500 Iron Chape-makers in the Counties of Wanvick and Stafford: That the Price of Chapes has been raised £. 15 per Cent. wit hin these Eighteen Months, owing to the great Demand for Exportat ion:

That if the Exportation of Chapes was prohibited, and they could be had at a reasonable Price, it would prevent Foreigners getting them, and by that means keep the Buckle Trade at home, and that he does not apprehend it will diminish the Number of Chnpe-makers: That the Chape-forgers can get 205". per Week, and the Filers from 9s. to 15^. per Week: That Chape-makers make much better Wages than other Manufacturers in the hard Ware, and may be kept conllantly employed, but they will work but Four or Five Days in a Week:

That the Chape-makers have entered into Combinations, and have declared they should raise their Prices 35. in the Pound; and that Chapes, that were formerly fold lor 18d. per Dozen, are now is. 9d. and not so good: i^id that this llife is owing to the foreign Demand: That he thinksChapes cannot be made abroad, as they have not many Materials sufficient for that Purpose:That the Chape-makers give the Preference to English Iron, and will not use foreign Iron; but that Foreigners might 16

endeavour to get English Iron, if they knew the Difference between that and foreign Iron:

That there are Secrets in the Buckle Trade, which Foreigners are Strangers to, which, induces him to think that Buckles canrtot be made so well abroad as in England:

That if the Exportation of Chapes was prohibited* the Exportation of Buckles would increase, and as many Hands be employed in Chape-making as at present.

And, being asked the Question; laid, That the Materials and Profits of the Mailer Buckle-maker is almost Half; for if a Master employs Forty Men, and gets £.40 per Week, he pays £.20 to his Journeymen, and that Journeymen’s Wages is as £.20 to £. 15.

Mr. John Scott, a Factor, being examined, laid, That he exports Toys in general:

That the exporting of Chapes is very ir jurious to Trade, and makes the Buckles come much dearer, and Foreigners can make them cheaper, by which means lie has had his Orders countermanded:

That Chapes 'which cost i8i\ or 195*. a Gross Eighteen Months ago,now coll 23s. or 245’. and not so good: That Foreigners give more for their Chapes than we can afford to give; for, if we were to give as much as they do, we should not be able to fell our Buckles; and that the foreign Demand for Buckles is owing to their being better manufactured in Birmingham than abroad: That bisCorrespondents will not submit to the advanced Price; and they will not pay any advanced Price more than original Pattern was lent at; and that their Orders come at such Prices now, they are not able to execute them: That the Chape-makers have advanced in their Prices from £.10 to £.15 per Cent, which obliges the Buckle-makers to raise the Price of their Buckles: That they formerly exported great Quantities of Buckles to Portugal; but they now fend none; but their Orders are now for Chapes, Tools, and Materials: That he has received Orders for 50 or 60 Gross of Chapes, Three or Four times in a Year; and that the Demand for Buckles decreases as the Demand lor Chapes increases: That Buckle Rings can be made here considerably cheaper and better than in Spain and Germany: That there are not Chapes enough madein the Country to answer the foreign Demand, and home Consumption; and that if the Chape-makers were to make 100 Gross more of Chapes per Week, they would all be taken off by the Buckle-makers: And therefore, if the Exportation of Chapes was prohibited, it would not lessen the Number of Chape-makers.

Mr. William Parkes, a Buckle-maker in Birmingham, being examined, said, That they now give 21 d. per Dozen for thofeSort of Chapes, for which they formerly gave but 18c/.; and be apprehends the Cause of such Rife is owing to the great Demand for Exportation: That Chapes cannot be made so well abroad as in England; and that he believes there are 2,000 Chape-makers in the Counties of Warxvick and Stafford:

That the Orders for Buckles in the Year 1759, were more than for any preceding Y"ear; but that not Half of them could be executed, because they could not get Chapes to put in their Buckles; and the Witness has now some Thousand Dozens of Buckle Rings by him, as dead Stock, for want of Chapes; and that he has discharged many of his Men for want of Chapes: and those that have advanced the Price of Chapes, have had their Orders countermanded:

That there are particular Arts in the Manufacturing of Buckles, which Foreigners are quite Strangers to; and that if Foreigners could attain the Knowledge of those Arts, it would destroy their Trade and the Toy Trade in general; and that if Half a Dozen Buckie-ninkers were seduced Abroad, they would easily communicate that Knowledge:

That he apprehends, if the Exportation of Chapeswere prohibited, there would be sufficient Employment for all the Chape-makers, as there are many other Parts of the Iron Manufactory, which they would readily come into; and those Trades are in Want of Hands.
