Mr. Elias Walling confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Parkes.

Mr. William Dairy 7:1 pie, a Spanish Merchant, being examined, said, That he hasaHouse in Spain, and deals in the Manufigures of Hard Ware in thisCountry :That there are some few Buckle Rings made in Spain, which are increased for some Time past, on account of getting Chapes from England: but that the Quality of those Rings are notfo good as ours: That the Carriage and Duty of English Rings to Spain comes to Half the Value of them; by which Means they can make them cheaper there; but that he never knew that any Chapes were made there; as they have no Coal Fire, and Labour is much dearer, and the Quality of their Iron not so tit for that Purpose; and that if the Exportation of Chapes was prohibited, the Spaniards would be obliged to take our Buckles and Chapes:

That he is many Months behind in his Orders from Spain, for want of Chapes.

Mr. Francis Ge/fon,nSpanish Merchant,confirmed the Evidence of My. Dahymple, and added, That he knows Chapes have been exported to the Spanish West Indies, to work their Rings there; and he is certain, that if Chapes were not sent there, they must take our Buckles and Chapes, as the}r cannot make Chapes there:

That he now wants above £.1,000 worth of Buckles; and that Buckles are advanced £. 15 per Cent, at Birmingham; and he could not get his Orders executed in Time, on Account of not having Chapes to put in their Rings; and that the Witness knows several Merchants, who have countermanded their Orders, because they could not get them in Time, owning to the Scarcity of Chapes.

Mr. John Bajkerville, being examined, said, That he knows the principal Buckle-makers in Birmingham, and he does not believe them to be a rich Body of People; and the Journeymen Buckle-makers are very poor; he does not think that any Master Buckle-maker in Birmingham, is worth £. 4,000; but there are Half a Score which he believes are worth £. 1,000.

That he does not apprehend Chapes can be manufactured so well in any other Country as in this, as he presumes Foreigners have not Ingenuity enough to make them so neat and cheap; but he does not doubt, but a few Foreigners may be taught to do it, but in general have not ingenuity:

That if the Exportation of Chapes to the Countries that now receive them was prohibited, he does not think it would be in their Power to make them.

Mr. John Floury, a Dealer in Hard Ware in Birming-ham, being examined, said. That Buckles are made of Brass, Spelter, and Copper: That the Buckle-maker’sBu-fmefs has greatly decreased for the last Eighteen Months, owing to the great Demand for Chapes from Abroad.

That the Journeymen Chape-makers are extremely poor, and desire that the Exportation of Chapes may not be prohibited: That the Toy Trade will be greatly prejudiced, if the Buckle-makers are seduced Abroad, more than it will be if the Chape-makers go Abroad; and that the Journeymen Buckle-makers are greater Artists than the Chape-makers:

That Iron has advanced 40 s. per Ton, since Christmas last.

And the Witness apprehends, That the Advance upon Iron and Materials for making Buckle Chapes, bear no Proportion to the Advance upon Chapes:

That Chapes are dearer now than they have been for Seven Years past; and that he never heard, that the Buckle-makers exported Rings without Chapes:

That the Rife of Chapes is owing to the great Demand: That the Buckle-makers could not get Chapes sufficient to answer their Demands:

That he has heard they make Chapes in Flanders; and yet they give the Preference to ours; but apprehends, if they could bring the Manufacture to Perfection, they would npt take ours.

Mr. William Parkes, being further examined, said. That the Demand for Buckles and Chapes increased to-VoL. 28.

gether; and that the Demand for Buckles was occasion- Exportation ed by the great Number of People going to settle in ic

Amenca; and that the Chape-makers have refused to make for the Home Trade, being obliged to answer their Demands from Abroad; and that a Merchant told him, that he could export all the Chapes that could be made in the Trade: That he used to employ above Twenty Hands; but he has not employed above Nine or Ten these Twelve Months.

To prove the Allegations of the Fourth-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Joseph Green, a Chape-maker in Birmingham, being examined, said, That he employs Fourteen Hands, about Four of whom are Men, and the rest are Children:

That the Business of the Chape-makers employs above as many more Hands as are employed in the making of Buckle Rings: That the Materials for making Chapes have rose; but that the Chapes have rose very little That there are not so many Manufacturers as formerly:

That many have infilled into the Army for want of Employment: That he does not make Chapes for Exportation:

That he has introduced a new Method of making Chapes, and produced One to your Committee, which he find, was in the State in which he delivers them to the Filer; and that they may be worked into that State as cheap, and are as strong, as in the old Method; One of which likewise in the state wherein they are delivered to the Filer, was also produced to your Committee; but appeared to require much more Labour to finidi it, than, that made in the new Method: That if the new Method was known, any Person might make them; he could teach them himself in Haifa Year; and that Charcoal id the best Fire to make the new Chape with, as the Heat is more intense; but could not teach them the old Method.

That he apprehends, if the Exportation^ Chapes was prohibited, it would be an Encouragement to the Workmen to go Abroad: That the Chape-makers Wages is very low; a Forger may get from 10s. to 15s. per Week; and the Filers about 8s. per Week, on an Average: That the advanced Price for Exportation, is£. 5 per Cent. and a little more upon Goods for Home Con* liimption:

That the Demand for Toys in general has been very great, which has laid the other Manufacturers under ad many Difficulties as the Buckle-makers, to get their Orders executed; not Two-thirds of them have been able to execute them: That the Business of Button-making is more considerable than the Buckle-makers; and that they have laboured under the same Inconveniencies: That it is owing to a Spanish Fleet, now fitting out; and that he apprehends there will be a Stagnation in the Toy Trade in general,when that Fleet is jailed

That if the Exportation of Chapes is prohibited, the Buckle-makers will lower the Price of Chapes; and if Foreigners cannot get them from hence, they will make them themselves: That lie could teach them by a Letter; and that there will not be Employment for the Manufacturers now in the Trade: That many Buckle-makers have Rings by them, but not any Chapes, which is owing to their Appreliension, that the Exportation of Chapes will be prohibited; and that they shall then get them at their own Prices:

That the Profits of the Buckle-makers greatly exceed the Profits of the Chape-makers.

That he served his Apprenticeship to a Button-maker; but hearing of the great Demand for Chapes, he invented a new Method of making them, by which he makes them as strong as by the old Method, and can fell them as cheap; and that Charcoal is the best Fire for his Invention.

That he never saw a soldered Chape before he invented them himself.

That if a Chape-maker was to employ Thirty Hands, he could not clear One-ihird as much as a Buckle-maker with the same Number of Hands.

Mr. John Merry, a Chape-maker near XValfall, being examined, said, That he has been in Business Thirty Years, and employs Twelve People-, and that their Wages are 7 s. Ss. 10s. and iis. per Week: That they have not raised their Prices: That the People in his Business are in general very poor:

That he makes Chapes for Exportation; and that there have been great Demands for Chapes and Toys in general lately; and that he has not been able to execute all his Orders; but that if the Exportation of Chapes is prohibited, he apprehends it will hurt him, as there will then be but one Market:

That he has known several Buckle-makers export Chapes without Rings; upon which the Chape-makers made Application to the Merchants, to have the Profits of Exporting as well as they: That there has not been any greater Demand for Chapes within these Eighteen Months, than the Chape-makers have been able to supply; and that he has not heard any Complaint for want of Chapes at Walsall; I know some Buckle-makers are against the Application, apprehending it will be of more Prejudice to them than the Chape-makers; and that the Home Consumption only would not be sufficient to employ the Chape-makers: That he has heard of some inconsiderate People at Bilston, who attempted to raise the Price of Chapes; but the leading People would not come intoit: That Chapes were dearer formerly than at present: That the Exportation of Chapes has decreased with respect to himself: That he has made Use of the Chapes invented by Mr. Green, and finds, they will wear as well, and are as good in every respect as the other:

That the Orders for Exportation are not now so great as usual: That when Merchants have applied to him, he has endeavoured to get them served as fall as possible, and could not always answer their Demands; but he always gave the Preference to the Buckle-makers Orders; and the Buckle-makers Price exceeded the Merchants: That the home and foreign Markets require the Commodities to be equally good: That a Gross of Chapes worth 20.V. The Witness could not say for what Time Mr. Heath had contra6led.

To prove the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition,

Mr. Simon JVilfon, a Merchant, being examined, said, That he is concerned in the Exportation of Hard Wares: That within these Eighteen Months, the foreign Demand for Chapes has increased considerably, and the Demand for Buckles has decreased: That he has given many Orders for Buckles lately, that have not been executed for want of Chapes; and that the Exportation of Chapes will greatly diminish the Orders for Buckles; and that he has countermanded Orders for Buckles: That if the Buckle-makers should raise their Prices, it will be a great Prejudice to Trade, because it will put Foreigners on attempting to make the same Manufactures; and that the great Demand arises from the low Price of the Buckles:

That he could have exported more Buckles if they could have been finiftied:

That he has not had more Orders for Tovs than he has

been able to execute, except for Buckles: That Buckles is by far the most considerable Article in the Toy Trade:

That the greatest Demand for Chapes has been from Portugal, which he apprehends is owing to the making Buckle Rings there, and to Buckles being prohibited from going there; and that the Prohibition took Place before the Demand for Chapes increased.

Mr. Bolton, being further examined, said, That the Orders for Chapes have greatly increased of late Years; and that the greatest Part of the Exportation has been in the common Sort of Buckles; and he produced to your Committee Specimens of Several Sorts of Buckles: —

That they cannot make Chapes in Spain and Portugal so good and cheap as in England, as they have no flitting or rolling Mills; and if they were to import Iron there, it would be of too high a Price for the Manufacture; and they have neither Workmen nor Coals: — That the Germans can make Chapes; but they take a great Quantity of us, as their Iron is not so fit for Chapes; and if they could make Chapes sufficient, they would not buy of us; and if we were deprived of our Chape-makers, we should be a long Time before others could be instructed; and by that means the Trade would be loft.

There mull be some invincible Impediment to making Chapes in Germany, because, if they could make them, they would make them £. 100per Cent, cheaper than we.

Mr. Edward Keep, a Merchant, being examined, said. That he is largely concerned in the Exportation of Hard Ware: That he has had large Orders for Buckles; but could not execute them for want of Chapes: Several of those Orders were given last September, and are not executed at this Time; and that the Buckle-makers write him Word, that the Rings are ready, but they flaud Hill for want of Chapes; and if the Exportation of Chapes is not prohibited, it will destroy the Buckle Trade in Time:

That if the Buckle-makers advance their Prices, Correspondents abroad will not pay them; he has in Consequence countermanded several Orders, because Foreigners would not give the advanced Price:

That a Foreigner, a Swiss, brought a Chape to him, which was made in his Country; and the Witness asked him, why he came here for Chapes? and heanswered, because you make them cheaper than we can; the Chape was well made, and fit for good work; it was not fit for that Sort of Buckle we commonly export; and he does not apprehend tJiey can make the common Sort of Chapes so well:

That there has been a Scarcity of Buckles for about Six Months, occasioned by the great Demand for Chapes from Abroad.

A Petition of Lieutenant Colonel Mordaunl Cracherode, late Lieutenant Governor of Fort AL Philip, in the Island of Minorca, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition* recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That in the Year 1753, the Petitioner exchanged his Government of Landguard Fort for that of Fort St. Philip, in the said Bland, at 40 s. per Diem, but the Petitioner not being sent thither before the Surrender of the said Bland, the King, under his Sign Manual, gave the Order, in the Petition mentioned, to his Majesty’s Paymaster General of Guards, Garrisons, and Land Forces, to dispense with the Petitioner’s Absence from the said Bland, and to continue his Pay to him from the Surrender of the said Castle to the 25th of 17

December 1756 5 and that the Petitioner did receive the Allowance of full Pay of 40 s. per Diem to 25 December 1756, but hath been reduced from that Time to Half Pay only, whereby the Petitioner is become a great Sufferer; and that the Petitioner would have applied to his Majesty for an Allowance in addition to his Half Payout has been informed, that he cannot receive any such Allowance, without rendering himself incapable of receiving his Half Pay, unless alfifted by Parliament; and repre-fenting to the House, that the Petitioner hath been in his Majesty ’s Service, in the Capacities mentioned in the Petition, lince the Year 1707: And therefore praying the House for Relief, the Petitioner having passed more than half a Century in Service to the Crown and Public, and once round the World; and that having been ready and willing to go where commanded, he may at lait be appointed to receive from 25 December 1756, the full Pay of 40.V. a Day, which he exchanged for, and that the same may from henceforth be allowed and continued to him, now in the 76th Year of his Age, finally to retire upon.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine and state to the House the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:

And it is referred to Major General Cormvallis, Lord North, Lord Carijsfort, Mr. Alderman Bedford, Mr.

GEORGE R,

Whereas by our Commission, bearing Date the 23d of November 1753, We thought fit to appoint Lieutenant Colonel Cratcherodc to be Lieutenant Governor of St. Philip's Cattle, in the Island of Minorca, in Consideration of his long Services; and were moreover pleased to excuse his going to hisGovernment,where his Presence was not wanted, as there was a Lieutenant Governor of the Island on the Spot, on account of his Age and Infirmities: And whereas he hath Alice been deprived of the Government to which We had thus appointed him, by the Surrender of the Cattle of St. Philips; therefore, that the said Lieutenant Colonel Cratcherodc may not he left without a Mark of our Royal Favour, and Approbation of his Serv ices, We are graciously pleased to continue his Pay to him, from the Surrender of the said Cattle of St. Philip's to the 25th December 1756. Our Will and Pica lure therefore is. That out of such Monies as arc or shall come to your Hands, arising from the Savings by the Surrender of Minorca, and the Reduction of the Statt Officers thereof* you do iffiuc to the said Lieutenant Colonel Cratcherodc his Pay, as Lieutenant Governor of St. Philip's Cattle, according to his former Establishment, from the 28th of June (the Day of the Surrender) to the 25th December 1756, exclusive; and for so doing this, with the Acquittance of the said Lieutenant Colonel Cratcherodc, or of his Assign, shall be your Warrant and Discharge. Given at our Court at Kensington, this 21 ft Day of May 1757, in the Thirtieth Year of Our Reign.

By his Majesty’s Command,

Barrington.

To Our Right trutty and Right well-beloved Cousin Henry Earl of Darlington, late Pay matter General, and our Right trutty and well-beloved Thomas Lord Vi f count Dupplin, Pay matter General of our Guards, Gamfons, and Land Forces.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill was committed.

And afterwards a Speech of the Lords Commissioners Lords Con was delivered to both Houses, by the Lord Keeper of miHioner*’ the Great Seal; which is as folloiveth; viz. Speech.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We have received the King’s Commands to put an End to this Session of Parliament; and, upon thisOccasion, to alTure you,that his Majesty looks back with intire Satisfaction on your Proceedings during the Course of it. The Duty and Affection which you have expressed for his Person and Government, and the Zeal and Unanimity which you have flievvn in maintaining the true Interest of your Country, can only be equalled by what his Majesty hath formerly experienced from this Parliament.

His Majesty has commanded us toacquaint you, That it would have given him the mofl sensible Pieafnre, to have been able to communicate to you, that his sincere Endeavours to promote a general Pacification, had met with more suitable Returns before this Time. His Ma-

jetty

34’Geo. II. Mail. — 170

jesty, in Conjunction with his good Brother and Ally the King of Prussia, chose to give their Enemies Proofs of this equitable Disposition, in the Midst of a Series of glorious Victories, an Opportunity the most; proper to <lo it with Dignity, and to manifest to all Europe, the Purity and Moderation of his Views; after such a Conduct, his Majesty has the Comfort to reflect, that the further Continuance of the Calamities of War cannot be imputed to him or his Allies; and trulls in the Blessing of Heaven upon the Justice of his Arms, and upon those ample Means which your Zeal, in so good a Cause, has wifely put into his Hands, that his future Succeflbs in carrying on the War, will not fall short of the pall; and that in the Event, the public Tranquillity will be rellored on solid and durable Foundations.

We are further commanded to acquaint you, That his Majesty has" taken the most effectual Care to augment the combined Anny in Germany; and at the same Time to keep up such a Force at Home, as may frustrate any Attempts of the Enemy to invade these Kingdoms, which have hitherto ended only in their own Confusion.

The Royal Navy was never in a more flourishing and respectable Condition; and the signal Victory obtained last Winter over the French Fleet, on their own Coasts, as it has added Lustre to his Majesty’s Arms, has given fresh Spirit to his Maritime Forces, and reduced the Naval Strength of France to a very low Ebb.

His Majesty has disposed his Squadrons in such a Manner, as may bell conduce to the Annoyance of his Enemies; to the Defence of his own Dominions, both in Europe and America \ and to the preferring and pur-iuing his Conquests, as well as to the Protection of the Trade of his Subjects, which be has extremely at Heart.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

Nothingcould relieve his Majesty’s Royal Mind, under the Anxiety which he feels for the Burthens of his faithful Subjects, but the public spiritedChearfulness, with which von have granted him such large Supplies; a.id his Conviction, that t hey are necessary for the Security and essential Interests of his Kingdoms: The King has enjoined us to return you his hearty Thanks for them, and to allure you of their due Application to the Purposes for which they have been given.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We have nothing further in Command from his Majesty, but to recommend toyoutheCoutinuancennd Improvement of that Union and good Harmony which he has observed with so much Plcafnre, and from which he Iras derived such important Effects. Make it your Study to promote these ddirable Objects, to support the King’s Government, and the good Order of your respective Countries, and to eonfult your own real Happiness and Prosperity; this Behaviour his Majesty graciously af-

HEREAS it hath pleased Almighty God, to call to his Mercy our late Sovereign Lord King George the Second, of Blessed Memory, by whose Decease the Imperial Crowns of Great Britain, France, and

Ireland, arefolely and rightfully come to the High and Mighty Prince, George Prince of Wales; We therefore,

Council, with Numbers of other principal Gentlemen of Quality, with the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens of London, do now hereby, with one Voice, and Consent of Tongue and Heart, publish and proclaim, That the High and Mighty Prince, George Prince of Wales, is now, by the Death of our late Sovereign, of happy Memory, become our only lawful and rightful Liege Lord, George the Third, by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France, and ^Ireland, Defender of the Faith, and so forth, to whom we do acknowledge all Faith and constant Obedience, with all hearty and humble Affection; beseeching God, by whom Kings and Queens do reign, to bless the Royal Prince, George the Third, with long and happy Years to reign over us.

the Lords Spiritual and Temporal of this Realm, being here assisted with those of his late Majesty’s Privy

At the COURT at CARLETON HOUSE, The Twenty-fifth Day of October, 1760. PRESENT,

The KING’s most Excellent Majesty in Council.

His M A J ESTY being this Day present in Council, was pleased to make the following Declaration 5 viz.

THE Loss that I and the Nation have sustained by the Death of the King my Grandfather, would have been severely felt at any Time, but coming at so critical a Juncture, and so unexpected, it is by many Circumstances augmented, and the Weight now falling upon be much increased: I feel my own Inefficiency to support it as I wish; but animated by the tendered Affection for this my native Country, and depending on the Advice, Experience, and Abilities, of your Lordships, on the Support and Assistance of every honest Man, I enter with Chearfulness into this arduous Situation, and shall make it the Business of my Life to ' promote, in every Thing, the Glory and Happiness of these Kingdoms, to preserve and strengthen both the Constitution in Church and State; and, as I mount the Throne in the Midst of an expensive, but just and ' necessary War, I shall endeavour to prosecute it in the Manner the moll likely to bring on an honourable and lasting Peace, in Concert with my Allies.

Whereupon the Lords of the Council made it their humble Request to his Majesty, That this his Majesty’s most gracious Declaration to their Lordships, might be made public; which his Majesty was pleased to order accordingly,

F. Vernon.

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE ft.

WHEREAS, at the Time of the Demise of our late Royal Grand father, of glorious Memory, this ptefent Parliament flood prorogued to Thursday the Thirteenth Day of this Instant November: And whereas, by virtue of an Act of Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of our late Royal Predecessor Queen Anne, of blessed Memory, intituled,<c An Act for the Security of her Majesty’s Person and Government, and of the Succession to the Crown of Great Britain in the Protestant Line/ it is required that the said Parliament should, immediately after such Demise, meet, convene, and fit, and should aft, notwithstanding such Demise, for and during the Term of Six Months, and no longer,unless the same should be sooner prorogued or dissolved, as in the said Act is provided: And whereas, We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, did order, That our said Parliament should be prorogued to Thursday the said Thirteenth Day of this Instant November; and the same hath been prorogued accordingly: Now We do hereby, with the Advice of our Privy Council, declare our Royal Will and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall be further

prorogued on the said Thirteenth Day of this Instant November, to Tuesday the Eighteenth Day of this Instant November; and We have given Order to our Keeper of the Great Seal of Great Britain, to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly; and We do hereby further declare our Royal Will and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Eighteenth Day of this Instant November, be held and fit for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners of Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster, on Tuesday the said Eighteenth Day of this Inllant November.

Given at our Court at St. James’s, the Sixth Day of November, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty, in the First Year of our Reign.

GOD save the King

Mr Speaker reported, That the House attended his Majesty on Tutfday fall, in the House of Peers; when his Majesty was pleased to make a moil gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

VOL. 28.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The just Concern which I have felt in my on Breach, on the sudden Death of the late King my Royal Grandfather, makes me not doubt but you mutt all have bee* deeply affected with so severe a Loss: The prefest critical and difficult Conjuncture has made tins L©4* the more fenfibie, as he was the great Support of tha* System, by which alone the Liberties of Eirrcpr, and the Weight and Influence of these Kingdoms, can be preserved; and gave Life to the Measures conducive to those important Ends.

1 need not tell you the Addition of Weight which immediately falls upon me, in being called to the Government of this free and powerful Country, at such a Time, and under such Circumstances: My Consolation is in the Uprightnefsof my own Intentions, your faithful and united Assistance, and the Bletting of Heaven upon our joint Endeavours, which I devoutly implore.

Bom and educated in this Country, I glory in the Name of Briton; and the peculiar Happiness of my Life will ever consist in promoting the Welfare of a People, whose Loyalty and warm Affection to me, I consider as the greatest and most permanent Security of myThrone; and, I doubt not, but their Steadiness in those Principles; will equal the Firmnefsofmy invariableRefolution, to adhere tOj and strengthen, this excellent Constitution in Church and State, and to maintain the Toleration inviolable. The civil and religious Rights of my loving Subjects are equally dear to me with the most valuable Prerogatives of my Crown; and, as the surest Foundation-of the Whole, and the best Means to draw down the Divine Favour on my Reign, it is my fixed Purpose to countenance and encourage the Practice of true Religion and Virtue.

I refled with Pleasure on the Successes with which the British Arms have been prospered this last Summer: The total Reduction of the vast Province of Canada, with the City of Montreal, is of the most interetling Consequence, and mutt be as heavy a Blow to my Enemies as it is a Conquest glorious to us; the mor£ glorious, because effected almost without Effusion of Blood, and with that Humanity which makes an amiable Part of the Character of this Nation.

Our Advantages gained in the East Indies have been signal, and mutt greatly diminish the Strength and Trade of France in those Parts, as well as procure the most solid Benefits to the Commerce and Wealth of my Subjects.

In Germany, where the whole French Force has been employed, the combined Army, under the wife and able Conduct of my General, Prince Ferdinand of Brunjivick, has not only flopped their Progress, but has gained Advantages over them, notwithstanding their boasted Superiority, and their not having hitherto come to a general Engagement.

My good Brother, and Ally, the King of Prnjia, although surrounded with numerous Armies of Enemies, has, with a Magnanimity and Perseverance ahnoft beyond Example, not only withstood their various Attacks, but has obtained very considerable Victories over them.

Of t hefe Events I shall say no more at this time, because the Nature of the War in those Parts has kept the Campaign there still depending.

As my Navy is the principal Article of our natural Strength, it gives me much Satisfaction to receive it in such good Condition; whilst the Fleet of France is weakened to such a degree, that the small Remains of it have continued blocked up by my Ships in their own. Ports, at the same time the French Trade is reduced to the lowed Ebb; and, vviih Joy of Heart, I fee the Commerce of my Kingdoms, that great Source of our Riches, and fixed Object of my never failing Cure and Protection, flourishing to an Extent unknown in any former War.

Addrefii on the lung's Speech.

20° Novembris. 1760,

The Valourand Intrepidity of my Officers and Forces, both at Sea and Land, have been distinguished so much to the Glory of this Nation, that I should be wanting in Justice to them, if I did not acknowledge it: This is a Merit which I shall constantly encourage and reward; and I take this Occasion to declare, that the zealous and useful Service of the Militia in the present arduous Conjuncture is very acceptable to me.

In this State I have found Things at my Accession to the Throne of my Ancestors; happy in viewing the prof-perous Part of it; happier dill should I have been, had I found my Kingdoms, whose true Interest I have intirely at Heart, in full Peace; but, fmee the Ambition, injurious Encroachments, and Dangerous Designs, of my Enemies, rendered the War both just and necessary; and the generous Overture made lall Winter towards a Congressfor a Pacification,has not yet produced a suitable Return; I am determined, with your chearful and powerful Assistance, to prosecute this War with Vigour, in order to that desirable Object, a safe and honourable Peace: For this Purpose, it is absolutely incumbent upon us to be early prepared; and I rely upon your Zeal and hearty Concurrence, to support the King of Prussia’, and the rest of my Allies, and to make ample Provision for carrying on the War, as the only Means to bring our Enemies to equitable Terms of Accommodation.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The greatest Uneasiness which I feel at this time is, in-considering the uncommon Burthens necessarily brought upon my faithful Subjects: I desire only such Supplies as shall be requisite to prosecute the War with Advantage; be adequate to the necessary Services; and that they may be provided for in the moll sure and effectual Manner. You may depend upon the faithful and punctual Application of what shall be granted: I have ordered the proper Estimates for the eh suing Year to be laid before you, and also an Account of the extraordinary Expences, which, from the Nature of the different and remote Operations, have been unavoidably incurred.

It is with peculiar ReluCiance that I am obliged, at such a Time, to mention any thing which personally regards myself; but, as the Grant of the greatest Part of the Civil List Revenues is now determined, I trust in your Duty and Affection to me, to make the proper Provision for supporting my civil Government with Honour and Dignity: On my Part, you may be assured of a regular and becoming Economy.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Eyes of all Europe are upon you; from your Resolutions the Protestant Interest hopes for Protection, as well as all our Friends for the Preservation of their Independency; and our Enemies fear the final Disappointment of their ambitious and destrudive Views: Let these Hopes and Fears be confirmed and augmented by the Vigour, Unanimity, and Dispatch, of your Proceedings.

In this Expectation I am the more encouraged by a pleasing Circuinllance, which I look upon as one of the most auspicious Omens of my Reign; that happy Extinction of Divisions, and that Union and good Harmony which continue to prevail amongst my Subjects, afford me the most agreeable Prospect; the natural Disposition and Wifliof my Heart are, to cement and promote them; and 1 promise myself, that nothing w ill aril’e, on your Part, to interrupt or dtfturb a Situation so essential to the true and lading Felicity of this great People.

Refulved, Xemine contra dicenteyli\\a!t an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to express the deep-. eft Sense of the great and severe Loss which his Majesty and these Kingdoms havesustained by the Death of his Majesty’s Royal Grandfather, our late most excellent Sovereign, the Memory of whose just and prof-perous Reign will be held in Reverence by latest Posterity:

To congratulate his Majesty upon his happy Accef-18

To return his Majesty the most humble Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to acknowledge, with the liveliest Sentiments of Duty, Gratitude, and Exultation of Mind,those most affecting and animating Words of our most gracious Sovereign, That born and educated in this Country, he glories in the Name of Briton; and to offer to his Majesty the full Tribute of our Hearts, for the warm Expressions of his truly Royal and tender Affection towards his People: That wTe venerate and confide in those sacred Assurances of his Majesty’s firm and invariable Resolution to adhere to and strengthen this excellent Constitution in Church and State, to maintain the Toleration inviolate, and to protect his faithful Subjects in the greatest of human Blessings, the secure Enjoyment of their religious and civil Rights:

To congratulate his Majesty on the various Successes, which, under the Protection of God, have attended the Brilijli Arms during the lall Summer, particularly in the Reduction of the City of Montreal, and the intire Province of Canada; a Conquest equally important and glorious, achieved w?ith Intrepidity, and closed with Humanity, the genuine Attributes of that British Spirit, which, under the benign Aulpices of his Majesty, will, we trust, continue, by the Divine Assistance, to give additional Lustre to the Arms of Great Britain: That this valuable and extensive Acquisition, joined to the signal Advantages gained in the East Indies, the flourishing State of our Commerce, the respectable Condition of his Majesty’s Navy, by which the Remains of the Enemy’s Fleet continue blocked up in their Harbours, whilst their Trade is almost annihilated, areCon-fiderations which fill our Hearts with the most pleasing Hopes that his Majesty will be thereby enabled to prosecute this just and necessary War to that great and desirable Object of establishing, in Conjunction with his Allies, a safe, honourable, and lading Peace:

That we fee with the greatest Pleasure, that the Progress of the French Armies in Germany, notwithstanding their Superiority of Numbers, has been Hopped, and, to the Honour of his Majesty’s Arms, their Attempts hitherto baffled, by the wife and able Conduct of his Serene Highness Prince Ferdinand of 1Brunswick: That when we consider the stupendous Efforts made in every Campaign, by his Majesty’s great Ally the King of Prussia, the Defeat of the Avjtrians in Silejia, and that recent and glorious Victory obtained over the Army commanded by Marshal Daun> we cannot sufficiently admire the invincible Constancy of Mind, and inexhaustible Refonrces of Genius, displayed by that magnanimous Monarch, to whom the most dangerous and difficult Situations have only administered frelli Occasions for Glory:

To make our most dutiful Acknowlegements to his Majesty for the Mention which he has so graciously made of the distinguished Valour and Intrepidity of his Officers and Forces at Sea and Land, and for the Declaration of his Majesty’s constant Resolution to encourage and reward such Merit; and to return our most humble Thanks to his Majesty for his favourable Acceptance of the zealous and useful Service of the Militia, in the present arduouslConjun&ure:

df our Hearts for the warm Expressions of your truly royal and tender Affection towards your People. We venerate and confide in those sacred Assurances of your Majesty’s firm and invariable Resolution, to adhere to and ltrengthen this excellent Constitution, in Church and State, to maintain the Toleration inviolate, and to protest your faithful Subjects in that greatest of hitman Bleffmgs, the secure Enjoyment of their religious and Civil Rights.

Permit us to congratulate yotir Majesty on the various Succoffes which, under the Protection of God, have attended the British Arms, during the last Summer particularly in the Reduction of the Gity of Montreal, and the intire Province of Canada, a Conquest equally important and glorious, atchieved with Intrepidity, and closed with Humanity, the Genuine Attributes of that British Spirit, which, under the benign Auspices of your Majesty, will, we trust, continue, by the Divine Assistance, to give additional Lustre to the Arms of Great Britain.

This valuable and extensive Acquisition, joined to the signal Advantages gained in the East Iridic:; the flourishing State of our Commerce; the respectable Condition of your Majesty’s Navy, by which the Remains of the Enemy’s Fleet continue blocked up in their Harbours, whiill their Trade is almost annihilated; are Considerations which fill our Hearts with the mofi pleasing hopes, that your Majesty will be thereby enabled to prosecute this just and necessary War, to that great and desirable Object of establishing, in Conjunction with your Allies, a sese, honourable, and lulling Peace.

We fee, with the greatest Pleasure, that the Progref* of the French Armies in Germany, notwithstanding their Superiority of Numbers, has been flopped, and, to the Honour of your Majesty’s Arms^ their Attempts hitherto baffled by the wife and able Conduct of his Serene Highness Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick.

When we eonfider the stupendous Efforts, made in every Campaign, by your Majesty’s great Ally, the King of Prnffia, the Defeat of the Aujlrians in Silefa, and that recent and glorious Victory obtained over the Army commanded by Marshal Daun, we cannot sufficiently admire the invincible Constancy of Mind and inexhaustible Resources of Genius, difpiayed by that magnanimous Monarch, to whom the most dangerous and difficult Situations have only administered fresh Occasions for Glory.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled. Approach your royal Presence to express the deepest Senie of the great and severe Loss which your Majesty and these Kingdoms have sustained, by the Death of your Majesty’s loyal Grandfather, our late most excellent Sovereign, the Memory of whose just and prof-perous Reign will be held in Reverence by latest rofterity.

We beg Leave to congratulate your Majesty on your happy Accession to the Throne, the only Consideration that cau alleviate our Grief for such a Loss; the Know-lege of your Majesty’s royal Virtues, Wisdom, and Firmness, opens to your faithful Subjects the faired ProfpetH for their future Happiuefs at home, and for the Continuance of that Weight and Influence of your Majesty's Crown abroad, so essentially necessary in this arduous and critical Conjuncture, for the Preservation of that System, upon which the Liberties of Europe depend.

We return your Majesty our humble Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne, and acknowlegde, with the livelielt Sentiments of Duty, Gratitude, and Exultation of Mind, those most affecting and animating Words of our most gracious Sovereign, That, born and educated in this Country, he glories in the Name of JBritvn; and we offer to your Majesty the full Tribute

Our most dutiful Acknowledgements are due to your Majesty, for the Mention which you have so graciously made of the distinguished V alonr and Intrepidity of your Officers and Forces at Sea and Land, and for the Declaration of your Majesty’sconftantRefolution toencourage and reward such Merit; and we return our most bumble Thanks to your Majesty for your favourable Acceptance of the zealous and useful Service of the Militia in the present arduous Conjuncture.

We assure your Majesty, that your faithful Commons, thoroughly sensible of this important Crisis, and delirous, with the Divine Assistance, to render your Majesty* Reign successfu land glorious in War, happy and honourable in Peace (the natural Return of a grateful People to a gracious and affectionate Sovereign) will concur in inch Measures as shall be requisite for the vigorous and effectual Prosecution of the War *, and that we will chearfully and speedily grant such Supplies as shall be found necessary, for that, Purpose, and for the Support of the King of Prussia, and the rest of your Majestys Allies; firmly relying on your Majesty’s Wisdom, Goodness, and Justice, that they will be applied in such a Manner as will most effectually answer the Ends for which they an* granted, and with the utmost Economy that the Nature of such great and extensive Operations will allow; and that we will make such an adequate Provision for your Majesty’s civil Government, us may be sufficient to maintain the Honour and Dignity of your Crown with all proper *nd becoming Lustre.

Your Majesty’s faithful Commons approach you royal Person, with Hearts penetrated by the warmest and livclieft Sense of your unbounded Tenderness and Concern for the Welfare of your People, and rejoicing at the high Satisfaction yotir Majesty takes in the Union which so univerially prevails throughout your Kingdoms a deep Sense of that national Strength and Prof-perity visibly derived from this salutary Source, and, above all, your Majesty’s Approbation of that happy Union, and the natural Disposition and With of your royal Heart to cement and promote it, are the strongest Incentives to Concord, and the surest Pledge of its Duration; the fixed Refutation which yoUr Majesty has declared, to countenance and encourage the Practice of true Religion and Virtue, will, we doubt not, prove the bell Means of drawing down the Favour of God upon a dutiful and united Nation; and we iliali never cease devoutly to offer up our ardent Vows to the Divine Providence, that, as a Recompehce for these royal Virtues, your Majesty may reign in the Hearts of a free and happy People; and that they, excited by your Majesty’s benevolent Care to discharge your royal Function, and animated by Gratitude for the Enjoyment of so many Blefiings, may make the due Return by a constant Obedience to your Laws, and by the most heady Attachment and Loyalty to yourPerson and Government.

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, assembled April the 15th 1760, at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace held for the County of Cornwall, and also the Gentlemen, Clergy, and principal Inhabitants, residing in or near the Boroughs of Penryn and IJelstone, in the said County, and the several Market Towns of Falmouth, Marazion, and Penzance, in the said County, was presented to the lIoufe, and read; setting forth, That the Great Pod Road leading from Falmouth aforesaid to a Place called the Land's End, in the Parish of Sennen, in the said County, and passing through the several Towns and Par ilhes of Penryn aforesaid, Male, Haddock, Con-Jlenton, Weldron, Helstone aforesaid, Sithney, Briage, Ger-moe, St. Hillary, Perranuthnoe, Marazion aforesaid, Ludg-van, Gulvall, Penzance aforesaid, Maddern, Sauer etc, Pauli, Burry an, and Sennen aforesaid; and also the Road leading from Heljtonc aforesaid to the Lizard Point, in the Parish of Landazvednack, and passing by and t hrough the several Parishes and Places following; viz. Killy Anchor, Bochim, Drytru, and Erifey Gate, in the Parishes o{Mawgan, Ruan Major, and Minor, and Grade; and also from Helfiom aforesaid, through Rofveor, in Mawgan aforesaid, and through Rclewas, and in and through the Parishes of Saint Martins and Manackan, to St. Kcvern Church Tozvn, in the Parish of St. Kevern, in the said County of Cornwall; are become very ruinous; and that many Parts thereof are so narrow, that Carriages cannot pass each other, and, in the Winter and rainy Seasons, are so deep and founderous, that Carriages, Horses laden, and even Travellers, pass in great Danger; and alleging, that the said Roads cannot be effectually repaired, widened, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course of Law: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant that Leave may be given for bringing in a Bill or Bills for the erecting asufficient Number of Turnpikes and Toll-houses on the said Roads, and for levying a Toll or Tolls upon the fame; and that, with the Money arising (therefrom, the said Roads may be repaired and widfehed, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Charlton, according to Order, reported from the Supply; Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred 30 consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for the Support of his Majesty’s Houftiold, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown, there be granted to his Majesty, during his Life, fitch a Revenue, as, together with the Annuities payable by virtue of any Acts of Parliament, made in the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, of blessed Memory, out of the Hereditary Civil List Revenues, shall amount to the clear yearly Sum of Eight hundred Thousand Pounds, to commence from the Demise of his said late Majesty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the said Revenue, for the Support of his Majesty’s Houiliold, and of the Honour arid Dignity of the Crown, be charged upon, and made payable out of, the Aggregate Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the several Revenues which were payable to his said late Majesty, during his Life, and had Continuance till the Time of his Demise, other than such Payments as were charged upon and bluing out of the Aggregate Fund, be granted and continued from the Time of the said Demise, to his present Majesty, during his Life; and the Produce of the said Revenues, together with the Produce of the Hereditary Revenues, which were settled or appointed to be, towards the Support of the Houftiold of his said late Majesty, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown, be, during the said Term, carried to, and made Part of, the Aggregate Fund.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Seventy thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty one, including Eighteen thousand Three hundred and Fifty-five Marines.

To prove the Allegations of tire said Petition,

Charles Dingley Esquire, being examined; said, That the present new Road from Paddington to Islington has been found of great Utility;

That the making a new Road from the Norlh-East Side of the Road called the Iflingtoli Road, over the Fields and Grounds, to Old Street Road, opposite the Doghouse Bar, and the repairingand widening the Road from the Doghouse Bar to the End of Chiswell Street, which is about a Quarter of a Mile in Length, will make an easter Communication into the City of London, and be a Quarter of a Mile nearer than the present Road through Old Street, and, by avoiding the Stones, and many Nuisances which attend the present Road, would be of further Utility and Benefit to the Public:

Mr. Isaac Majfeter, being examined, said. That he has surveyed the Premises through which the said Road is intended to be made, which is Seven Eights of a Mile and Fourteen Perches in Length; and that he could foresee no Inconvenience in making the Road* it being a good Soil, and mostly Gravel.

Clergy, Freeholders, Tradesmen, Farmers, and others, of the County of Durham; was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the jfame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Ralph Lodge and Mr. Robert Wenfley, being examined, severally laid, That the Roads leading from the Turnpike Road upon Gatherley Moor, near Didderjley Hilly to and through the Town of Caldwell, in the County of York, and from thence to and through Win-flon, in the County of Durham, to Stai?idrop, in the said County and also the Roads leading from the said Turnpike Road, near Smallways, to and through the Town of Hutton-long Fillers, in the said County of York, and from thence to and through the Town of Oinngton, to the Ford across the River Tees, to Winslow,\w the said County of Durham; are in a very ruinous Condition, and in many Parts very narrow and incommodious; and that the same cannot be effectually widened and repaired by the Laws in being.

And the Witnesses further said. That the Ford across the River Tees, from the Yorkshire Side, to Winslow, in the County of Durham, is very dangerous, and frequently impassable, by Reason of the frequent Floods in the said River: That the repairing and widening the said Roads (upon which great Quantities of Coals are carried), and the building a Bridgea cross the said River at or near the said Ford, will make a more commodious and near Communication between the North-Welt Parts of the County of York and the South W eft-Parts of the County of Durham, and be a great Convenience to the Inhabitants and ^Traders thereof, and to the Public in general.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making, amending, widening, turning, and repairing, the Roads leading from the Turnpike Road upon Gatheiiey Moor, near Didderjley Hill, to and through the Town of Caldxvell, in the County of York, and from thence to and through the Town of Winslow, in the County of Durham, to the Town of Staindrop, in the said County; and also from the said Turnpike Road near Smallways, to and through the Town of Hutton long Fillers, in the said County of York, and from thence to and through the Town of Ovington, to the Ford across the River Tecs, to the Town of Winjion, in the said County of Durham; and for building a Bridge over the River Tees, at or near Winsion Ford: And that Mr. Hewett and Mr. Thornton do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Charlton, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of One Million be granted to his Majesty, to enable his Majesty to discharge the like Sum raised in pursuance of an Act made in the last Session of Parliament., and charged upon the First Aids or Supplies to be granted in this Session of Parliament.

Rcjhlvcd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifteen thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, to be applied towards the improving, widening, and enlarging, the Passage over and through London Bridge.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Convention /FR. Secretary Pitt presented to the House, by his with Prussia. _1\JL Majesty’s Command,

Copy of a Convention between his Majesty and the King of Prussia, concluded and signed at London, the 12th of December 1760, and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation were read.

The said Copy is preserved among!! the other Papers of this 'Session; and the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

Translation of a Convention between his Majesty and the King of Prussia, concluded and signed at Ijon-don, the 12th of December 1760.

Be it known to all whom it concerns, or may concern. That the burthensome War wherein his Pnffian Majesty is engaged putting him under the Necessity of making new Efforts for his Defence again!! the great Number of Enemies by which his Dominions are attacked; and being the refore obliged to enter into a new Concert with his Britannic Majesty, in order to provide reciprocally and jointly with him for their common Defence and Safety 5 and his Majesty the King of Great Britain, having made known, at the same time, the Delire he had toflrengthen the Bonds of Friendship which subsist between the Two Courts, and to come to a new Agreement on this Occasion; and, for this End, by an express Convention, relating to the Succours by which he may give to his Prussian Majesty most expeditious and mol! efficacious Assistance, their said N1 a jellies have therefore, for this Purpose, named and authorized their respectiveMinisters; to wit, in the Name and on the Part of his Britannic Majesty, his Privy Counsellors Robert Lord Henley, Baron of Grainge, Keeper of his Great Seal of Great Britain, John Earl Granville, Presid cut of his Council, Thomas Holies Duke of Newcastle, First Lord Commissioner of his Treasury, Robert Earl of Hot-demeffc, One of his principal Secretaries of State, Philip Earl of JIardwicke, and William Pitt, another of his principal Secretaries of State; and, in the Name and on the Part of his Pnffian Majesty, the Sieurs Dodo Henry, Baron of KnyphauJ'en, his Privy Counsellor of Em bally and Minister Plenipotentiary at the Court of h\s Britannic Majesty, and Lewis Michell, his Minister at the said Court; who, after the Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

1.

It is agreed that all the preceding Treaties which fnb-fist between the Tw o Courts, of whatever Date or Nature Yql. 28.

Decembris. 991

they may be, and particularly that of Westminster, of the

I Gth of January 1756, as well as the Convention of the

II th of April in the Year 1 758, and that of the 7th of December of the same Year, as also the Convention of the 9th of November of the last Year, shall be deemed to be renewed and confirmed by the present Convention in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses, and shall be of the same Force as if they were inserted herein Word for Word.

2.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to cause to be paid, in the City of London, into the Hands of the Person or Persons who shall be authorized for that Purpose by his Majesty the King of Prussia, the Sum of Four millions of German Crowns, amounting to Six hundred and Seventy thousand Pounds Sterling, which intire Sum shall be paid at once, immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications, upon the Requifttion of his Prussian Majesty.

3-

His Majesty the King of Prussia engages, on his Part, to employ the said Sum in keeping up and augmenting his Forces, which shall acte in the most advantageous Manner for the common Cause, and for the End proposed by their aforesaid Majesties, of reciprocal Defence and mutual Security.

_ 4-

The high contracting Parties moreover engage; viz. on the one Part, his Britannic Majesty, both as King and as Elector, and, on the other Part, his Prussian Majesty, not to conclude any Treaty of Peace, Truce, or Neutrality, or any other Convention or Agreement whatsoever, with the Powers who have taken Part in the prefect War, but in Concert, and by mutual Consent, and expressly comprehending each other therein.

5-

This Convention shall be ratified, and the Ratifications thereof shall beexchanged on both Sides within the Term of Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Date of the Signing of the present Convention, or sooner, if possible. In Witness whereof, we the under-written Ministers of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and of his Majesty the King of Prussia, by virtue of our full Powers, have signed the present Convention, and have set the Seals of our Arms thereto. Done at London, the Twelfth Day of December in the Year of our Lord 1760.

(L. S.) Henley, C. S. (L. S.) Granville, P.

(L. S.} Holies Newcastle, (L. S.J Holder nc/fe,

(L. S.) Hardwickey (L. S.) W. Pitt.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, an additional Duty be paid for every Barrel, of Beer or Ale, above Six Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise, brewed by the common Brewer, or any other Person or Persons, who doth or shall fell or tap out Beer or Ale, publickly or privately, to be paid by the common Brewer, or by such other Person or Persons respectively, of Three Shillings, and so proportionably, for a greater or lesser Quantity.

Sir Charles Kemys Tynte reported from the Com- Bath Reads, mittee, to whom the Petition of the Trustees appointed for carrying into Execution the several Acts of Parliament, for erecting Turnpikes, and for the repairing the Roads round the City of Bath, and of several other Persons who are obliged to travel on the said Roads, or some of them, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, made in the Thirty-second Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, was produced, and read.

Mr. Thomas Butler, being examined, said, That he knows the Road directed by the said Act to be made, between the Bridge at Bath and Rush Hill: That the said Road will be about Eleven Miles; and it will be necessary to purchase several Lands, in order to make the said. Roads: that the Materials near the said intended Road are very bad; and, if the said Road should be made, the Hills therein would be inconvenient for Travellers:

That if a Road were made from the Cross Hands, in the Parish of Compton Dando, to join the Turnpike Roads leading to Shepton Mallet and Wells, at Rush Hill, it would be leis expensive, and more convenient to the Public, as the said Road would be no more than Six or Seven Miles long. Two Miles of which are already in good Repair, and good Materials are to be found on the Spot all the Way for repairing the said Road That the said Road will be more level, and very little Land necessary to be purchased.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the loll owing Resolutions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners ha\e fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are subscribed. Merchants, and Owners of Ships, Vessels, and other Craft belonging to and using the Port of London, and Inhabitants and Occupiers of Wharfs, Yards, and Premises, adjoining to the River Thames, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table.

Ordered, That Mr. Cooke have Leave to make a Motion, it being near Four of the Clock:

And he moved the House accordingly.

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Mr. Alexander Mathifon, being examined, said. That Bum Boats are in general small Boats, that carry from between Fifteen hundred to a Ton Weight: That they go about the River, under Pretence of felling Brooms, Greens, and Fruit, and sometimes spirituous Liquors, to Persons on board Ships, but in reality they bring Stores from the Ships, such as Hemp, Cordage, Corn, Coals, Tobacco, Sugar, and Iron Bolts, which the Witness imagines they get fraudulently: That there are Four Persons in his Neighbourhood, who have between them about Fifty of these Boats, which they lett out at zd.per' Day each Boat; and that the Goods are sold to the Owners of these Boats, who keep Warehouses, Where they receive and dispose of the Things brought to them from the Ships by these Boats: That he cannot tell what Prices are given for them, but he imagines very low ones, as they are generally fold cheaper than they can be bought for elsewhere.

Mr. John Nichols, being examined, said. That he is Owner of Four or Five Vessels, and is Rigger to the King and the East India Company: That he has frequently seen Bum Boats in his Passage up and down the River: That he saw Coils of Rope taken out of an East /tfrf/«Ship (the Bombay Castle) by a Bum Boat, which he supposes might be worth about 15.9. or 20£.: That he took the Boat inPoffellion, and carried her alongside the Ship; and delivered in Charge to the Officer, who chained her alongside the Ship; that there was a Man and a Woman in her: That the Woman threw the Rope overboard, and told the Officer he might do his worst, for that he could not get any Proof: That he has seen many bad PraQices of the same Kind.

Captain John Thompson, being examined, said, That liehas been Master of a Ship Fifteen Years, and is now an Owner: That he has frequently had his Servants corrupted: That they have acknowledged to him they have fold Goods to these Bum Boats, once in particular, to the Amount of Five Pounds: That they cannot keep a Buoy to their Anchors: That he himself has loft several; by which means many Anchors have been loft: That he has seen Buoys brought ashore in these Boats: That he saw one of these Boats loading all Sorts of old Stores out of a Prize Ship that lay at Deptford, which he is very fqre no one on board could have any Right to dispose

Januariu A. 1761.

of: That these Bum Boats fire of no Use, but in general are a very great Nuisance: That a total Prohibition of the said Boats was most deftrabte; but that if they were put under the Regulation of the Trinity House, and no Boats under the Burthen of Three Tons allowed, it might be a great Means of preventing the Evil.

Mr. John Addijbn, being examined, said. That he is Owner of Shipping, and has been Master: That he came from the Baltic about 18 or 20 Months ago; and when became to his Moorings at Limehouse, he saw one of these Boats come and cut the Anchor Buoy and Part of the Buoy Rope away, by which means he might have loft his Anchor, or the Ship or any other Vessel might have gone upon the Anchor and funk.

Mr. William Leg rove, being examined, said, That he has been a Lighterman 28 Years: That he has seen Coals taken out of Lighters by these Bum Boats: That he has known several Lighters cut from their Moorings, by having their Headfaft taken away, by which means Craft have gone adrift, got upon bad Ground, very often funk, and the Coals loft.

Mr. CoverdaleRichardson, Merchant, being examined, said, That the best Way to prevent these Mischiefs, would be, to seize all Boats with Ships Stores in them, that could not give a just Account how they came by them: That he apprehends the Amount of these Robberies is more than £.10,000 per Annum.

And all the Witnesses said, That the Bum Boats, carry spirituous Liquors on board Ships, and by that mean# encourage Drunkenness among the Sailors.

Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That many Thefts and Frauds are frequently committed .» by Persons navigating the Boats, commonly called Bum Boats, upon the River Thames, and thereby great Lodes are sustained by Merchants and Owners of Ships, Vessels, and other Craft.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next. Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Thomas Tomlyn, being examined, said, That he is Surveyor and Clerk to the said Trustees: That great Progress has been made in repairing the said Roads; and that £. 100 is now due upon Bond, on the Credit of the said Acts; and that upwards of £. 430 is due to him, upon the Balance of his Account.

That Part of the said Roads, directed by the said Acts to be repaired, is extremely bad, and dangerous; and that some Part of the said Road between North-feet and Gravesend cannot be made safe for Travellers, without altering the Course thereof, as it goes at present near the Side of a very deep Chalk Pit; and that the Trustees are not impowered by the present Acts to turn it:

And that the Trustees cannot complete the necessary Repairs of the said Roads, and discharge the Money due on the Credit of the Tolls, during the subsisting Term of the said Act.

A State of the Fafts contained in the said Petition is as follows; viz.

Mr. John Chamier, Merchant, being examined, said,

He did not know of any Verdigrease being made in E??gla?id, except by Mr. Bindley and Mr. Maud:

That Verdigrease is imported from the South of France: That he never heard of any being brought from any other Place; and that he apprehends the People of England never knew how to make it till nowi That he has been told, the French make it from the Mart or Hulls of the Grapes, after the Juice has been pressed out for Wine; and that he does not know, that any of the Materials used in France in making Verdigrease are subject to Duties:

That it is the general Opinion, That Verdigrease is made in France only: That it is now a considerable Article imported at JLeghorn: That he never heard of any imported from any where else, but from the South of France: and that he has imported it himself from Marseilles.

Mr. EdmundTaylor, being examined, said, he had been a Broker in the Drug Way 21 Years; that Verdigrease is used in Coach Painting, andother Painting; and very much in the dying of Hats; that when it is wet, it fells for about One Shilling per Pound, and when very dry, from 18 d. to 20 d.; but on an Average, from One Shilling to 20d. according to the Dryness.

Mr. John Planner and Mr. James Bindley, being severally examined, said. That they had seen the Manufactory of Verdigrease carried on by the Petitioners, in the several Stages, and had collected some of it from the Copper Plates, on which it vegetated; when they took it off the Plates, they put it into a Bag, and put their Seals on it; that it remained under their Seals about 3 Days, during which Time, it was dried: That they then delivered some of this Verdigrease to Mr. Primate, a Chemist; some to Mr. Cra/e, a Coach Painter; some to Mr. Cornelius Taylor, a Paper Stainer; and some to Mr. Pemberton, a Coach and House Painter; and that a Part of it was delivered by the said Mr. James Bindley to Mr. JackJ'on, a Hatter.

Mr. John Cluimier, Merchant, being again examined, laid. That he*ha$ received Verdigrease from Mr. James Bindley and Mr. Planner, that he compared it with some French Verdigrease, and thinks it equally good; that the Price has varied for Ten Years palt, from 15 d> to 18 d. per Pound: That there was a little Rife for about Twelve Months, and then it was fold for 20rf.; that about a Year or a Year and Half ago, there was a great Scarcity, and then it fold for 22 d. per Pound, and the Manufacturers were in great Distress for want of it: That it is used in the dying.of Hats.

Being aiked, Why in the Years 1753, 1754,31^1755, so large a Quantity was imported, inComparifon with the Four succeeding Years: He said it was owing to the falling off of the Hat Trade; for that many thousand Dozen of Hats lefswere exported in the last Period, than i’ ^the Three preceding, Years.

Mr. Edmund Taylqr, being again called, and aiked, If he knew of any Verdigrease having been made here; he said, he had a Sample of some, which was said to be made in England, which he produced to your Committee; but that it was so bad, that he had not been able to fell it, though he had had it by him Six Years:

That he had seen some of Mr. Bindley' sand Maud's Verdigrease, and knows no Difference between that and foreign Verdigrease, in Point of Goodness; a Peice of Mr. Bindley s Verdigrease was then produced to Mr. Tayloi*, which he said was as good as Foreign; and he added, that he knew the other English Verdigrease, which he had produced to your Committee, to be a Mixture of French Verdigrease and Whiting, by way of Imposition; and that he does not know of any Person that makes Verdigrease in England, except the Petitioners.

Mr. William Primate, Chymilt, being examined, said. That he received some Verdigrease from Mr. Planner mid Mr. James Bindley, in ordertomake anExperiment, to try whether or no it was real Verdigrease; and that in the Experiment, it had all the Properties of real Verdigrease; that by dissolving it in Vinegar, he can extract the Colour from it, and the Goodness depends upon the id

Purity of it; that he tried it against some French., which was very good in Quality: That 11 Ounces very good foreign Verdigrease, produced,

From which Experiments, he said, it appears that the Two Sorts are nearly equal in Goodness; and that upon the Whole, he apprehends no Preference can' be given to the French:

That lie does not know of any other Persons, except Mr. Bindley and Mr. Maud, who are possessed of the Secret of making Verdigrease here; and he apprehends it is a new Invention.

Mr. ComeliitsTaylor, Paper Stainer, being examined, said, That he received some Verdigrease from Mr* Planner and Mr. James Bindley, which he ground with Oil, and compared it with some of French Manufacture: ThatMr.BiWfeys answered rather better in Col our, and was rather stronger in Body; and that he never used any better: That he knows the Difference between this and the foreign Verdigrease; that the Acid is different; and he told Mr. Planner, he knew it was not French by the Smell:

That he has seen Verdigrease which was made in England, within these Three or Four Years; but could not use it, as it would not grind.

Mr. William Pemberton, Coach Painter, being exr amined, said. That he received some Verdigrease from Mr. Planner, which he ground in Oil, and tempered with White Lead, which is the Way they use it; That he tried it against French Verdigrease, and it proved equally good in all respects; and that he never heard of arty made in England before.

Mr. George Jackson, Hat-maker, being examined, said, That he dyed a Dye of Hats, confiding of 120, withe some Verdigrease, which he received from Mr. James Bindley; That he used the same Quantity that he does of French Verdigrease; that it went as far, and the Hats, when dyed, were as good a Colour; that he had tried it more than once; and he added, that Hats cannot be dyed without Verdigrease:

That in the lad War, Verdigrease was at a very high Price, being fold for 2s. 6d. per Pound; but a great Quantity was hurried in before the breaking out of the War, which has kept down the Price so much, that he

That if the French were to flop the making of it, or prohibit the Exportation, we could not make a Hat: That he uses about Six Pounds of it in a Week; and that he never heard of any being made in England except by Mr. Bindley and Mr. Maud.

Then Mr. Bindley, one of the Petitioners, informed your Committee, That he is very sure they can make a much larger Quantity of Verdigrease in a Year than can possibly he consumed here.

A Petition of the several Proprietors of Lands and He- Burton Pidfea reditaments lying in the open Fields, Pastures, and Carrs, Inclosure. called the North Field, the South Field, the Greens, the Jug Carr, and the Deep Carr, in Burton Pidfea, in IIolder ne/je, in the County of York, whose Names are Subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; alleging,

That the Petitioners are informed, that a Bill is depending for dividing and inclosing the said Fields, Carrs, and Lands, in pursuance of Articles of Agreement entered into for that Purpose; and that if the said Bill should pass into a Law, it would be attended with great Loss and Inconvenience to the Landholders at Burton Pidfea in general, and to the Petitioners in particular; and that a very considerable Part of the Lands intended to be divided, is Copyhc^ld, in Bondage, subject to high Fines, and Part to a Loras Rent of Twenty Pence an Acre, and other Part of Eight Pence an Acre, and is in general of so bad a Quality, as to be capable of very little if any Improvement, by Inclosure, and absolutely unable to bear the Expence of it; and that no public or general Notice was given to the said Proprietors of the intended Inclosure, nor any Meeting called to consider of the Utility of such a Scheme, nor, if it should be judged expedient, of the proper Means to carry it into Effect: but that the whole Proceeding has been planned and conducted in a private Manner, by One or Two of the Proprietors only, who have taken upon themselves, / without any Authority from the rest, to agree with the Impropriator of the Tythes, for a high and unreasonable Composition or Tythe Rent, and to prepare, and settle the Articles, which have not been executed by the Owners of more thaih One Half of the Lands proposed to be inclosed, many of whom reside at a Distance from Burton Pidfea, and are unacquainted with the Nature and Condition of the said Lands: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill; and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for the better securing and encouraging the Trade of his Majesty's Sugar Colonies in America, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for extending an Act, intituled, An Act todiscontinue, for a limited Time, the Duties payable on Tallow imported from Ireland, to Hogs Lard and Grease, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to indemnify Persons who have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices and Employments; and to indemnify Justices of the Peace, Deputy Lieutenants, Officers of the Militia, and others, who have omitted to register, or to deliver in, their Qualifications, within the Time limited by Law; and for giving further Time for those Purposes; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from Fisherton Bridge, to the Turnpike Road at Willoughby Hedge, in West Knoyle, and from Wilton Bridge, to the Turnpike Road at the Western End of Heytesbury; and also the Road from the Turnpike Road at the Top of Red Hone Hill, in the Parish of Urjhfont, to the Mile Stone at the West End of Fisherlon Street, in the County of Wilts; without any Amendment: and also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting the Plantation and Estate of John Walter Esquire, and Netolon his Wife, late Newton Walker Spiafter, in the Island of Barbadoes, in Trustees, for raising Money to be applied in purchasing of Stock, and for other Purposes, for the Improvement of the same Plantation and Estate: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

Separate Article.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain engages, in case that, contrary to all Expectation, the Dominions of the Mod Serene Landgrave of Hesse Cajfel should be again invaded and laid under Contribution, to grant to his Most Serene Highness a reasonable Succour in Money, to be settled if the same should exist, and the present separate Article has been made for this Purpose; which shall have the same Force as if it was inserted word for word in the Convention concluded and signed this Day* and shall be ratified in the same Manner.
