Whitebaven Harbour and Rank.

Sir Janies Lowther reported from the Committee, to whom Part of the Petition of the Trusteos for repairing the Harbour of Whitehaven, in the County of Cumberland, and the Gentlemen, Merchants, Matters and Owners of Ships, and of the Freeholders, Farmers, and Occupiers of Laud, lying in and near the said Town of JYhitchaveni

and of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act; made in the 13H1 Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for making more effectual Two Acts of Parliament, passed in the Seventh and Tenth Years of her late Majesty Q11 ecu Anne, for preserving and enlarging the Harbour of Whitehaven, in the County of Cumberland: and for repairing and amending the high Roads leading to the said Harbour and Town of Whitehaven; and also of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act, made in the 23d Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Roads leading from Egremont to Duddon Bridge, Sant on Bridge, and Salt house, in the County of Cumberland; was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter o( such Part of the said Petition as was referred to them; and had directed him to repost the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

The Agent for the Petitioners produced an Act, of the 7th}Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, whereby it appeared, that certain Duties upon Coals and other Goods, and upon Shipping, were granted, for preserving and enlarging the Harbour of Whitehaven; which were further continued by an Act, of the 10th Yrear of her said Majesty’s Reign:

And likewise an Act, of the 13th Y’ear of King George the Second: whereby the said Duties are further continued, from the loth of April 1740, for the Term of 21 Years; which Term expires on the 10th of April 1761: But a Moiety of the said Duties uponTonnageof Ships and Vessels arc to continue for ever, to be applied for the Preservation of the said Harbour of Whitehaven: And Power was given in the said Act to borrow Money upon the Credit of the Duties thereby granted, to be applied for those Purposes.

Then, in order to prove the Improvements made in the said Harbour, in pursuance of the Act of the 13th of his late Majesty,

Peter John Hayward Esquire, produced to your Committee, a Plan of the present Harbour; which contains the Works already done, and those proposed to be further added in Consequepce of the present Application to Parliament; by which, and also by an Account produced by him to your Committee, and signed by the Accountant to the said Harbour, it appeared, that the Sum of £.26,117 6^. o\d. had been expended in improving the said Harbour, and in paying the Interest of the Money borrowed for that Purpose, since the Commencement of the said Act of the 13th of his late Majesty; and by another Account, likewise produced by him, it also appeared, That the Sum of £. 2,970 now remains due upon the Credit of the said Harbour Duties; which Duties, as appeared by another Account likewise produced to your Committee, amounted at an Average, ftnee the Commencement of the late Act, to about £. 1,159 /*r Annum.

Then the Witness proceeded to explain to your Committee the Nature and Conveniency of the Extension of the said Harbour, and of the new Works proposed to be erected in Consequence thereof; and said, That if the said Harbour was extended, and a new* Mole erected on the North-east Side thereof, it would prevent the Roughness of the Sea caused by a North*weft Wind, which renders the said Harbour dangerous and incommodious, and would likewise facilitate the Ingress and| Egress of Ships, which in a North-weft Wind can feldora get out of the Harbour, which they might easily do if the proposed Mole was ere5ted% -J

Which Evidence of ML Hayzvard was severally coi firmed by'M.r.JohnKelfwick and Mr. William Sfojroi Who both declared, They were perfectly acquainted wil the said Harbour of Whitehaven: And they fever; ‘ added, that if the said additional Works were made,

said Harbour would admit Vessels of greater Burthen* of the said Road from Whiuhouse, over Workington Moot, be a further Security to the Navigation of those Seas* to Distington, through the Moor Fields, to Htin day Gate, and of greater Utility to the Public. leading to Workington; which several Roads are in a

Then the said Act of the 7th of Queen Anne being ruinous Condition, and cannot be repaired by the Laws again readmit appeared,that several Duties were granted in being; and that, if the same were repaired, it would

thereby upon several Goods in the said Act particularly enumerated; but that no mention was therein made of the several Species of Goods following; viz. Rice, Log-wood,. Deer Skins, and Battery: And,

Mr. Hayzvard, being examined, informed your Committee, That great Quantities of those Commodities are at this Time annually imported at Whitehaven:

And by the said Act it further appeared, That Ships driven into the said Harbour by Stress of Weather are only subjected to pay One Fourth Part of the Duties thereby laid upon other Shipping: And,

Mr. Haijzvard further informed your Committee, That Ships under those Circumstances very often flay in the Harbour a long Time; and, as they frequently have received Damage* it becomes necessary to station them in the most secure and convenient Places, which they occupy for One Fourth Part of the Expence which is laid upon other Shipping, which neither enjoy such convenient Births, nor receive so much Benefit from the Use of the said Harbour:

That the additional Works will be very expensive, and Will necessarily. require an Increase of the said Harbour Duties on Tonnage of Shipping and Goods:

That there is a small Rivulet, called the Poe, which runs t hrough the Market Place of the Town of White-haven into the said Harbour, which at present is very detrimental thereto; For though all Persons are by the said Acts prohibited from throwing any Filth, Rubbish, or other Things, into the said Harbour* yet they constantly do it into the said Rivulet, and it is waihed dowrn into the said Harbour, to the great Detriment thereof; and that if the Trustees of the said Harbour were im-povverea to cover the said Rivulet, and to open, widen* deepen or pen up, the fame, it might be made very useful in cleaning the said Harbour from Filth and Rubbish, which in its present Situation it contributes to bring into the fame;

That there is likeWife another small Rivulet* called Branjly Beck, which at prefect runs just without the intended Limits of the Harbour; which, if turned into the Harbour, would be useful for the same Purpose: And that it is of the utmost Consequence to keep the said Harbour clear from Rubbish, Ballast, and other Obstructions.

Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Keswick and Mr. Skyron.

Then your Committee proceeded to examine that Part of the Petition which relates to the repairing the Roads therein mentioned.

And Mr. Hayzvard produced to your Committee, an Account, which he said he had taken from the Accounts of the Trustees, whereby it appeared, that the Sum of jf-575 remains due upon the Credit of the Tolls granted by the said Act of the 13th of his late Majesty for repairing the Roads therein mentioned,

Then an Act, pasted in the 23d Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for repairing the Road leading from Eggre-mont to Dudden Bridge, Santon Bridge, and Salthonfe, in the County of Cumberland, was produced to your Committee, and read: And,

Mr. Hayward informed your Committee, That the Trustees appointed by the said last mentioned Act had found it>impracticable to repair that Part of the Road directed to be repaired by the said Act, which lies between Calder Bridge and Eggremont; which is at present very ruinous, and cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law; and that the same is a Road much frequented, being the great London Road; and, if it could be repaired, would be of public Utility:

Mr. Speaker also reported, That his Majesty was afterwards pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament*; of which, Mr. Speaker laid, he had, to prevent Mistakes obtained a

x7

Copy: Which he read to the loweth; viz*

A. 1761.

House; and is as fol-

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Upon granting new Commissions to the Judges, the present State of their Offices fell naturally under Consideration.

In consequence of the Act, passed in the Reign of my late glorious Predecessor King William the Third, for settling the Succession of the Crown in my Family, their Commissions have been made during their good Behaviour; but, notwithstanding that wife Provision, their Offices have determined upon the Demise of the Crown, or at the Expiration of Six Months afterwards, in every Instance of that Nature which has happened.

I look upon the Independency and Uprigbtness of the Judges of the Land as essential to the impartial Administration of Justice, as one of the bed Securities to the Rights and Liberties of my loving Subjects, and as nnofi conducive to the Honour of the Crown; and I come now to recommend this interetling Object to the Consideration of Parliament, in order that such farther Provision may be made, for Securing the Judges in the Enjoyment of their Offices, during their good Behaviour, notwithstanding any such Demise, as shall be most expedient.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I mull desire you in particular, that I may be enabled to grant and establish upon the Judges such Salaries as I shall think proper, so as to be absolutely secured to them during the Continuance of their Commissious.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I have nothing to add but my Thanks for the great Unanimity and Application with which you have hitherto carried on the public Business; and to deflre you to proceed with the same good Disposition, and with such Dispatch, that this Session may be soon brought to a happy Conclusion.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Ad- A(j<lrdsot dress be present ed to his Majesty to return his Majesty the Kinj’i the most humble Thanks of this House, for his most Speech, gracious Speech from the Throne:

To express thp grateful Sense which this House has of his Majesty’s Attention to an Object so interesting to his People, as the impartial Administration of Justice, and the Integrity and Independency of the Judges of the Land: And to assure his Majesty, that his faithful Commons fee,with Joy and Veneration,the warmRegard and Concern which animate his Royal Bread, for the Security of the Religion, Laws Liberties, and Properties, of his Subjects; and that this House will immediately proceed upon the important Work recommended by his Majesty, with such tender Care of his People, and will enable his Majesty to establish the Salaries of Judges in so permanent a Manner, that the same may be enjoyed during the Continuance of their Commissions:

To return his Majesty the fmcere Acknowledgments of this House for his gracious Acceptance of the Services of his faithful Commons; and to allure his Majesty, that they will proceed with Unanimity and Dispatch to finish the remaining Business of this Session of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know his Majesty’s Pleafur^, when he will be attended by this House.

Use of A Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, Yeo-broadWheels, men, Farmers, and others, residing in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners have long laboured under great Inconveniences and Losses, from the Necessity they are under of drawing with no more than Four Horses, and by an Act of King George the First, with 110 more than Three, with narrow Wheels; and that most Part of that Country being either hilly or sandy, the Petitioners find themfclres particularly afteded by these Restrictions, as the cross Roads off the Turnpikes are incapable of being travelled on with broad Wheels; which, in Compliance with the Spirit of the Law, the Petitioners would, if possible, have acquiesced in, and as the Turnpike Roads themselves are so deep and heavy, that in many Places it is scarce practicable with even Four Horses to draw their Corn to Market, or Manure to make their Seasons; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners do not presume to dictate the Manner of Redress; but humbly to lay before the House their Grievances, which‘in their Cafes call atoud for Afiifiance of Parliament, and which the Petitioners implore, in whatever Manner shall seem meet to the House.

Treaty with . The Lord Barrington presented to the House, by the Landgrave his Majesty s Command,

A Paper, intituled, " Protocol, March 3d 1761,’* Caird- and Tranflation.

And the Titles of the said Paper and Translation were read.

The said Paper is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

Protocol, March 3d 1761. Translation.

The Hejfian Ministers having, by their Memorial of the 7th February, claimed, in the Name of the Most Serene Landgrave their Master, the Execution of the separate Article concluded and signed the lftof April, in the Year 1760, and having required that the Sum should be fixed to which the reasonable Succour demanded by the Most Serene Landgrave might amount: And whereas it seems expedient to come to a final Agreement thereupon during the Course of the present Session of Parliament, which is drawing to an End, It has been proposed to those Ministers, as the Ultimatum on the Part of England, that his Britannic Majesty, in Execution of the* separate Article above-mentioned, should cause to be paid to the Most Serene Landgrave the Sum of Two hundred Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling; including therein the extraordinary Subsidy of Sixty thousand Pounds Sterling, in the Manner following; viz.

The Sum of One hundred Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling immediately.

The Sum of Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling in the Course of the Year 1762.

The remaining Fifty thousand Pounds Sterling in the Course of the Year 1763.

The Hessian Ministers, on their Part, accept the Proposal made oh behalf of his Britannic Majesty.

In Witness whereof, we have signed the present Protocol, and have caused the Seals of Our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at London this Third Day of March 1761.

(L.S.) Holder nefle. (L.S.) J. G. WUtorffy

(L.S.) J. H. Alt.

Mr. Bacon, according to Order, reported from the Privilege Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint made to the House, upon the 4th Day of this instant March, That, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, Sir Richard Per-. rot hath entered into Possession of a Cellar, in the Occupation of aTenantof Charles Fitzroy SaMamore Eiq u ire, a Member of this House; and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed; viz.

To prove what is alleged in the said Complaint,

Mr. Nathan Draper, being examined, said, That Sir Thomas Rob inf on, between Lady-day and Midjinnmer lall, took a House in Scotland Yard, of Air. Fitzroy Scudamore; That the Cellar now in dispute was repaired the same time that the House was; and that the Key was delivered to him, and waspn his Possession till after Lord Gower succeeded to the Office of Mafier of the Great Wardrobe: That he kept the Key, as Officer of the Great Wardrobe under SxrTJiomas Robinson, and delivered it to Mr. Lander, Porter of the Wardrobe, in November last: That in his Time no One made life of it but Sir Thomas Robinson, as Tenant to Mr. Fitzroy.

Mr. William Lander, being examined, said, That he took the Lock off the Cellar Door about the End of January lad (when the Cellar was in Lord Gozocr's Possession, as Colonel Fitzroy's Tenant) in order to have it cleaned: That Sir Richard Perrot in the mean time took Possession of the Cellar, which is under Part of the House inhabited by him; put another Lock on; and told the Witness,'That he had taken Possession, and would keep it; for he had bought the Lease of some Ground, in which this Cellar was included; although he was often told, that it belonged to Colonel Fitzroy.

Thotmas Gilbert Esquire, being examined, informed the Committee, That he, as Deputy to Lord Gower, came into the House rented by Lord Gower of Colonel Fitzroy, about a Month ago, and understood, that the Cellar in Dispute belonged to that House: That upon applying to Sir Richard Per rot, on his having taken Possession of the Cellar, Sir Richard told him, he had a Grant of it from the Crown, which he would abide 'by, and keep Possession: And upon being again applied to about a Fortnight after, and being repeatedly asked to give up Possession, or try his Title at Law, he refused; and has kept Possession everfince, although the Witness told him, that probably a Complaint would be made against him, of having committed a Breach of Privilege: And the 'Witness said, he has enquired, and can’t find, that any One has any Right to the said House and Cellar but Colonel Fitzroy: and that the only Opening from the Cellar was into the Yard.

Sir Richard Perrot, the Person complained of, being called, and not appearing, nor any One on his Behalf,

Mr William Whit tam (One of the Messengers attending this House), being examined, said, That he had left a Copy of the Order for his Attendance at his Place of Residence, in Scotland Yard, on Friday lad; but that he did not fee him; but a Woman, who has the Care of his House, undertook to deliver it.

Upon the whole, the Committee came to the folloiv-in Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir Richard Perrot, having entered into Possession of a Cellar, in the Occupation of a Tenant of Charles Fitzroy Scudamore Esquire, a Member of this House, is thereby guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the Thanks of Vote of this House be given to Mr. Speaker, for his constant and ^S^eiki unwearied Attendance in the Chair, during the course p of above Thirty-three Y'ears, in Five successive Parliaments; for the unftiaken Integrity and fteadv Impar-. tiality of his Conduct there; and for the indefatigable Pains he has, with uncommon Abilities, constantly taken, to promote the real Interest of his King and Country, to maintain the Honour and Dignity of Parliament, and to preserve inviolable the Rights and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain.

Upon which Mr. Speaker said:

I was never under so great a Difficulty in my Life to know what to say in this Place, as I am at present —

Indeed it is almost too much for me — -lean Hand against Misfortunes and Distresses: I have stood against Misfortunes and Distresses; and may do so again r But I am not able to stand this Overflow of Good Will and Honour tome. It overpowers me: and had I all the Strength of Language, I could never express the full Sentiments of my Heart upon this Occasion, of Thanks and Gratitude. If I have been happy enough to perform any Services here,that are acceptable to the House, I am sure 1 now receive the noblest Reward for them; the noblest that any Man can receive for any Merit, far superior, in my Efiimation, to all the other Emoluments of this World. I owe every thing to this House: I not only owe to this House that I am in this Place, but that I have had their constant Support in it; and to their Good Will and Assistance, their Tenderness and Indulgence towards me in my Errors, it; is, that I have been able to perform my Duty here to any Degree of Approbation:

Thanks therefore are not so much due'to me for these Services, as to the House itself, who made them to be Services in me.

When I began my Duty here, I set out with a Resolution, and Promise to the House, to be impartial in every Thing, and to shew Respe6l to every Body. The first I know I have done, it is the only Merit lean assume: If I have failed in the other, it was unwillingly, it was inadvertently; and I a(k their Pardon, moil lincerely, to whomsoever it may have happened — I can truly say, the giving Satisfaction to oil has been my constant Aim, my Study, and my Pride.

And now. Sirs, I am to take my last Leave of You,

It is, I confess, with Regret, because the being within these Walls has ever been the chief Pleasure of my Life:

The King’t After which his Majesty was pleased to make a most Speech* gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot put an End to this Session without declaring my intire Satisfaction in your Proceedings, during the course of it. The Zeal you have shewn for the Honour of niy Crown, as well as for my true Interest, and that of your Country, which are ever the fame, is the clearest Demonrtration of that Duty and Affection to my Person and Government, of which you so tmanimourty allured me at your first Meeting. Nothing could" so much add to the pleasure which these Confkleraiions afford me, as that I am now able to acquaint ycu with the great Progress made of late by the Combined Army in Germany, under the Command of Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick. I formerly told you, that the Nature of the War in those Parts had kept the Campaign there Hill depending; and it now appears, to the Surprise of my Enemies, that the superior Ability and indefatigable Activity of my General, and the Spirit and Ardour of my Officers and Troops, have greatly profited of this Perseverance, notwithstanding all the Difficulties anting from the Season.

I3y your Artiftance I have taken the belt Care to recruit that Army in an effectual Manner; and have made such a Disposition of my Fleet for the next Summer as may most advantageously defend my Kingdoms, protect the Commerce of my Subjects, maintain and extend our Possessions and Acquisitions, and an-ioy the Enemy.

As in all my Measures I have nothing in View but the Security and Felicity of my Dominions, the Support of my Allies, and the restoring of the public Tranquillity, I trull in the Divine Providence to give a happy Issue to our farther Operations.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I cannot furticiently thank you for your Unanimity and Dispatch, in providing for the Expences of my Civil Government, and the Honour and Dignity of the Crown: And I think myself as much obliged to you for the prudent Use which, in framing that Provision, you have made of my Consent to leave my own Hereditary Revenues to such Disposition of Parliament as might bed conduce to the Utility and Satisfaction of the Public, as for what more immediately concerns myself.

In making my Acknowledgments for the large and extensive Supplies which you have granted me this Session, I am at a Loss whether moll to applaud your Chearfulnels in giving or your Wisdom in proportioning them to the extraordinary Occasions of the Public, notwithstanding those uncommon Burthens, which I heartily regret. No Care rtiall be wanting on my Part to fee them duly applied to the National Ends for which you intended them.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Expiration of this Parliament now drawing very near, I will forthwith give the necessary Orders for calling a new One. But I cannot take my Leave of you, without returning my Thanks for the many eminent Proofs you have given of your Fidelity and Affection to my Family and Government, and of your Zeal for this happy and excellent Constitution.

During this Parliament the Flame of War was kindled, by the injurious Encroachments and Ufurpatious of our Enemies; and therefore it became just and necessary on our Part. In the Prosecution of it you have given such Support to my Royal Grand fat lie r and myself, and such Artiftance to our Allies, as have manifested your public-spirited Concern for the Honour of the Nation, and the Maintenance of its undoubted Rights and Polfeftions, and been attended with glorious Successes and great Acquisitions in various Parts of the World, particularly in the intire Reduction of 6V/-nada; a Conquest of the utmost Importance to the Security of our Colonies in North America, and to the Extension of the Commerce and Navigation of my Subjects.

May God Almighty grant Continuance to these Successes! The Use which I propose to make of them is to secure and promote the Welfare of my Kingdoms, and to carry on the War with Vigour, in order to procure to them the Blessings of Peace, on safe and honourable Conditions for me and my Allies, to which I have been always ready to hearken.

Firm in these Resolutions I do, with intire Confidence, rely on the good Dispositions of my faithful Subjects in the Choice of their Representatives; and I make no Doubt but they will thereby demonstrate the Sincerity of those Assurances which have been so cordially and universally given me, in the loyal, affectionate, and unanimous, Addresses of my People.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty’s parliaromt Command, said, prorogued.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued until Tuesday the Seventh Day of April next, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued until Tuesday the Seventh Day of April next.
